title: Designing for Ethical AI: HCI Feature Considerations to Improve Fairness and User Experience in AutoML use for Human Resources
comment: 295 pages; Doctoral Thesis;28 figures; 42 tables; 248 references
summary: This thesis examines the fairness of Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) tools in human resource hiring systems through the combined lenses of regulation, business strategy, and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). It argues that fairness is no longer merely an ethical concern but a critical determinant of usability, trust, legal compliance, and organizational adoption. While AutoML platforms improve efficiency by simplifying model selection and deployment, they also risk perpetuating discriminatory outcomes when trained on biased historical hiring data. Existing platforms prioritize technical performance over fairness, leaving non-expert business users unable to detect or mitigate bias effectively. The study investigates fairness gaps in AutoML tools through four research questions focused on fairness mechanisms, interface transparency, human oversight, and product design priorities. Drawing on frameworks such as the Technology Acceptance Model, Innovation Diffusion Theory, Human-Centered AI, Cognitive Load Theory, and Affordance Theory, the research evaluates both usability and fairness alignment. Using qualitative HCI audits and quantitative testing of eight AutoML platforms on HR datasets, the findings reveal widespread deficiencies in transparency, user control, and bias mitigation support. The thesis proposes a five-dimensional HCI-based fairness evaluation framework and recommends embedding fairness directly into AutoML product design to improve accountability, adoption, and ethical sustainability in AI-driven hiring systems.

AI.tldr: This thesis investigates fairness deficiencies in AutoML tools used for HR hiring, finding that current platforms prioritize technical performance over bias mitigation. It proposes a five-dimensional HCI-based fairness evaluation framework and recommends embedding fairness directly into AutoML product design.
AI.motivation: AutoML tools simplify model selection and deployment for non-expert business users but risk perpetuating discrimination when trained on biased historical hiring data. Existing platforms lack adequate fairness mechanisms, leaving business users unable to detect or mitigate bias. Fairness has evolved from a purely ethical concern into a critical factor for usability, trust, legal compliance, and organizational adoption.
AI.method: The study combines qualitative HCI audits and quantitative testing across eight AutoML platforms using HR datasets. It employs multiple theoretical frameworks (Technology Acceptance Model, Innovation Diffusion Theory, Human-Centered AI, Cognitive Load Theory, and Affordance Theory) to evaluate usability and fairness alignment. Four research questions guide the investigation, addressing fairness mechanisms, interface transparency, human oversight, and product design priorities.
AI.result: The findings reveal widespread deficiencies across AutoML platforms in transparency, user control, and bias mitigation support. Current tools fail to equip non-expert users with the means to detect or address discriminatory outcomes effectively.
AI.conclusion: The thesis proposes a five-dimensional HCI-based fairness evaluation framework and argues for embedding fairness directly into AutoML product design. This approach aims to improve accountability, adoption, and ethical sustainability in AI-driven hiring systems, positioning fairness as integral to both regulatory compliance and business strategy.

title: Cross-Model Humor Preference Modeling with Cards Against Humanity
summary: This paper investigates whether one large language model can approximate the humor preferences of another in a controlled Cards Against Humanity-style task. Two models - GPT-4o as Czar and Claude Opus-4.5 as Player - are evaluated on a binary humor-selection task constructed so that success cannot follow from self-preference. A reflected-cell stability procedure isolates 244 hands on which the two models hold deterministic but opposite preferences, partitioned into a 97-hand context pool and a 147-hand held-out test pool. The Player is then evaluated across five graded conditions: default self-preference, generic Czar-modeling instruction, model-identified Czar, prior Czar selections, and prior Czar selections with rationales. This gradient is designed to separate two sources of improvement: framing effects, in which the Player is told to attend to a Czar without seeing any of the Czar's behavior, and direct behavioral evidence, in which the Player is shown the Czar's prior choices. Player accuracy increased from 0.7% in Condition 1 to 19.0% and 25.9% in the framing-only conditions, and then rose to 72.8% and 82.3% once behavioral evidence and rationales were provided. An omnibus Cochran's Q test and pairwise McNemar tests confirmed that each step in the gradient produced a significant improvement. The results indicate that role instruction and model identity yield only modest gains, while behavioral evidence - especially when accompanied by rationales - supports substantial cross-model preference modeling. The findings are interpreted as theory-of-mind-like behavior in an operational rather than representational sense: the Player shifts away from self-preference toward another agent's demonstrated preferences, without any claim about an underlying representation of mental states.

AI.tldr: GPT-4o and Claude Opus-4.5 were tested on a Cards Against Humanity-style humor task where they held opposite preferences. Instruction-based framing alone yielded modest gains (19–26% accuracy), but providing behavioral evidence with rationales boosted cross-model preference alignment to 72–82%, suggesting operational theory-of-mind-like behavior without requiring internal mental state representations.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a large language model can approximate the humor preferences of another model, and to disentangle whether improvements arise from mere framing/role-play instructions versus exposure to the target model's actual behavioral evidence and rationales.
AI.method: A binary humor-selection task was constructed from Cards Against Humanity prompts. A reflected-cell stability procedure isolated 244 hands where GPT-4o (Czar) and Claude Opus-4.5 (Player) held deterministic but opposite preferences. The Player was tested across five graded conditions: (1) default self-preference, (2) generic Czar-modeling instruction, (3) model-identified Czar, (4) prior Czar selections, and (5) prior Czar selections with rationales. Cochran's Q and pairwise McNemar tests assessed significance across conditions.
AI.result: Player accuracy rose from 0.7% (Condition 1) to 19.0% and 25.9% (framing-only Conditions 2–3), then to 72.8% and 82.3% (behavioral evidence Conditions 4–5). Each step in the gradient produced statistically significant improvement. Framing yielded modest gains; behavioral evidence with rationales drove substantial cross-model preference alignment.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can engage in operational theory-of-mind-like behavior: they shift from self-preference toward another agent's demonstrated preferences when given behavioral evidence and rationales. Role instructions and model identity alone are insufficient for robust cross-model preference modeling. The effect is interpreted in an operational rather than representational sense, without attributing genuine mental state representations to the models.

title: From Human-Centered Design to Human-AI Collaboration: Why the Future of HCI Still Starts With People
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to the CHIWORK 2026 Workshop: Interrogating GenAI Augmentation for CHIworkers
summary: Generative AI is reshaping HCI work by accelerating brainstorming, writing, prototyping, and interface generation. However, faster production does not automatically produce human-centered design. This position paper argues that GenAI should be treated not as a replacement for human-centered methods, but as a co-thinking partner driven by human goals, ethics, cognition, and accountability. After reflecting on HCI coursework, design activities, and AI-assisted workflows, I argue that traditional HCD principles become more important as AI systems become more capable. Users still bring limited attention, mental models, trust issues, and cognitive biases into interaction, while GenAI introduces new risks around over-reliance, de-skilling, shallow reasoning, hallucination, unclear authorship, and reduced accountability. The future of HCI should therefore focus on human-AI collaboration that preserves human agency, critical thinking, and responsibility.

AI.tldr: Generative AI accelerates HCI workflows but threatens human-centered principles; the paper argues GenAI should serve as a co-thinking partner that preserves human agency, critical thinking, and accountability rather than replacing human-centered methods.
AI.motivation: The tension between GenAI's rapid production capabilities and the risk of eroding human-centered design practices. Faster output does not guarantee human-centered outcomes, and traditional HCD principles risk being sidelined as AI capabilities grow.
AI.method: Position paper based on reflective analysis of HCI coursework, design activities, and AI-assisted workflows, examining both enduring human cognitive limitations (attention, mental models, trust, biases) and GenAI-specific risks.
AI.result: GenAI introduces novel risks — over-reliance, de-skilling, shallow reasoning, hallucination, unclear authorship, and reduced accountability — while users' pre-existing cognitive constraints persist. Traditional HCD principles become more, not less, critical as AI systems advance.
AI.conclusion: The future of HCI must prioritize human-AI collaboration frameworks that safeguard human agency, critical thinking, and responsibility, positioning GenAI as a co-thinking partner driven by human goals, ethics, cognition, and accountability.

title: Generative AI as Support, Not Replacement, in Human-Centered Design
comment: This position paper is part of the CHIWORK '26 Workshop Interrogating GenAI Augmentation for CHIworkers: Strategies for Professional Autonomy and Accountability (June 22, 2026, Linz, Austria)
summary: Traditional human-centered design is grounded in human needs, behaviors, and experiences, especially throughout the development of products and services. Recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning, accelerated by the public launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, have created a wave of AI adoption across research, industry, and design practice. While some of this rapid adoption reflects the current enthusiasm and overuse surrounding AI tools, it has also introduced lasting changes to how designers and researchers understand users, generate ideas, evaluate systems, and make design decisions. This position paper examines how AI is reshaping human-centered design and argues that some of these changes are likely to extend beyond short-term hype. It also considers the risks and limitations introduced by this shift, including over-reliance on AI, reduced human judgment, bias, data security concerns, and unclear accountability. Finally, the paper suggests that AI literacy, careful ethical judgment, and clearer boundaries for AI use are necessary for preserving the human-centered focus of design.

AI.tldr: This position paper examines how the rapid adoption of AI tools (accelerated by ChatGPT) is fundamentally reshaping human-centered design practices, arguing these changes will outlast current hype while highlighting risks like over-reliance, bias, and accountability gaps, and calling for AI literacy and ethical boundaries.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of AI tools—accelerated by ChatGPT's public launch in November 2022—has introduced lasting changes to design practice. The authors seek to examine which of these shifts are enduring rather than ephemeral hype, and to critically assess the implications for human-centered design.
AI.method: This is a position paper, meaning it presents a structured, argument-driven analysis grounded in critical reflection on current trends in AI adoption across design research and practice, rather than empirical experimentation.
AI.result: The paper identifies that AI is reshaping how designers understand users, generate ideas, evaluate systems, and make design decisions. It also surfaces key risks: over-reliance on AI, diminished human judgment, bias amplification, data security concerns, and unclear accountability.
AI.conclusion: To preserve the human-centered core of design, the field must cultivate AI literacy, exercise careful ethical judgment, and establish clearer boundaries for appropriate AI use in design processes.

title: Zero-Trust Federated Learning for Connected Aftermarket Devices
summary: Connected aftermarket devices extend vehicle diagnostics, repair workflows, and over-the-air software maintenance beyond original equipment manufacturer boundaries, yet their heterogeneous ownership and long service life complicate conventional perimeter security. This paper develops Zero Trust Federated Learning for Connected Aftermarket Devices (ZT FL CADE), an edge-learning architecture that combines device-level access control, privacy-preserving federated learning, and adversarial validation for over-the-air update and predictive maintenance decisions. The evaluation uses a single synthetic dataset of 144,000 telemetry windows from 240 devices, 12 vendor domains, and 180 days of operation. Features include bus entropy, update latency, attestation age, signature retries, environmental signals, fault-code rates, packet loss, drift, mileage, and trust score, with targets for maintenance risk, update intrusion, and access action. ZT FL CADE trains local temporal models, aggregates privacy-bounded updates, scores each device against behavioral and update integrity evidence, and routes update requests to allow, challenge, or quarantine actions. Synthetic experiments improve maintenance risk F1 from 0.837 for Fed Avg to 0.883, improve intrusion F1 from 0.856 to 0.897, and preserve 0.842 intrusion recall when 20 percent of selected clients are adversarial. Mean access-decision latency remains 44 MS, below the 100 MS operational budget used in the simulation. The results do not establish field validation, but they indicate that zero-trust policy enforcement and federated learning can be evaluated jointly rather than as separate aftermarket security controls. Index Terms Zero trust architecture, federated learning, connected aftermarket devices, over-the-air updates, adversarial machine learning, edge artificial intelligence, predictive maintenance, automotive cybersecurity

AI.tldr: ZT FL CADE combines zero-trust access control with privacy-preserving federated learning on edge devices for secure OTA updates and predictive maintenance in connected aftermarket automotive environments, demonstrating improved F1 scores and adversarial robustness on synthetic telemetry data.
AI.motivation: Connected aftermarket devices face heterogeneous ownership, long service life, and perimeter security limitations, requiring a joint zero-trust and federated learning architecture to secure over-the-air updates and predictive maintenance across multiple vendor domains.
AI.method: ZT FL CADE integrates device-level access control, privacy-preserving federated learning with bounded updates, and adversarial validation. Local temporal models are trained on telemetry features (bus entropy, update latency, attestation age, signature retries, etc.) from 240 devices across 12 vendor domains over 180 days. Devices are scored on behavioral and update integrity evidence, routing update requests to allow, challenge, or quarantine actions.
AI.result: On a synthetic dataset of 144,000 telemetry windows: maintenance risk F1 improved from 0.837 (FedAvg) to 0.883; intrusion detection F1 improved from 0.856 to 0.897; intrusion recall retained at 0.842 with 20% adversarial clients; mean access-decision latency was 44 ms, well below the 100 ms operational budget.
AI.conclusion: The synthetic results lack field validation but demonstrate that zero-trust policy enforcement and federated learning can be jointly evaluated as an integrated security framework rather than as separate aftermarket controls.

title: Preserving Item Semantics for Free: Rethinking Token Initialization in LLM-Based Generative Recommendation
summary: Recent advances in generative recommendation (GR) leverage large language models (LLMs) as recommender backbones, enabling LLMs to directly generate recommendations conditioned on item-interaction histories. In these systems, items are often represented through semantic IDs (SIDs) added to the LLM vocabulary as special tokens. Ideally, SIDs imbue item token representations with semantic priors, thereby improving model generalization. However, standard vocabulary expansion typically initializes these tokens as random Gaussian vectors, discarding the SIDs' underlying continuous geometry and forcing the LLM to relearn token relationships from interaction data. To demonstrate the consequences of this design, we first show that training from this initialization tends to organize SID embeddings around item popularity rather than semantics. We further show that, despite partially reducing the reliance on popularity and improving cold item performance, the computationally expensive process of continual pretraining (CPT) fails to reliably recover the original semantic geometry. To address these findings, we propose a simple, parameter-free intervention that initializes SID token embeddings directly from their corresponding centroids in the semantic embedding space. Requiring only a few lines of code and no additional training or inference overhead, this drop-in approach improves pure-SFT Recall@5 by up to 16%, reaches peak performance with up to 40% fewer SFT steps, and improves cold-item Recall@5 by up to 60%. Moreover, on datasets that benefit from additional CPT, centroid initialization reaches comparable performance while requiring half as many CPT epochs. Together, our findings show that preserving SID geometry, beyond shared-prefix structure, provides a simple and effective semantic prior for LLM-based GR.

AI.tldr: Standard random initialization of semantic ID (SID) tokens in LLM-based generative recommendation discards semantic geometry and biases embeddings toward popularity. The authors propose centroid initialization—a parameter-free method that initializes SID embeddings from semantic space centroids—yielding up to 16% Recall@5 improvement, 40% fewer SFT steps, and 60% better cold-item performance.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based generative recommendation, SID tokens are typically initialized as random Gaussian vectors during vocabulary expansion, discarding the continuous semantic geometry inherent to the SID space. This forces the LLM to relearn token relationships from scratch, leading to embeddings organized around item popularity rather than semantics, and cold items suffer as a result. Even costly continual pretraining (CPT) fails to reliably recover the original semantic structure.
AI.method: The paper proposes a parameter-free intervention: instead of random initialization, SID token embeddings are initialized directly from the centroid of each SID's corresponding items in a pre-computed semantic embedding space. This requires only a few lines of code with no additional training or inference overhead. The approach is evaluated against standard random initialization and CPT baselines, measuring Recall@5 for both warm and cold items, as well as training efficiency.
AI.result: Centroid initialization improves pure-SFT Recall@5 by up to 16%, reaches peak performance with up to 40% fewer SFT steps, and improves cold-item Recall@5 by up to 60%. On datasets benefiting from additional CPT, centroid initialization matches CPT-level performance while requiring only half the CPT epochs. Analysis confirms that random initialization organizes SID embeddings by popularity, while centroid initialization better preserves semantic geometry.
AI.conclusion: Preserving SID geometry through centroid initialization provides a simple, effective semantic prior for LLM-based generative recommendation. The method is drop-in, parameter-free, and significantly outperforms standard random initialization while reducing or eliminating the need for costly CPT. This highlights that explicitly encoding semantic structure into token embeddings—beyond shared-prefix structure—is crucial for model generalization in GR systems.

title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose long-horizon tasks across supervisors and subagents, but delegated goals do not necessarily carry their original authorization boundaries. Existing safety benchmarks mainly study adversarial compromise, while work on constraint drift lacks controlled architecture-level evaluation. We introduce MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across eight domains. Each task pairs required work with reserved actions. MasDrift compares single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion and authorization preservation. Across generic multi-agent conditions, centralized hierarchies achieve 93.9--98.6% task completion versus 85.7--87.0% for peer networks, while unauthorized actions occur in 2.7--19.8% of tasks versus 0.6--0.8%, a gap that widens with hierarchy depth. We further compare two defenses that differ in where authorization evidence resides. One re-anchors every pending call to the original user request. The other carries an attenuated policy along the delegation chain. Re-anchoring reduces unauthorized actions in every model configuration we evaluate, at a cost of 1.6 points of pooled completion. Chain propagation blocks required work instead, forfeiting up to 36.3 points. A heterogeneous case study confirms that the failure follows from coordination rather than model strength. MasDrift exposes a centralization tradeoff and makes authorization preservation a measurable property of MAS design.

AI.tldr: MasDrift is a benchmark of 600 multi-agent tasks revealing that centralized coordination achieves higher task completion (93.9–98.6%) but suffers more unauthorized actions (2.7–19.8%) than decentralized peer networks (85.7–87.0% completion, 0.6–0.8% unauthorized). Two defenses are tested: re-anchoring to the original request reduces unauthorized actions with minimal completion loss, while chain propagation severely degrades task completion.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent system safety research focuses on adversarial compromise rather than benign constraint drift during delegated task execution. There is no controlled, architecture-level evaluation framework for measuring how authorization boundaries degrade across delegation chains in non-adversarial settings.
AI.method: The authors construct MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across 8 domains, where each task pairs required work with reserved (forbidden) actions. They systematically compare single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination architectures while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion rate and authorization preservation. They further evaluate two defense strategies: re-anchoring (verifying every pending call against the original user request) and chain propagation (carrying an attenuated policy along the delegation chain).
AI.result: Centralized hierarchies achieve 93.9–98.6% task completion vs. 85.7–87.0% for peer networks. However, unauthorized actions occur in 2.7–19.8% of centralized tasks vs. only 0.6–0.8% in peer networks — a gap that widens with hierarchy depth. The re-anchoring defense reduces unauthorized actions across all model configurations at a cost of only 1.6 pooled completion points. Chain propagation, by contrast, forfeits up to 36.3 completion points by blocking required work. A heterogeneous case study confirms failures stem from coordination structure rather than model capability.
AI.conclusion: MasDrift reveals a fundamental centralization tradeoff in MAS design: centralized coordination improves task completion at the expense of authorization drift. Authorization preservation should be treated as a measurable, first-class property in MAS architecture design, and re-anchoring is an effective mitigation with minimal performance cost.

title: DevIntent: How Much Does LLM-Generated Code Violate Developer Intent?
summary: Code generated by LLMs can violate a developer's implicit intentions when given an ambiguous prompt, yet standard benchmarks measure only whether code passes its stated test. We introduce the Intent Violation Rate (IVR) and a 49-problem pilot benchmark derived from HumanEval+. Each problem strips implicit constraints from a clarified prompt and encodes them as hidden constraint tests. IVR measures the fraction of LLM-generated solutions that pass the stated (visible) tests yet fail hidden constraint tests that capture unstated intent. Evaluating Claude Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI GPT 4.1, we find both pass over 92\% of stated tests yet violate intent in over half of problems (54.5\% and 63.5\%), following a systematic, bimodal pattern consistent across both models. Out findings indicate that pass rates overstate how well generated code reflects developer intent.

AI.tldr: LLMs achieve high pass rates on stated coding tests but frequently violate implicit developer intent. The authors introduce the Intent Violation Rate (IVR) and a benchmark showing both Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-4.1 exceed 92% on visible tests yet violate hidden constraints in over half of all problems.
AI.motivation: Standard code generation benchmarks only evaluate whether generated code passes explicitly stated tests, ignoring whether the code respects a developer's unstated but implied intentions. This creates a gap where high benchmark scores may overstate real-world utility.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Intent Violation Rate (IVR) metric and construct a 49-problem pilot benchmark derived from HumanEval+. Each problem takes a clarified prompt and strips away implicit constraints, encoding them instead as hidden constraint tests. IVR measures the fraction of solutions that pass visible (stated) tests but fail the hidden tests capturing unstated intent. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI GPT-4.1 are evaluated using this framework.
AI.result: Both models pass over 92% of stated tests. However, Claude Sonnet 4.6 violates intent on 54.5% of problems, and GPT-4.1 on 63.5% of problems. The violation pattern is systematic and bimodal, consistent across both models.
AI.conclusion: Pass rates on standard benchmarks significantly overstate how well LLM-generated code aligns with developer intent. The systematic nature of intent violations suggests this is a fundamental limitation of current LLMs rather than sporadic error.

title: Unified Hallucination Fuzzing for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Hallucination remains a persistent challenge for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), severely limiting their reliability in high-stakes applications. Existing evaluations, predominantly based on static benchmarks, suffer from narrow taxonomical coverage and rapid performance saturation, failing to reflect model robustness in evolving real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic evaluation framework integrating a comprehensive benchmark with self-evolving stress testing. First, we introduce UniHall, a fine-grained dataset grounded in a unified taxonomy spanning Object, Instruction, and Knowledge dimensions. Second, to address benchmark saturation, we propose Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing (SAMF), a self-adaptive framework that employs evolutionary mutation strategies to explore the boundaries of model hallucinations. Crucially, to ensure reliable assessment of dynamic inputs, SAMF incorporates a structured metric suite driven by an ensemble of multi-modal oracles. Our extensive experiments reveal that state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit significant performance degradation under fuzzing compared to conventional settings, exposing a dissociation between reasoning capabilities and factual grounding. Furthermore, we identify a helpfulness-hallucination trade-off, where reinforcement learning alignment inadvertently exacerbates sycophancy in instruction-following tasks. The framework, code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/LanceZPF/EvalHall.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces UniHall, a fine-grained hallucination benchmark for MLLMs organized across Object, Instruction, and Knowledge dimensions, paired with SAMF (Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing), an evolutionary stress-testing framework that dynamically probes model robustness. Experiments reveal MLLMs degrade significantly under fuzzing, expose a reasoning–grounding dissociation, and identify a helpfulness–hallucination trade-off exacerbated by RL alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM hallucination evaluations rely on static benchmarks with narrow taxonomical coverage and rapid performance saturation. These benchmarks fail to reflect model robustness in evolving real-world scenarios, creating a critical gap for high-stakes applications.
AI.method: The authors propose two complementary components: (1) UniHall, a fine-grained dataset built on a unified taxonomy with three dimensions — Object (entity-level errors), Instruction (task-following failures), and Knowledge (factual grounding errors); and (2) SAMF (Self-Adaptive Multimodal Fuzzing), an adaptive framework using evolutionary mutation strategies to dynamically generate stress-test inputs that explore model hallucination boundaries. SAMF includes a structured metric suite powered by an ensemble of multi-modal oracles for reliable evaluation of dynamic inputs.
AI.result: State-of-the-art MLLMs show significant performance degradation under SAMF fuzzing compared to conventional static evaluation, revealing a dissociation between reasoning ability and factual grounding. Additionally, a helpfulness–hallucination trade-off emerges where reinforcement learning alignment increases sycophantic behavior in instruction-following tasks.
AI.conclusion: The unified benchmark plus self-evolving fuzzing framework provides a more robust and ecologically valid approach to evaluating MLLM hallucinations. The findings highlight fundamental vulnerabilities overlooked by static benchmarks and caution against RL alignment strategies that may unintentionally amplify hallucinatory sycophancy.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence for Fraudulent Banking Operations Recognition
summary: This study considers the task of applying artificial intelligence to recognize bank fraud. In recent years, due to the COVID19 pandemic, bank fraud has become even more common due to the massive transition of many operations to online platforms and the creation of many charitable funds that criminals can use to deceive users. The present work focuses on machine learning algorithms as a tool well suited for analyzing and recognizing online banking transactions. The study`s scientific novelty is the development of machine learning models for identifying fraudulent banking transactions and techniques for preprocessing bank data for further comparison and selection of the best results. This paper also details various methods for improving detection accuracy, i.e., handling highly imbalanced datasets, feature transformation, and feature engineering. The proposed model, which is based on an artificial neural network, effectively improves the accuracy of fraudulent transaction detection. The results of the different algorithms are visualized, and the logistic regression algorithm performs the best, with an output AUC value of approximately 0,946. The stacked generalization shows a better AUC of 0.954. The recognition of banking fraud using artificial intelligence algorithms is a topical issue in our digital society.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and compares machine learning models for detecting fraudulent banking transactions, addressing challenges like imbalanced datasets and feature engineering. An artificial neural network is proposed, with logistic regression achieving an AUC of ~0.946 and stacked generalization improving it to 0.954.
AI.motivation: The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift to online banking and charitable funds, creating more opportunities for bank fraud. There is a pressing need for robust AI-based tools to automatically recognize fraudulent transactions in this expanding digital financial landscape.
AI.method: The authors develop machine learning models (including an artificial neural network) for fraud detection. They employ techniques for handling highly imbalanced datasets, feature transformation, and feature engineering. Multiple algorithms are compared, including logistic regression and stacked generalization, with performance visualized and evaluated using AUC.
AI.result: Logistic regression achieved an AUC of approximately 0.946, while stacked generalization outperformed it with an AUC of 0.954, demonstrating the effectiveness of ensemble methods for this task.
AI.conclusion: AI-based fraud detection in banking is a critical need in modern digital society. The study demonstrates that machine learning, particularly when enhanced with proper data preprocessing and ensemble techniques like stacking, can yield high-accuracy fraud detection models suitable for real-world application.

title: Towards an Argumentative Foundation for Evaluative AI
summary: Evaluative AI (EAI) has been recently proposed as a way to support human decision-making, not by producing a single recommendation, but by presenting competing hypotheses together with evidence for and against each. In this position paper, we advocate (computational) argumentation as a particularly suitable paradigm to provide a formal, computable foundation for forms of EAI that are explainable and contestable, setting the ground for a long-term research agenda towards distributed and human-centred EAI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper advocates for using computational argumentation as a formal foundation for Evaluative AI (EAI), which supports decision-making by presenting competing hypotheses with supporting and opposing evidence rather than single recommendations.
AI.motivation: Traditional AI systems typically output single recommendations, limiting transparency and user agency. There is a need for AI systems that are explainable, contestable, and human-centred, enabling users to weigh competing alternatives with explicit evidence.
AI.method: The authors propose adopting computational argumentation — a formal paradigm for representing, evaluating, and resolving conflicting arguments — as the underlying framework for building Evaluative AI systems. This position paper outlines a research agenda rather than presenting empirical results.
AI.result: As a position paper, no experimental results are reported. The contribution is the articulation of a research roadmap connecting computational argumentation to Evaluative AI, emphasizing explainability, contestability, and distributed architectures.
AI.conclusion: Computational argumentation offers a promising formal basis for building EAI systems that are inherently explainable and contestable, paving the way for long-term research into distributed, human-centred AI decision support.

title: Using the gameplay and user data to predict and identify causes of cybersickness manifestation in virtual reality games
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2006.15432
summary: Virtual reality (VR) is an imminent trend in games, education, entertainment, military, and health applications, as the use of head-mounted displays is accessible to everyone. While VR provides immersive experiences, it still does not offer an entirely perfect situation, mainly due to cybersickness (CS) issues. In this work, we propose a novel approach for predicting upcoming CS symptoms. Our solution is able to suggest whether the user of VR is entering into an illness situation. We adopted random forest classifiers and validated our solution using 16 different machine-learning techniques, which presented the best results. For training purposes, we built our own dataset through a CS profile questionnaire that we also propose in the present work. The questionnaire is focused on registering and identifying the user's susceptibility to CS, considering their historical conditions and also their response to the immersive environment developed by us. In this method, 86 individuals are selected and the developed questionnaire was put to them on different days, and the answers are compiled as dataset. Our proposal also identifying attributes responsible (causes and individual's parameters) for the observed stressful and uncomfortable situations.

AI.tldr: A random forest classifier is proposed to predict upcoming cybersickness in VR users, trained on a custom questionnaire dataset from 86 participants to identify susceptibility factors and causes.
AI.motivation: VR is increasingly accessible across games, education, military, and health, but cybersickness (CS) undermines the immersive experience. There is a need for a predictive approach that can anticipate CS symptoms before they fully manifest.
AI.method: The authors developed a novel CS susceptibility questionnaire capturing users' historical conditions and responses to a custom immersive environment. Data were collected from 86 individuals on multiple days. A random forest classifier was trained and benchmarked against 16 other machine learning techniques. The model also identifies key attributes responsible for stressful and uncomfortable situations.
AI.result: The random forest classifier outperformed 16 alternative machine learning techniques in predicting upcoming cybersickness symptoms. The approach successfully identified both causal factors and individual parameters linked to CS.
AI.conclusion: Random forest classification, combined with a purpose-built CS susceptibility questionnaire, provides an effective early-warning system for VR cybersickness, enabling proactive rather than reactive mitigation strategies.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Deep OCR Systems
summary: Deep-OCR (DeepSeek-OCR) advances document recognition by treating the visual modality as an optical compression medium, enabling long-context OCR at low token cost. However, its increased complexity may introduce new security vulnerabilities. In this paper, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first pure black-box adversarial attack against a generative OCR vision-language model, where only the decoded string can be queried and no gradients, logits, or model internals are available. We recast the attack as a zeroth-order optimization problem driven by a bounded scalar loss defined directly on the string output via sequence similarity, and estimate the gradient with a random-direction finite-difference scheme whose query cost is independent of the image dimension. An Adam update with ell_infinity projection yields imperceptible perturbations for both untargeted and targeted objectives. Pilot experiments on Deep-OCR validate the string-only attack and evaluation pipeline and expose severe qualitative decoder failures, including repetition, truncation, and prompt leakage. They also show that controlled targeted rewriting remains substantially harder than untargeted degradation; we avoid claiming targeted success until the pre-registered evaluation is complete.

AI.tldr: First pure black-box adversarial attack against generative OCR vision-language models (Deep-OCR), using only decoded string output. Recasts attack as zeroth-order optimization with sequence-similarity loss and random-direction finite-difference gradient estimation, revealing decoder vulnerabilities like repetition, truncation, and prompt leakage.
AI.motivation: Deep-OCR's increased architectural complexity may introduce new security vulnerabilities. Existing attacks rely on white-box access (gradients, logits), but real-world deployments expose only decoded strings. Thus, a pure black-box attack framework is needed to assess and expose robustness failures in generative OCR models.
AI.method: The attack is formulated as a zeroth-order optimization using a bounded scalar loss based on sequence similarity (e.g., edit distance) between the decoded output and a target string. Gradients are estimated via a random-direction finite-difference scheme with query cost independent of image dimension. An Adam optimizer with ℓ∞ projection generates imperceptible adversarial perturbations for both untargeted degradation and targeted rewriting objectives.
AI.result: Pilot experiments on Deep-OCR validated the string-only attack pipeline. Severe qualitative decoder failures were exposed: repetition, truncation, and prompt leakage. Untargeted degradation succeeded, but controlled targeted rewriting proved substantially harder; the authors withhold claiming targeted success pending full pre-registered evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Pure black-box adversarial attacks are feasible against generative OCR models using only string-level feedback. The observed decoder failures highlight critical robustness gaps in Deep-OCR. Targeted attacks remain challenging, warranting further investigation through pre-registered evaluation before definitive claims.

title: PushDualGen: Enabling LLMs to Generate Semantic IDs with Interpretable Copy for Industrial Push Recommendation
summary: Push recommendation in KuaiShou proactively delivers personalized content to nearly one billion users to facilitate their engagement. Recently, generative recommendation has achieved end-to-end user personalization through semantic ID. However, their black- box characteristics make recommendation logics difficult to trace, hindering their deployment. OneRec-Thinking addresses this by incorporating CoT before generating SIDs, but this significantly increases inference cost. To support large-scale industrial applications, we propose PushDualGen, a lightweight generator, which first generates the SID and then produces a copy as a skippable explanation. PushDualGen has been deployed in Kuaishou's push recommendation system. Online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness of PushDualGen, delivering significant improvements in both user attraction and satisfaction. The effective play rate for videos recommended to users has relatively increased by 8.50%, while the dissatisfaction rate has relatively fallen by 37.70%. In the long term, PushDualGen optimises the content ecosystem, providing more exposure for long-tail videos.

AI.tldr: PushDualGen is a lightweight generative recommendation model deployed at Kuaishou that generates semantic IDs followed by a skippable explanation, achieving an 8.50% relative increase in effective play rate and a 37.70% relative decrease in dissatisfaction rate in online A/B tests.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation systems using semantic IDs (SIDs) offer strong personalization but suffer from black-box opacity, making their recommendation logic untraceable and difficult to deploy. While OneRec-Thinking addresses traceability by adding Chain-of-Thought (CoT) before SID generation, it incurs substantial inference cost, rendering it impractical for large-scale industrial applications serving nearly one billion users.
AI.method: PushDualGen is a lightweight generator that first generates the semantic ID (SID) for the recommended content, and then produces a copy of that SID framed as a skippable explanation. This design preserves interpretability without the heavy inference overhead of full CoT generation, enabling efficient deployment at scale in Kuaishou's push recommendation system.
AI.result: Online A/B tests in Kuaishou's production environment show that PushDualGen significantly improves both user attraction and satisfaction. The effective play rate relatively increased by 8.50%, and the dissatisfaction rate relatively dropped by 37.70%. Long-term, the model also optimizes the content ecosystem by increasing exposure for long-tail videos.
AI.conclusion: PushDualGen successfully balances the trade-off between generative recommendation personalization and industrial scalability. By generating SIDs with skippable explanations instead of full CoT reasoning, it achieves strong online performance gains while remaining computationally lightweight, and it further contributes to a healthier content ecosystem through improved long-tail content exposure.

title: Mobility, Memory, and Network Structure in Agent-Based Models of Convention Tipping and Convergence
comment: Under review at the Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS)
summary: Tipping-point dynamics describe the critical conditions under which a committed minority drives a population to abandon an established convention in favor of a new one. We present a transparent agent-based model of this process, in which agents hold one of two behavioral states and a mobile committed minority attempts to overturn the incumbent convention. Our goal was to examine how localized mobility, bounded agent memory, and network topology jointly influence the tipping threshold. Using a custom agent-based simulation framework, we found that in many configurations, tipping becomes effectively inevitable: given sufficient time, the population always converges to the minority state. This observation motivated a complementary analysis focused on the pace of convergence rather than its feasibility. We introduce a unified predictive model that accurately estimates how structural and behavioral parameters determine the time required for complete adoption, showing that mobility is the dominant accelerator while memory and connectivity modulate convergence in systematic ways. Together, these results extend classical tipping-point research by linking structural and behavioral factors not only to the likelihood of convention change but also to the timescale on which it unfolds. While we frame the model in terms of convention-like binary behavioral adoption, the same mechanisms bear on norm change and other contagion-like social processes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an agent-based model examining how localized mobility, bounded memory, and network topology jointly influence tipping-point dynamics, finding that under many configurations tipping becomes inevitable; the authors thus shift focus to convergence speed, offering a unified predictive model for adoption time with mobility as the dominant accelerator.
AI.motivation: Classical tipping-point research has focused primarily on the critical conditions under which a committed minority can overturn an established convention, but has underexplored how structural and behavioral factors—specifically localized mobility, bounded agent memory, and network topology—jointly influence not only whether tipping occurs but how quickly it unfolds.
AI.method: The authors developed a custom agent-based simulation framework featuring agents with two behavioral states and a mobile committed minority. They systematically varied localized mobility, bounded memory, and network topology parameters to observe their effects on tipping dynamics, then derived a unified predictive model linking these parameters to convergence time.
AI.result: In many configurations, tipping becomes effectively inevitable given sufficient time. Mobility emerged as the dominant accelerator of convergence, while memory and network connectivity modulated convergence speed in systematic, quantifiable ways. The unified predictive model accurately estimates adoption time from structural and behavioral parameters.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend tipping-point research by linking structural and behavioral factors to both the likelihood and the timescale of convention change, with implications for norm change and contagion-like social processes beyond binary behavioral adoption.

title: Refining LLM-based Directed Test Input Generation via Runtime Value Feedback
summary: LLM-based directed input generation techniques have shown promising effectiveness at producing target-reaching test inputs. However, due to the constraint of available code information and inherent unpredictability of LLM inference, reliable directed input generation requires mechanisms to ground the process in observed runtime behavior. We propose ReDig, a runtime feedback-guided refinement framework which adds a control loop around an LLM-based directed test input generation technique to refine the directed input generation with runtime values observed in prior target-missing test executions. In the case studies with Poppler and Libsndfile, we found that ReDig effectively derive runtime value feedback to diagnose why the previous test script failed to reach the target lines, and also effectively leverage given runtime value feedback to refine the test scripts in subsequent steps.

AI.tldr: ReDig is a runtime feedback-guided refinement framework that wraps LLM-based directed test input generation with a control loop, using runtime values from failed executions to diagnose and fix test scripts so they can reach target code lines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based directed input generation techniques are limited by incomplete code information and the unpredictability of LLM inference, making it difficult to reliably produce target-reaching test inputs without grounding the generation process in observed runtime behavior.
AI.method: ReDig introduces a control loop around an LLM-based directed test input generation technique. It captures runtime values from prior target-missing test executions, uses that feedback to diagnose why the test script failed to reach the target lines, and then leverages the diagnosis to refine subsequent test scripts iteratively.
AI.result: In case studies with Poppler and Libsndfile, ReDig effectively derived runtime value feedback to diagnose failure causes and successfully used that feedback to refine test scripts, enabling them to reach previously missed target lines.
AI.conclusion: Runtime feedback-guided refinement significantly improves the reliability of LLM-based directed input generation by closing the loop between generation and execution, allowing the system to learn from failed attempts and iteratively converge on target-reaching inputs.

title: DocAtlas: Long-Document Understanding as Mutable-State Interaction
summary: Long-document understanding requires models to find and combine evidence across many pages, layouts, tables, figures, and charts. Existing retrieval-augmented systems usually select evidence from a static index before generation, while recent agentic systems add multi-turn tool use but often rely on frozen proprietary backbones whose behavior is set by prompts. We present DocAtlas, a system that treats long-document understanding as a mutable-state information-seeking process. We instantiate DocAtlas as a mutable document harness: an external environment that determines what document information is searched, read, stored, reviewed, and shown to the model at each step. Given a document and question, the harness exposes search, reading, note-taking, and review tools, maintains a hierarchical tree and note store, and updates both as the agent records evidence. DocAtlas combines self-improving retrieval, selective evidence access, and active working memory under a fixed context budget. The same harness supports inference-time use with large VLMs and end-to-end reinforcement learning for compact VLM agents. With GPT-5.4, DocAtlas reaches 71.4\% on MMLongBench-Doc, exceeding the human-expert reference of 65.8\%. A Qwen3.5-4B VLM trained with end-to-end RL in the DocAtlas environment reaches 63.7\%, compared with a 54.4\% direct-input baseline, showing that mutable document-harness design can improve compact document agents by a large margin.

AI.tldr: DocAtlas is a system for long-document understanding that treats the task as a mutable-state information-seeking process. It uses an external "document harness" with search, reading, note-taking, and review tools, maintaining a hierarchical tree and note store. With GPT-5.4 it achieves 71.4% on MMLongBench-Doc (surpassing human experts at 65.8%), and a Qwen3.5-4B VLM trained with end-to-end RL reaches 63.7%, significantly outperforming the 54.4% direct-input baseline.
AI.motivation: Long-document understanding requires models to find and combine evidence across many pages with diverse elements (layouts, tables, figures, charts). Existing retrieval-augmented systems select evidence statically before generation, and agentic systems rely on frozen proprietary models steered only by prompts. Neither approach provides a dynamic, mutable environment where evidence can be actively searched, stored, reviewed, and updated step-by-step under a fixed context budget. There is also a need for compact models to benefit from such architectures via end-to-end RL training.
AI.method: DocAtlas instantiates a mutable document harness — an external environment exposing search, reading, note-taking, and review tools. It maintains a hierarchical tree and a note store, both updated as the agent records evidence. The system combines self-improving retrieval, selective evidence access, and active working memory under a fixed context budget. The same harness supports both inference-time use with large VLMs and end-to-end reinforcement learning for training compact VLM agents.
AI.result: With GPT-5.4, DocAtlas reaches 71.4% on MMLongBench-Doc, exceeding the human-expert reference of 65.8%. A Qwen3.5-4B VLM trained end-to-end with RL in the DocAtlas environment reaches 63.7%, compared to a 54.4% direct-input baseline — a gain of 9.3 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Mutable document-harness design — treating long-document understanding as a dynamic, stateful information-seeking process — significantly improves performance for both large proprietary VLMs and compact VLMs. The approach enables compact models to bridge much of the gap toward large-model performance via end-to-end RL training in the harness environment.

title: Data-Driven Fire-Zone Segmentation for Improved Short-Term Wildfire Prediction
summary: Wildfire prediction models typically discretize study areas into uniform grids, ignoring the heterogeneous spatial distribution of ignitions. We challenge this paradigm by showing that how data is discretized matters more than which model is used. We propose an unsupervised fire-zone segmentation algorithm combining watershed detection with K-means clustering to define prediction units directly from historical fire patterns. Experiments across six French departments and six forecasting models show that fire-zone segmentation consistently outperforms grid-based approaches, with mean IoU improvements of +3--6% depending on spatial scale. The method is computationally lightweight (<10s per configuration) and fully parallelizable. Our results demonstrate that optimizing spatial discretization yields significant, reproducible performance gains for short-term wildfire forecasting.

AI.tldr: Paper shows that spatial discretization method matters more than model choice for wildfire prediction. An unsupervised fire-zone segmentation method combining watershed detection and K-means clustering outperforms uniform grids by +3–6% mean IoU across six French departments and six models, while remaining computationally lightweight.
AI.motivation: Conventional wildfire prediction models use uniform grids for spatial discretization, which ignores the inherently heterogeneous spatial distribution of ignition events. The authors argue this paradigm is suboptimal and contend that how data is discretized matters more than which predictive model is selected.
AI.method: An unsupervised fire-zone segmentation algorithm that combines watershed detection with K-means clustering to delineate prediction units directly from historical fire patterns, rather than imposing arbitrary grid boundaries. Tested across six French departments and six distinct forecasting models.
AI.result: Fire-zone segmentation consistently outperforms grid-based approaches, yielding mean IoU improvements of +3–6% depending on spatial scale. The method is computationally lightweight (<10s per configuration) and fully parallelizable.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing spatial discretization provides significant, reproducible performance gains for short-term wildfire forecasting, and should be considered a critical design choice alongside model selection.

title: Flow-by-Flow:Content-Judgment Bypass for Governing AI Output in High-Loss Domains
summary: Prior work showed that human-in-the-loop oversight becomes structurally untenable in high-loss domains when AI output velocity V exceeds human cognitive capacity C_max. The operative constraint, however, is not V alone but V x L, where L denotes per-item cognitive load. L consists of triage, judgment, and response, which respond asymmetrically to AI capability improvement. Triage cost does not decline as models become more capable, because semantic indeterminacy is inherent in general-purpose design. Response cost is invariant to accuracy improvements. Only judgment cost faces downward pressure, and this pressure often operates by inducing omission rather than genuine reduction. Capability improvement therefore restructures L rather than reducing it. Governance mechanisms based on evaluating whether AI output is correct either delegate that evaluation to AI and inherit hallucination risk, or delegate it to humans and face the V x L ceiling. We propose Flow-by-Flow, a governance paradigm that controls supervisory load without evaluating content. A cognitive cost score based on formal, countable features imposes nonlinear costs on high-volume production, while an institutional capacity cap keeps processing volume within C_max. We derive four design invariants for any content-judgment-bypass exceedance pathway: no content judgment, no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, identity-bound per-application friction, and no batch clearance. One reference implementation is discussed to show that these invariants are jointly satisfiable, while its practical difficulties are explicitly acknowledged. An illustrative Monte Carlo analysis across 1,000 parameter draws suggests that composite multi-metric flow control outperforms supervision reinforcement alone in 90.8% of trials.

AI.tldr: Human oversight of AI fails when output volume × cognitive load exceeds human capacity. AI capability improvements restructure cognitive load rather than reducing it, because triage and response costs remain fixed. The authors propose "Flow-by-Flow," a governance paradigm that controls supervisory load without evaluating content, using countable features and institutional capacity caps, and show it outperforms supervision reinforcement in ~91% of simulated trials.
AI.motivation: Traditional human-in-the-loop AI oversight becomes structurally impossible in high-stakes domains when AI output velocity (V) exceeds human cognitive capacity (C_max). The core problem is that the true constraint is V × L (cognitive load per item), and current governance mechanisms — whether human or AI-driven evaluation — either hit the V × L ceiling or inherit hallucination risk. There is a need for a governance approach that bypasses content judgment entirely.
AI.method: The authors decompose cognitive load L into three components (triage, judgment, response) and analyze how each responds asymmetrically to AI capability improvements. They then propose Flow-by-Flow, a governance paradigm with four design invariants: no content judgment, no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, identity-bound per-application friction, and no batch clearance. A cognitive cost score uses formal, countable features to impose nonlinear costs on high-volume production, paired with an institutional capacity cap. Validation is done via a reference implementation discussion and a Monte Carlo analysis across 1,000 parameter draws.
AI.result: Capability improvement restructures L rather than reducing it: triage cost persists due to semantic indeterminacy in general-purpose design; response cost is invariant to accuracy improvements; only judgment cost faces downward pressure, often by inducing omission. Composite multi-metric flow control outperforms supervision reinforcement alone in 90.8% of Monte Carlo trials (1,000 parameter draws).
AI.conclusion: Governance mechanisms relying on evaluating AI output correctness are structurally bounded by the V × L ceiling. Flow-by-Flow offers a viable alternative by controlling supervisory load through formal, non-content-based features, and its four design invariants provide a blueprint for any content-judgment-bypass governance pathway.

title: Humour as Resistance: Visceralizing the Environmental and Social Impact of AI through Humour-based Creative Practices
summary: The growth of AI does not come without cost. While we hear about the economic costs, the environmental and social costs are often obfuscated by mainstream narratives, and even when acknowledged, are accompanied by a sense of helplessness. To counter this, we, a group of designers and researchers, reflect on our experience leading a humour-based creative campaign surfacing the material impact of AI infrastructures. Through graphics design, physical installations, digital content creation and co-creation workshops, we leaned into humour as a creative practice to provoke collective reflection. Drawing on event ethnography, surveys and interviews with campaign engagers, we examine four roles of humour-based creative work in HCI: a connector to critical friends, a visceral and emotional harbour, social glue, and resistance to power. We argue for the importance of creative practices in bridging social and emotional gaps between people and concerns around technology, and in surfacing hidden perspectives for more inclusive conversations.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how a humour-based creative campaign—using graphic design, installations, and workshops—can surface the hidden environmental and social costs of AI infrastructure, identifying four key roles of humour in HCI: connecting critical friends, providing emotional harbour, acting as social glue, and resisting power.
AI.motivation: Mainstream narratives around AI typically emphasize economic costs while obscuring environmental and social impacts; even when these are acknowledged, they are often accompanied by public helplessness. The authors aim to counter this by exploring creative, humour-driven approaches that make these hidden costs visible and emotionally accessible.
AI.method: The authors, a group of designers and researchers, conducted a humour-based creative campaign involving graphic design, physical installations, digital content creation, and co-creation workshops. They gathered data through event ethnography, surveys, and interviews with campaign engagers to analyze the campaign's effects.
AI.result: The analysis revealed four distinct roles that humour-based creative work plays in HCI contexts: (1) a connector to critical friends, (2) a visceral and emotional harbour, (3) social glue, and (4) resistance to power.
AI.conclusion: Creative practices are essential for bridging social and emotional gaps between people and technology-related concerns, and for bringing hidden perspectives into more inclusive conversations around AI's material impacts.

title: Can AI Write Compliant Code, and to What Extent? Evaluating SOC 2 Compliance of Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Opus 5 Across Four Use Cases
summary: Software teams now delegate production code to language models, including code that provisions storage, handles credentials, and stores regulated data, so we asked whether a model applies the controls a SOC~2 program expects (encryption, restricted access, logging, retention) when nobody mentions security, and how much one sentence naming the standard changes the answer. We tested three frontier models (Claude Fable~5, Opus~4.8, and Opus~5) across four use cases (an S3 CLI, an authentication service, an RDS Terraform module, and a file-upload handler holding personal data), each generated once from a neutral task statement and once with a single SOC~2 sentence added, scoring all 24 outputs against binary rubrics mapped to specific Trust Services Criteria and hand-verifying every failure and flagged act. Unprompted conformance ran from 47\% to 88\% and tracked whether a control is part of how the code is normally written, so password hashing and \texttt{storage\_encrypted} appear unasked while S3 hardening calls, retention, and MFA hooks do not. The neutral prompt also shipped real vulnerabilities, including a reachable Werkzeug debugger allowing remote code execution, an unauthenticated download, and an endpoint returning every stored name and email, all scored clean by our first checklist, with a fourth defect passing because its value was computed by a conditional. One SOC~2 sentence moved every case to 86--100\%, worth 23 to 50 points, and removed every insecure construction, though controls outside the model's conception of the task survived it, including MFA hooks, cookie flags, and account lifecycle. Model choice mattered least, with same-generation models within one rubric item across all eight cells, and the pattern-matching scorer proved unreliable, disagreeing with semantic grading on 27 of 216 judgments and passing a real defect, so it needs replacing with semantic checks.

AI.tldr: When code generation tasks omit security requirements, frontier LLMs inconsistently apply SOC 2 controls (47–88% conformance) and can introduce real vulnerabilities. Adding a single sentence referencing SOC 2 boosts conformance to 86–100% and eliminates all insecure constructions, though some controls remain missing. Model choice matters little, and pattern-matching scorers are unreliable compared to semantic grading.
AI.motivation: As organizations increasingly delegate production code generation to LLMs—including code handling credentials, storage, and regulated data—it is critical to understand whether these models implicitly apply security controls expected by compliance frameworks like SOC 2, and how easily compliance can be induced.
AI.method: Three frontier models (Claude Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 5) were tested across four use cases (S3 CLI, authentication service, RDS Terraform module, file-upload handler with personal data). Each case was generated twice: once from a neutral prompt and once with a single SOC 2 sentence added. All 24 outputs were scored against binary rubrics mapped to Trust Services Criteria, with every failure and flagged action hand-verified. Pattern-matching scoring was compared against semantic grading.
AI.result: Unprompted conformance ranged from 47% to 88%, with controls like password hashing and storage_encrypted appearing automatically while S3 hardening, retention, and MFA hooks did not. The neutral prompt produced real vulnerabilities including a reachable Werkzeug debugger (RCE), an unauthenticated download, and an endpoint exposing all stored names and emails. One SOC 2 sentence raised every case to 86–100% (a 23–50 point gain) and removed all insecure constructions, though MFA hooks, cookie flags, and account lifecycle controls remained absent. Same-generation models differed by at most one rubric item across all cells. The pattern-matching scorer disagreed with semantic grading on 27 of 216 judgments and passed a real defect.
AI.conclusion: LLMs do not reliably apply SOC 2 security controls unless explicitly prompted, and a minimal compliance cue dramatically improves outcomes—but does not guarantee complete coverage. Reliable security in AI-generated code requires moving beyond pattern-matching evaluation to semantic verification.

title: Give the Long-tail More SPACE: Promoting Provider Fairness in Next POI Recommendation
comment: 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys '26), September 27-October 02, 2026, Minneapolis, MN, USA
summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation predicts users' future destinations from historical mobility sequences and has become a key component of location-based services. However, mainstream models often concentrate exposure on a small set of popular POIs, leaving long-tail merchants systematically under-exposed. While provider fairness has recently attracted increasing attention, directly applying existing provider-fairness techniques to POI recommendation is problematic: (i) users face execution constraints; and (ii) POIs face resource supply constraints. To address this, we propose SPACE (Supply- and Physics-Aware Conditional Embedding generation), a model-agnostic framework that improves long-tail POI exposure via virtual user generation under explicit feasibility and supply control. SPACE consists of three stages: (1) community inference to capture heterogeneous user execution constraints; (2) unbalanced optimal-transport allocation to decide how many virtual users each tail POI should receive from which communities under POI-specific supply budgets; and (3) constraint-guided latent diffusion to generate POI-conditional, community-consistent virtual user embeddings. The generated user-POI pairs can be seamlessly used to train existing recommenders without modifying their architectures. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that SPACE substantially improves provider fairness while maintaining and often improving recommendation accuracy across multiple backbone models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Anniran1/SPACE-main.

AI.tldr: SPACE is a model-agnostic framework that improves long-tail POI exposure in next-POI recommendation by generating virtual users under explicit feasibility and supply constraints, using community inference, unbalanced optimal transport allocation, and constraint-guided latent diffusion.
AI.motivation: Mainstream POI recommenders systematically under-expose long-tail POIs, and existing provider-fairness techniques fail because they ignore two critical constraints: (i) users' physical execution constraints (mobility limits) and (ii) POIs' resource supply constraints (capacity limits).
AI.method: A three-stage framework: (1) Community inference to capture heterogeneous user execution constraints; (2) Unbalanced optimal-transport allocation to distribute virtual users from communities to tail POIs under supply budgets; (3) Constraint-guided latent diffusion to generate POI-conditional, community-consistent virtual user embeddings. The generated pairs train existing recommenders without architectural modification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show SPACE substantially improves provider fairness while maintaining or often improving recommendation accuracy across multiple backbone models.
AI.conclusion: SPACE effectively addresses provider fairness in POI recommendation by respecting both user execution constraints and POI supply constraints through virtual user generation, achieving a practical, model-agnostic solution.

title: Per-Shipment Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Intermodal Freight Routing Under Hurricane Disruption
summary: Intermodal freight networks face growing disruption risk from climate extremes that degrade multiple corridors simultaneously. To address this, we formulate freight routing as a Dec-POMDP with per-shipment action granularity and train Independent PPO (IPPO) under Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution, comparing against two heuristic baselines with privileged state access on a 15-hub network under hurricane disruption. Across 30 matched episodes, no single policy dominates: IPPO achieves the highest throughput ($+12.7\%$) and delivery rate while a capacity-aware heuristic leads on Resilience Index (RI) and delay. Under demand surge (2.9:1 capacity ratio), IPPO's RI advantage grows to $+6.4\%$, suggesting learned routing is most valuable when capacity is scarce. A Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) variant collapses under train-eval queue mismatch ($\mathrm{RI} = 0.811$); retraining recovers RI to $1.018$ but IPPO still leads on throughput, pointing to residual limitations in centralized critics under per-shipment dispatch.

AI.tldr: This paper models intermodal freight routing under climate-induced disruptions as a Dec-POMDP, trains agents using Independent PPO with CTDE, and benchmarks against heuristic baselines on a 15-hub hurricane-affected network. IPPO achieves highest throughput (+12.7%) and delivery rate; a capacity-aware heuristic leads on Resilience Index. Under demand surges, IPPO's RI advantage grows, and a MAPPO variant suffers from train-eval queue mismatch.
AI.motivation: Intermodal freight networks are increasingly vulnerable to climate extremes (e.g., hurricanes) that can disrupt multiple corridors simultaneously. Existing approaches lack per-shipment granularity and decentralized execution capable of adapting to such disruptions, motivating a multi-agent RL formulation that balances throughput, resilience, and delay under stochastic capacity degradation.
AI.method: Freight routing is formulated as a Dec-POMDP with per-shipment action granularity. Independent PPO (IPPO) agents are trained under Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE). Two heuristic baselines with privileged state access serve as benchmarks. A Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) variant with centralized critics is also evaluated. Experiments run on a 15-hub network under hurricane disruption scenarios, including a demand surge condition (2.9:1 capacity ratio).
AI.result: No single policy dominates across all metrics. IPPO achieves the highest throughput (+12.7%) and delivery rate. The capacity-aware heuristic leads on Resilience Index (RI) and delay. Under demand surge (2.9:1 capacity ratio), IPPO's RI advantage grows to +6.4%, indicating learned routing is most valuable when capacity is scarce. MAPPO collapses under train-eval queue mismatch (RI = 0.811); retraining recovers RI to 1.018, but IPPO still leads on throughput, highlighting residual limitations of centralized critics under per-shipment dispatch.
AI.conclusion: Learned multi-agent routing via IPPO with CTDE provides robust throughput gains under disruption, especially in capacity-constrained regimes. However, centralized critics (MAPPO) introduce fragility due to queue distribution mismatch between training and evaluation. The findings suggest that decentralized policies with independent learning strike a favorable balance between performance and robustness for real-world intermodal freight networks facing climate extremes.

title: Verication-driven closed-loop multi-agent large language modelframework for code-compliant structural design
summary: Multi-agent large language model(LLM)systems are applied to structural design,yet most use one-shot generation and cannot verify their output,leaving themill-suited to safety-critical tasks.Rather than trusting LLM self-correction,thisframework injects feedback from an external physics-based verier into a closedrepair loop.The framework couples a three-layernite-element verication systemwith a dual-node loop.Node 1 turns code violations into hard repair constraints,Node 2 turns a four-dimensional quality score into safety-rst soft constraints,and a retrieval-augmented code base makes every violation traceable to a clause.Overve structure types and 44 cases,code compliance rises from 56.8%to 98.6%and the composite score from 63.8 to 71.4(p<0.000001),using about 5.8%lessmaterial.Removing either node degrades performance,and compliance does notchange detectably across the two backbone LLMs tested,indicating that it ishere attributed to the external verier rather than the model.The framework,the 44-case benchmark and all experiment scripts are released as open source forreplicability.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework for structural design that replaces self-correction with an external physics-based verifier in a closed repair loop, achieving 98.6% code compliance across 44 cases while using less material. Performance gains are attributed to the verifier, not the LLM.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems for structural design rely on one-shot generation without verification, making them unsuitable for safety-critical tasks. LLM self-correction is unreliable; an external, trustworthy verification mechanism is needed.
AI.method: A framework coupling a three-layer finite-element verification system with a dual-node repair loop: Node 1 converts code violations into hard constraints, Node 2 transforms a four-dimensional quality score into safety-first soft constraints, and a retrieval-augmented code base ensures every violation is traceable to a clause. Tested across 5 structure types and 44 cases with two different backbone LLMs.
AI.result: Code compliance improved from 56.8% to 98.6%; composite quality score rose from 63.8 to 71.4 (p < 0.000001); approximately 5.8% less material used. Removing either node degraded performance. Compliance did not change detectably across two backbone LLMs, attributing gains to the external verifier rather than the model.
AI.conclusion: Injecting external physics-based verification into a closed-loop repair framework dramatically improves structural design compliance and quality, independent of the underlying LLM. The framework, benchmark (44 cases), and scripts are open-sourced for replicability.

title: WuYuEval: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Large Language Models in Solid Waste Management
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as technical assistants, but their competence in solid waste management (SWM) remains difficult to assess because existing benchmarks emphasize general knowledge rather than professional decisions under engineering, environmental, and policy constraints. We introduce WuYuEval, a multi-level benchmark for evaluating LLMs in SWM across foundational knowledge, domain reasoning, and expert decision-making. After quality auditing, WuYuEval contains a Foundation Module with 4,590 closed-ended multiple-choice questions across six task types and eight domain categories, together with an Expert Module with 247 scenario-based open-ended questions involving multi-objective optimization, constraint trade-offs, and system design. For expert tasks, we combine anchor-calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring with Elo-based pairwise comparison. Across 33 LLMs, performance varied widely. The leading model reached 94.64\% accuracy on the Foundation Module, but average accuracy still fell from 84.14\% on easy questions to 42.50\% on hard questions, with lower performance concentrated in calculation, experimental design, urban planning, and open-ended expert tasks. Reasoning-oriented Thinking modes improve most matched model pairs after auditing, but the gains depend on baseline capability and are not uniformly positive. These results suggest that visible deliberation helps only when it remains anchored to units, assumptions, and engineering constraints; otherwise, it may drift from decisive answer boundaries. WuYuEval therefore provides both an evaluation resource and an empirical basis for developing SWM-oriented foundation models with professional reasoning chains and explicit constraint control.
