AI.tldr: WuYuEval is a multi-level benchmark for evaluating LLMs in solid waste management, comprising a Foundation Module (4,590 multiple-choice questions) and an Expert Module (247 open-ended scenario questions). Testing 33 LLMs revealed strong performance on easy questions but significant drops on hard tasks, with reasoning-mode gains being uneven and dependent on baseline capability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks emphasize general knowledge rather than professional SWM decisions under real engineering, environmental, and policy constraints, making it difficult to assess LLM competence in this domain.
AI.method: WuYuEval consists of two modules: a Foundation Module (4,590 closed-ended MCQs across six task types and eight domain categories) and an Expert Module (247 scenario-based open-ended questions with multi-objective optimization and constraint trade-offs). Expert tasks are evaluated using anchor-calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge scoring combined with Elo-based pairwise comparison. 33 LLMs were benchmarked, with special attention to reasoning-oriented Thinking modes.
AI.result: The leading model achieved 94.64% accuracy on the Foundation Module, but average accuracy dropped from 84.14% on easy questions to 42.50% on hard questions. Weaknesses concentrated in calculation, experimental design, urban planning, and open-ended expert tasks. Reasoning-oriented Thinking modes improved most matched pairs after auditing, but gains were not uniformly positive and depended on baseline capability.
AI.conclusion: Visible deliberation (reasoning chains) helps only when anchored to units, assumptions, and engineering constraints; otherwise it may drift from correct answer boundaries. WuYuEval serves as both an evaluation resource and an empirical basis for developing SWM-oriented foundation models with professional reasoning and explicit constraint control.

title: Evolving Safety Landscape of Multi-modal Large Language Models: A Survey of Emerging Threats and Safeguards
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Principled Design for Trustworthy AI
summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) integrate heterogeneous modalities through modality alignment and fusion, enabling stronger understanding and reasoning. However, this architectural shift reshapes the safety landscape of machine learning. Increased model complexity and cross-modal interactions give rise to novel threats, including compromised modality integration, modality misalignment, and fused safety risks, reflecting shifts in threat modeling beyond uni-modal assumptions. These shifts, in turn, impose new constraints on safety solutions not captured by existing frameworks rooted in uni-modal learning. Motivated by these challenges, this survey provides a systematic analysis of the evolving safety landscape of MLLMs. We first propose a multimodal grounded taxonomy of safety threats and analyze shifts in threat models, covering adversarial attacks, data poisoning, jailbreaks, and hallucinations. We then summarize updated safety assumptions and organize recent advances in MLLM safety strategies accordingly. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions to inform the development of more principled and scalable safety mechanisms for multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically analyzes emerging safety threats in multi-modal large language models (MLLMs), proposing a multimodal-grounded taxonomy of threats and organizing safety strategies in response to the unique risks arising from cross-modal integration and fusion.
AI.motivation: The architectural shift from uni-modal to multimodal LLMs introduces novel safety threats—such as compromised modality integration, modality misalignment, and fused safety risks—that are not adequately captured by existing uni-modal safety frameworks. A systematic understanding of this evolving safety landscape is urgently needed.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic survey organized around: (1) a proposed multimodal-grounded taxonomy of safety threats; (2) analysis of shifts in threat models including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, jailbreaks, and hallucinations; (3) summarization of updated safety assumptions; and (4) organization of recent advances in MLLM safety strategies.
AI.result: The survey reveals that cross-modal interactions fundamentally reshape the threat landscape, giving rise to novel attack vectors and imposing new constraints on defense mechanisms. It categorizes existing safety strategies under revised assumptions and identifies open challenges for scalable, principled safety mechanisms in multimodal systems.
AI.conclusion: MLLM safety requires rethinking beyond uni-modal paradigms. The paper calls for more principled and scalable safety mechanisms that account for the unique vulnerabilities introduced by modality alignment and fusion, and outlines future research directions to address these open challenges.

title: Determinization in Structure Theories: A Unified Framework via Closure, Comparability, and Joint Admissibility
comment: Formal framework paper on canonicalization and determinization in structure theories; version v2.16.4; 29 pages
summary:
We develop a formal framework for constructing canonical interpretations from plural structure theories. A structure theory is a triple T = (Σ, A, I) consisting of a signature, axioms, and an inference policy, whose admissible interpretation family collects all globally consistent assignments of structural conclusions.
  We distinguish three levels of canonicalization: closure stabilization (per-seed convergence), global completion (seed-independent convergence), and determinization (a unique admissible interpretation). Non-determinism is classified into epistemic plurality (Type E) and structural plurality (Type S), with a refined Type S-strong subclass characterized by the absence of common upper bounds.
  Two canonicalization mechanisms arise: operator-based completion and selector-based construction. We provide sufficient structural conditions under which these mechanisms exist, and show that pure inference-based completion reduces to a saturated closure operator under positive, non-retractive rules with an additional soundness condition. For Type E theories, closure stabilization is established, while full determinization depends on a global confluence property that remains open. For Type S-strong theories, determinization is achieved via canonical selection.
  We further show that multi-level canonicalization forms a structurally non-commutative system via staged operators, and provide a conditional classification theorem reducing theory-intrinsic mechanisms to closure or selection. The framework also applies to LLM-assisted reasoning, where hallucination can be viewed as unsupported canonicalization.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a formal framework for constructing canonical (unique, stabilized) interpretations from "structure theories" — triples of signature, axioms, and inference policy. It classifies non-determinism into epistemic (Type E) and structural (Type S) plurality, with a strong subclass, and shows how closure-based and selector-based mechanisms achieve varying degrees of canonicalization under different structural conditions.
AI.motivation: Interpretation of pluralistic or non-deterministic theories often lacks a principled way to converge on a single canonical result. The authors aim to formalize when and how canonical interpretations can be systematically derived, distinguishing different sources of non-determinism and the mechanisms (closure vs. selection) that resolve them.
AI.method: The framework defines a structure theory as a triple (Σ, A, I). Admissible interpretations are globally consistent assignments. Three levels of canonicalization are defined: closure stabilization, global completion, and determinization. Non-determinism is taxonomized into Type E (epistemic) and Type S (structural, with a strong variant lacking common upper bounds). Two mechanisms — operator-based completion and selector-based construction — are analyzed with sufficient structural conditions. Multi-level canonicalization is modeled via staged, non-commutative operators, yielding a conditional classification theorem.
AI.result: For Type E theories, closure stabilization holds, but full determinization remains contingent on an open global confluence property. For Type S-strong theories, determinization is achieved via canonical selection. Pure inference-based completion reduces to a saturated closure operator under positive, non-retractive rules with a soundness condition. Multi-level canonicalization forms a structurally non-commutative system.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous classification of non-determinism in structure theories and identifies precise structural conditions under which canonical interpretations can be constructed. It bridges abstract canonicalization theory with practical concerns, including LLM hallucination framed as unsupported canonicalization.

title: A Symbolic Machine Learning Approach for Cybersickness Potential-Cause Estimation
summary: Virtual reality (VR) and head-mounted displays are constantly gaining popularity in various fields such as education, military, entertainment, and bio/medical informatics. Although such technologies provide a high sense of immersion, they can also trigger symptoms of discomfort. This condition is called cybersickness (CS) and is quite popular in recent publications in the virtual reality context. This work proposes a novel experimental analysis using symbolic machine learning that ranks potential causes for CS. We estimate the CS causes and rank them according to their impact on the classification capabilities of CS. The experiments are performed using two distinct virtual reality games. We were able to identify that acceleration triggered cybersickness more frequently in a race game in contrast to a flight game. Furthermore, participants less experienced with VR are more prone to feel discomfort and this variable has a greater impact in the race game in contrast to the flight game, where the acceleration is not controlled by the user.

AI.tldr: This paper uses symbolic machine learning to rank the causes of cybersickness (CS) in VR, finding that acceleration is the dominant trigger in a race game versus a flight game, and that VR inexperience significantly increases discomfort, especially when the user controls acceleration.
AI.motivation: VR and HMDs are widely adopted but frequently induce cybersickness (CS), a discomfort condition. The authors aim to move beyond merely detecting CS to systematically identifying and ranking its causal factors, enabling better mitigation strategies.
AI.method: A novel experimental analysis employing symbolic machine learning is proposed. CS causes are estimated and ranked by their impact on classification performance. Experiments are conducted using two distinct VR games (a race game and a flight game) to compare causal factor salience across different interaction paradigms.
AI.result: Acceleration triggers CS more frequently in the race game than the flight game. VR inexperience is a significant predictor of discomfort, with greater impact in the race game where the user controls acceleration, compared to the flight game.
AI.conclusion: Cybersickness causation is context-dependent: the same factor (acceleration) varies in its CS-inducing impact based on the type of VR experience and user agency. User experience level also modulates susceptibility differently across game types.

title: The Anatomy of a Prompt Injection: A Component Model for Structured Analysis
summary: Four years after prompt injection was first identified in 2022, attacks are still predominantly documented as verbatim strings rather than structured exploits, despite advancing agent capabilities and threat actors embedding injections to subvert AI-assisted security analysis. This paper formalizes the structure of prompt-injection artifacts, enabling defenders, red teamers, and cyber threat intelligence (CTI) teams to label, compare, and mutate attacks without relying on fragile string matching. Because large language models compile varied natural-language realizations into identical executable actions, labeling must track attacker intent (tool targets, sinks, and effects) rather than surface wording. We propose a seven-component model (carrier, delivery vector, concealment, context-break, privilege escalation, payload, and return channel) consisting of five artifact fields and two environment fields. This framework unifies roles partially addressed by HOUYI's payload decomposition, the Promptware Kill Chain, and campaign taxonomies, while framing minimal jailbreak frameworks like ReNeLLM as projections onto a restricted subspace. We provide clear labeling rules, a logical analysis record mapping directly to industry CTI schemas, worked examples including EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) and an in-the-wild malware AI-evasion sample, and an illustrative agentic flowchart.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes prompt injection attacks as structured artifacts using a seven-component model, moving beyond brittle string-matching to track attacker intent, with labeling rules mapped to industry CTI schemas and validated against real-world examples like EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711).
AI.motivation: Despite prompt injection being known since 2022, attacks remain documented as verbatim strings rather than structured exploits, making defense, comparison, and mutation fragile. With advancing agent capabilities and threat actors embedding injections to subvert AI-assisted security analysis, a formal structure that tracks attacker intent—rather than surface wording—is urgently needed.
AI.method: The authors propose a seven-component model comprising five artifact fields (carrier, delivery vector, concealment, context-break, privilege escalation) and two environment fields (payload and return channel). This framework unifies elements from HOUYI's payload decomposition, the Promptware Kill Chain, and campaign taxonomies, with minimal jailbreak frameworks like ReNeLLM treated as projections onto a restricted subspace. Labeling rules and a logical analysis record are provided, mapped to industry CTI schemas, and demonstrated through worked examples.
AI.result: The framework successfully labels and structures real-world attacks including EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) and an in-the-wild malware AI-evasion sample. An illustrative agentic flowchart demonstrates practical applicability for defenders, red teamers, and CTI teams.
AI.conclusion: Structured, intent-based labeling of prompt injection artifacts enables robust attack comparison, mutation, and defense that string-matching cannot provide. The seven-component model bridges gaps between existing frameworks and operational CTI workflows, offering a foundation for systematic prompt injection threat intelligence.

title: Search over the Visual World: Persistent Visual Memory, Layered Indexes, and Source-Grounded Evidence
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 17 tables. Technical report. Benchmark configurations and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/video-db/search-over-the-visual-world
summary: Most video-retrieval systems assume a bounded corpus and return ranked files or timestamps. Agents operating over cameras, screens, streams, and archives face a different systems problem: observations arrive continuously; models interpret them at different temporal granularities; context must be selected without replaying the complete visual record; and results must stay connected to inspectable source evidence. We argue that search over such a corpus is an infrastructure problem that cannot be reduced to ranking video files. We develop a conceptual and formal model of search over the visual world built on analyzer-defined scenes, persistent understanding artifacts, visual memory as coexisting scene spaces over shared source time, and capability-declared indexes, distinguishing memory (everything retained), context (what is selected for a task), and evidence (the source intervals that ground it). The VideoDB data format (VDB) realizes this model in production, exposed through a typed search surface spanning planned retrieval, stateful investigation, direct access, and grounded synthesis. We contrast this model-agnostic infrastructure, where segmentation, sampling, model choice, embeddings, and ranking are system decisions and live streams are first-class sources, with video-native foundation models offered as fixed APIs. In a semantic-retrieval comparison against a commercial video-native engine spanning 9,800+ queries over four public datasets, a pipeline of general-purpose components achieves higher macro-averaged Recall@1/@3/@10 (73.09/83.39/91.20 versus 65.75/77.13/89.10), while the baseline is higher at Recall@50 (96.42 versus 96.07). Retrieval quality over the visual world is today governed more by system design than by video-specific pretraining, and visual-memory infrastructure can deliver it while keeping playable, source-grounded evidence first-class.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that video retrieval over continuous, unbounded visual streams is fundamentally an infrastructure problem rather than a ranking problem. It introduces a conceptual model based on scenes, visual memory, and grounded evidence, implemented as the VideoDB (VDB) format. Empirical results show that a general-purpose pipeline built on this infrastructure outperforms a commercial video-native foundation model on Recall@1/3/10 across 9,800+ queries, suggesting system design matters more than video-specific pretraining for visual-world retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing video-retrieval systems assume a bounded, static corpus and return ranked files or timestamps. Real-world agents operating over live cameras, screens, streams, and archives face a different problem: continuous observation ingestion, heterogeneous model granularities, the need to select context without replaying everything, and the requirement that results remain traceable to inspectable source evidence. The authors argue this cannot be reduced to ranking video files and requires rethinking retrieval as an infrastructure problem.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual and formal model of visual-world search built on several key constructs: (1) analyzer-defined scenes, (2) persistent understanding artifacts, (3) visual memory as coexisting scene spaces over shared source time, and (4) capability-declared indexes. It distinguishes memory (everything retained), context (what is selected for a task), and evidence (the source intervals that ground it). This model is realized in the VideoDB (VDB) data format, exposed through a typed search surface supporting planned retrieval, stateful investigation, direct access, and grounded synthesis. The approach is model-agnostic: segmentation, sampling, model choice, embeddings, and ranking are system-level decisions, and live streams are treated as first-class sources. For evaluation, a general-purpose component pipeline is compared against a commercial video-native foundation model on 9,800+ queries across four public datasets.
AI.result: The general-purpose pipeline achieves higher macro-averaged Recall@1 (73.09 vs. 65.75), Recall@3 (83.39 vs. 77.13), and Recall@10 (91.20 vs. 89.10). The commercial video-native engine scores higher only at Recall@50 (96.42 vs. 96.07). The authors conclude that retrieval quality over the visual world is governed more by system design than by video-specific pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Visual-memory infrastructure can deliver superior retrieval quality at practical recall thresholds while preserving playable, source-grounded evidence as a first-class citizen. The results challenge the assumption that video-native foundation models are necessary for high-quality video retrieval, suggesting that investments in system architecture — segmentation, indexing, and context management — yield greater returns.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Urban Traffic Management via Spatio-Temporal Mobility Profile Planning
summary: As modern cities face increasingly severe traffic congestion, connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) have emerged as a crucial enabling technology for next-generation intelligent traffic management. However, fully realizing this potential is hindered by the limitations of current paradigms. Existing approaches typically optimize localized interactions rather than system-wide efficiency, incur severe communication overhead, or lack the deterministic guarantees required for safe kinematic execution. Furthermore, current multi-agent adaptations are frequently restricted to small predefined scenarios, failing to scale across large and complex urban networks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces VeloCity, a decentralized multi-agent spatio-temporal mobility profile planning framework designed for CAVs operating in arbitrary urban areas. To minimize vehicles' travel times, VeloCity distributes mobility profile optimization directly to individual CAVs. Vehicles query a localized traffic coordinator for a reservation table, independently compute their fastest conflict-free mobility profile, and reserve their requested space-time slots back with the coordinator. By natively adapting to any arbitrary road topology, the framework manages highly irregular urban areas without requiring scenario-specific tuning, all while guaranteeing collision-free and physically executable vehicle trajectories. Extensive simulations across four large-scale real-world urban maps (Tokyo, Manhattan, Rome, and Bologna) demonstrate the framework's scalability. Compared to established state-of-the-art models, VeloCity yields drastically lower travel times, tightly bounds delay variance, and successfully prevents congestion gridlocks even under extremely high vehicular densities.

AI.tldr: VeloCity is a decentralized multi-agent framework for CAVs that distributes mobility profile optimization to individual vehicles using a reservation-table mechanism. It scales to arbitrary urban topologies, guarantees collision-free trajectories, and across four major city maps demonstrates drastically lower travel times, bounded delay variance, and prevention of congestion gridlocks compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Current CAV traffic management paradigms suffer from three key shortcomings: (1) they optimize only localized interactions rather than system-wide efficiency, (2) they incur severe communication overhead, and (3) they lack deterministic safety guarantees for kinematic execution. Additionally, multi-agent approaches fail to scale beyond small predefined scenarios to large, complex urban networks. A framework is needed that simultaneously achieves system-level optimization, low communication cost, deterministic safety, and scalability to arbitrary road topologies.
AI.method: VeloCity is a decentralized multi-agent spatio-temporal mobility profile planning framework. Each CAV independently queries a localized traffic coordinator to obtain a reservation table, computes its fastest conflict-free mobility profile (space-time trajectory), and reserves those slots back with the coordinator. The framework natively adapts to arbitrary road topologies without scenario-specific tuning and guarantees collision-free, physically executable trajectories.
AI.result: Extensive simulations on four large-scale real-world urban maps (Tokyo, Manhattan, Rome, Bologna) demonstrate VeloCity's scalability. Compared to state-of-the-art models, it achieves drastically lower travel times, tightly bounds delay variance, and prevents congestion gridlocks even under extremely high vehicular densities.
AI.conclusion: VeloCity bridges the gap between decentralized decision-making and system-wide traffic efficiency, offering a scalable, safe, and communication-efficient solution for coordinating CAVs across large, irregular urban networks.

title: Stateful Multi-Agent LLMs for Cross-View Interface Alignment in Automotive Model-Based Systems Engineering
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) can accelerate Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) for software-defined vehicles, their probabilistic nature causes "architectural drift", fabricating interfaces in behavioral views that lack structural foundations. To enforce deterministic interface alignment, we propose a stateful, multi-agent validation pipeline. The framework utilizes a sequential generation matrix (Class->Activity->Sequence) and Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS)-grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). An independent AI Validator Agent dynamically audits outputs against a strict error taxonomy, triggering state-preserving backtracking loops to resolve incompatibilities. Evaluated on an Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) scenario, standard RAG yielded 0% Entity Traceability. Conversely, our multi-agent workflow eradicated cross-phase hallucinations, achieving 97% Entity Traceability, 87% Signal Conservation, and an 85% F1-score. This proves adversarial auditing enables LLMs to reliably synthesize zero-error MBSE architectures.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent validation pipeline with adversarial auditing eliminates architectural drift in LLM-generated MBSE models, achieving 97% entity traceability versus 0% for standard RAG.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for MBSE in software-defined vehicles suffer from "architectural drift"—hallucinating interfaces in behavioral views (activity, sequence diagrams) that have no corresponding structural foundation (class diagrams). This breaks traceability and consistency across SysML/UML views, rendering LLM-generated architectures unreliable for safety-critical automotive systems.
AI.method: A stateful, multi-agent validation pipeline featuring: (1) a sequential generation matrix enforcing Class→Activity→Sequence diagram ordering; (2) VSS-grounded RAG to anchor outputs in the Vehicle Signal Specification ontology; (3) an independent AI Validator Agent that audits outputs using a strict error taxonomy; and (4) state-preserving backtracking loops that re-trigger generation upon detecting incompatibilities without losing prior valid state.
AI.result: Standard RAG achieved 0% Entity Traceability. The proposed multi-agent pipeline achieved 97% Entity Traceability, 87% Signal Conservation, and an 85% F1-score on an ADAS case study, effectively eliminating cross-phase hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial auditing with stateful backtracking enables LLMs to synthesize zero-error MBSE architectures, proving that deterministic interface alignment is achievable when generation is coupled with independent validation and domain-grounded retrieval.

title: Search-G1: Grounded Search Agents via Representation-Based Intrinsic Rewards
summary: Search-augmented language agents should retrieve external information only when necessary and ground their answers in retrieved evidence. Existing external rewards provide either sparse outcome supervision or richer feedback from process annotations and LLM judges. Outcome rewards scale readily but cannot distinguish grounded retrieval from redundant search, whereas richer signals require costly annotation or inference during training. Internal rewards based on policy-side signals such as entropy, likelihood, or information gain are graded and inexpensive to evaluate, yet mainly reflect model confidence rather than evidence grounding. We propose Search-G1, a representation-based intrinsic reward framework that measures the operational grounding of an agent's answers through two intervention-calibrated readouts. A prompt-state readout predicts closed-book sufficiency, whose complement defines policy-relative retrieval necessity; an answer-commit readout estimates evidence reliance from answer-stage sensitivity to evidence deletion. Together, they provide additional credit to correct searched trajectories when retrieval is estimated necessary and the answer is evidence-sensitive, favor correct direct answers when closed-book knowledge suffices, and penalize repeated search. After calibration, reward scoring requires neither process annotations nor LLM-as-judge inference during policy optimization. Because reinforcement learning changes policy representations, Search-G1 periodically refits both readouts on trajectories from the latest checkpoint, allowing the reward to co-evolve with the policy. Experiments across multiple search-based question-answering benchmarks and two model scales show that Search-G1 improves the grounding--search-cost trade-off, producing shorter response-side trajectories at competitive task accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/Rosy0912/Search-G1.

AI.tldr: Search-G1 is an intrinsic reward framework for training search-augmented language agents that uses representation-based readouts to measure retrieval necessity and evidence reliance, eliminating the need for process annotations or LLM judges during reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for training retrieval-augmented agents suffer from a trade-off: sparse outcome rewards scale well but cannot distinguish necessary retrieval from redundant search, while richer process-based rewards require costly annotations or LLM inference. Internal signals like entropy are cheap but only reflect model confidence, not evidence grounding. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a reward that explicitly measures grounded retrieval without annotation overhead.
AI.method: Search-G1 introduces two intervention-calibrated readouts derived from policy representations: (1) a prompt-state readout that predicts closed-book sufficiency, whose complement defines retrieval necessity; (2) an answer-commit readout that estimates evidence reliance by measuring answer-stage sensitivity to evidence deletion. These provide credit to correct trajectories when retrieval is necessary and the answer is evidence-sensitive, favor correct closed-book answers when knowledge suffices, and penalize redundant search. The readouts are periodically refitted on trajectories from the latest checkpoint so the reward co-evolves with the policy during RL.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple search-based QA benchmarks and two model scales show Search-G1 improves the grounding--search-cost trade-off, achieving competitive task accuracy with shorter, more efficient search trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Search-G1 provides an effective, annotation-free intrinsic reward that enables search-augmented agents to learn when to retrieve and how to ground answers in evidence, yielding more efficient and trustworthy retrieval behavior.

title: Tracing sources of epistemic uncertainty in deep learning predictions: homo- and hetero-scedastic linearized estimators
summary: We adapt two classical statistical estimators for quantifying uncertainty to modern deep learning, in order to provide clearer insights into uncertainty attributable to two sources : aleatoric uncertainty, or locally scarce data. Our approach leverages recent advances in approximate Fisher Information Matrices, to enable scaling to actual architectures. Experimental results demonstrate how each test points is differentially impacted by both sources, highlighting the practical utility of our estimators in improving the robustness of real-world applications.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts two classical statistical estimators using approximate Fisher Information Matrices to quantify both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in deep learning models, enabling scalable uncertainty decomposition for modern architectures.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models often lack interpretable uncertainty estimates. Existing methods fail to cleanly separate aleatoric uncertainty (inherent data noise) from epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty due to scarce data) in a manner that scales to modern deep architectures. The authors aim to bridge this gap by resurrecting classical statistical estimators.
AI.method: The authors adapt two classical statistical uncertainty estimators and scale them to deep neural networks using recent advances in approximate Fisher Information Matrices (FIM). This allows efficient computation of uncertainty decomposition at the per-test-point level, distinguishing between aleatoric and epistemic sources.
AI.result: Experimental results show that each test point is differentially affected by both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, demonstrating that the proposed estimators effectively disentangle the two sources and provide actionable, instance-level uncertainty insights.
AI.conclusion: The adapted classical estimators, enabled by approximate FIM scaling, offer a practical and interpretable framework for uncertainty quantification in deep learning, with potential to improve robustness in real-world applications.

title: Emotion in an active inference model of human driving
summary: Active inference has emerged as a principled framework for modeling adaptive behavior by balancing goal-directed action with uncertainty reduction. It has been successfully applied across biological and artificial systems, including recent work on human driving. However, existing active inference models of driving have yet to address an important determinant of behavior in traffic: affective state, which significantly influences decision-making. Prior work in non-traffic domains has explored active inference agents in which emotions are represented along the axes of valence and arousal in the circumplex model. However, this work has been limited to simplified settings with discrete state spaces. In this work, we propose an expanded formulation of valence and arousal that can be extracted from a more complex active inference model of driving with continuous states. In particular, we condition affective estimates not only on the current state but also on predicted future outcomes. We evaluate the proposed approach in two interactive driving scenarios and show that the resulting emotion signals correspond to affective patterns reported in similar scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper extends active inference models of driving by incorporating affective states (valence and arousal) derived from continuous state spaces, conditioning them on both current states and predicted future outcomes, and validating the approach in interactive driving scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing active inference models of driving ignore affective state, a key determinant of traffic behavior. Prior work combining active inference with emotion (via the circumplex model of valence/arousal) has been limited to discrete state spaces and simplified settings, leaving a gap for richer, continuous driving environments.
AI.method: The authors propose an expanded formulation of valence and arousal extracted from a continuous-state active inference driving model. Affective estimates are conditioned on both the current state and predicted future outcomes, enabling richer emotional inference. The approach is evaluated in two interactive driving scenarios.
AI.result: The resulting emotion signals correspond to affective patterns reported in similar driving scenarios, suggesting the model successfully captures context-appropriate emotional dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed continuous-state affective active inference model effectively generates plausible emotion signals in driving contexts, bridging a gap between affect modeling and real-world adaptive behavior under the active inference framework.

title: SafeStudent Driving: A Multimodal Driver-Safety System to Support Teen Drivers Using Computer Vision and Mobile Sensing
summary:
Teen drivers face disproportionately high crash rates, often due to inexperience and inconsistent attention to basic traffic rules. SafeStudent Driving addresses this problem with a multimodal coaching system deployed on both a Raspberry Pi device and a Flutter-based mobile app. The system uses three YOLO-based computer-vision models to detect traffic lights, light-bulb colors, and road signs, an OCR module to read speed-limit values, and an audio model plus IMU data to infer whether turn signals are used during turns. An analysis layer smooths detections over time and triggers prioritized voice prompts through text-to-speech or pre-recorded audio.
  Key challenges included achieving sufficient model accuracy in varied lighting, running inference fast enough on limited hardware, and designing prompts that inform without distracting the driver [3]. Experiments on sign detection and turn-signal recognition highlight strengths and failure modes, guiding future improvements. Overall, the project demonstrates a practical, low-cost way to help novice drivers build safer habits in real traffic.

AI.tldr: A low-cost, multimodal coaching system using computer vision, OCR, and audio/IMU models on Raspberry Pi and a mobile app to help teen drivers build safer habits by detecting traffic elements and providing real-time voice prompts.
AI.motivation: Teen drivers have disproportionately high crash rates due to inexperience and inconsistent attention to traffic rules. There is a need for a practical, affordable in-vehicle coaching solution that provides real-time feedback without distracting the driver.
AI.method: A multimodal coaching system deployed on a Raspberry Pi device and a Flutter mobile app. It employs three YOLO-based models (traffic lights, bulb colors, road signs), an OCR module for speed-limit reading, and an audio model combined with IMU data to infer turn-signal usage. An analysis layer smooths temporal detections and triggers prioritized voice prompts via TTS or pre-recorded audio.
AI.result: Experiments on sign detection and turn-signal recognition demonstrated both strengths and failure modes. Key challenges included maintaining model accuracy under varied lighting, meeting inference speed constraints on limited hardware, and designing informative yet non-distracting prompts.
AI.conclusion: The project demonstrates a practical, low-cost approach to helping novice drivers develop safer habits in real traffic, with identified failure modes guiding future improvements.

title: China RealDID: Verifiable Credentials Anchored in Legal Identity
summary: Verifiable credentials (VCs) and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) enable selective disclosure but lack legal anchoring: without a trusted identity root, verifiers cannot distinguish a genuine holder from a fabricated identity. State identity systems provide biometric-grounded verification but impose three costs: verifiers must collect subjects' full personally identifiable information, infrastructure concentrates on a single API, and the state observes every transaction. We present China RealDID, a three-layer architecture -- CTID (centralized legal identity), RealDID (decentralized anchor on an open permissioned blockchain), and VCs with SD-JWT-based selective disclosure -- evaluated against five adversary classes and six security goals. The central mechanism is a content-blind government relay: the state authenticates participants and counter-signs every credential but cannot read the payload, encrypted by the issuer to the holder's public key. We describe the VC lifecycle, triple-signature chain, open template registry, and the architecture's metadata-level privacy limits, including the credential graph at the relay and presentation linkability from single-DID reuse. The design yields an asymmetric, state-bounded trust model: the state cannot impersonate or read contents; the user cannot fabricate identity or evade metadata observation. We analyze alignment with China's Personal Information Protection Law and the EU's GDPR, including the tension between immutable registries and erasure rights, and discuss generalizability through cross-border deployments with Singapore and Hong Kong.

AI.tldr: China RealDID proposes a three-layer architecture (CTID, RealDID, VCs) that combines state-verified biometric identity with decentralized verifiable credentials using a content-blind government relay. The state authenticates and counter-signs credentials without reading their encrypted payload, creating an asymmetric trust model where the state can observe metadata but cannot impersonate users or access content, while users cannot fabricate identity.
AI.motivation: Verifiable credentials and DIDs enable selective disclosure but lack a trusted legal identity root, allowing fabricated identities. State identity systems offer biometric verification but impose three costs: full PII collection by verifiers, single-API infrastructure concentration, and complete state surveillance of every transaction. RealDID aims to reconcile these tensions — providing legally grounded identity without requiring the state to read credential contents or verifiers to collect full PII.
AI.method: A three-layer architecture: (1) CTID — China's centralized legal identity system providing biometric-grounded authentication; (2) RealDID — a decentralized identity anchor on an open permissioned blockchain; (3) VCs with SD-JWT-based selective disclosure. The core innovation is a content-blind government relay where the state counter-signs every credential but cannot read its payload, which is encrypted by the issuer to the holder's public key. The design uses a triple-signature chain (issuer, state relay, holder) and an open template registry. Security is evaluated against five adversary classes and six security goals.
AI.result: The architecture yields an asymmetric, state-bounded trust model: the state cannot impersonate users or read credential contents; users cannot fabricate identity or evade metadata observation. The design aligns with China's Personal Information Protection Law and the EU's GDPR, though immutable blockchain registries create tension with erasure rights. Cross-border deployments with Singapore and Hong Kong demonstrate generalizability.
AI.conclusion: RealDID demonstrates that legal anchoring and selective disclosure are not mutually exclusive when mediated by a content-blind relay. The architecture provides a practical model for state-bound decentralized identity, though metadata-level privacy limits — credential graph visibility at the relay and linkability from single-DID reuse — remain acknowledged residual risks requiring further attention.

title: DS@GT ARC at Touché: Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Debate
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in the CLEF 2026 Best of Labs proceedings
summary: We extend the DS@GT ARC working-note submission to the Touché 2025 Retrieval-Augmented Debate task. The task has two subtasks: generating the next utterance in a simulated debate, and evaluating debate responses according to the Gricean maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner. The DS@GT ARC submission consisted of six leading LLMs from three providers through a retrieval-augmented prompting pipeline. We summarize the results from the working paper and explore whether multi-LLM evaluator agreement is a reliable proxy for official evaluation performance. The analysis shows that frontier LLM systems are strong response generators, and as evaluators they agree strongly within model families. However this consensus does not reliably track the official evaluation target, with the largest gap on the Quality maxim. The accompanying source code for this paper is located at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/touche-2025-rad and https://github.com/dsgt-arc/touche-2025-rad-analysis.

AI.tldr: An extension of the DS@GT ARC submission for Touché 2025's Retrieval-Augmented Debate task, investigating whether multi-LLM evaluator agreement serves as a reliable proxy for official evaluation performance. The study finds that while frontier LLMs generate strong debate responses and exhibit high intra-family agreement as evaluators, this consensus does not reliably correlate with official evaluation scores — particularly on the Quality maxim.
AI.motivation: To assess whether agreement among multiple LLM-based evaluators can serve as a dependable proxy for official human-judged evaluation performance in the Retrieval-Augmented Debate task, thereby exploring the limits of LLM-as-judge reliability.
AI.method: The authors employ six frontier LLMs from three providers in a retrieval-augmented prompting pipeline. These models serve dual roles: generating debate utterances and evaluating responses according to the four Gricean maxims (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner). The analysis compares inter-evaluator agreement patterns against official evaluation scores to determine alignment.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs perform strongly as debate response generators. As evaluators, they exhibit strong agreement within model families (same provider), but this within-family consensus does not reliably track the official evaluation target. The largest divergence occurs on the Quality maxim.
AI.conclusion: High multi-LLM evaluator agreement, particularly within model families, is an unreliable proxy for official evaluation performance. Caution is warranted when using LLM consensus as a substitute for human evaluation, especially for nuanced criteria like the Gricean maxim of Quality.

title: AOC-CBS: Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search for Generalised Multi-Agent Path Finding
summary: Many research fields share a common structure: a set of agents, each pursuing its own goal, whose actions must be coordinated so that no two of them conflict. Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is a concrete instance of this structure, with applications from warehouses to road traffic and airports. Much of MAPF research assumes discrete time, circular agents sharing one spatial graph, a single goal per agent, and that an agent must remain at its goal once reached, precluding heterogeneous fleets, non-geometric conflicts, task sequences, and agents that move on after completing them. We generalise the MAPF formulation to lift these assumptions, and present Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search (AOC-CBS), an exact and solution-complete solver for it. AOC-CBS guarantees the eventual return of an optimal solution, while reporting an incumbent with a known optimality gap upper bound throughout its runtime; it is configurable with a portfolio of repair functions, one of which we introduce (Tier-Prioritized Safe Interval Path Planning), and can exploit multiple processor cores. We demonstrate AOC-CBS on a mixed fleet of non-convex agents moving along smooth, kinodynamically feasible trajectories. Preliminary experiments against the exact solver OC-CBS, on well-known benchmarks and roadmaps we sample from them, show AOC-CBS is comparable at finding optimal solutions while extending scalability from the tens to the hundreds of agents when a bounded optimality gap is accepted.

AI.tldr: AOC-CBS generalizes Multi-Agent Path Finding beyond discrete-time, circular agents on a shared graph to handle heterogeneous fleets, non-geometric conflicts, task sequences, and continuous-time kinodynamic trajectories, while providing anytime-optimal solutions with known optimality gap bounds.
AI.motivation: Classical MAPF formulations make restrictive assumptions: discrete time steps, circular agents sharing one spatial graph, single goals per agent, and agents remaining stationary at goals. These preclude real-world needs like heterogeneous vehicle fleets, non-geometric conflicts (e.g., communication interference), sequential tasks, and agents that continue moving after task completion. The paper aims to lift all these assumptions within a unified, exact solver framework.
AI.method: The authors propose Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search (AOC-CBS), an exact, solution-complete solver for the generalized MAPF formulation. It uses a portfolio of repair functions — including a novel Tier-Prioritized Safe Interval Path Planning (TP-SIPP) — and supports multi-core parallelization. AOC-CBS guarantees eventual return of an optimal solution while continuously providing an incumbent solution with a provable upper bound on the optimality gap.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments on well-known benchmarks (with sampled roadmaps) compare AOC-CBS against the exact solver OC-CBS. AOC-CBS shows comparable performance in finding optimal solutions while scaling from tens to hundreds of agents when a bounded optimality gap is acceptable.
AI.conclusion: AOC-CBS successfully generalizes MAPF to a broader class of coordination problems, maintains exact solution guarantees, and achieves significantly better scalability through its anytime-optimal framework, making it applicable to real-world multi-agent coordination scenarios with heterogeneous, non-convex agents and complex constraints.

title: HugSelect: An Explainable Multi-Criteria Decision-Support Framework for foundation-model selection
comment: Pages: 29, Figures: 5. Corresponding authors: Alireza Joonbakhsh (alireza.joonbakhsh@hafez.shirazu.ac.ir) and Siamak Farshidi (siamak.farshidi@wur.nl)
summary:
Foundation models are increasingly reused as software components, making model selection a critical software-engineering decision. Current model hubs primarily support discovery through popularity metrics, often neglecting functional capabilities, operational constraints, and community-perceived quality. We argue that foundation-model selection should be treated as an explicit, auditable software-component selection task rather than as keyword search, popularity ranking, or opaque conversational advice.
  This paper proposes HugSelect, an explainable decision-support framework for foundation-model selection. HugSelect builds a knowledge base of 71,274 models by combining repository metadata, extracted functional capabilities, and perceived quality attributes derived from community discussions into a unified pipeline. It ranks candidate models using a weighted additive model that exposes criterion-level score decompositions.
  We evaluated HugSelect through pipeline validation, comparative case studies against four commercial LLM-based recommendation systems (44 scenarios), fine-grained ablation, and an exploratory user study (n = 10). Extraction pipelines achieved an F1 score of 0.801 for functional features and an accuracy of 0.84 for quality-attribute mapping. HugSelect achieved a model-level Coverage@10 of 0.61 and family-level Coverage@10 of 0.91, showing recommendation quality comparable to that of the evaluated commercial systems, with no significant overall differences in ranking quality, while providing stable, traceable, and inspectable reasoning. Ablation confirmed that functional features were the main driver of retrieval accuracy, and preliminary user feedback suggests that the framework is useful and intuitive.

AI.tldr: HugSelect is an explainable decision-support framework for foundation-model selection that builds a knowledge base from repository metadata, functional capabilities, and community-perceived quality to rank models with transparent criterion-level reasoning, achieving performance comparable to commercial LLM-based recommenders.
AI.motivation: Current model hubs (e.g., Hugging Face) rely on popularity metrics for model discovery, neglecting functional capabilities, operational constraints, and community-perceived quality. Foundation-model selection should be treated as an explicit, auditable software-component selection task rather than keyword search or opaque conversational advice.
AI.method: HugSelect constructs a knowledge base of 71,274 models by integrating repository metadata, extracted functional capabilities (via NLP pipelines, F1=0.801), and quality attributes from community discussions (accuracy=0.84). It ranks candidates using a weighted additive model that exposes criterion-level score decompositions for explainability. Evaluation included comparative case studies against four commercial LLM recommenders (44 scenarios), ablation studies, and a user study (n=10).
AI.result: HugSelect achieved model-level Coverage@10 of 0.61 and family-level Coverage@10 of 0.91, with recommendation quality comparable to commercial LLM-based systems and no significant differences in ranking quality. Ablation confirmed functional features as the primary driver of retrieval accuracy. User feedback indicated the framework is useful and intuitive.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model selection benefits from being framed as an auditable software-component selection problem. HugSelect demonstrates that combining extracted functional capabilities with community quality signals yields competitive, transparent, and traceable recommendations, offering a viable alternative to opaque commercial recommenders.

title: Scaling Inherently Interpretable Language Models
summary:
Interpretability is often treated as a tax on capability: language models are trained as opaque systems, then explained after the fact, with methods whose reliability is difficult to establish. In this work, we challenge this premise. Rather than reverse-engineering a model, we make interpretability a constraint of the training pipeline, optimized alongside the language modeling objective. Across three orders of magnitude of compute, on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, interpretability scales with capability rather than against it. Surprisingly, model representations become more disentangled and aligned with human-understandable concepts with scale.
  We instantiate the training-time recipe with Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model with a causal attention mask. For any group of generated tokens, Steerling-8B attributes the output to relevant input tokens, human-understandable concepts, and training data. This enables closed-loop intervention: diagnose an output through its concept or feature attribution, retrieve similar training data, and correct the behavior through concept steering without retraining. Steerling-8B remains competitive with open peer models trained on substantially 2-16x more compute, suggesting a different scaling paradigm: interpretability can be designed into training, and it improves with scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes training language models with interpretability baked into the objective rather than applied post-hoc, showing that interpretability scales with capability. They instantiate this via Steerling-8B, a diffusion LM enabling attribution, concept steering, and training-data retrieval without retraining.
AI.motivation: Interpretability is traditionally treated as an afterthought — models are trained opaquely and then explained using unreliable post-hoc methods. The authors challenge this premise, arguing that interpretability should be a first-class training constraint rather than a tax on capability.
AI.method: The authors design a training pipeline where interpretability is optimized jointly with the language modeling objective. They instantiate this recipe with Steerling-8B, a diffusion language model using a causal attention mask. The model attributes generated token groups to relevant input tokens, human-understandable concepts, and training data. This enables closed-loop intervention: diagnose outputs via concept/feature attribution, retrieve similar training data, and steer concepts without retraining.
AI.result: Across three orders of magnitude of compute, on both autoregressive and diffusion LMs, interpretability scales with capability rather than against it. Model representations become more disentangled and aligned with human-understandable concepts as scale increases. Steerling-8B remains competitive with open peer models trained on 2–16× more compute.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability can be designed into training from the start and improves with scale, suggesting a fundamentally different scaling paradigm where capability and interpretability are not in tension but are mutually reinforcing.

title: SkillConsist: Detecting Inconsistencies in Agent Skills via Bidirectional Graph Alignment
summary: Agent Skills provide reusable capabilities to LLM agents. Agent Skill inconsistencies can expose undisclosed dangerous behavior or cause wrong Skill selection. Recent Agent Skill research has increasingly examined Agent Skill consistency detection. Existing methods evaluate behaviors or security-property graphs against predefined categories or declared scopes. More recently, PL-HCL uses an LLM-based model to learn consistency across metadata, instructions, and resources. However, declaration and implementation behavior can be mixed across text and code, and a concise declaration can correspond to multiple connected implementation steps. We present SkillConsist to address both challenges. An LLM separates declaration and implementation content into behavior records on the implementation and declaration sides, while static analysis supplements implementation records. These records form declaration and implementation behavior graphs, respectively. Starting from a behavior record on either side, bidirectional graph alignment searches the other graph for a candidate subgraph and expands it along behavior relations until it completely expresses the source-side behavior. Graph differencing identifies conflicts between aligned subgraphs and outputs the detection results. We construct a 633-Skill benchmark from ClawHub's 500 most-downloaded public Skills and 133 Skill-Inject packages. The benchmark contains 319 inconsistent and 314 consistent Skills and 442 localized inconsistency annotations. On this benchmark, SkillConsist achieves 86.85% precision, 89.03% recall, and 87.93% F1 for package-level detection, improving F1 over the best baseline by 20.43 percentage points. For localization, it achieves 67.60% precision, 58.14% recall, and 62.52% F1.

AI.tldr: SkillConsist detects inconsistencies between declared and implemented behaviors in LLM Agent Skills by constructing behavior graphs from both sides, performing bidirectional graph alignment, and identifying conflicts through graph differencing, achieving 87.93% F1 on a custom 633-Skill benchmark.
AI.motivation: Agent Skills can suffer from inconsistencies between their declared capabilities (metadata/instructions) and actual implementation (code/resources), which can hide dangerous behaviors or cause incorrect Skill selection. Existing methods either rely on rigid predefined categories or struggle with the mixed text-code nature of Skills where concise declarations map to multiple implementation steps.
AI.method: SkillConsist uses an LLM to extract behavior records separately from declaration and implementation content, supplemented by static analysis for implementation records. These records form declaration and implementation behavior graphs. Bidirectional graph alignment then searches for candidate subgraphs matching a source-side behavior record, expanding along behavior relations until full expression is achieved. Graph differencing identifies conflicts between aligned subgraphs to produce detection and localization results.
AI.result: On a 633-Skill benchmark (319 inconsistent, 314 consistent, with 442 localized inconsistency annotations), SkillConsist achieves package-level detection: 86.85% precision, 89.03% recall, 87.93% F1 (20.43 pp improvement over best baseline). For inconsistency localization: 67.60% precision, 58.14% recall, 62.52% F1.
AI.conclusion: SkillConsist effectively addresses the dual challenges of mixed text-code behavior specification and complex declaration-to-implementation mappings in Agent Skills, significantly outperforming existing consistency detection methods and providing both package-level and fine-grained localization of inconsistencies.

title: Training Variable Long Sequences with Data-Centric Parallel
summary: Training deep learning models on variable long sequences poses significant computational challenges. Existing methods force a difficult trade-off between efficiency and ease-of-use. Simple approaches use static configurations that cause workload imbalance low efficiency, while complex methods introduces significant complexity and code change for new models. To break this trade-off, we introduce Data-Centric Parallel (DCP). Its core principle is to let the data itself drive the runtime. It achieves this by dynamically adjusting direct runtime settings (e.g., parallel size, gradient accumulation, recomputation) based on each batch's sequence length. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves up to a 2.88$\times$ speedup on 32 H200 GPUs. Designed for generalization, it can be integrated into any model with 10 lines of code. We anticipate this simple yet effective approach will serve as a robust baseline and facilitate future advancements in distributed training for variable long sequences.

AI.tldr: Data-Centric Parallel (DCP) dynamically adjusts runtime settings (parallel size, gradient accumulation, recomputation) based on per-batch sequence length, achieving up to 2.88× speedup on 32 H200 GPUs while requiring only 10 lines of code for integration.
AI.motivation: Training on variable-length sequences forces a trade-off: static configurations cause workload imbalance and low efficiency, while existing adaptive methods introduce significant complexity and require substantial code changes for new models. The authors seek to break this trade-off.
AI.method: DCP is a data-centric runtime approach where the data (specifically, each batch's sequence length) drives runtime decisions. It dynamically adjusts three key settings: parallel size, gradient accumulation steps, and recomputation strategies, all tuned per-batch based on sequence length characteristics.
AI.result: DCP achieves up to 2.88× speedup on 32 H200 GPUs compared to static configurations.
AI.conclusion: DCP provides a simple yet effective baseline for distributed training on variable-length sequences, offering both high efficiency and ease of integration (10 lines of code), and is expected to facilitate future research in this area.

title: Large Language Models Explain Experts Better Than Experts Themselves
summary: Tacit knowledge, or the "know-how" embedded in experience, is difficult to articulate, making its transfer a challenge in organizations. Tacit knowledge is hard to externalize (transform into explicit knowledge), and expertise is often poorly documented and lost when experts leave. This study examines whether LLMs can externalize tacit knowledge from experts' behaviors and whether such externalized knowledge supports downstream decision-making and transfer to novices. Across two studies, we show that LLM-externalized tacit knowledge improves decision quality and enables novices to approach expert-level performance, often outperforming knowledge articulated by human experts. These findings provide empirical support for Polanyi's Paradox -- that we can know more than we can tell -- and highlight the potential of LLMs as scalable tools that can help overcome human experts' articulation bottleneck. Mechanism analyses and robustness checks show that LLMs meaningfully learn and extract knowledge from expert conversations, and findings generalize across models and retrieval methods.

AI.tldr: LLMs can externalize tacit knowledge from expert behaviors, improving decision-making and enabling novices to approach expert-level performance—often surpassing human-articulated knowledge. This provides empirical support for Polanyi's Paradox and positions LLMs as tools to overcome the articulation bottleneck in organizations.
AI.motivation: Tacit knowledge—the "know-how" embedded in experience—is notoriously difficult to articulate, document, and transfer. When experts leave organizations, their expertise is often lost. This study investigates whether LLMs can overcome this articulation bottleneck by externalizing tacit knowledge directly from experts' behaviors, addressing a fundamental challenge in organizational knowledge management.
AI.method: Two empirical studies were conducted. LLMs were used to extract tacit knowledge from expert behaviors/conversations. The quality of LLM-externalized knowledge was then evaluated on downstream decision-making tasks and on its ability to transfer expertise to novices, with performance benchmarked against knowledge articulated directly by human experts. Mechanism analyses and robustness checks were performed to validate that LLMs meaningfully learn from expert data, with generalization tested across different models and retrieval methods.
AI.result: LLM-externalized tacit knowledge improved decision quality and enabled novices to approach expert-level performance, often outperforming knowledge explicitly articulated by human experts. Mechanism analyses confirmed meaningful knowledge extraction from expert conversations, and findings generalized across different LLMs and retrieval methods.
AI.conclusion: The results provide empirical evidence for Polanyi's Paradox—"we can know more than we can tell"—and demonstrate that LLMs can serve as scalable tools to externalize tacit knowledge, overcoming the articulation bottleneck that limits human experts. This has significant implications for knowledge management and expertise transfer in organizations.

title: Capability-Routed Guard: Defending Large Reasoning Models Against Reasoning-Centric Jailbreaks
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) expose a new safety failure mode: adversarial prompts can manipulate reasoning context, task decomposition, or capability interpretation so that harmful objectives are processed as legitimate reasoning steps. Existing safeguards, including safety reminders, external classifiers, and self-checking wrappers, are often brittle because they either inspect the adversarial prompt directly or ask the target model to perform additional safety reasoning on the same surface that attacks exploit. We introduce Capability-Routed Guard (CRG), a model-agnostic inference-time guardrail for closed-source LRMs, where defenders cannot inspect hidden reasoning traces or modify model weights. CRG reframes prompt defense as a capability-routing problem: a side-channel controller first constructs a trusted representation of the user's authorized task, active context, safety evidence, and capability-transfer risk, separating executable intent from untrusted reasoning context. This representation supports route-specific execution, allowing CRG to block high-risk requests, constrain ambiguous ones, and forward low-risk requests through trusted active context. Finally, CRG applies TraceCheck to verify consistency with the authorized task and invokes a restricted fallback to preserve utility for low-risk benign prompts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CRG effectively mitigates diverse reasoning-centric jailbreaks while preserving benign utility and avoiding common over-refusal issues. Further analysis shows that its components contribute complementary benefits, highlighting the importance of coordinated defense mechanisms for securing large reasoning models.

AI.tldr: CRG is a model-agnostic inference-time guardrail for closed-source large reasoning models that reframes prompt defense as a capability-routing problem, using a side-channel controller to separate authorized intent from untrusted reasoning context, and applies TraceCheck for consistency verification, effectively mitigating reasoning-centric jailbreaks while preserving benign utility.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models (LRMs) exhibit a new safety failure mode where adversarial prompts manipulate reasoning context, task decomposition, or capability interpretation, causing harmful objectives to be processed as legitimate reasoning steps. Existing safeguards (safety reminders, external classifiers, self-checking wrappers) are brittle because they inspect adversarial prompts directly or rely on the same reasoning surface being exploited. For closed-source LRMs, defenders cannot inspect hidden reasoning traces or modify model weights, necessitating a new defense paradigm.
AI.method: CRG operates as a side-channel controller with three stages: (1) constructing a trusted representation of the user's authorized task, active context, safety evidence, and capability-transfer risk, separating executable intent from untrusted reasoning context; (2) route-specific execution that blocks high-risk requests, constrains ambiguous ones, and forwards low-risk requests through trusted active context; and (3) TraceCheck verification for consistency with the authorized task, with a restricted fallback mechanism to preserve utility for benign low-risk prompts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CRG effectively mitigates diverse reasoning-centric jailbreaks while preserving benign utility and avoiding common over-refusal issues. Ablation analysis confirms that CRG's components contribute complementary benefits, underscoring the importance of coordinated defense mechanisms for LRM security.
AI.conclusion: Coordinated, multi-component defense mechanisms like CRG are essential for securing large reasoning models against reasoning-centric adversarial attacks. The capability-routing paradigm offers a promising model-agnostic approach that works even when internal reasoning traces are inaccessible, balancing safety with utility.

title: Personalized Communication Skills for Agentic Recommender Systems
summary: Agentic recommender systems increasingly employ large language model-based UserAgents to evaluate candidate items through simulated feedback before recommendations are delivered. However, existing UserAgents typically reason in isolation based on limited personal histories, which may lead to perspective narrowing: the agent evaluates candidates from a local and incomplete view, overlooks relevant preference facets, and consequently produces inaccurate judgments. A natural way to alleviate this problem is to introduce other users as advisor agents, whose diverse histories provide complementary evidence that helps the target user reconsider overlooked preference signals. Nevertheless, a generic user-advisor communication process is insufficient, as different user decision states require different forms of external advice. Based on this insight, we propose AgentCom, a personalized communication skill framework for agentic recommender systems. AgentCom organizes reusable communication skills into a shared why--what--how--who skill bank: why identifies the decision deficiency that necessitates communication, what specifies the information task, how determines the advisor interaction protocol, and who retrieves advisors capable of executing that protocol. To make the shared skill bank personalized at use time and adaptive over time, AgentCom introduces two complementary mechanisms: personalized skill routing and failure-driven skill evolution. Personalized skill routing constructs a communication path by sequentially selecting suitable skills for each user and recommendation context. Failure-driven skill evolution learns from unsuccessful communication cases and enriches the shared bank with reusable skills that address previously uncovered communication needs. Experiments show that AgentCom consistently improves recommendation performance across traditional, social, and agentic recommenders.

AI.tldr: AgentCom is a personalized communication skill framework for agentic recommender systems that mitigates "perspective narrowing" in LLM-based UserAgents. It organizes communication skills into a why-what-how-who bank and employs personalized skill routing plus failure-driven skill evolution to enable adaptive advisor interactions, improving recommendation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based UserAgents in agentic recommender systems reason in isolation using limited personal histories, leading to "perspective narrowing" — where agents evaluate candidates from an incomplete local view, miss relevant preference facets, and produce inaccurate judgments. While introducing advisor agents with diverse histories can help, a generic communication process is insufficient because different user decision states require different forms of external advice.
AI.method: AgentCom proposes a shared why-what-how-who skill bank that codifies communication skills across four dimensions: why (identifying decision deficiencies), what (specifying information tasks), how (determining advisor interaction protocols), and who (retrieving suitable advisors). Two complementary mechanisms operationalize this: (1) personalized skill routing, which dynamically constructs a communication path by sequentially selecting skills tailored to each user and recommendation context; and (2) failure-driven skill evolution, which learns from unsuccessful communication cases to enrich the shared bank with new reusable skills addressing previously uncovered needs.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that AgentCom consistently improves recommendation performance across traditional, social, and agentic recommender systems.
AI.conclusion: AgentCom effectively addresses perspective narrowing by enabling personalized, adaptive, and evolving advisor communication, yielding robust recommendation gains across diverse recommender paradigms.

title: Fluid Structure, Rigid Record: A Layered Organizational Design Framework for Agent-Native Organizations
summary: An agentic organization should not be a set of model instances with corporate titles, despite most MAS still operationalizing organization as a conversational topology, a role prompt, or a fixed workflow. This paper develops an agent-native organizational structure framework that separates the persistent and dynamic layers of operations. The persistent layer consists of a four-store record architecture and a pool of resident specialization agents. A coordination layer defines Permission as the boundary of the operational world available to an agent, and Privilege as the set of organizational state changes that the agent is authorized to initiate. Together, these mechanisms compile task-specific operational worlds. A runtime layer combines an external Workflow Protocol with an isolated runtime store to dynamically assemble Task Groups. A human-interaction layer exposes the organization through a Control Plane mediated by a non-decision-making Translation Agent. Three orthogonal Role Groups further separate Operation, Review, and Supervision. Operators execute within narrowly scoped leases; reviewers receive elevated but demand-activated authority to modify organizational state; supervisors retain broad observational access while holding limited modification authority. The resulting architecture is fluid at the execution surface but structurally rigid underneath: tasks and events may alter team composition, topology, views, tools, and workflows, while records, write constraints, authority boundaries, and separation of powers remain persistent. The architecture has been implemented as a prototype and evaluated in small-sample experiments. Large-scale empirical validation remains incomplete, therefore no general performance claimed is made yet. Instead, the contribution is a coherent and falsifiable framework for designing, governing, recovering, and evaluating agent-native organizations.

AI.tldr: Proposes an agent-native organizational framework separating persistent structural layers (four-store records, specialization agents) from dynamic runtime layers (workflow protocol, task groups), with formalized Permission/Privilege mechanisms and three orthogonal Role Groups (Operation, Review, Supervision) to create organizations that are fluid at the execution surface but structurally rigid underneath.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent systems (MAS) reductively operationalize organization as conversational topology, role prompts, or fixed workflows — essentially treating agents as model instances with corporate titles. This lacks the structural persistence, authority boundaries, and separation of concerns needed for genuine agent-native organizations.
AI.method: The framework comprises four layers: (1) a persistent layer with a four-store record architecture and resident specialization agent pool; (2) a coordination layer defining Permission (operational world boundary) and Privilege (authorized state-change scope) that compile task-specific operational worlds; (3) a runtime layer combining an external Workflow Protocol with isolated runtime stores to dynamically assemble Task Groups; and (4) a human-interaction layer exposing the organization via a Control Plane mediated by a non-decision-making Translation Agent. Three orthogonal Role Groups — Operation (narrowly scoped leases), Review (elevated, demand-activated modification authority), and Supervision (broad observation, limited modification) — enforce separation of powers.
AI.result: A prototype implementation was evaluated in small-sample experiments. Large-scale empirical validation remains incomplete; no general performance claims are made. The contribution is positioned as a coherent, falsifiable framework for designing, governing, recovering, and evaluating agent-native organizations.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a principled architectural framework rather than empirical performance results. Its core insight is that agent-native organizations require structural rigidity (persistent records, authority boundaries, separation of powers) beneath operational fluidity (dynamic task groups, evolving workflows), with formal Permission/Privilege semantics and orthogonal role separation providing the governance substrate.

title: Synthesizing Behavioural Models of CPS Using Automata Learning and Statistical Machine Learning
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication in the Automated Software Engineering journal
summary:
Inferring behavioural models from system executions is essential for supporting formal verification and analysis of complex, heterogeneous cyber-physical systems (CPS). Automata learning provides an effective way to infer state machine models from system executions. However, CPS inputs and outputs often consist of numeric time-series data, while automata learning algorithms assume inputs over a finite symbolic alphabet. As a result, raw numeric data must first be abstracted into a finite set of symbols. In this article, we present MELA, a passive automata learning approach enhanced with machine learning to synthesize behavioural models from numeric time-series data generated by CPS. MELA systematically combines statistical machine learning with automata learning to automatically abstract raw numeric signals into interpretable intervals that are strongly correlated with system states. Specifically, MELA uses information-theoretic variable selection and decision-tree-based range abstraction to transform numeric traces into symbolic representations suitable for automata learning. We evaluate MELA on two CPS: a commercial network intrusion detection system developed by our industry partner, RabbitRun Technologies, and a publicly available industrial autopilot benchmark from the aerospace domain. Compared with expertise-based numeric data abstraction, MELA reduces the number of states and transitions in the learned state machines by 49.20% on average, while improving accuracy by 41.71% on average. Furthermore, the learned state machines support system-level requirement verification and help practitioners explore behaviours that are not explicit in the system requirements. We make our implementation and experimental data available online.
  Keywords: Automata learning, Cyber-physical systems, Behavioural model synthesis, Decision trees, Model checking, Intrusion detection, Simulink.
