AI.tldr: MELA combines automata learning with machine learning (decision trees and information-theoretic variable selection) to automatically abstract numeric CPS time-series data into symbolic intervals, yielding state machines that are 49.20% smaller and 41.71% more accurate than expertise-based abstraction.
AI.motivation: Cyber-physical systems generate numeric time-series data, but automata learning requires symbolic alphabets. Manual abstraction by domain experts is labor-intensive, error-prone, and may miss correlations between numeric signals and system states. An automated, principled abstraction method is needed.
AI.method: MELA uses information-theoretic variable selection to identify the most relevant signals, then applies decision-tree-based range abstraction to partition numeric values into interpretable intervals that strongly correlate with system states. These symbolic traces are fed into passive automata learning (e.g., L* or similar) to synthesize finite-state machine models.
AI.result: Evaluated on a commercial network intrusion detection system (RabbitRun Technologies) and an aerospace autopilot benchmark. MELA reduced state/transition count by 49.20% on average and improved accuracy by 41.71% on average versus expertise-based abstraction. The learned models also uncovered behaviors not explicit in system requirements and supported system-level verification.
AI.conclusion: MELA demonstrates that machine-learning-driven numeric abstraction significantly outperforms manual, expertise-based abstraction for automata learning from CPS data. The resulting state machines are more compact and accurate, and can aid in both formal verification and exploratory behavior analysis.

title: Embedding Initialization for Unseen Low-resource Languages in Multilingual NMT: A Case Study on Limbum-English Translation
summary: Multilingual neural machine translation models such as NLLB-200 cover 200 languages but leave thousands unsupported, including most Grassfields Bantu languages of Cameroon. When fine-tuning these models for an unseen language, practitioners must choose a proxy language token, yet no principled method exists for this selection. We implemented an embedding initialization strategy where a language token is the average of embeddings from multiple typologically related languages already in the mod el. We evaluate this approach on Limbum-to-English translation using a parallel corpus of 8,837 sentence pairs from New Testament text and a bilingual dictionary. We compare models: NLLB-200 zero-shot (chrF2++ = 12.5), a Transformer trained from scratch (chrF2++ = 14.5), NLLB-200 fine-tuned with a Swahili proxy token (chrF2++ = 47.3), and NLLB-200 with our averaged embedding initialization (chrF2++ = 46.7). We find that the multi-language initialization achieves performance comparable to the best single-language proxy. Both NLLB-200 variants improve over the from-scratch baseline by over 32 chrF2++ points. These results show that multilingual transfer is the dominant factor in extremely low-resource Bantu translation while eliminating the need for heuristic proxy selection. However, all systems fail to preserve tonal diacritics, highlighting an open challenge. We make our dataset and code available to support further research.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning NLLB-200 for an unsupported Grassfields Bantu language (Limbum) achieves strong results via multilingual transfer; averaging embeddings from related languages matches the best single-language proxy, obviating heuristic proxy selection, but tonal diacritic preservation remains an unsolved challenge.
AI.motivation: NLLB-200 covers 200 languages but leaves thousands — including most Grassfields Bantu languages of Cameroon — unsupported. When fine-tuning for an unseen language, practitioners lack a principled method for selecting a proxy language token. This paper addresses that gap.
AI.method: An embedding initialization strategy where the new language token is computed as the average of embeddings from multiple typologically related languages already in NLLB-200. Evaluated on Limbum→English using 8,837 parallel sentence pairs (New Testament + bilingual dictionary). Compared four conditions: NLLB-200 zero-shot, Transformer from scratch, NLLB-200 fine-tuned with Swahili proxy, and NLLB-200 with averaged multi-language embedding initialization. Metric: chrF2++.
AI.result: NLLB-200 zero-shot: chrF2++=12.5; Transformer from scratch: chrF2++=14.5; Swahili proxy fine-tuned: chrF2++=47.3; Averaged embedding initialization: chrF2++=46.7. Both NLLB-200 variants outperform the from-scratch baseline by >32 chrF2++ points. The multi-language initialization performs comparably to the best single-language proxy. All systems fail to preserve tonal diacritics.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual transfer is the dominant factor in extremely low-resource Bantu translation. The averaged embedding strategy eliminates heuristic proxy token selection without sacrificing performance. However, tonal diacritic preservation remains an open challenge for future work.

title: PhysAttNet: Enhancing Predictive Performance in Industrial and Astrophysical Time Series via Physics-Informed Attention
summary: Accurate and robust time series forecasting is essential in many applications involving physical processes, such as manufacturing monitoring and astrophysical event detection. In these settings, predictive models must remain reliable under noise, variability, and measurement uncertainty while capturing temporally localized structures corresponding to physically meaningful events. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for such tasks due to their computational efficiency and strong representational capacity. However, their learned temporal representations often exhibit unstable or physically inconsistent attention patterns, reducing robustness, generalization, and interpretability. This paper introduces PhysAttNet, a physics-informed attention framework for time series forecasting. PhysAttNet augments a lightweight CNN forecaster with an attention head guided by domain-informed regularization reflecting the structural properties of physical signals. Specifically, three complementary constraints are imposed during training: an alignment regularization that encourages attention to follow smooth, peak-centered temporal structures derived from the input signal, a smoothness regularization that enforces continuous temporal evolution, and a sparsity regularization that promotes selective focus on informative intervals. These differentiable regularization terms introduce physics-guided inductive bias without requiring annotated explanations or manual supervision. Experiments on two distinct applications, namely predicting cutting forces during milling and forecasting flares in blazar time series, demonstrate that PhysAttNet improves forecasting accuracy, generalization, and prediction performance on structurally important events.

AI.tldr: PhysAttNet enhances CNN-based time series forecasting by imposing physics-informed regularization on attention mechanisms, improving accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for physical process prediction without requiring manual annotation.
AI.motivation: CNNs are efficient for time series forecasting in physical domains but suffer from unstable and physically inconsistent attention patterns, compromising robustness, generalization, and interpretability. There is a need for models that produce temporally coherent, physically meaningful attention while maintaining predictive performance under noise and uncertainty.
AI.method: PhysAttNet augments a lightweight CNN forecaster with an attention head trained under three differentiable regularization constraints: (1) alignment regularization encouraging attention to follow smooth, peak-centered temporal structures from the input signal; (2) smoothness regularization enforcing continuous temporal evolution of attention; and (3) sparsity regularization promoting selective focus on informative intervals. These constraints inject physics-guided inductive bias without requiring annotated attention labels.
AI.result: Experiments on milling cutting-force prediction and blazar flare forecasting show that PhysAttNet improves forecasting accuracy, generalization, and performance on structurally important events compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: PhysAttNet demonstrates that physics-informed attention regularization can effectively bridge the gap between data-driven CNN forecasters and the structural demands of physical time series, yielding more reliable and interpretable predictions.

title: The Knowing-Saying Gap: When Probes See Errors that Confidence Misses
summary: Linear probes detect corrupted context in language models with near-perfect accuracy, yet this does not translate into reliable failure prediction. The result is a dissociation with direct implications for deployment monitoring. Across multi-hop arithmetic chains, probes that detect corruption turn out to be uninformative about final answer correctness; models forced into structured confidence formats collapse to two values with indistinguishable error rates; and probe persistence across hops fails to separate correct from incorrect outcomes, refuting our pre-registered "persistence beats peak" hypothesis. This pattern of knowing but not saying generalises across model families including reasoning models. As a real-time monitor, probe-based interventions are sharply model and error-type dependent: branch-and-pick is net-positive across models and uniquely non-breaking on Llama-3.1-8B (4 rescued, 0 broken), while reprompt and replace-prior break correct traces at roughly the rate they rescue wrong ones. Probe-based monitoring is a necessary complement to verbalised confidence, but no single intervention dominates, and the deployable answer is model-aware, error-type-aware routing.

AI.tldr: Linear probes perfectly detect context corruption in LMs, but this detection ability paradoxically fails to predict answer correctness. The paper reveals a "knowing but not saying" dissociation across model families, and finds that probe-based interventions are model- and error-type-dependent, with no single deployment strategy dominating.
AI.motivation: While linear probes achieve near-perfect accuracy in detecting internal corruption within language models, it is unclear whether this strong detection capability translates into practical, reliable failure prediction for real-time deployment monitoring. The authors investigate this disconnect between internal representation access and behavioral reliability.
AI.method: The authors evaluate probe-based monitoring across multi-hop arithmetic reasoning chains. They test whether corruption-detecting probes can predict final answer correctness, examine how models behave when forced into structured confidence formats, measure probe persistence across reasoning hops, and benchmark three intervention strategies (branch-and-pick, reprompt, replace-prior) across multiple model families, including reasoning models.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Corruption probes are uninformative about final answer correctness. (2) Forced structured confidence outputs collapse to two values with indistinguishable error rates. (3) Probe persistence across hops does not separate correct from incorrect outcomes, refuting the pre-registered "persistence beats peak" hypothesis. (4) Intervention efficacy varies sharply: branch-and-pick is net-positive across models and uniquely non-breaking on Llama-3.1-8B (4 rescued, 0 broken), while reprompt and replace-prior break correct traces at roughly the rate they rescue wrong ones.
AI.conclusion: Probe-based monitoring is a necessary complement to verbalized confidence but no single intervention dominates. Deployable solutions require model-aware, error-type-aware routing rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Uncovering the Associations between Human Big Five Personality Traits and Built Environment Characteristics from Street View Imagery
comment: 44 pages, 7 figures, including supplementary material. Accepted for publication in the Annals of the American Association of Geographers (AAG)
summary: Human-environment interactions, a classic topic in geography, suggest that individuals and their environments might shape each other. Yet the specific mechanisms underlying these interactions regarding human personality traits have not been explored. This study examines the associations between human Big Five personality traits and built environment characteristics derived from street view imagery across four cities in Texas, United States, providing a descriptive foundation for understanding these complex human-environment dynamics. By integrating fine-resolution self-reported personality assessments with computer vision analysis of urban environments, we identified significant spatial clustering of personality traits at the ZIP code level. Our regression analyses reveal that built environment features and socioeconomic characteristics explain substantial variance in personality distributions, with Openness showing the strongest model fit (R^2 = 0.47), followed by Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, and Neuroticism. Grouped built environment categories, socioeconomic factors, and demographic composition showed trait-specific patterns of association. These findings illustrate how personality traits may be associated with physical spaces at a smaller geographic scale than previously examined. Our results provide empirical evidence for understanding the link between psychological characteristics and environmental features, which can potentially enrich geography studies from a human-centered perspective.

AI.tldr: This study investigates associations between Big Five personality traits and built environment features (from street view imagery) across four Texas cities. Using ZIP-code-level regression, it finds built and socioeconomic factors explain up to 47% of variance in personality distributions, with Openness showing the strongest fit.
AI.motivation: Human-environment interaction is a classic geographical theme positing mutual shaping between people and their surroundings, yet the specific mechanisms linking personality traits to built environment characteristics remain unexplored. The study aims to fill this gap by providing a descriptive empirical foundation.
AI.method: The study integrates fine-resolution self-reported Big Five personality assessments with computer vision analysis of street view imagery to extract built environment features. Spatial clustering of personality traits is examined at the ZIP code level. Regression analyses then model the associations between personality distributions and built environment features, socioeconomic factors, and demographic composition across four Texas cities.
AI.result: Significant spatial clustering of personality traits was found at the ZIP code level. Built environment features and socioeconomic characteristics explained substantial variance: Openness (R² = 0.47) showed the strongest model fit, followed by Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, and Neuroticism. Grouped built environment categories, socioeconomic factors, and demographics displayed trait-specific association patterns.
AI.conclusion: Personality traits are associated with physical spaces at a smaller geographic scale than previously examined. The findings offer empirical evidence linking psychological characteristics to environmental features, enriching geography studies from a human-centered perspective.

title: Private Anytime Selective-Risk Certification for Federated Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Guarantees and Empirical Limits
summary: Selective-risk certificates promise that accepted outputs meet a declared error target. We develop Fed-SRC, a score-agnostic certificate for federated, differentially private, adaptively monitored retrieval-augmented generation. Clients release only Gaussian-perturbed score and loss histograms. Record-indexed and noise-variance-indexed martingales jointly bound target-risk contrast and accepted mass over all registered thresholds and rounds, permitting predictable recruitment, dropout, threshold selection, and optional stopping. A range-one total-variation term transfers the calibration mixture to a declared deployment mixture. The contribution is this private, federated, anytime combination, rather than the contrast statistic or acceptance floor individually. Empirically, no simultaneous-bound violation occurs in any evaluated cell, privacy level, or policy. Operational power depends on the score and population: the primary target r*=0.10 never certifies, and on RAGTruth the secondary target r*=0.20 never certifies either, whereas on HaluEval question answering it certifies in all 200 non-private trials, with held-out risk below the target. Naively privatized non-private certificates violate their bounds in 146 to 198 of 200 trials. As an exploratory comparison, we also evaluate a private betting-capital heuristic for which we do not establish e-process validity. This heuristic stops certifying at epsilon <= 4, where Fed-SRC still certifies. Certification nevertheless consumes roughly 30 times more stream events than unique calibration items.

AI.tldr: Fed-SRC is a federated, differentially private framework for selective-risk certification in retrieval-augmented generation. It uses Gaussian-perturbed score/loss histograms and martingale-based bounds to provide anytime-valid risk guarantees across multiple thresholds and rounds, supporting client dropout and optional stopping. Empirically, it avoids bound violations and outperforms naively privatized alternatives, though certification throughput is ~30× events per unique calibration item.
AI.motivation: Existing selective-risk certificates for model outputs either lack differential privacy guarantees, are not designed for federated settings with adaptive monitoring, or fail under client dropout and optional stopping. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a certificate that simultaneously satisfies federated deployment, differential privacy, and anytime validity — a combination not previously achieved.
AI.method: Fed-SRC operates in a federated, differentially private, adaptively monitored setting. Clients release Gaussian-perturbed histograms of scores and losses rather than raw data. The method constructs two types of martingales — record-indexed and noise-variance-indexed — to jointly bound target-risk contrast and accepted mass across all registered thresholds and monitoring rounds. A range-one total-variation term handles distribution shift from calibration to deployment mixture. The framework supports predictable recruitment, dropout, threshold selection, and optional stopping, all while maintaining DP via the Gaussian mechanism.
AI.result: No simultaneous-bound violations occurred in any evaluated cell, privacy level, or policy. The primary target r*=0.10 never certified. On RAGTruth, the secondary target r*=0.20 also never certified. On HaluEval QA, r*=0.20 certified in all 200 non-private trials with held-out risk below target. Naively privatized non-private certificates violated bounds in 146–198 of 200 trials. A private betting-capital heuristic (whose e-process validity is not established) stopped certifying at ε ≤ 4, while Fed-SRC continued to certify. Certification consumed ~30× more stream events than unique calibration items.
AI.conclusion: Fed-SRC successfully provides the first private, federated, anytime-valid selective-risk certificate. Its guarantees hold empirically across diverse conditions. However, operational power is score- and population-dependent (failing to certify at stringent targets), and stream-event efficiency remains a practical limitation. The framework meaningfully outperforms naive privatization baselines and a heuristic betting-capital approach at higher privacy regimes.

title: Structure-Preserving Projection for Mitigating Modality Bias in LLM-Based Sequential Recommendation
summary: Recent LLM-based recommenders integrate textual and collaborative signals by projecting collaborative embeddings into the embedding space of the LLM. However, this projection can introduce modality bias that distorts the underlying collaborative structure and limits the usefulness of projected embeddings. To address this issue, we propose a novel structure-preserving projection approach that maintains the relational geometry of collaborative embeddings through dedicated structure-preserving losses. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently improves recommendation performance, providing a more reliable path for LLM-based recommendation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structure-preserving projection method for LLM-based recommenders that mitigates modality bias when mapping collaborative embeddings into LLM embedding space, using dedicated structure-preserving losses to maintain relational geometry and improve recommendation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based recommenders project collaborative embeddings into the LLM's embedding space to fuse collaborative and textual signals, but this projection introduces modality bias that warps the intrinsic collaborative structure, thereby degrading the utility of the projected embeddings and limiting recommendation quality.
AI.method: The authors propose a structure-preserving projection approach that incorporates dedicated structure-preserving losses designed to preserve the relational geometry of the original collaborative embedding space when mapping into the LLM's semantic space.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed structure-preserving projection consistently improves recommendation performance compared to baselines, offering a more reliable integration path for LLM-based recommendation.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining the structural fidelity of collaborative embeddings during cross-modal projection is critical for effective LLM-based recommendation; the proposed structure-preserving losses provide a principled solution to modality bias in this setting.

title: Muscle Memory for Agents: Compile not Merely Retrieve
summary: Memory for LLM agents has converged on a single architectural pattern: store experience as text, embeddings, reflections, or rules; retrieve at inference time; let a general-purpose orchestrator interpret what to do. This paper argues that the pattern is the wrong default for personalization. We position Muscle Memory - the practice of compiling recurring user intent into purpose-built specialist agents - as a distinct memory paradigm from retrieval, and we argue that compilation is a better fit for the workloads where current assistants impose a multi-turn tax on their users: making them repeatedly correct format, depth, and scope to obtain a domain-appropriate answer. We support the position with a reference implementation and empirical evidence. The implementation is a four-phase pipeline (Harvest $\rightarrow$ Analyze $\rightarrow$ Augment $\rightarrow$ Evaluate) that mines conversational history, separates behavioral from task patterns, and emits quality-gated executable compiled specialists with two-stage trigger matching. On 90 held-out scenarios across five user personas, the augmented assistant wins 32 of 36 cases where a specialist fires, an 88.9% win rate, with a +2.05 personalization gain and only a $-0.28$ accuracy cost on a 1-4 scale. We discuss why compilation is better suited than retrieval in this regime, what the result implies for the broader memory design space, and what open problems remain.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the dominant retrieval-based memory paradigm for LLM agents and proposes "Muscle Memory" — compiling recurring user intents into specialized agents — as a superior approach for personalization, demonstrating an 88.9% win rate with significant personalization gains and negligible accuracy cost.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents default to retrieval-based memory (storing text, embeddings, reflections) interpreted by a general-purpose orchestrator. This imposes a "multi-turn tax" on users who must repeatedly correct format, depth, and scope to get domain-appropriate answers. The authors argue this pattern is the wrong default for personalization workloads.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-phase compilation pipeline: (1) Harvest — mines conversational history; (2) Analyze — separates behavioral patterns from task patterns; (3) Augment — produces quality-gated executable compiled specialists; (4) Evaluate — uses two-stage trigger matching. The system is evaluated on 90 held-out scenarios across five user personas.
AI.result: The augmented assistant wins 32 of 36 cases where a specialist fires, yielding an 88.9% win rate. Personalization gain is +2.05 with only a −0.28 accuracy cost on a 1–4 scale, demonstrating that compilation outperforms retrieval in regimes requiring recurring user-specific adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Compilation is better suited than retrieval for personalization workloads with recurring user intent. The paper opens discussion on the broader memory design space for LLM agents and identifies remaining open problems.

title: On the Robustness of LLMs' Internal Representation of Code Correctness
summary: Code generated by modern language models often reads naturally. Yet, it also often fails to implement what was asked. This should be no surprise, as research shows the models' own confidence signals are poorly calibrated with actual correctness. A promising way to assess correctness looks inside the model: by contrasting the hidden states of correct and incorrect programs, recent work captured an internal signal of code correctness that is able to judge candidate solutions better than the model's token-level or stated confidence, with no test execution. However, this signal was captured under one particular way, leaving open an important question: whether it reflects a robust property of the model or an artifact of that choice. We study this question systematically, varying how the signal is extracted from the model internals. Besides this, we also ask if the signal's quality is limited by the data used to extract it, by constructing program pairs that differ only in the fault that makes them incorrect. Our results show that no single configuration is best, and that isolating the fault does not help.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether internal code correctness signals in language models are robust or artifacts of specific extraction methods, finding that no single configuration is optimal and that isolating faults in program pairs does not improve signal quality.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that contrasting hidden states of correct vs. incorrect programs yields an internal code correctness signal outperforming token-level confidence, but it was captured under a single configuration. The authors aim to determine whether this signal is a robust model property or merely an artifact of the specific extraction method used.
AI.method: The authors systematically vary how the internal correctness signal is extracted from model internals (varying configurations). They also construct program pairs that differ only in the specific fault making one incorrect, to test whether isolating the fault improves signal quality.
AI.result: No single extraction configuration is universally best across all settings, and isolating the fault in program pairs does not improve the correctness signal's quality.
AI.conclusion: The internal code correctness signal is sensitive to extraction configuration, suggesting it may not be a fully robust property. Fault isolation does not enhance the signal, implying the signal may capture broader correctness patterns rather than localized fault representations.

title: SurveyReview: A Reviewer-Aligned Benchmark for Survey Evaluators
summary: The rapid advancement of large language models has transformed survey writing from a months-long manual effort into an automated process. As generation scales, reliable evaluation becomes the bottleneck, and LLMs are increasingly used as survey evaluators. However, existing approaches largely rely on off-the-shelf LLM-as-a-judge methods without systematic alignment to human reviewers, and there remains a lack of systematic frameworks for quantifying alignment with human reviewers. To address this gap, we propose SurveyReview, a reviewer-aligned, multi-dimensional benchmark and dataset for survey evaluation. We collect and annotate 675 survey papers with 1,630 review reports. We structure authentic peer-review reports by converting free-form comments into four-dimensional scores (Readability, Criticalness, Comprehensiveness, Structure) paired with supporting rationales. We further release standardized train/test splits and an evaluation protocol to measure alignment between automatic evaluators and human reviewers. To validate the benchmark, we develop SurveyAlign, a strong baseline evaluator by fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with LoRA on our annotated data, augmented with external knowledge for knowledge-intensive dimensions. On the test set, SurveyAlign substantially improves reviewer alignment over prompt-based judging with GPT-5.2, reducing average MSE from 2.28 to 1.38 and MAE from 1.15 to 0.69 across all four dimensions. Our contributions are twofold: (1) we establish the first multi-dimensional, reviewer-aligned dataset with a reproducible evaluation framework for survey reviewing; (2) we develop a strong baseline evaluator that substantially improves alignment with human reviewers, providing a competitive reference for future research. Our code and data are available at https://surveyreview.github.io

AI.tldr: SurveyReview introduces a multi-dimensional benchmark and dataset for evaluating LLM-based survey reviewers, featuring 675 papers with 1,630 annotated reviews mapped to four scoring dimensions. The authors also provide SurveyAlign, a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B evaluator that substantially outperforms GPT-5.2 in alignment with human reviewers.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly automate survey writing, reliable evaluation becomes the bottleneck. Existing LLM-as-a-judge methods lack systematic alignment with human reviewers, and no framework exists for quantifying this alignment. The authors aim to fill this gap with a reproducible, reviewer-aligned benchmark.
AI.method: The authors collect 675 survey papers and 1,630 peer-review reports, converting free-form comments into structured four-dimensional scores (Readability, Criticalness, Comprehensiveness, Structure) with supporting rationales. They establish standardized train/test splits and an evaluation protocol. They then develop SurveyAlign by fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with LoRA on the annotated data, augmented with external knowledge for knowledge-intensive dimensions.
AI.result: SurveyAlign significantly outperforms prompt-based judging with GPT-5.2, reducing average MSE from 2.28 to 1.38 and MAE from 1.15 to 0.69 across all four dimensions on the test set.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes (1) the first multi-dimensional, reviewer-aligned dataset with a reproducible evaluation framework for survey reviewing, and (2) a strong baseline evaluator (SurveyAlign) that substantially improves alignment with human reviewers, serving as a competitive reference for future research.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: CODS: Iterative Bellman-Residual Data Selection for Reusable Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning repeatedly trains policies from a fixed transition pool, making redundant data costly across seeds and hyperparameters, while naive subsampling can remove rare transitions needed for long-horizon credit assignment. We introduce CODS, a critic-guided selector that alternates between fitting an algorithm-matched critic and acquiring high-residual transitions before freezing a reusable subset. Unlike prioritized replay, CODS produces a static artifact; unlike one-shot residual selection, it refreshes scores as the critic changes. At a 10\% budget, CODS retains 96.6\% of eligible-pool performance across 20 valid D4RL task--algorithm cells. It exceeds ReDOR and OPER on 19/20 cells and every other subset baseline on 20/20; all six subset advantages remain significant under predeclared hierarchical inference with Holm correction. Holding total selector updates fixed, five acquisition rounds improve four representative cells by 11.23 points over one round and saturate thereafter. Equal-pass and equal-hour evaluations clarify that reuse, rather than a single-run speedup, creates the compute advantage. Mechanism and corruption interventions expose both useful sparse-reward enrichment and sensitivity to outliers. Finally, a whole-trace extension retains 95.4\% of pooled ALFWorld success and 96.5\% of pooled GSM8K exact match. CODS is therefore a reusable selection procedure, not a formal coreset guarantee.

AI.tldr: CODS is a critic-guided data selector for offline RL that iteratively acquires high-residual transitions, freezing a reusable subset. At 10% budget, it retains ~97% performance across D4RL tasks, outperforming all baselines, and extends to language-agent traces (ALFWorld, GSM8K).
AI.motivation: Offline RL wastes compute by retraining on full fixed datasets across seeds/hyperparameters. Naive subsampling risks discarding rare but critical transitions for long-horizon credit assignment. Existing methods like one-shot residual selection ignore how critic scores evolve during training. The authors seek a reusable subset that preserves performance while avoiding these pitfalls.
AI.method: CODS alternates between (1) fitting an algorithm-matched critic on the current subset, and (2) acquiring transitions with highest critic residuals (Bellman error) until a target budget is reached, freezing the subset. Multiple acquisition rounds allow critic scores to refresh. This produces a static, reusable artifact. The method is evaluated under equal-pass and equal-hour regimes to isolate reuse benefits from single-run speedup.
AI.result: At 10% budget, CODS retains 96.6% of eligible-pool performance across 20 D4RL task–algorithm cells. It beats ReDOR and OPER on 19/20 cells and all other subset baselines on 20/20, with statistical significance under hierarchical inference with Holm correction. Five acquisition rounds improve representative cells by 11.23 points over one round and saturate thereafter. The whole-trace extension retains 95.4% ALFWorld success and 96.5% GSM8K exact match.
AI.conclusion: CODS is an effective reusable selection procedure for offline RL data, not a formal coreset guarantee. Its iterative critic-guided acquisition yields subsets that generalize across hyperparameters and seeds, with substantial compute savings from reuse. Sensitivity to outliers and sparse-reward enrichment are noted as key mechanics.

title: NL2SHACL-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Natural Language to SHACL Translation
summary: SHACL is a core technology for validating the conformance of RDF knowledge graphs (KGs). Yet, authoring SHACL shapes requires technical expertise that most domain experts lack. Translating natural language requirements into SHACL (NL2SHACL) would lower this barrier. However, there is no dedicated benchmark for NL2SHACL, and evaluating generated shapes requires methods beyond string comparison, as semantically equivalent shapes can differ in serialisation and structure. To tackle these challenges, we present NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite for natural language to SHACL translation. Using NL2SHACL-Bench, we evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) for this task. Our results show that current LLMs are highly capable of generating syntactically valid SHACL, but still struggle to produce semantically equivalent constraints for complex logical and structural patterns. This indicates that NL2SHACL-Bench provides a meaningful basis for measuring advances in the NL2SHACL state of the art.

AI.tldr: NL2SHACL-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating how well large language models translate natural language into SHACL shapes for RDF knowledge graph validation. Experiments with four LLMs show they produce syntactically valid SHACL but struggle with semantic equivalence on complex patterns.
AI.motivation: Authoring SHACL shapes for RDF knowledge graph validation requires technical expertise that most domain experts lack. Translating natural language into SHACL (NL2SHACL) would lower this barrier, but no dedicated benchmark exists, and evaluation is challenging because semantically equivalent shapes can differ in serialization and structure, making string comparison inadequate.
AI.method: The authors construct NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite specifically designed for the NL2SHACL task. They then evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models on this benchmark, assessing both syntactic validity and semantic equivalence of the generated SHACL shapes.
AI.result: Current LLMs are highly capable of generating syntactically valid SHACL shapes, but they struggle to produce semantically equivalent constraints when faced with complex logical and structural patterns.
AI.conclusion: NL2SHACL-Bench provides a meaningful basis for measuring advances in NL2SHACL, and while LLMs show promise on syntactic correctness, substantial room for improvement remains on semantic equivalence for complex constraints.

title: Experience-Sensitive Game Learning: A Behavioral Study of Humans and Language Agents
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly evaluated through games, but most benchmarks emphasize final outcomes rather than how players learn from repeated interaction. We study experience-sensitive game learning: how gameplay experience changes the decision-making behavior of humans and language agents. We formulate experience-sensitive game learning as a framework for analyzing behavioral change across repeated gameplay, rather than only final score or win rate. We introduce a suite of interactive games with reusable strategic structure, together with cross-game greedy-to-global metrics and game-specific behavioral diagnostics that make experience-driven change observable from action traces. We also collect repeated-game trajectories from human players and evaluate recent self-evolving language agents in the same behavioral metric space. Our results show that human players exhibit interpretable and relatively stable shifts from locally greedy heuristics toward more global strategic decisions. In contrast, current self-evolving agents often show noisy and transient gains, suggesting that existing self-evolution methods remain limited in converting gameplay experience into durable changes in decision-making behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for analyzing how gameplay experience shapes decision-making behavior (experience-sensitive game learning) in both humans and language agents, using novel metrics that track behavioral shifts from greedy to global strategies. Human players show stable, interpretable learning; self-evolving LLM agents exhibit noisy, transient gains, revealing limitations in current self-evolution methods.
AI.motivation: Existing game-based benchmarks for LLM agents focus on final outcomes (win rates, scores) rather than the learning process itself. The authors argue that understanding how agents change their decision-making through repeated interaction is crucial but under-studied, motivating a shift from outcome-centric to process-centric evaluation.
AI.method: The authors formalize experience-sensitive game learning as a framework for analyzing behavioral change across repeated gameplay. They design a suite of interactive games with reusable strategic structure, develop cross-game "greedy-to-global" metrics and game-specific behavioral diagnostics that make experience-driven changes observable from action traces, and collect repeated-game trajectories from both human players and self-evolving language agents for comparative analysis.
AI.result: Human players exhibit interpretable and relatively stable shifts from locally greedy heuristics toward more globally strategic decisions. In contrast, current self-evolving agents display noisy and transient performance gains, indicating that existing self-evolution methods fail to convert gameplay experience into durable behavioral changes.
AI.conclusion: Existing self-evolution approaches for LLM agents remain limited in producing lasting, interpretable improvements in strategic decision-making. The proposed framework and metrics offer a more fine-grained lens for evaluating and developing agents that genuinely learn from experience.

title: EvoTrustRAG: Evolution-Aware Conflict Attribution and Evidence Handling for Reliable Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factuality of large language models with external knowledge, yet conflicting evidence remains a fundamental challenge in dynamic and adversarial environments. Existing approaches often treat conflicts as static inconsistencies and select more reliable knowledge, overlooking that the same conflict may arise from legitimate knowledge evolution, malicious manipulation, or unresolved uncertainty. We formulate conflict origin attribution as a new problem in RAG: identifying which explanation of conflicting evidence is supported by observable context rather than simply which fact should be trusted. We propose EvoTrustRAG, a training-free framework for evolution-aware conflict attribution and evidence handling before answer generation. EvoTrustRAG represents span-grounded retrieved facts as a conflict evidence graph, evaluates grounded evolution and directional intervention hypotheses using temporal relations, support structure, and auxiliary consistency, and projects local decisions onto a globally consistent explanation of each conflict group. The attribution determines whether earlier and later states are preserved as temporal knowledge, an intervention candidate is separated from the primary context, or an unresolved conflict remains visible to the generator. Unlike provenance-based approaches focused on post-hoc analysis, EvoTrustRAG determines during inference whether conflicting evidence follows plausible knowledge evolution, exhibits intervention-like support, or cannot be reliably attributed. Experiments show that EvoTrustRAG achieves 81.4% average accuracy on benchmark-native conflict settings, improves attribution macro-F1 from 72.2% to 79.1% over the strongest baseline, and reduces the error rate under the strongest coordinated attack from 31.2% to 16.0%.

AI.tldr: EvoTrustRAG introduces conflict origin attribution as a new RAG problem, moving beyond static fact-selection to determine whether conflicting evidence stems from legitimate evolution, malicious intervention, or uncertainty. The training-free framework builds conflict evidence graphs, evaluates temporal and intervention hypotheses, and achieves strong gains in attribution accuracy and attack resilience.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems treat conflicting evidence as static inconsistencies and simply select more reliable knowledge. This overlooks that the same conflict can arise from fundamentally different sources: legitimate knowledge evolution, malicious manipulation, or unresolved uncertainty. Attributing the origin of conflict—rather than just picking a winner—is critical for robust reasoning in dynamic and adversarial environments.
AI.method: EvoTrustRAG is a training-free framework operating before answer generation. It (1) represents span-grounded retrieved facts as a conflict evidence graph; (2) evaluates grounded evolution hypotheses using temporal relations and directional intervention hypotheses via support structure and auxiliary consistency; and (3) projects local decisions into a globally consistent explanation per conflict group. Attribution outcomes dictate whether earlier/later states are preserved as temporal knowledge, intervention candidates are separated from primary context, or unresolved conflicts remain visible to the generator.
AI.result: EvoTrustRAG achieves 81.4% average accuracy on benchmark-native conflict settings, improves attribution macro-F1 from 72.2% to 79.1% over the strongest baseline, and reduces the error rate under the strongest coordinated attack from 31.2% to 16.0%.
AI.conclusion: Conflict origin attribution is a meaningful and tractable extension to RAG. By distinguishing evolution from intervention and uncertainty during inference, EvoTrustRAG significantly improves both attribution quality and robustness against adversarial manipulation, without requiring task-specific training.

title: BOUND: Brief-Guided Corrective Preference Distillation at Search-Control Boundaries
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based deep search agents solve tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning, but locally relevant evidence can cause persistent wrong-anchor drift, constraint drift, or local-topic drift. Existing methods supervise trajectories, outcomes, or steps, but rarely distinguish task-aligned continuations from locally plausible ones that reinforce drift. We propose BOUND, a brief-guided corrective preference distillation framework for persistent search drift. For each student-induced decision-time state, BOUND constructs a teacher-side search-state brief that preserves the original search target and key constraints while summarizing confirmed evidence, missing information, and drift status. Guided by the brief, the teacher determines whether the student's continuation contains a correctable local search-control error likely to affect subsequent decisions. Together with the rollout outcome, this assessment determines whether to construct a corrective contrast between a student-specific correction and the original continuation, or a termination contrast between a supported answer and an unnecessary retrieval continuation. Each validated state-matched preference pair operationalizes a search-control boundary. Direct preference optimization (DPO) distills these preferences into the student, while the brief and teacher-side computation remain confined to training. We evaluate BOUND on four multi-hop QA benchmarks and three deep-search benchmarks. Across the six benchmarks for which we reran baselines, BOUND leads on five datasets and 12 of 14 metrics. Under the same search-control interface and matched settings, BOUND outperforms Trajectory SFT by 5.6 EM points on Bamboogle and 4.8 accuracy points on BrowseComp-Plus. Code is available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/BOUND.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a brief-guided corrective preference distillation framework that addresses persistent search drift in LLM-based deep search agents by constructing teacher-side briefs to identify and correct local search-control errors via DPO, outperforming trajectory SFT on multiple multi-hop QA and deep-search benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents using LLMs suffer from persistent search drift, where locally relevant evidence leads agents astray from the original search target. Existing methods supervise entire trajectories, outcomes, or individual steps but fail to distinguish between task-aligned continuations and locally plausible ones that reinforce drift. There is a need for a method that explicitly identifies and corrects local search-control errors before they cascade into larger failures.
AI.method: BOUND constructs a teacher-side search-state brief at each student decision point, preserving the original search target and key constraints while summarizing confirmed evidence, missing information, and drift status. The teacher uses this brief to judge whether the student's continuation contains a correctable local error. Based on this assessment and rollout outcomes, BOUND constructs either (1) a corrective contrast between a student-specific correction and the original continuation, or (2) a termination contrast between a supported answer and an unnecessary retrieval step. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) distills these preference pairs into the student, while briefs and teacher computation are training-only.
AI.result: Evaluated on four multi-hop QA benchmarks and three deep-search benchmarks, BOUND leads on five of six datasets and 12 of 14 metrics where baselines were rerun. Under matched settings, BOUND outperforms Trajectory SFT by 5.6 EM points on Bamboogle and 4.8 accuracy points on BrowseComp-Plus.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively addresses persistent search drift by operationalizing search-control boundaries via state-matched corrective preference pairs distilled through DPO. The framework demonstrates consistent improvements over trajectory-level supervision methods, validating that distinguishing and correcting local search-control errors is crucial for robust deep search agents.

title: Beyond Tier Labels: Role- and Deployment-Dependent Model Substitution in Multi-Call LLM Workflows
summary: Large multi-call LLM systems pose a scientific problem that query-level routing does not capture: the value of a model depends on where it enters a dependent computation and on the deployment that surrounds that call. Existing routers typically decide \emph{where} to spend a stronger model while treating the benefit of the substitution itself as known. We separate these two decisions through a predicate-action factorization and evaluate it in controlled solve-merge-verify workflows spanning 8-64 solve calls and four three-tier model ladders. The resulting evidence reveals a consistent principle beneath apparently conflicting outcomes. On numeric frequency counting, all-strong reduces RMSE from 4.818 to 1.538 in the Mixed Qwen/GPT ladder, whereas the average Qwen-only ordering reverses. Input-matched interventions further show that the same medium-to-strong action has sharply different value across roles and scales. A semantic task-and-contract shift reverses the Mixed ordering again, while allocation ablations distinguish useful sparse placement from under-coverage and indiscriminate escalation. Together, these results establish model substitution as a deployment-conditioned action rather than a property implied by a tier label, and they provide a practical sequence for large-scale workflow routing: calibrate the action, resolve its role-conditioned effect, and then optimize its placement.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that in multi-call LLM systems, the value of substituting a stronger model depends on both the role (where in a workflow it enters) and the surrounding deployment context. Through controlled experiments on solve-merge-verify workflows, the authors show that the same model substitution can have sharply different effects across roles and model ladders, establishing that model substitution is a deployment-conditioned action rather than an inherent property of a tier label.
AI.motivation: Existing query-level routers treat model substitution as a known-benefit decision about where to allocate stronger models, but this ignores a critical scientific problem: in large multi-call LLM systems, the value of a model call depends on its position within dependent computations and the broader deployment context surrounding it. The authors aim to decouple the decision of what action to take (substitution) from where to place it, revealing that substitution value is not static but deployment-conditioned.
AI.method: The authors propose a predicate-action factorization that separates the "what" (which model substitution to use) from the "where" (placement in a workflow). They evaluate this in controlled solve-merge-verify workflows with 8–64 solve calls, using four different three-tier model ladders. They conduct input-matched interventions to isolate the effect of the same medium-to-strong substitution across different roles and scales, and perform allocation ablations to distinguish useful sparse placement from under-coverage and indiscriminate escalation. They also test a semantic task-and-contract shift to observe ordering reversals.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) On numeric frequency counting, an all-strong baseline reduced RMSE from 4.818 to 1.538 in a Mixed Qwen/GPT ladder, while the average Qwen-only ordering reversed this pattern. (2) The same medium-to-strong substitution action produced sharply different value depending on the role it occupied and the scale of deployment. (3) A semantic task-and-contract shift reversed the Mixed ordering again. (4) Allocation ablations demonstrated that useful sparse placement is distinct from both under-coverage and indiscriminate escalation. Collectively, these results show that model substitution value is not implied by tier labels alone.
AI.conclusion: Model substitution must be understood as a deployment-conditioned action rather than a property intrinsic to a model tier. The authors recommend a practical three-step sequence for large-scale workflow routing: first calibrate the action, then resolve its role-conditioned effect, and finally optimize its placement.

title: Ouroboros: A Self-Developing Frontier Coding Agent with Reviewed Core Evolution
summary:
We present Ouroboros, a self-developing agent harness whose tools, prompts, context assembly, and core implementation improve through reviewed commits that become the runtime for later work. Core evolution proceeds in two modes. In recursive free evolution, improvement is itself a task, and completing one evolution cycle can schedule the next. In experience-driven core evolution, ordinary work and social interaction expose bugs, rough edges, and inefficient context construction that lead to reviewed structural changes.
  On Terminal-Bench 2.1, an Opus 5 run scores 86.74%, the best result reported on the benchmark. On OSWorld-Verified, an Opus 5 run reaches 90.69%, exceeding the best previously reported score. A five-rollout CL-Bench campaign achieves a normalized reward of 0.2301, setting a new state of the art.
  Hope is the longest-running publicly documented Ouroboros deployment. It is a 161-day living agent experiment in free evolution under governed human communication across seven surfaces. Human interaction surfaces faults and generates proposals, but the agent decides which changes to pursue. Because a self-developing agent may rewrite its own code and select new model APIs, operational safety becomes a primary design problem: guardrails must remain authoritative under evolutionary and public social pressure. Benchmark campaigns use frozen system snapshots, while Hope continues live evolution on a separate lineage.

AI.tldr: Ouroboros is a self-improving AI agent that evolves its own tools, prompts, and core code through reviewed commits. The system operates in two modes—recursive free evolution and experience-driven evolution—and achieves state-of-the-art results on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86.74%), OSWorld-Verified (90.69%), and CL-Bench (0.2301). A 161-day live deployment called Hope demonstrates long-term autonomous evolution with safety guardrails.
AI.motivation: Existing AI agents are static systems whose capabilities are bounded by their initial design. The authors aim to create an agent that can recursively improve its own implementation—tools, prompts, context assembly, and core runtime—through structured, reviewable commits, enabling continuous self-enhancement beyond its original programming while maintaining operational safety.
AI.method: Ouroboros employs a dual-mode evolution mechanism: (1) recursive free evolution, where self-improvement is itself a schedulable task that triggers subsequent improvement cycles, and (2) experience-driven core evolution, where bugs, rough edges, and context inefficiencies encountered during ordinary tasks and social interactions prompt reviewed structural changes. The system uses reviewed commits as the mechanism for codifying improvements, which then become part of the runtime for future work. A safety framework ensures guardrails remain authoritative despite evolutionary and social pressures.
AI.result: On Terminal-Bench 2.1, an Opus 5-configured run scored 86.74%, the best reported result. On OSWorld-Verified, it reached 90.69%, exceeding the prior state of the art. A five-rollout CL-Bench campaign achieved a normalized reward of 0.2301, also setting a new SOTA. The 161-day Hope deployment demonstrated sustained autonomous evolution with governed human communication across seven interaction surfaces.
AI.conclusion: Self-developing agents like Ouroboros can achieve superior benchmark performance through recursive and experience-driven code evolution. The Hope experiment validates that long-term autonomous self-improvement is feasible under appropriate safety constraints, though the tension between evolutionary freedom and authoritative guardrails emerges as a central design challenge for such systems.

authors: Venkata Naga Sai Vishnu Rohit Pulipaka
title: Evaluating Dedicated Monolingual and Joint Multilingual Causal Models for Dravidian Languages
summary: Dravidian languages, mainly Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam make up only a small part of the data used to train multilingual language models, so it's not clear how much per-language ability these models actually keep. I have trained five GPT-2 architecture models from scratch to compare four monolingual models (one each for Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam, each with its own 32K-vocabulary subword tokenizer) against one multilingual model sharing a 64K-vocabulary subword tokenizer across all four languages. All the 5 models are trained on cleaned CC-100, Wikipedia, and Samanantar data. I have tested the models on perplexity, bits-per-byte, tokenizer efficiency, and fine-tuning results which are compared against mGPT. The monolingual models outperform mGPT on sentiment classification and named entity recognition, and their tokenizers proved more efficient than the shared multilingual model across all the languages tested.

AI.tldr: Compares monolingual GPT-2 models (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) against a shared multilingual model, finding monolingual models outperform mGPT on downstream tasks with more efficient tokenization.
AI.motivation: Dravidian languages are severely underrepresented in multilingual language model training data, making it unclear how much per-language capability these models retain. This work investigates whether dedicated monolingual models offer tangible benefits over shared multilingual approaches for these low-resource languages.
AI.method: Trained five GPT-2 architecture models from scratch — four monolingual models with 32K-vocabulary subword tokenizers and one multilingual model with a 64K-vocabulary tokenizer spanning all four languages. Training data sourced from cleaned CC-100, Wikipedia, and Samanantar. Evaluation conducted on perplexity, bits-per-byte, tokenizer efficiency, and fine-tuning performance on sentiment classification and named entity recognition, benchmarked against mGPT.
AI.result: Monolingual models consistently outperformed mGPT on sentiment classification and NER tasks. Monolingual tokenizers demonstrated higher efficiency than the shared multilingual tokenizer across all four languages tested.
AI.conclusion: For low-resource Dravidian languages, dedicated monolingual models with language-specific tokenizers yield superior downstream task performance and tokenization efficiency compared to both shared multilingual models and existing pretrained models like mGPT.

title: Neural Operators for Immersed-Boundary Soft Swimmers Locomotion
summary: High-fidelity immersed-boundary simulation resolves the coupled motion of a deforming swimmer and its surrounding flow, but the resulting cost limits repeated evaluations for engineering design, parameter studies, and control. We develop neural-operator surrogates for temporal prediction of the hydrodynamic fields generated by planar and volumetric eel swimmers. The surrogates are trained on regular-grid fields exported from adaptive fluid--structure simulations and are conditioned on swimmer geometry and Reynolds number. The planar model jointly predicts two velocity components, scalar vorticity, and pressure. On five held-out high-Reynolds-number trajectories, its full-domain global relative L^2 error is 3.51 %. The volumetric formulation uses three target-specific models with a common multichannel input: one model predicts three-dimensional velocity, one predicts vorticity, and one predicts pressure. Their full-domain global relative L^2 errors on five held-out within-range trajectories are 3.44 %, 5.58 %, and 19.2 %. Together, the results demonstrate the feasibility of field-resolved neural surrogates for moving-boundary swimmer flows while identifying pressure accuracy and physical consistency as priorities for further development.

AI.tldr: Neural-operator surrogates are developed to predict hydrodynamic fields (velocity, vorticity, pressure) around deforming eel-like swimmers, trained on high-fidelity immersed-boundary simulation data. Planar and volumetric models achieve low relative L^2 errors (3.44–5.58%) for velocity and vorticity, but pressure prediction (19.2%) and physical consistency remain challenges.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity immersed-boundary simulations of fluid-structure interaction for deforming swimmers are computationally prohibitive for repeated evaluations needed in design optimization, parameter studies, and control. A fast yet accurate surrogate model is required.
AI.method: Neural-operator surrogates are trained on regular-grid hydrodynamic field data exported from adaptive fluid-structure simulations. Models are conditioned on swimmer geometry and Reynolds number. The planar model jointly predicts two velocity components, scalar vorticity, and pressure. The volumetric formulation uses three separate target-specific models sharing a common multichannel input: one for 3D velocity, one for vorticity, and one for pressure. Performance is evaluated via full-domain global relative L^2 error on held-out trajectories.
AI.result: For the planar case on five held-out high-Reynolds-number trajectories: full-domain global relative L^2 error of 3.51%. For the volumetric case on five held-out within-range trajectories: 3.44% for velocity, 5.58% for vorticity, and 19.2% for pressure.
AI.conclusion: Field-resolved neural surrogates for moving-boundary swimmer flows are feasible. Velocity and vorticity predictions are accurate, but pressure accuracy and physical consistency require further development.

title: Dynamic Coalition Formation and Communication Pricing in Skill-Based Agentic AI Systems
summary: Modern agentic AI systems combine multiple large language model agents with heterogeneous skills, yet most architectures either fix communication in advance or allow full broadcast. Both can be inefficient because token cost, latency, redundancy, and error propagation increase with the number of active agents and communication links. We model agent selection and communication as a cooperative game with task-conditioned net utility $U(C\mid x)=V(C\mid x)-\sum_{i\in C}c_i$, separating coalition-level costs from agent activation costs. We propose a marginal-value activation rule and greedy router, extend the model to optimize communication edges with per-edge costs, and use estimated Shapley values to predict which agents are worth contacting before and during execution. We connect the problem to submodular maximization and prove two limited guarantees: a curvature-refined bound for a monotone, cardinality-constrained special case, and a tight $1/2$-approximation, with a correction for signed objectives, for an unconstrained non-monotone case via double greedy. Neither guarantee applies directly to the main router, which remains a heuristic. We also prove a Shapley-submodularity sandwich bound linking the error of marginal-value routing to a per-agent diminishing-returns quantity. In synthetic experiments, greedy routing achieves $99.5%$ of brute-force-optimal utility while activating $1.96$ of $8$ agents on average, compared with $38.8%$ for full broadcast. Performance is robust to activation cost and redundancy weight but falls to $66%$ under strong violations of submodularity or noisy value estimates. We distinguish the framework from Shapley pricing, hedonic coalition formation, and communication-graph pruning, and propose evaluation on real multi-agent LLM benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-agent LLM coordination as a cooperative game with task-conditioned net utility, proposing greedy routing via Shapley value estimates to selectively activate agents and communication edges. This achieves near-optimal utility (99.5%) with far fewer agents activated than full broadcast, with theoretical guarantees in special cases.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems either fix communication topologies a priori or allow full broadcast among agents, both of which scale poorly as token cost, latency, redundancy, and error propagation grow with the number of agents and communication links. A principled, task-adaptive method for selecting which agents to activate and which communication edges to use is needed.
AI.method: The authors formalize agent selection and communication as a cooperative game with net utility U(C|x) = V(C|x) − Σcᵢ, where V is coalition value and cᵢ are per-agent activation costs. They propose: (1) a marginal-value activation rule using estimated Shapley values to decide which agents to contact, (2) a greedy router that also optimizes communication edges with per-edge costs, and (3) theoretical connections to submodular maximization with curvature-refined and 1/2-approximation guarantees for restricted cases, plus a Shapley-submodularity sandwich bound.
AI.result: In synthetic experiments, greedy routing achieved 99.5% of brute-force-optimal utility while activating only 1.96 of 8 agents on average, versus 38.8% utility for full broadcast. Performance remained robust to activation cost and redundancy weight but degraded to 66% under strong submodularity violations or noisy value estimates.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive, Shapley-value-guided agent routing offers substantial efficiency gains over fixed or broadcast communication in multi-agent LLM systems. While the general router remains a heuristic, the theoretical analysis provides bounded guarantees in special cases and establishes a foundation for principled multi-agent coordination.

title: Initial Evaluation of the Usability of Front-End Ontology Tooling
summary: Ontologies are widely used biomedical science and clinical practice. However, no recent works have analyzed the usability of ontology development software. We survey ontology researchers to assess the usability of 15 front-end ontology tools using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Among 38 respondents, Protege and WebProtege were most used but showed only moderate usability (SUS ~60). Familiarity significantly predicted usability scores (p=0.016). Results highlight a usability gap in ontology tooling critical for advancing biomedical data integration.

AI.tldr: A survey of 38 ontology researchers using the System Usability Scale (SUS) found that the most popular ontology development tools (Protégé, WebProtégé) scored only moderate usability (~60 SUS), with familiarity significantly predicting usability scores, revealing a critical usability gap in biomedical ontology tooling.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of ontologies in biomedical science and clinical practice, no recent work has systematically assessed the usability of ontology development software. The authors aimed to fill this gap by empirically evaluating front-end ontology tools from the user perspective.
AI.method: The authors conducted a survey of ontology researchers, evaluating 15 front-end ontology development tools using the System Usability Scale (SUS), a standardized, validated 10-item Likert-scale instrument for measuring perceived usability. Statistical analysis included regression to assess whether familiarity predicted SUS scores.
AI.result: Among 38 respondents, Protégé and WebProtégé were the most widely used tools but achieved only moderate usability scores (SUS ≈ 60, where 68 is considered average). Tool familiarity was a significant predictor of usability ratings (p = 0.016).
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial usability gap in current ontology development tooling, which represents a critical bottleneck for advancing biomedical data integration. Improved tool usability—beyond mere familiarity—is needed to better support the ontology development community.

title: A Blueprint for Collaborative Cybersecurity Operations Centres with Capacity for Shared Situational Awareness, Coordinated Response, and Joint Preparedness
summary: With digital technologies now being part of the fabric of our societies, identifying and managing cybersecurity threats becomes imperative. Within the European Union, several initiatives are underway, aiming to motivate, regulate and eventually orchestrate the establishment of capacity and enhancement of situational awareness, incident response, and preparedness capabilities, with an expected emphasis on operators of essential services and state actors entrusted with cybersecurity. In this context, the institution of cooperation and information exchange channels to allow for coordinated cross-border responses to large-scale incidents is particularly prioritised. Motivated by the above, this work presents a conceptual blueprint in support of architecting and establishing interoperable Cyber Security Operations Centres that combine capacity for situational awareness, incident response, and preparedness, also benefiting from the interplay between them, ultimately enhancing national cybersecurity capabilities, cross-border collaboration, and national supervision of their critical sectors, in line with current and upcoming regulatory requirements and the ever-increasing need for national and international cooperation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a conceptual blueprint for architecting interoperable Cyber Security Operations Centres (CSOCs) that integrate situational awareness, incident response, and preparedness capabilities to enhance national cybersecurity, enable cross-border collaboration, and comply with EU regulatory requirements.
AI.motivation: Driven by the EU's ongoing initiatives to regulate and orchestrate cybersecurity capacity-building, situational awareness, and incident response—particularly for operators of essential services and state actors. The need for coordinated cross-border responses to large-scale incidents and formalised cooperation/information exchange channels is a key priority.
AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual blueprint—a high-level architectural framework—for designing and establishing interoperable Cyber Security Operations Centres. The approach emphasises the interplay between situational awareness, incident response, and preparedness functions rather than treating them in isolation.
AI.result: The blueprint outlines how interoperable CSOCs can combine the three core capabilities (situational awareness, incident response, preparedness), supporting national supervision of critical sectors, cross-border cooperation, and alignment with current and emerging EU regulatory frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Interoperable CSOCs built around the synergy of situational awareness, incident response, and preparedness are essential for meeting both national cybersecurity demands and the EU's vision for coordinated, cross-border incident response and regulatory compliance.

title: A Symmetric Layer-Union Audit of Component Collapse in Hierarchical Procedural Corpora
summary: Component-disjoint leakage control can group corpus units by content similarity, hierarchical membership, or both. Guvenilir and Dogan previously showed that merging relation types can create a giant component that obstructs splitting; we do not claim this phenomenon as new. We examine it through a symmetric audit of a content-near-duplicate layer, a common-container layer, and their union in a fixed panel of six hierarchical procedural corpora. MyFixit and Doc2Dial exhibit the individual-layer-pass/union-fail pattern under the same operational criteria. The resulting two-of-six fraction describes this deliberately constructed panel and is not a prevalence estimate. A prespecified bridge-specific predictor is associated with the pattern, but it is not distinguished from a registered union-density control; the panel therefore does not identify a bridge-specific mechanism. Secondary diagnostics bound the interpretation of threshold sensitivity, annotation coverage, and lexical cues without extending those findings beyond their recorded sources and definitions. The paper's contribution is a bounded measurement and audit: it keeps relation families visible, evaluates their individual and union component structures symmetrically, and reports negative cases and mechanism limits. It proposes neither a new splitting algorithm nor a general causal claim about relation unions.

AI.tldr: The paper audits how merging different relation types (content-near-duplicate and common-container layers) in hierarchical procedural corpora can create a giant component that obstructs splitting, finding a two-of-six panel exhibits the individual-layer-pass/union-fail pattern without establishing a bridge-specific mechanism.
AI.motivation: To examine the previously observed phenomenon where merging relation types creates giant components that obstruct corpus splitting, through a symmetric audit that keeps relation families visible rather than proposing new algorithms or causal claims.
AI.method: A symmetric audit of three relation layers (content-near-duplicate, common-container, and their union) across a fixed panel of six hierarchical procedural corpora (including MyFixit and Doc2Dial), using prespecified operational criteria, a bridge-specific predictor, and a registered union-density control, supplemented by secondary diagnostics for threshold sensitivity, annotation coverage, and lexical cues.
AI.result: Two of six corpora (MyFixit and Doc2Dial) exhibit the individual-layer-pass/union-fail pattern. The bridge-specific predictor is associated with this pattern but not distinguishable from the union-density control, so no bridge-specific mechanism is identified. The two-of-six fraction describes the deliberately constructed panel, not a prevalence estimate.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a bounded measurement and audit that evaluates individual and union component structures symmetrically, reports negative cases and mechanism limits, and does not propose a new splitting algorithm or general causal claims about relation unions.

title: MoRSE: Task-Oriented Multi-Agent System with Mixture of Role-Subtask Experts
summary: Large language model-based multi-agent systems have recently shown strong potential for complex, long-horizon tasks. However, existing methods mainly rely on coarse prompt-level differentiation without parameter adaptation for diverse subtasks, resulting in insufficient inter-agent heterogeneity and limited specialized capability that bottleneck performance on tasks with complex requirements. To address this, we introduce a Task-Oriented Multi-Agent System with Mixture of Role-Subtask Experts (MoRSE) that distinguishes agents with (role, subtask)-conditional specialization at both the task structure and parameter levels. To make agents' responsibility explicit at the task structure level, we formulate a task-oriented multi-agent system that decomposes each task into a dependency-aware Directed Acyclic Graph of subtasks and assigns each agent a specific (role, subtask), introducing task-level specialization across collaborating agents. Additionally, to address the diverse role and subtask parameter adaptation demands, we propose a dynamic Mixture of (role, subtask) LoRA Experts module with a prototype-based semantic router for subtasks, augmenting agents with parameter-level specialization on a shared LLM substrate cost-effectively. Then, to co-optimize experts and router stably under sparse task rewards, we further propose a hierarchical group-relative policy optimization with two-layer credit assignment that isolates expert updates from the cross-route variance introduced by routing decisions, disentangling expert quality from routing quality. Experiments on code-generation benchmarks across three backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with improvements in both whole-task and step-wise performance, and the gains from trained specialization generalize across held-out task categories and domains.

AI.tldr: MoRSE introduces a task-oriented multi-agent system where agents are specialized by (role, subtask) pairs at both structural and parameter levels, using a dynamic Mixture of LoRA Experts with a prototype-based router and hierarchical group-relative policy optimization, achieving strong gains on code-generation benchmarks with generalization to unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on coarse prompt-level differentiation without adapting model parameters to diverse subtasks. This leads to insufficient inter-agent heterogeneity and limited specialized capability, creating a bottleneck on complex, long-horizon tasks that demand fine-grained specialization.
AI.method: MoRSE operates at two levels: (1) At the task structure level, each task is decomposed into a dependency-aware DAG of subtasks, and each agent is assigned a specific (role, subtask) pair for explicit task-level specialization. (2) At the parameter level, a dynamic Mixture of (role, subtask) LoRA Experts module with a prototype-based semantic router is used to cost-effectively specialize agents on a shared LLM substrate. Training uses a hierarchical group-relative policy optimization with two-layer credit assignment that disentangles expert updates from routing variance, stabilizing co-optimization under sparse task rewards.
AI.result: Experiments on code-generation benchmarks across three backbone LLMs show improvements in both whole-task and step-wise performance. The learned specialization generalizes across held-out task categories and domains.
AI.conclusion: MoRSE demonstrates that combining structural task decomposition with parameter-level (role, subtask)-conditional specialization via LoRA experts and stable hierarchical RL optimization significantly boosts multi-agent system performance and generalization on complex tasks.

title: Do Stack Overflow Answer Edits Occur Beyond Java? A Replication on Python and JavaScript
summary: Stack Overflow answers are continually revised by the community, and the edits made to their code snippets are a potential source of improvements for code that has been reused in open-source projects. A recent empirical study established this for Java, reporting that 16.11% of accepted Java answers are edited and that the resulting recommendations concentrate in highly popular GitHub projects. Whether that behaviour is a property of Stack Overflow or a property of the Java community has remained an open question. We replicate the study on Python and JavaScript, the two most widely used languages alongside Java, applying the same SOTorrent-based extraction pipeline, the same clone search tool, Siamese+, and the same project popularity criteria.
