Analysing 840,132 accepted Python answers and 1,144,185 accepted JavaScript answers, we find that 41.25% and 39.10% respectively have been edited at least once, roughly two and a half times the Java rate, while the number of revisions per edited answer is almost invariant across the three languages at 2.78, 2.68 and 2.82. Searching 100 GitHub projects per language, we find that the number of matched answer edits increases monotonically from low- to medium- to high-popularity projects in both languages, from 80 to 156 to 977 for Python and from 32 to 71 to 353 for JavaScript. The difference is statistically significant for Python but not for JavaScript. The central findings of the original study therefore generalise beyond Java, with the supply of candidate improvements considerably larger in both replication languages than in the original.

AI.tldr: This paper replicates a prior study on Stack Overflow answer edits in Java, extending it to Python and JavaScript. It finds that Python (41.25%) and JavaScript (39.10%) answers are edited at roughly 2.5× the Java rate, while revisions-per-answer remain constant (~2.7–2.8). Edits concentrate in high-popularity GitHub projects, confirming the original findings generalize beyond Java, with a substantially larger supply of candidate improvements in both languages.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the previously observed phenomenon — that Stack Overflow answer code edits propagate into popular open-source projects — is specific to the Java community or generalizes across programming languages.
AI.method: A replication study targeting Python and JavaScript. The authors reuse the original SOTorrent-based extraction pipeline, the Siamese+ clone detection tool, and identical project popularity criteria. They analyze 840,132 accepted Python answers and 1,144,185 accepted JavaScript answers, then search across 100 GitHub projects per language, stratified by popularity (low, medium, high).
AI.result: 41.25% of Python and 39.10% of JavaScript accepted answers are edited at least once (~2.5× Java's 16.11%). Mean revisions per edited answer: Python 2.78, JavaScript 2.68, Java 2.82 — nearly invariant. Matched edits rise monotonically with project popularity: Python (80→156→977), JavaScript (32→71→353). The trend is statistically significant for Python but not JavaScript.
AI.conclusion: The original study's central findings generalize beyond Java. Both Python and JavaScript exhibit substantially higher rates of answer editing, implying an even larger pool of candidate code improvements available to open-source projects than previously documented.

title: The No-Meaning Falsity: The Structural Impossibility of the Arbitrary Sign in Classical Arabic
summary: This paper investigates whether the postmodern claim of unrestricted semantic indeterminacy, and its foundational Saussurean axiom of the arbitrary sign, are compatible with the structural architecture of Classical Arabic. We develop a formal mathematical model of Arabic non concatenative morphology in which lexical meaning is determined by the interaction between an invariant root and a morphosyntactic pattern. Within this framework, we establish a Morphological Correspondence Theorem, demonstrating that every lexical item is uniquely generated by a root pattern pair, and a Semantic Localization Theorem, proving that lexical meaning is determined at the derivational level prior to surface realization. To address Saussurean weaker notion of relative arbitrariness, we formalize it via conditional Kolmogorov complexity, defining arbitrariness algorithmically as the no rule property. We prove that general relative arbitrariness is formally undecidable, while Arabic relative arbitrariness is decidable and provably less than 1 for its motivated signifiers (Levels W and M), establishing a strict system complexity asymmetry over Indo-European languages.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges postmodern semantic indeterminacy using a mathematical model of Classical Arabic morphology, proving that root-pattern pairs uniquely determine lexical meaning and that Arabic exhibits provably lower semantic arbitrariness than Indo-European languages.
AI.motivation: To test whether the postmodern claim of unrestricted semantic indeterminacy and the Saussurean principle of the arbitrary sign hold under the structural constraints of Classical Arabic's non-concatenative morphology, thereby questioning the universality of these linguistic-philosophical doctrines.
AI.method: A formal mathematical model of Arabic non-concatenative morphology is constructed. Two theorems are proved: a Morphological Correspondence Theorem (unique root-pattern generation) and a Semantic Localization Theorem (meaning fixed at derivational level). Saussurean relative arbitrariness is formalized via conditional Kolmogorov complexity as the "no-rule property," and decidability/undecidability results are derived.
AI.result: General relative arbitrariness is formally undecidable. Arabic relative arbitrariness is decidable and strictly less than 1 for motivated signifiers (Levels W and M), establishing a strict system-complexity asymmetry favoring Arabic over Indo-European languages.
AI.conclusion: The postmodern claim of unrestricted semantic indeterminacy and the Saussurean arbitrary sign axiom fail to generalize to Classical Arabic. The language's root-pattern architecture enforces deterministic meaning assignment and provably lower arbitrariness, exposing a cross-linguistic asymmetry that undermines the universality of these foundational claims.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: Finite Constant Frontiers and Auditable Regret Certificates for Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: Average-reward reinforcement-learning regret is known up to logarithmic factors, but the numerical content of published guarantees is difficult to compare because probability mode, structural parameter, logarithmic normalization, prior information, and planning assumptions differ. We introduce a constant-aware comparison protocol and derive an explicit finite lower certificate for communicating MDPs. The construction is a binary tree of two-state blocks; its proof uses exact trajectory-level Bernoulli KL divergence and keeps action budget, diameter, occupancy, navigation cost, and terminal bias explicit. A common closed-form envelope improves the published coefficient $0.015$ across a finite frontier: $0.0200$ in a moderate regime and up to $0.0291$ under stronger action, diameter, and horizon conditions, a $94\%$ increase. The limiting coefficient is $\frac1{32}\sqrt{(A-3)/A}$. For upper bounds, we give an auditable composition rule for a span-constrained optimistic learner, but do not claim a coefficient while adaptive directional-variance and planning certificates remain open. We also formalize valid expectation conversion and constant comparability. Controlled diagnostics test diameter dependence, bonus-by-width interactions, span misspecification, and the finite lower certificate on its exact family.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a constant-aware comparison protocol for average-reward reinforcement learning regret bounds, derives an explicit finite lower certificate for communicating MDPs using a binary tree construction, improves the published coefficient from 0.015 to up to 0.0291 (a 94% increase), and establishes a limiting coefficient of (1/32)√((A-3)/A).
AI.motivation: Published average-reward RL regret guarantees are difficult to compare due to differing assumptions on probability mode, structural parameters, logarithmic normalization, prior information, and planning. The authors aim to create a standardized, constant-aware comparison framework that makes numerical content explicit and comparable across algorithms.
AI.method: The authors construct a binary tree of two-state blocks as a lower-bound instance for communicating MDPs. The proof employs exact trajectory-level Bernoulli KL divergence and keeps action budget, diameter, occupancy, navigation cost, and terminal bias explicit. A closed-form envelope is derived to improve the constant coefficient. For upper bounds, an auditable composition rule for a span-constrained optimistic learner is provided, though adaptive directional-variance and planning certificates remain open problems.
AI.result: The lower certificate improves the published coefficient from 0.015 to 0.0200 in a moderate regime and up to 0.0291 under stronger conditions—a 94% increase. The limiting coefficient is derived as (1/32)√((A-3)/A). Controlled diagnostics validate diameter dependence, bonus-by-width interactions, span misspecification, and the finite lower certificate on its exact family.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous constant-aware comparison framework for average-reward RL regret, providing explicit finite lower certificates and improved coefficients. For upper bounds, an auditable composition rule is given, but the authors do not claim a final coefficient due to open problems in adaptive directional-variance and planning certificates. Valid expectation conversion and constant comparability are also formalized.

title: MetaSpace: Metamorphic Testing for Spatial Cognition in Embodied Agents
comment: 30 pages, 17 figures. Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA1)
summary:
An embodied agent is an intelligent entity that interacts with its environment through a physical body. Currently, the evaluation of embodied agents primarily relies on two paradigms: (1) manually annotated Visual Question Answering (VQA) pairs and (2) high-level task completion metrics, such as success in navigation or manipulation. The former is labor-intensive and subject to variability in annotation quality. The latter may obscure critical vulnerabilities, allowing agents to complete tasks through suboptimal means or safety violations, thereby concealing safety risks and inefficiencies. Given that spatial cognition is the cornerstone for executing embodied tasks, there is a pressing need to assess whether embodied agents possess robust spatial cognition during task execution.
  Inspired by metamorphic testing principles in software engineering, we propose MetaSpace, a novel framework designed to evaluate the spatial cognition of agents. By leveraging spatiotemporal multimodal states derived from real execution trajectories, MetaSpace automatically generates test cases based on predefined metamorphic relations (MRs) grounded in logical rules and physical laws. Crucially, we encode these MRs as executable rules in a logic programming language (Prolog). Violations of these relations indicate failures in spatial cognition. Our empirical evaluation across three embodied scenarios demonstrates that MetaSpace successfully detects 90,422 spatial cognition errors in state-of-the-art (SOTA) MLLM-driven agents. We introduce the Spatial Cognition (SC) score to quantify performance. Results indicate that all SOTA agents achieve average scores between 0.44 and 0.52, significantly lower than the human benchmark of 0.96.

AI.tldr: MetaSpace is a framework that automatically evaluates spatial cognition in embodied agents by applying metamorphic testing principles. It generates test cases from real execution trajectories using Prolog-encoded physical and logical rules, detecting 90,422 spatial cognition errors in SOTA MLLM-driven agents. All tested agents scored 0.44–0.52, far below the human benchmark of 0.96.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation paradigms for embodied agents are inadequate: manual VQA annotation is labor-intensive and inconsistent, while high-level task completion metrics can mask critical vulnerabilities, safety risks, and inefficiencies by rewarding suboptimal or unsafe task completion. Since spatial cognition underpins embodied task execution, there is a pressing need for robust, automated spatial cognition assessment.
AI.method: MetaSpace leverages metamorphic testing principles from software engineering. It extracts spatiotemporal multimodal states from real agent execution trajectories and automatically generates test cases based on predefined metamorphic relations (MRs) grounded in logical rules and physical laws. These MRs are encoded as executable rules in Prolog (a logic programming language). Violations of these relations signal spatial cognition failures. A new metric, the Spatial Cognition (SC) score, quantifies agent performance.
AI.result: MetaSpace detected 90,422 spatial cognition errors across SOTA MLLM-driven agents in three embodied scenarios. All SOTA agents achieved average SC scores between 0.44 and 0.52, substantially below the human benchmark of 0.96.
AI.conclusion: Current SOTA embodied agents exhibit significant deficits in spatial cognition despite succeeding at high-level tasks. MetaSpace provides an automated, principled approach to uncovering these hidden failures and quantifying spatial cognition, highlighting a critical gap between agent and human spatial reasoning capabilities.

title: A Survey On Digital Reading Materials and Personal Study of Christian Religious Texts
summary: Religion is an important part of many people's lives, with reading from religious texts being among the most common and important regular practices. Modern technology has in many ways changed the way this religious reading takes place, but the effects of these changes have not yet been studied. While there have been plenty of studies examining the effects of digital media on reading comprehension and similar topics, the study of religious texts is often primarily focused on achieving a religious experience, so the existing research is not sufficient to explore these changes. In our study, we used surveyed students from two universities to ask individuals how they use technology in their personal study of religious texts and religious education courses. Our respondents were predominately Christian. Through qualitative and quantitative analysis of the results, we aim to learn how technology interacts with study of religious texts, in what situations technology is preferred over print and vice versa, and the rationale for choosing the medium for a given task. In particular, we have found that paper scriptures are still frequently used even with the prevalence of technology. Additionally, individuals do not strictly use one particular medium during study; they tend to choose different mediums depending on the circumstances.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how individuals use technology versus print when studying religious texts, finding that paper scriptures remain prevalent alongside digital tools, and that medium choice is situational rather than fixed.
AI.motivation: Existing research on digital media and reading comprehension does not adequately address religious text study, which prioritizes spiritual experience over mere comprehension. The effects of modern technology on religious reading practices remain unexamined.
AI.method: Survey of students from two universities (predominately Christian), employing both qualitative and quantitative analysis to assess technology use in personal religious text study and religious education courses.
AI.result: Paper scriptures remain frequently used despite widespread technology availability. Individuals do not adhere to a single medium; they flexibly switch between print and digital formats depending on context and task.
AI.conclusion: Technology has not displaced print in religious text study; rather, both media coexist, with users making situational choices about which medium best serves their needs for a given religious study task.

title: BASIS: Breach-Aware Selective Prompt Injection Shielding with Prefill Attention Probes
summary: Prompt injection is a critical security threat in large language model (LLM) applications, where attackers hijack model behavior by embedding malicious instructions in user or external data. Existing detection methods only detect the presence of injection and refuse to respond upon detection, overlooking the fact that for many modern aligned models, well-crafted instructions can resist most injection attacks. This means that the injection robustness varies significantly across instructions and models. This leads to widespread unnecessary over-refusal: inputs containing injections that the model could have handled correctly are rejected incorrectly. To deal with this over-refusal issue, we propose BASIS (Robustness-Aware Prompt Injection Defense). This defense method uses the Attention Competition Ratio ($ρ$) as features to train two sparse linear probes: an existence probe and a breach probe. Both probes make defense decisions through cascaded gating, which does not require additional LLM inference. BASIS comprises three stages: injection existence detection, per-sample breach prediction, and instruction robustness assessment; the online cascade refuses only when the model would actually be compromised and thus avoids over-refusal on robust instructions. Experiments across four tasks and six open-source LLMs show that BASIS maintains near-perfect injection detection while substantially reducing over-refusal on safe attack samples, especially under robust instruction templates.

AI.tldr: BASIS is a prompt injection defense that uses attention-based probes and cascaded gating to detect injections and predict whether a given instruction will actually be breached, thereby avoiding unnecessary over-refusal on robust instruction-model combinations.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt injection detectors blindly refuse all inputs containing injections, ignoring that many well-crafted instructions can resist injection attacks in modern aligned LLMs. This causes widespread over-refusal — rejecting inputs the model could have safely handled.
AI.method: BASIS uses the Attention Competition Ratio (ρ) as features to train two sparse linear probes: an existence probe (detects injection presence) and a breach probe (predicts whether the injection will actually compromise the model). These probes operate via cascaded gating without additional LLM inference. The three-stage pipeline consists of: (1) injection existence detection, (2) per-sample breach prediction, and (3) instruction robustness assessment. The cascade only refuses when the model would truly be compromised.
AI.result: Experiments across four tasks and six open-source LLMs show BASIS maintains near-perfect injection detection while substantially reducing over-refusal on safe attack samples, especially under robust instruction templates.
AI.conclusion: BASIS effectively addresses the over-refusal problem in prompt injection defense by conditioning refusal on predicted breach likelihood rather than mere injection presence, achieving a practical balance between security and utility.

title: Difficulty-Gated Fusion of Reasoning Views for Temporal Retrieval
summary: Reasoning-intensive temporal retrieval requires matching a query to documents whose relevance depends on shared temporal reasoning rather than lexical overlap. Expanding a query into several reformulations that make its temporal intent explicit, and retrieving with each, supplies this reasoning, but fusing the resulting rankings with equal weights wastes accuracy: for any single query, only some reformulations are reliable. We propose query-difficulty-gated fusion of reasoning views. From each view we read an eight-dimensional signature of its score distribution, built from query-performance-prediction quantities such as softmax entropy, score gaps, and dispersion, and a gate of roughly one thousand parameters maps these signatures to per-query view weights. The fused ranking uses no relevance labels at inference, no re-ranking, and no fine-tuning of the retriever; the gate is trained leave-one-task-out. On the \textsc{Tempo} benchmark, the method improves all six retrievers we evaluate, from BERT encoders to 7B decoder retrievers, with the largest gains on the weaker backbones. The strongest retrievers reach $0.297$ and $0.303$ nDCG@10, and the per-query gain over the original query is significant under a paired bootstrap ($p<0.001$). A per-query oracle reaches $0.364$ against our realized $0.297$, exposing headroom that identifies per-query view selection as a concrete next step.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method for reasoning-intensive temporal retrieval where multiple query reformulations (views) are fused using a learned gate that assigns per-query weights based on score distribution signatures. The gate, trained leave-one-task-out, improves all six evaluated retrievers on the Tempo benchmark without requiring relevance labels at inference, re-ranking, or retriever fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: In temporal reasoning retrieval, expanding a query into multiple reformulations helps capture temporal intent, but fusing them with equal weights is suboptimal because only some reformulations are reliable for any given query. The key insight is that per-query weighting of reformulation views can recover accuracy that uniform fusion wastes.
AI.method: The method generates multiple query reformulations (reasoning views), retrieves documents with each, and extracts an eight-dimensional signature from each view's score distribution using query-performance-prediction features (softmax entropy, score gaps, dispersion). A lightweight gate (~1K parameters) maps these signatures to per-query view weights for weighted fusion. The gate is trained leave-one-task-out, requiring no relevance labels at inference, no re-ranking, and no retriever fine-tuning.
AI.result: The method improves all six retrievers on Tempo, from BERT encoders to 7B decoder retrievers, with larger gains on weaker backbones. Top retrievers reach 0.297 and 0.303 nDCG@10, with per-query gains over the original query significant under paired bootstrap (p<0.001). A per-query oracle reaches 0.364, revealing substantial headroom for future per-query view selection.
AI.conclusion: Query-difficulty-gated fusion of reasoning views is an effective, lightweight approach for temporal reasoning retrieval that generalizes across retriever architectures. The gap between realized performance (0.297) and oracle (0.364) identifies per-query view selection as a promising direction for future work.

title: Distributed Team Orchestration via Supervisor Networks: Convergence, Optimality, and Resilience
summary: In this paper, we study zero-sum potential team games with a supervisor network, where agents rely on supervisor-provided belief information rather than accurate common beliefs. The main challenge is that such belief information can be inaccurate because of supervisors' belief-estimation errors and the misreporting of joint actions by Byzantine teams. We propose the distributed team-orchestrating algorithm (DTOA), which combines team fictitious play with supervisor-based distributed belief learning. We prove the convergence of supervisors' belief estimates and establish that the induced learning dynamics converge to a near team-Nash equilibrium (TNE) in terms of the team-Nash gap (TNG). In the Byzantine setting, we consider a misreporting attack model and develop a Byzantine-resilient DTOA. We further provide probabilistic guarantees for Byzantine-team identification and establish an asymptotic bound on the honest TNG. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical findings, compare DTOA with baseline learning methods, and evaluate its performance in a Markov decision process setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes DTOA, a distributed learning algorithm for zero-sum potential team games where agents use supervisor-provided beliefs. Combines team fictitious play with distributed belief learning, proving convergence to near team-Nash equilibrium. Extends to Byzantine settings with a resilient variant offering probabilistic guarantees for identifying malicious teams.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent team games, agents often rely on supervisors for belief information rather than maintaining accurate common beliefs. However, supervisor-provided beliefs can be corrupted by estimation errors or deliberate misreporting by Byzantine (adversarial) teams. Existing methods lack robustness to such inaccuracies, motivating the need for a learning algorithm that can converge to equilibrium despite unreliable belief information.
AI.method: DTOA integrates team fictitious play with supervisor-based distributed belief learning. Supervisors estimate beliefs and share them with agents, who then update strategies. For Byzantine settings, a resilient variant incorporates a misreporting attack model and Byzantine-team identification mechanism. Theoretical analysis covers convergence of belief estimates, learning dynamics, and TNG bounds.
AI.result: Proved convergence of supervisors' belief estimates; established that DTOA dynamics converge to a near team-Nash equilibrium with bounded team-Nash gap. In the Byzantine setting, provided probabilistic guarantees for Byzantine-team identification and derived an asymptotic bound on the honest TNG. Numerical experiments validated theoretical findings and demonstrated superior performance over baselines, including in MDP settings.
AI.conclusion: DTOA effectively enables learning in zero-sum potential team games under unreliable supervisor belief information, with theoretical guarantees on convergence and robustness. The Byzantine-resilient extension further ensures reliable operation under adversarial conditions, with empirical results supporting the theoretical claims.

title: Tangent: An Empirical Study of Testing Practices for LLM-Based Agent Applications
summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build applications that perform complex, multi-step tasks involving reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments. Despite rapid progress in benchmarking LLM-based agents, very few studies have attempted to understand how such systems are tested in practice. In particular, testing levels, objectives, data patterns, test complexity, and validation strategies for agent applications remain underexplored. In this paper, we present an empirical study of testing practices in LLM-based agent applications using a large corpus of mined open-source projects. We construct a large-scale dataset of agent applications, tools, and tests, and manually label 2,572 test methods from 240 modules. From this analysis, we derive a taxonomy of 23 testing patterns across test fixtures, data, objectives, and assertions, and characterize tests by level (unit, module, integration). We complement this with structured interviews of 10 senior industry practitioners building agentic systems. Our results show that testing of LLM-based agent applications is dominated by narrowly scoped unit tests, with limited coverage of complex interactions, realistic scenarios, and non-functional requirements. Tests frequently rely on simplistic inputs, heavy mocking, and shallow validation, and agent-related tests exhibit low structural complexity. While industry practice places greater emphasis on non-functional testing than open-source projects, both reveal common gaps, including the lack of formal testing foundations, unclear test objectives, and challenges in generating high-quality test data. Based on these findings, we outline research directions toward more systematic and rigorous testing of agent applications, including foundations for agent testability, formalized test objectives, and fault-based testing techniques.

AI.tldr: An empirical study analyzing testing practices in LLM-based agent applications through mining open-source projects (2,572 test methods, 240 modules) and interviewing 10 industry practitioners. The study derives a taxonomy of 23 testing patterns and reveals that agent testing is dominated by narrow unit tests with simplistic inputs, heavy mocking, shallow validation, and limited coverage of complex interactions or non-functional requirements.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based agent benchmarks, very few studies examine how such systems are actually tested in practice. Testing levels, objectives, data patterns, test complexity, and validation strategies remain underexplored, creating a gap between benchmarking research and real-world testing needs.
AI.method: Mixed-methods empirical study: (1) mined a large corpus of open-source LLM-based agent projects to construct a dataset of applications, tools, and tests; (2) manually labeled 2,572 test methods from 240 modules; (3) derived a taxonomy of 23 testing patterns across test fixtures, data, objectives, and assertions; (4) characterized tests by level (unit, module, integration); (5) conducted structured interviews with 10 senior industry practitioners building agentic systems.
AI.result: Testing is dominated by narrowly scoped unit tests with limited coverage of complex interactions, realistic scenarios, and non-functional requirements. Tests frequently rely on simplistic inputs, heavy mocking, and shallow validation. Agent-related tests exhibit low structural complexity. Industry practice emphasizes non-functional testing more than open-source, but both share common gaps: lack of formal testing foundations, unclear test objectives, and challenges in generating high-quality test data.
AI.conclusion: The authors outline research directions toward more systematic and rigorous testing of agent applications, including foundations for agent testability, formalized test objectives, and fault-based testing techniques.

title: Jako Tako or Fluent? Presenting PoVisLE: A Polish Vision-Language Evaluation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on tasks such as image captioning, visual question answering, and image-to-text generation. However, they are predominantly trained on English-centric data, which limits their ability to handle culturally grounded visual understanding and leads to failures in interpreting region-specific meanings, symbolic content, and context-dependent visual cues. Existing benchmarks for cultural competence are often template-driven and focused on surface-level recognition, making them insufficient for evaluating deeper linguistic and pragmatic understanding in culturally situated settings. We introduce PoVisLE, a monocultural vision-language benchmark for Polish designed to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding under a grounded evaluation paradigm, where language is interpreted in interaction with visual context. The dataset contains 1,117 images and 2,366 manually annotated VQA pairs. Overall, our dataset provides a controlled and challenging resource for assessing culturally grounded vision-language understanding beyond surface-level recognition.

AI.tldr: PoVisLE is a Polish monocultural vision-language benchmark (1,117 images, 2,366 VQA pairs) designed to evaluate culturally grounded multimodal understanding beyond surface-level recognition, addressing the English-centric bias in existing VLMs.
AI.motivation: VLMs are predominantly trained on English-centric data, causing failures in interpreting culturally specific, region-bound visual content, symbolic meanings, and context-dependent cues. Existing cultural benchmarks rely on template-driven, surface-level recognition and lack depth in evaluating pragmatic, linguistically nuanced understanding in culturally situated settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce PoVisLE, a monocultural vision-language benchmark for Polish, comprising 1,117 images and 2,366 manually annotated VQA pairs. It employs a grounded evaluation paradigm where language understanding is assessed in tight interaction with visual context, targeting deeper linguistic and pragmatic competence rather than superficial recognition.
AI.result: The paper presents PoVisLE as a controlled, challenging resource for evaluating culturally grounded vision-language understanding. Specific experimental results on VLM performance are not detailed in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: PoVisLE fills a critical gap in vision-language evaluation by providing a non-English, culturally specific benchmark that tests pragmatic, context-bound multimodal understanding, moving beyond template-driven surface recognition.

title: LUCID: Latent-Skill Unified Control via Imagined Dynamics for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation requires composing versatile whole-body skills and reliable high-level decision making. Existing methods often coordinate pretrained skills with scripted planners, finite-state machines or task-specific model-free policies, restricting their ability to handle complex task sequences. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{LUCID}, a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that plans over reusable skills through imagined rollouts of a learned dynamics model. LUCID first trains a structured latent-conditioned low-level policy via adversarial imitation and then freezes it while jointly learning a high-level policy and macro-dynamics world model. The world model predicts the temporally extended state transitions induced by latent decisions, enabling high-level policy optimization through imagined rollouts. We evaluate our framework across various simulated multi-object rearrangement scenarios. Experimental results show that LUCID improves the full-task success and partial-completion rates compared to prior baseline methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in complex sequential loco-manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: LUCID is a hierarchical model-based RL framework that trains a low-level policy via adversarial imitation, then freezes it while jointly learning a high-level policy and world model. The world model enables planning over reusable skills through imagined rollouts, improving performance on long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation rely on scripted planners, finite-state machines, or task-specific model-free policies to coordinate pretrained skills. These methods lack the flexibility to handle complex, diverse task sequences.
AI.method: LUCID employs a two-stage hierarchical framework: (1) a structured latent-conditioned low-level policy is trained via adversarial imitation learning to produce reusable whole-body skills; (2) this low-level policy is frozen, and a high-level policy is jointly learned with a macro-dynamics world model that predicts temporally extended state transitions induced by latent skill decisions. The high-level policy is optimized through imagined rollouts in the learned world model.
AI.result: Evaluated on simulated multi-object rearrangement scenarios, LUCID achieves improved full-task success rates and partial-completion rates compared to prior baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: LUCID demonstrates that hierarchical model-based RL with a learned macro-dynamics model and reusable low-level skills is effective for complex sequential loco-manipulation tasks, outperforming prior approaches that use scripted or model-free coordination.

title: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
summary: As LLM agents move from decision support to autonomous procurement, firms need to know whether delegated negotiators create value, divide it predictably, and avoid money-losing contracts. We study this in a canonical supply chain bargaining problem: a buyer with private demand information negotiates a quantity-payment contract with an uninformed seller. We benchmark nine LLMs from OpenAI, Google, and Alibaba against a validated Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium across 9,840 LLM-to-LLM negotiations. First, capability governs value creation. Agents agree in 98.9% of negotiations and capture 95.4% of first-best surplus undiscounted, but average 2.98 rounds against the benchmark's 1.25, and this delay erodes 21-34% of surplus. Capability also governs reliability: baseline models accept individually irrational contracts in 19.2% of cases, versus 0.0-0.6% at mid-tier and flagship, making automated profit verification the binding guardrail below that threshold. Second, surplus capture is relational. Provider identity predicts who captures surplus better than capability rank: self-play buyer shares average 40% for OpenAI, 50% for Google, and 70% for Alibaba's Qwen, an ordering that survives restricted communication and no discounting. Reversing which provider sells moves the division by 7-18 percentage points, and the capable Qwen flagship is the weakest cross-family seller: vendor choice is a first-order distributional decision. Third, the prompt is a strategic lever. Delegation separates the principal's economic patience from the agent's prompted strategic patience, a free deployment choice that is the single strongest driver of surplus division (90% of explained variance). Together these establish an equilibrium-referenced audit of AI agents along three dimensions: discounted efficiency, distributional profile, and operational reliability.

AI.tldr: This paper audits nine LLMs (OpenAI, Google, Alibaba) as autonomous negotiators in a supply chain bargaining game with private buyer demand. Against a Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium benchmark across 9,840 agent-to-agent negotiations, it finds: (1) capability governs value creation and reliability — all models agree often and capture most surplus, but low-tier models frequently accept loss-making contracts; (2) surplus division is relational, driven by provider identity rather than capability rank; and (3) the prompt is the strongest strategic lever, with delegated patience explaining 90% of variance in surplus division.
AI.motivation: As firms increasingly deploy LLM agents for autonomous procurement and negotiation, there is no systematic framework for auditing whether these delegated negotiators create value, divide it predictably, and avoid money-losing contracts. The paper fills this gap by benchmarking LLM negotiators against a rigorous game-theoretic equilibrium in a canonical supply chain bargaining setting.
AI.method: The authors use a canonical supply chain bargaining problem: a buyer with private demand information negotiates a quantity-payment contract with an uninformed seller. They benchmark nine LLMs (from OpenAI, Google, Alibaba) across capability tiers against a validated Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium (PBE). The experiment runs 9,840 LLM-to-LLM negotiations, varying provider pairings, capability levels, prompting strategies (strategic patience), and communication regimes. Outcomes are evaluated along three audit dimensions: discounted efficiency (value creation net of bargaining delay), distributional profile (surplus division), and operational reliability (rate of individually irrational contract acceptance).
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Capability governs value creation and reliability — agents agree in 98.9% of negotiations and capture 95.4% of first-best surplus, but average 2.98 rounds vs. the benchmark's 1.25, and delay erodes 21–34% of surplus. Baseline models accept individually irrational contracts in 19.2% of cases vs. 0.0–0.6% for mid-tier/flagship models. (2) Surplus capture is relational — provider identity predicts surplus division better than capability rank: self-play buyer shares are ~40% (OpenAI), ~50% (Google), ~70% (Qwen/Alibaba). Reversing seller identity shifts division by 7–18 ppts. (3) Prompted strategic patience is the single strongest driver of surplus division, explaining 90% of variance, making the prompt a free and powerful strategic lever.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes an equilibrium-referenced audit framework for AI negotiating agents across three dimensions: discounted efficiency, distributional profile, and operational reliability. It demonstrates that LLM negotiators are broadly capable but that provider identity, capability tier, and prompt design are first-order strategic considerations. Critically, automated profit verification is a binding guardrail below flagship-tier models, and prompt engineering constitutes a free deployment choice with outsized distributional consequences.

title: The Transparency Trap: How AI Disclaimers Create Overconfidence in High-Stakes Decisions
summary: Current AI disclaimers often fail to function as intended due to warning habituation and a transparency paradox. As AI-generated information becomes pervasive in everyday decision-making, effective risk communication is increasingly critical for responsible design. This exploratory study examines how disclaimer placement and persuasive cues shape trust, perceived accuracy, and disclaimer engagement across three high-stakes domains: finance, medicine, and AI-generated content. Using a mixed within-between experimental design with 378 stimulus-level responses from 52 participants, we find that advisory content was generally trusted across conditions, even when disclaimers were present. A significant domain effect showed that medical content received the highest trust ratings. In the AI domain, the findings reveal a transparency paradox: some participants interpreted disclaimers not as warnings, but as signs of system self-awareness and honesty, paradoxically increasing perceived trustworthiness. Evidence of banner blindness further suggests that standardized AI disclaimers are insufficient to prevent over-reliance. Finance and medicine provide useful comparison domains by showing how users interpret warnings differently depending on context and perceived risk. These findings have vital implications for responsible AI design, algorithmic fairness, and consumer protection when users act on potentially misleading information in high-stakes settings.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how disclaimer placement and persuasive cues affect trust, perceived accuracy, and engagement with AI disclaimers across finance, medicine, and AI-generated content domains. Findings reveal a transparency paradox where disclaimers can increase trust in AI systems, alongside banner blindness that renders standardized warnings ineffective.
AI.motivation: Current AI disclaimers fail due to warning habituation and a transparency paradox. As AI-generated content permeates high-stakes decision-making, effective risk communication becomes critical for responsible design, yet little is known about how placement and persuasive cues influence user responses.
AI.method: A mixed within-between experimental design with 378 stimulus-level responses from 52 participants, testing disclaimer placement and persuasive cues across three domains: finance, medicine, and AI-generated content.
AI.result: Advisory content was generally trusted regardless of disclaimer presence. Medical content received the highest trust ratings (significant domain effect). In the AI domain, a transparency paradox emerged: disclaimers were interpreted as signals of system self-awareness and honesty, paradoxically increasing trust. Banner blindness indicated standardized disclaimers are insufficient to prevent over-reliance.
AI.conclusion: The findings carry vital implications for responsible AI design, algorithmic fairness, and consumer protection, particularly in high-stakes settings where users act on potentially misleading information. Standardized disclaimers alone are inadequate; context-sensitive warning strategies are needed.

title: Algebraic Attack on Convolutional Neural Networks with Max Pooling
summary:
Recovering the weights and biases of deep neural networks (DNNs) via black-box input-output queries, known as parameter extraction attacks, has been extensively studied for ReLU-based fully connected neural networks (FCNNs), but remains unexplored for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the max pooling function, a core architecture for computer vision and multimedia processing. The key challenge lies in the CNN max pooling layer, which introduces an additional non-linearity and hides ReLU critical points, rendering existing FCNN extraction methods inapplicable. To address this gap, we propose the first cryptanalytic extraction attack tailored for CNNs with the max pooling function.
  First, we establish an algebraic representation of CNNs, formally proving that CNNs are piecewise linear functions enabling the extension of linearity-based extraction principles. We then identify two novel types of critical points in CNNs: ReLU-Pooling Critical Points (RPCPs) and Pooling Switching Points (PSPs). We design complementary extraction techniques: a pattern matching method for RPCPs to recover partial signatures and signs, and an internal differential extraction attack for PSPs, inspired by cryptographic internal differential analysis, to recover high-accuracy signatures. Given that PSPs are far more abundant than RPCPs and yield a highly efficient extraction method, and that RPCPs are indispensable for bias recovery, we integrate both methods: the PSP method enables efficient signature extraction, while a single RPCP recovers the sign and bias.
  We evaluate our attack on multiple CNN architectures, including modern adaptations of LeNet-5, trained on random data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves high extraction accuracy with polynomial query complexity and runtime, even for deep CNN layers. This work fills a research gap in CNN security.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first parameter extraction attack against convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with max pooling, overcoming the non-linearity challenges that previously limited such attacks to fully connected ReLU networks. The authors identify two novel critical point types (RPCPs and PSPs) and develop complementary extraction methods, achieving high-accuracy parameter recovery with polynomial query complexity.
AI.motivation: Prior parameter extraction attacks via black-box queries have been extensively studied only for ReLU-based fully connected neural networks (FCNNs). CNNs with max pooling — a core architecture for computer vision — introduce additional non-linearity that hides ReLU critical points, making existing FCNN extraction methods inapplicable. This gap in CNN security analysis motivates the work.
AI.method: The authors first establish an algebraic representation proving CNNs are piecewise linear functions. They then identify two novel critical point types: ReLU-Pooling Critical Points (RPCPs) and Pooling Switching Points (PSPs). Two complementary extraction techniques are designed: (1) a pattern matching method for RPCPs to recover partial signatures and signs, and (2) an internal differential extraction attack for PSPs (inspired by cryptographic internal differential analysis) for high-accuracy signature recovery. The methods are integrated: PSPs enable efficient signature extraction, while a single RPCP suffices for sign and bias recovery.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on multiple CNN architectures (including modern LeNet-5 adaptations trained on random data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10) demonstrates high extraction accuracy with polynomial query complexity and runtime, even for deep CNN layers.
AI.conclusion: This work fills a significant research gap in CNN security by demonstrating that parameter extraction attacks are feasible against CNNs with max pooling, extending the threat landscape beyond FCNNs to architectures central to computer vision and multimedia processing.

title: What Would Fix This RAG Failure? Auditing Counterfactual Response with Paired Evidence Interventions
summary: A failed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answer can be consistent with several unseen responses to evidence repair. We introduce Pair-ID, an offline audit that holds one query, retrieval state, and reader constant, then crosses two operations, adding missing support and deleting verified nonsupport, to measure a same-failure counterfactual response vector. A complete funnel over 19,981 benchmark queries identifies 11,105 eligible Qwen failures, from which a prospectively fixed SHA-256 ordering selects 1,200 before generating any sampled response. Among 1,190 regenerated-valid failures, support addition repairs 197/600 JOINT cases (0.328, 95% CI [0.292, 0.367]), and deletion repairs 162/1,190 cases (0.136, 95% CI [0.117, 0.155]); length- and position-matched shams retain semantic contrasts of 0.223 and 0.101. The original view carries partial predictive signal for individual response cells (macro AUROC 0.678; Brier 0.152 versus 0.160 for a marginal baseline), but exact-vector accuracy, 0.637, does not exceed the 0.646 majority-vector baseline, and vector macro-F1 is 0.170. Across four readers, both marginal sensitivities recur, while pooled exact-vector agreement is 0.675-0.765 and JOINT-only agreement falls to 0.538-0.691. These results show that evidence sensitivity occurs at meaningful rates in the hash-selected eligible-failure sample, is only partially predictable from the observed failure, and is conditional on the reader. The evidence supports a frame-scoped offline response audit, not an information-theoretic impossibility result, reader-independent taxonomy, or runtime repair policy.

AI.tldr: Pair-ID is an offline audit method that fixes retrieval and reader while measuring how RAG failures respond to two counterfactual operations—adding missing support and deleting nonsupport. In 1,190 validated Qwen failures, support addition repairs 32.8% of JOINT cases and deletion repairs 13.6%; repair outcomes are only partially predictable from the original failure and vary across readers, supporting frame-scoped offline auditing rather than runtime repair or reader-independent taxonomies.
AI.motivation: Current RAG evaluation treats failures as monolithic, but a single failed answer may be consistent with multiple counterfactual repairs. The paper aims to quantify evidence sensitivity—whether adding or removing evidence changes the answer—within a rigorous, preregistered offline audit framework that avoids the confounds of online repair policies.
AI.method: Pair-ID fixes query, retrieval state, and reader; then applies two atomic operations (adding missing support, deleting verified nonsupport) to produce a counterfactual response vector. A funnel over 19,981 benchmark queries yields 11,105 eligible Qwen failures, from which a prospectively fixed SHA-256 ordering selects 1,200 cases before any generation. Sham controls (length- and position-matched) provide semantic contrast baselines. Predictive modeling uses macro AUROC, Brier scores, exact-vector accuracy, and macro-F1 against majority baselines. Four readers are tested for cross-reader agreement and sensitivity generalization.
AI.result: Support addition repairs 197/600 JOINT cases (0.328; 95% CI [0.292, 0.367]); deletion repairs 162/1,190 (0.136; 95% CI [0.117, 0.155]). Sham contrasts are 0.223 and 0.101. Predictive signals are partial: macro AUROC 0.678, Brier 0.152 vs. marginal 0.160; exact-vector accuracy 0.637 does not beat majority baseline (0.646); macro-F1 is 0.170. Across four readers, marginal sensitivities recur, pooled exact-vector agreement is 0.675–0.765, but JOINT-only agreement drops to 0.538–0.691.
AI.conclusion: Evidence sensitivity is real, occurs at meaningful rates, is only partially predictable from observed failures, and is conditional on the reader. These findings support a frame-scoped offline response audit methodology rather than an information-theoretic impossibility result, a reader-independent failure taxonomy, or a runtime repair policy.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a new benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coding systems on real-world full-stack projects. It uses 10 authentic projects, hierarchical rubrics, and a dynamic probing grader (TAgent) to jointly measure functional success, latency, and token cost. Experiments across 100 runs reveal that organizational topology rivals model capability in determining the speed–cost–quality trade-off, with structured pipelines outperforming heavy managerial oversight.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks suffer from three key limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, (2) conflation of reasoning with communication, and (3) reward signals that only capture superficial task completion. There is no rigorous, reproducible standard for evaluating how multi-agent teams actually build software in real-world settings.
AI.method: MSEval is grounded in 10 authentic full-stack projects spanning 10 domains, scored via hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate through periodic sync intervals and deploy via native CI/CD pipelines. The automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to measure functional success, wall-clock latency, and prefix-cached token cost simultaneously.
AI.result: Across 100 runs, organizational topology was found to rival model capability in shaping the speed–cost–quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying topology shifted scores by over 30 points and doubled wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converged fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degraded performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. It demonstrates that how agents are organized (topology) is as critical as which models they use, and the benchmark is publicly released to facilitate further research.

title: Generics-Aware Fuzz Target Generation for Rust Libraries via Structured API Analysis
summary: Fuzzing Rust library APIs requires constructing well-typed, compilable call sequences that satisfy ownership rules, generic parameters, and trait bounds; existing tools ignore these constraints or use shallow heuristics, yielding low coverage. We present GRAFT, which extracts structured API information from Rust documentation, builds an API dependency graph via recursive generics-aware type matching, and uses topology-guided traversal plus LLM synthesis with compiler-error feedback to produce compilable fuzz targets. On 13 crates from crates.io, GRAFT achieves 80.75% macro-average API coverage at 96.19% compilation success, outperforming RULF and RPG by 4.76x and 2.43x, and reaching 1.41x the average API coverage of deepSURF on crates with unsafe-reaching APIs.

AI.tldr: GRAFT is a fuzzing framework for Rust library APIs that leverages documentation-extracted API dependency graphs, topology-guided traversal, and LLM-based synthesis with compiler feedback to generate well-typed, compilable fuzz targets, achieving 80.75% API coverage and 96.19% compilation success.
AI.motivation: Existing Rust API fuzzing tools either ignore Rust's strict type system constraints (ownership, generics, trait bounds) or rely on shallow heuristics, leading to low API coverage and high compilation failure rates.
AI.method: GRAFT extracts structured API information from Rust documentation (rustdoc), constructs an API dependency graph using recursive, generics-aware type matching, then generates fuzz targets via topology-guided graph traversal combined with LLM-based synthesis that iteratively refines code using compiler-error feedback until compilation succeeds.
AI.result: Evaluated on 13 crates.io crates, GRAFT achieves 80.75% macro-average API coverage at 96.19% compilation success rate, outperforming RULF by 4.76x and RPG by 2.43x in coverage, and reaching 1.41x the average API coverage of deepSURF on crates containing unsafe-reaching APIs.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT demonstrates that combining structured API knowledge extraction with LLM-guided synthesis and compiler feedback is a highly effective approach for automated fuzz target generation in strongly-typed languages like Rust.

title: On the use of foundation models in cognitive science
summary: A host of recent studies have evaluated the cognitive and developmental alignment of Foundation Models (FMs). These investigations include evaluations of their correspondence to adult performance across a range of cognitive domains, as well as whether aspects of model training track children's cognitive development. However, using FMs as candidate cognitive models poses significant methodological and conceptual challenges. A key question underlies this effort: under what conditions does behavioral alignment justify treating FMs as explanatory models of cognition? In this paper, we articulate a four-stage inferential framework for evaluating FMs as cognitive and developmental models: adapting human experimental tasks to model-compatible formats, specifying linking hypotheses that map model outputs to human measures, evaluating behavioral correspondence, and comparing across candidate models or manipulations. We clarify the role of linking hypotheses in mapping model outputs to human behavioral measures, identify challenges that constrain alignment claims, and propose principles for theory-driven and comparative evaluation. Throughout, we argue that behavioral fit alone is insufficient. Alignment becomes scientifically meaningful only when embedded within explicit theoretical commitments, theory-diagnostic tasks, and systematic contrastive evaluation across candidate models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a four-stage inferential framework for evaluating Foundation Models as cognitive and developmental models, arguing that behavioral alignment alone is insufficient—meaningful alignment requires explicit theoretical commitments, theory-diagnostic tasks, and systematic contrastive evaluation across candidate models.
AI.motivation: Recent work has increasingly evaluated whether Foundation Models align with human cognitive performance and developmental trajectories. However, using FMs as candidate cognitive models raises methodological and conceptual challenges. The paper aims to clarify the conditions under which behavioral correspondence between FMs and humans can justifiably support explanatory claims about cognition.
AI.method: The authors articulate a four-stage inferential framework: (1) adapting human experimental tasks to model-compatible formats, (2) specifying linking hypotheses that map model outputs to human behavioral measures, (3) evaluating behavioral correspondence, and (4) comparing across candidate models or experimental manipulations. The framework emphasizes the critical role of linking hypotheses and theory-driven, contrastive evaluation.
AI.result: The paper identifies key challenges that constrain alignment claims, including the insufficiency of behavioral fit alone, and proposes principles for rigorous comparative evaluation. It demonstrates that alignment becomes scientifically meaningful only when embedded in explicit theoretical commitments and systematic contrastive model comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral alignment between FMs and humans does not, on its own, warrant treating FMs as explanatory models of cognition. Scientific validity requires embedding such alignment within a clear theoretical framework, using theory-diagnostic tasks, and conducting systematic comparisons across candidate models to rule out alternative explanations.

title: From Benchmark Performance to Tool Deployment: Human-in-the-Loop Anomaly Detection
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Accepted as a regular paper at the 25th International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA 2026)
summary:
Automated anomaly detection methods often report strong performance on curated academic benchmarks, but their behavior under real-world industrial conditions is less clear. In this work, we evaluate 19 unsupervised anomaly detection models on the BowTie dataset, a challenging manufacturing dataset with reflective surfaces, subtle defects, and profile-specific variation. In contrast to benchmark results, we observe that model performance is less stable than typically reported on standard benchmarks such as MVTec AD, highly sensitive to preprocessing, and inconsistent across conditions, with no single approach emerging as uniformly robust; a consensus audit further indicates that nominal-data quality affects deployment.
  Motivated by these findings, we developed and initially deployed a unified human-in-the-loop framework for manufactured-part inspection that combines image annotation, AI-assisted defect detection, and an integrated validation engine, replacing a prior manual visual inspection and documentation workflow. The system supports heatmap-guided defect review, SAM-refined candidate regions for inspector acceptance, rejection, or boundary adjustment, mask evaluation where annotations exist, and review history for inspector consistency and onboarding. Together, the results highlight the gap between benchmark performance and deployment reality, and provide a practical framework for addressing it.

AI.tldr: An evaluation of 19 unsupervised anomaly detection models on a challenging industrial manufacturing dataset reveals significant performance instability compared to curated benchmarks, motivating the development of a human-in-the-loop inspection framework combining AI-assisted detection, SAM-refined regions, and validation tools.
AI.motivation: Benchmark results for anomaly detection models (e.g., on MVTec AD) do not reflect real-world industrial performance, where reflective surfaces, subtle defects, and profile variation degrade reliability. The authors aim to quantify this gap and address it practically.
AI.method: First, a systematic evaluation of 19 unsupervised anomaly detection models on the BowTie dataset, assessing sensitivity to preprocessing and cross-condition consistency, with a consensus audit on nominal-data quality. Second, a deployed human-in-the-loop framework integrating image annotation, AI-assisted detection with heatmap guidance, SAM-refined candidate proposals, mask evaluation, and review history for inspector workflows.
AI.result: Model performance is unstable, highly preprocessing-sensitive, and inconsistent across conditions; no single model is uniformly robust. Nominal-data quality significantly affects deployment outcomes. The human-in-the-loop system successfully replaced prior manual inspection with a validated, auditable workflow.
AI.conclusion: A substantial gap exists between benchmark and real-world anomaly detection performance. Integrating human oversight via a structured framework with AI assistance, region refinement, and validation tools offers a practical path toward reliable industrial deployment.

title: TREAT: Evaluating Access to Formal Knowledge across Equivalent Mathematical Representations
comment: Accepted at 28th International Symposium on Symbolic and Numeric Algorithms for Scientific Computing (SYNASC 2026)
summary: AI systems increasingly operate between flexible input representations and formal objects used by downstream tools. A key challenge is recognizing when an unfamiliar formulation denotes a known formal object. We study this challenge through theorem recognition: given an equivalence-preserving transformation of a theorem condition, a model must recover the theorem identity associated with the standard statement. We introduce TREAT, a benchmark for evaluating whether large language models can recover known theorem identities from equivalence-preserving formula-level transformations. Rather than paraphrasing theorem text, TREAT changes the mathematical form of theorem conditions themselves, expressing known results through residual equations, witness statements, optimization identities, set relations, operator forms, and proof-intermediate characterizations. Starting from scraped theorem pages, we filter for entries with usable mathematical expression forms, extract canonical theorem conditions, and generate transformed variants with recorded assumptions and inverse mappings. The final corpus contains 737 theorem identities and 29,480 transformed rows. On a test panel, the best model retrieves the correct theorem identity in only 60.73% of cases. Other systems reveal different failure modes, including abstention, wrong detection, and malformed outputs. These suggest that theorem knowledge can be fragile under equivalent changes in representation. TREAT therefore provides a controlled testbed for evaluating representation-robust access to formal knowledge, with broader relevance to domains that require stable target objects, explicit equivalence relations, validation procedures, and auditable scoring.

AI.tldr: TREAT is a benchmark that tests whether large language models can recognize known theorems when their mathematical conditions are expressed in equivalent but non-standard forms (e.g., residual equations, optimization identities, set relations). Across 737 theorem identities and 29,480 transformed variants, the best model achieves only 60.73% accuracy, revealing that theorem knowledge in LLMs is fragile under representation changes.
AI.motivation: AI systems increasingly bridge flexible input representations and formal downstream tools. The core challenge is recognizing when an unfamiliar formulation denotes a known formal object. Theorem recognition serves as a controlled testbed for this problem: can a model identify a known theorem when its condition is rewritten in an equivalence-preserving but mathematically different form?
AI.method: The authors construct TREAT by scraping theorem pages, filtering entries with usable mathematical expressions, extracting canonical theorem conditions, and generating transformed variants through six transformation types: residual equations, witness statements, optimization identities, set relations, operator forms, and proof-intermediate characterizations. Each transformation preserves logical equivalence and is accompanied by recorded assumptions and inverse mappings. The final dataset comprises 737 theorem identities and 29,480 transformed rows.
AI.result: On the test panel, the best-performing model retrieves the correct theorem identity in only 60.73% of cases. Other systems exhibit distinct failure modes including abstention (refusing to answer), wrong detection (incorrect theorem identification), and malformed outputs, indicating that theorem knowledge is brittle under equivalent representational changes.
AI.conclusion: TREAT provides a controlled testbed for evaluating representation-robust access to formal knowledge. The findings have broader implications for domains requiring stable target objects, explicit equivalence relations, validation procedures, and auditable scoring — highlighting a significant weakness in current LLMs' ability to maintain semantic understanding across mathematically equivalent reformulations.

title: How to Ask the AI: A User Perspective Survey for Large Language Model Prompting
summary: AI tools like ChatGPT and DeepSeek, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), allow users to obtain instant and effective content responses simply by typing requests, such as ``plan a three-day Vienna trip'', ``solve the attached mathematical problem'', ``draft an email to inquire review progress'', etc., which are also known as LLM prompts. Crafting clear and well-structured prompts leads to more appropriate LLM feedback, which effectively bridges human-LLM interaction. Although prompting appears accessible to non-expert users, precisely organizing effective prompts is a highly systematic and skillful process, presenting potential challenges even for experienced users. This survey explores the principles, taxonomy, and organization of prompts from a user-centered perspective. Differing from the existing surveys that primarily focus on technical principles and application scenarios of LLMs, this paper provides actionable guidelines for formulating effective LLM prompts across diverse real-world tasks and specifically contributes by: 1) developing an intuitive evaluation strategy for prompt efficacy, 2) providing prompting workflow demonstrations on representative applications, and 3) maintaining a dynamically updated open-source project to ensure the core takeaways remain up-to-date. These measures lower the threshold for users to correctly understand and craft prompts that align with evolving application scenarios. This work will be maintained as a living GitHub project \href{https://github.com/Yunfan-Zhang/TAI_Guideline-Table}{\textcolor{blue}{here}}.

AI.tldr: A user-centered survey that provides actionable guidelines, an evaluation strategy, and workflow demonstrations for crafting effective LLM prompts, supported by a living open-source repository.
AI.motivation: While LLM prompting appears accessible, crafting clear and well-structured prompts is a highly systematic skill that challenges even experienced users. Existing surveys focus on technical LLM principles and application scenarios, leaving a gap in practical, user-centered guidance for prompt formulation across diverse real-world tasks.
AI.method: The authors adopt a user-centered perspective to survey prompting principles, taxonomy, and organization. They contribute: (1) an intuitive evaluation strategy for assessing prompt efficacy, (2) prompting workflow demonstrations on representative applications, and (3) a dynamically updated open-source GitHub project to keep guidance current with evolving LLM capabilities.
AI.result: The survey delivers structured, actionable guidelines that lower the barrier for non-expert and experienced users alike to understand and craft effective prompts. The living repository ensures long-term relevance as application scenarios evolve.
AI.conclusion: Effective prompting is a teachable, systematic skill. By shifting the focus from LLM internals to user-facing prompt design strategies and maintaining a continuously updated resource, this work bridges the gap between human intent and LLM response quality, democratizing effective LLM interaction.

title: Defending Retrieval-Augmented Intrusion Detection Against Knowledge Poisoning and Prompt Injection
comment: 14 pages with Appnedix, 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE CIC 2026, Research Track (double-blind review)
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models to classify network flows and generate human-readable incident reports by retrieving semantically similar historical traffic from a vector knowledge base. However, the retrieval layer introduces vulnerabilities to knowledge poisoning and prompt-injection attacks. We present RAG-IDS, a three-tier multi-agent intrusion detection framework with a retrieval-boundary defense combining soft trust scoring, label-embedding consistency checking (LECC), and prompt sanitization, designed to recover classification quality under retrieval-layer attack. Experiments on CIC-UNSW-NB15 show recovery relative to clean undefended performance ranging from R=1.0 at 1% poisoning to R=0.57 at 30%, with negligible clean-performance overhead. Under prompt injection, multi-document retrieval limits label-flip success to 0.6-2.4%, compared with 35-55% for single-document retrieval. Ablation results show that LECC is the primary contributor to robustness, while soft trust-based demotion outperforms hard filtering. The defended RAG pipeline offers an explainable, attack-resilient foundation for intrusion detection, well suited for hybrid deployment alongside high-throughput classifiers.

AI.tldr: RAG-IDS is a three-tier multi-agent intrusion detection framework that defends against knowledge poisoning and prompt-injection attacks on RAG-based network flow classification, using soft trust scoring, label-embedding consistency checking (LECC), and prompt sanitization to recover classification quality with minimal clean-performance overhead.
AI.motivation: RAG enhances LLMs for network intrusion detection by retrieving similar historical traffic, but the retrieval layer is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning and prompt-injection attacks. Existing defenses are insufficient, motivating a robust, explainable defense framework tailored for RAG-based IDS.
AI.method: A three-tier multi-agent framework combining: (1) soft trust scoring to demote suspicious retrieved documents; (2) label-embedding consistency checking (LECC) to verify alignment between document labels and embeddings; and (3) prompt sanitization to neutralize injected malicious content. Multi-document retrieval further limits attack surface compared to single-document retrieval.
AI.result: On CIC-UNSW-NB15: recovery relative to clean undefended performance ranges from R=1.0 at 1% poisoning to R=0.57 at 30% poisoning. Multi-document retrieval limits prompt-injection label-flip success to 0.6–2.4% vs. 35–55% for single-document. LECC is the primary robustness contributor; soft trust-based demotion outperforms hard filtering.
AI.conclusion: The defended RAG pipeline provides an explainable, attack-resilient foundation for intrusion detection, well suited for hybrid deployment alongside high-throughput classifiers.

title: Guardian Crawler: Retrieval-First Knowledge Discovery with Bounded LLM Augmentation for Noisy Web Intelligence
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted as a Short Paper at KDIR 2026 (International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Information Retrieval)
summary: Retrieving relevant evidence from noisy web data is challenging, particularly in sensitive domains containing incomplete reports, heterogeneous language, and irrelevant content. We present Guardian Crawler, a reproducible retrieval-first testbed for controlled experiments on knowledge discovery and evidence-grounded summarization over synthetic web-like corpora. The architecture combines BM25 retrieval with risk-aware, embedding-augmented, and hybrid reranking, followed by constrained retrieval-augmented generation with explicit document citations. Experiments on a synthetic 900-document corpus and 10 queries produced the highest descriptive retrieval scores under risk-based reranking, with P@10 = 1.00 and NDCG@10 = 0.94, compared with 0.94 and 0.81 for BM25. The best hybrid and BM25+Semantic configurations reached NDCG@10 values of 0.94 and 0.88, respectively. All 41 evaluable generated bullets passed the lexical coverage threshold; an automated LLM judge classified 36 as supported, one as partially supported, and four as unsupported. These results demonstrate the feasibility of Guardian Crawler as a controlled testbed but do not establish statistical superiority, human-validated faithfulness, or transfer to live-web investigative environments.

AI.tldr: Guardian Crawler is a retrieval-first testbed for evidence-grounded summarization over synthetic web-like corpora, combining BM25 retrieval with risk-aware and hybrid reranking. Experiments on a 900-document corpus show risk-based reranking achieves P@10=1.00 and NDCG@10=0.94, outperforming vanilla BM25, though results do not establish statistical superiority or real-world transfer.
AI.motivation: Retrieving relevant evidence from noisy, heterogeneous web data is difficult, especially in sensitive domains with incomplete reports and irrelevant content. Existing approaches lack a reproducible, controlled experimental framework for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation pipelines in such settings.
AI.method: The system integrates: (1) BM25 as a baseline retriever; (2) risk-aware, embedding-augmented, and hybrid reranking strategies applied post-retrieval; (3) constrained retrieval-augmented generation with explicit document citations. Evaluation uses a synthetic 900-document corpus with 10 queries, measuring Precision@10, NDCG@10, lexical coverage of generated bullets, and automated LLM-based support classification.
AI.result: Risk-based reranking yielded the highest scores: P@10=1.00, NDCG@10=0.94, versus BM25 baseline of 0.94 and 0.81 respectively. Hybrid and BM25+Semantic configurations reached NDCG@10 of 0.94 and 0.88. Of 41 evaluable generated bullets, all passed lexical coverage thresholds; an LLM judge classified 36 as supported, 1 as partially supported, and 4 as unsupported.
AI.conclusion: Guardian Crawler demonstrates feasibility as a controlled, reproducible testbed for retrieval-first evidence-grounded summarization. However, the study does not claim statistical superiority, human-validated faithfulness, or generalizability to live-web environments.

title: Fusing UI Structure & Semantics for Feature-Oriented App Screen Retrieval & Clustering
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026), Benevento, Italy
summary:
User Interface (UI) programming is challenging due to the complex abstraction gap between code and graphical software representations. To bridge this gap, UI programming tools often rely on screen retrieval and clustering, which require accurate similarity measures based on overlapping features. However, computing feature-oriented similarity is difficult because screens with similar functionality often exhibit design variations.
  To address this, we propose FRAME (ReinForced UseR InterfAce Screen EMbedding with Graphical Structural ComprEhension), a multi-modal, neuro-symbolic embedding technique. FRAME constructs symbolic, graph-based representations of UI components to encode salient relationships and capture feature patterns across different screens. It leverages large vision-language models for visual and lexical encoding, alongside a novel UI-specific computational geometry algorithm that enables weighted embedding propagation. Across three benchmarks, FRAME outperforms strong baselines by up to 13% MRR in search and 7.6 percentage points in clustering accuracy. A comprehensive ablation study further confirms the benefit of each component, demonstrating FRAME's potential for enhancing automated UI design and testing tools.

AI.tldr: FRAME is a multi-modal, neuro-symbolic embedding technique for UI screens that combines graph-based symbolic representations with large vision-language models and a novel geometry-aware propagation algorithm, outperforming baselines by up to 13% MRR in retrieval and 7.6 pp in clustering.
AI.motivation: UI programming tools rely on screen retrieval and clustering, which demand accurate similarity measures.
