However, computing feature-oriented similarity is difficult because functionally similar screens often exhibit significant design variations, making overlap-based feature comparison unreliable.
AI.method: FRAME constructs symbolic, graph-based representations of UI components to encode salient spatial and structural relationships. It integrates large vision-language models for visual and lexical encoding and introduces a novel UI-specific computational geometry algorithm that performs weighted embedding propagation across the graph structure.
AI.result: FRAME outperforms strong baselines by up to 13% MRR in screen retrieval/search and up to 7.6 percentage points in clustering accuracy across three benchmarks. A comprehensive ablation study validates the contribution of each component.
AI.conclusion: FRAME demonstrates strong potential for enhancing automated UI design and testing tools by providing robust, feature-oriented screen embeddings that are resilient to design variations.

title: "Many Are My Names": The Anatomy of the Assistant and Its Personas via Sparse Autoencoders
summary: How a language model internally represents who is speaking, the Assistant, an assigned roleplay persona, or a narrated story character, remains underexplored. We study speaker representations using a dataset of user-expressed emotional text and corresponding model responses. We decompose three generation settings (Assistant, Roleplay, and Story) into sparse autoencoder features extracted at turn-boundary and pronoun-token positions and selected through a filtering pipeline for different depths. We characterize each surviving feature through its steering effects and activation distribution. Our main finding is that the Assistant and roleplay personas are not independent alternatives: personas retain the Assistant-associated feature core while progressively differentiating from it across layers, starting from operational machinery towards behavioral and stylistic features. Meanwhile, generated story characters lack the Assistant-associated core. Both Story and Roleplay can be distinguished from the Assistant with Immersive Simulation Mode. However, the Assistant can sometimes enter or slowly drift into it even in the default setting.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how language models internally represent different speaker identities (Assistant, Roleplay persona, Story character) using sparse autoencoder features. The key finding is that roleplay personas retain an Assistant-associated feature core while progressively differentiating across layers, whereas story characters lack this core entirely.
AI.motivation: Understanding how language models internally represent speaker identity — whether acting as the default Assistant, adopting a roleplay persona, or narrating a story character — remains largely unexplored. This gap motivates a mechanistic interpretability investigation into speaker representations.
AI.method: The authors use a dataset of user emotional text paired with model responses across three generation settings: Assistant, Roleplay, and Story. They decompose representations using sparse autoencoder features extracted at turn-boundary and pronoun-token positions, filtered through a depth-based selection pipeline. Surviving features are characterized via steering effects and activation distribution analysis.
AI.result: The primary finding is that the Assistant and roleplay personas are not independent alternatives: roleplay personas retain an Assistant-associated feature core while progressively differentiating from it across layers, moving from operational machinery toward behavioral and stylistic features. In contrast, generated story characters lack this Assistant-associated core. Both Story and Roleplay modes can be distinguished from Assistant via an "Immersive Simulation Mode," though the Assistant can sometimes enter or drift into this mode even in default settings.
AI.conclusion: Speaker identity in language models exhibits a hierarchical structure where roleplay personas build upon and differentiate from an Assistant core, whereas story characters form distinct representations. The phenomenon of "Immersive Simulation Mode" suggests fluid boundaries between speaker modes, with implications for understanding and controlling model behavior.

title: The Sample Complexity of Policy Learning with Mu-Resets
summary: We study policy-based reinforcement learning under the $μ$-resets interaction protocol of Kakade and Langford [KL02]. This interaction protocol enables the learner to sample trajectories from a given exploratory reset distribution $μ$, in addition to the starting distribution. We resolve the question raised by [KLS25] on the role of policy realizability for the sample complexity of this problem. Critically, the dependence on horizon $H$ is governed by the notion of coverage assumed of the reset distribution. Under bounded all-policy concentrability, we show a $\exp(Ω(H))$ sample complexity lower bound; with bounded pushforward concentrability, we show the dependence on horizon is tightly characterized as $\exp(Θ(\sqrt H))$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies policy-based RL under the μ-resets protocol and resolves the sample complexity dependence on horizon H under different coverage assumptions of the reset distribution. Under bounded all-policy concentrability, the lower bound is exponential in H (exp(Ω(H))); under bounded pushforward concentrability, the dependence tightens to exp(Θ(√H)).
AI.motivation: Kakade and Langford introduced the μ-resets interaction protocol, where the learner can sample from an exploratory reset distribution μ in addition to the starting distribution. Recent work [KLS25] raised the question of how policy realizability affects sample complexity in this setting. This paper aims to resolve that open question, specifically characterizing how the horizon H affects sample complexity under different coverage assumptions on μ.
AI.method: The authors derive sample complexity lower bounds under two different concentrability (coverage) assumptions: (1) bounded all-policy concentrability, and (2) bounded pushforward concentrability. They prove a exp(Ω(H)) lower bound under the former and a tight exp(Θ(√H)) characterization under the latter, demonstrating how the choice of coverage notion fundamentally governs the horizon dependence.
AI.result: Under bounded all-policy concentrability, the sample complexity has an unavoidable exp(Ω(H)) dependence on horizon. Under bounded pushforward concentrability, the horizon dependence is sharply characterized as exp(Θ(√H)), which is significantly milder. This shows that the coverage assumption on μ critically determines the horizon-dependent difficulty of the problem.
AI.conclusion: The role of policy realizability in the μ-resets RL setting is resolved: the horizon dependence is governed by which concentrability notion bounds the reset distribution. Pushforward concentrability yields substantially better (though still exponential) dependence than all-policy concentrability, providing a tight characterization.

title: An AI Scientist that Doesn't Drift: Taste, Structure, and Falsifiable Findings in a Quadruped Navigation Research Loop
summary: Autonomous research loops driven by large language models can run machine-learning experiments at scale but tend to drift toward local refinements of whichever metric they optimise rather than testing the hypotheses that motivate the experiments. We address this structurally and present an AI Scientist for studying generalisation in quadruped robot navigation policies in simulation. Building on the autoresearch paradigm of Karpathy, our loop adds three components: an immutable experiment card that pairs each iteration's prediction with its outcome under a fixed schema, so a falsified hypothesis cannot be retconned; specialised subagents restricted to mechanical roles; and kkanbu, a preference oracle that holds the user's research taste as a typed knowledge graph and is the only component permitted to make subjective judgements. To isolate the oracle we run the identical loop twice across eleven research streams, with and without kkanbu. Neither arm drifts: both falsify roughly three quarters of their own hypotheses, and the best trained policy comes from the oracle-less arm. What the oracle changes is direction, not score: it alone explores test-time adaptation, it authored the winning designs where its arm led, and it carried lessons across streams that the other arm repeatedly re-derived. The scaffold keeps the loop honest; kkanbu decides where it looks.

AI.tldr: An AI Scientist loop for robot navigation is augmented with an immutable experiment card, role-restricted subagents, and a user-preference oracle (kkanbu) encoded as a knowledge graph. In an ablation across 11 research streams, both oracle and oracle-less arms falsify ~75% of hypotheses; the oracle doesn't improve best-policy score but steers exploration toward test-time adaptation, cross-stream knowledge transfer, and more innovative designs.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM-driven research loops tend to drift toward local metric optimization rather than genuine hypothesis testing. The authors aim to structurally enforce honest falsification and introduce a mechanism for injecting user research taste without corrupting the objectivity of experimental outcomes.
AI.method: Building on Karpathy's autoresearch paradigm, the authors add three components: (1) an immutable experiment card that locks each iteration's prediction–outcome pair under a fixed schema to prevent retroactive reinterpretation; (2) specialized subagents restricted to purely mechanical roles; (3) kkanbu, a preference oracle that encodes the user's research taste as a typed knowledge graph and is the sole component allowed to make subjective judgments. The loop is run twice across eleven research streams — once with kkanbu, once without — to isolate the oracle's effect.
AI.result: Both arms falsify approximately 75% of their own hypotheses, demonstrating no drift. The best trained policy emerges from the oracle-less arm. However, kkanbu changes research direction: it alone explores test-time adaptation, authors the winning designs in streams where its arm leads, and transfers lessons across streams that the other arm repeatedly re-derives.
AI.conclusion: The scaffold (immutable experiment card + role-restricted subagents) keeps the research loop honest by preventing hypothesis drift. The kkanbu preference oracle does not improve raw metric scores but shapes where the loop looks — enabling exploration of richer ideas like test-time adaptation and cross-stream knowledge reuse.

title: EmoPatient: An Emotion-Directed Patient Simulator for Realistic Palliative Care Communication Training
summary: Effective communication during palliative care discussions is a critical clinical skill, yet training clinicians to manage complex patient emotions remains challenging. Large language model (LLM)-based patient simulators provide a scalable approach for communication training, but most existing systems treat patient emotion as static and fail to capture the dynamic emotional shifts observed in clinical interactions. We present EmoPatient, an emotion-directed patient simulator designed to generate evolving emotional responses during palliative care discussions. The system introduces an Emotion Director agent that estimates the patient's emotional state and generates turn-level control signals for emotional intensity, regulatory stability, and interactional guidance. We evaluate EmoPatient through controlled multi-turn physician-patient dialogue simulations and compare it with baseline simulators. Results show improvements across four theory-informed emotional realism metrics and robustness across conversational personality variants, suggesting that modeling emotional dynamics can improve the realism of LLM-based patient simulators for palliative care communication training.

AI.tldr: EmoPatient is an LLM-based patient simulator that uses an Emotion Director agent to generate dynamic, evolving emotional states in palliative care dialogues, outperforming static baselines on emotional realism metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based patient simulators for communication training treat patient emotion as static, failing to capture the dynamic emotional shifts that characterize real palliative care interactions. This limits their realism and training effectiveness.
AI.method: EmoPatient introduces an Emotion Director agent that estimates the patient's emotional state at each conversational turn and generates control signals for emotional intensity, regulatory stability, and interactional guidance. The system is evaluated through controlled multi-turn physician-patient dialogue simulations, compared against baseline simulators using four theory-informed emotional realism metrics, with robustness testing across conversational personality variants.
AI.result: EmoPatient showed improvements over baseline simulators on all four theory-informed emotional realism metrics, with results remaining robust across different conversational personality variants.
AI.conclusion: Modeling emotional dynamics through an explicit Emotion Director agent can significantly improve the realism of LLM-based patient simulators, offering a more effective scalable tool for palliative care communication training.

title: Compositional Threat Analysis of Latent Compromise in LLM Agent Systems: The Order 66 Scenario
summary: In the fictional Order 66, catastrophe does not arise from a powerful command alone: a trusted population is preconditioned, a short directive activates the concealed condition, and protective authority turns against the system. This paper translates that mechanism into an origin-neutral security analysis of tool-using large language model (LLM) agents. A representative scenario combines a deployed artifact or shared memory bearing a dormant destructive rule, a later email, document, update, or peer message that activates it, and an agent harness granting operational and recovery authority. We introduce a compositional model explaining why no component is catastrophic alone, yet their conjunction can produce correlated destructive action. We separate three population-reach routes --- release-time pre-positioning, post-release durable seeding, and peer replication --- from a common core of dormancy, activation, authority, reachable targets, and failed recovery. This yields defensive cut sets and shows why checkpoint scanning or prompt filtering cannot close every route. A two-class example shows that cross-class feedback can sustain spread even when both within-class reproduction terms are below one; isolation and persistence controls suppress the loop. Published work instantiates constituent mechanisms, while incidents demonstrate autonomous boundary crossing, malicious agent extensions, agent-assisted reconnaissance, and public-package propagation, but not the full dormant-implant composition. We found no public observation, in evidence reviewed through 5 August 2026, traversing the complete Order 66 graph. The result is neither dismissal nor prediction: the scenario is componentwise credible under stated assumptions, damage depends on the harness, and the strongest defenses are capability mediation, durable-state provenance, propagation isolation, and protected recovery.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the "Order 66" fictional scenario as a metaphor to analyze how dormant malicious instructions in LLM agent ecosystems can be activated through coordinated triggers, showing that while no single component is catastrophic, their conjunction enables correlated destructive action. It proposes a compositional security model and defensive cut sets.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that catastrophic failures in LLM agent systems can emerge from the conjunction of individually benign components — dormant implanted rules, activation triggers, and operational authority — and that existing defenses like checkpoint scanning and prompt filtering are insufficient to cover all attack routes.
AI.method: A compositional threat model decomposing the attack into stages: dormancy, activation, authority, reachable targets, and failed recovery. Three population-reach routes are analyzed (release-time pre-positioning, post-release durable seeding, peer replication). A two-class epidemic-inspired model demonstrates cross-class feedback sustaining spread. Empirical grounding via published work and incident review through 5 August 2026.
AI.result: No public observation through 5 August 2026 was found traversing the complete Order 66 attack graph. However, constituent mechanisms are individually instantiated in published work and real incidents (autonomous boundary crossing, malicious extensions, agent-assisted reconnaissance, public-package propagation). The two-class model shows cross-class feedback can sustain spread even when within-class reproduction terms are below one.
AI.conclusion: The scenario is componentwise credible under stated assumptions but not an inevitability. Damage depends on the agent harness. The strongest defenses are capability mediation, durable-state provenance, propagation isolation, and protected recovery — not merely scanning or filtering.

title: PreGress: Ranking-Native Pre-training and Prompting for Graph Node Ranking
summary: Node ranking is a fundamental problem in graph information retrieval, measuring the relative importance of nodes and supporting a wide range of applications such as influence analysis, recommendation, and graph-based retrieval augmented generation. However, exact computation of graph-based ranking measures is often computationally prohibitive at scale. Existing GNN-based ranking methods provide scalable approximations, but they are typically tailored to individual ranking criteria and require retraining for each downstream task, which limits their transferability and efficiency. Recent graph pre-training approaches aim to enable knowledge transfer across tasks, yet their learning objectives are largely misaligned with node ranking, resulting in suboptimal adaptability to ranking-oriented applications. To address these limitations, we propose PreGress, the first ranking-native pre-training and prompting framework for supporting a wide range of node ranking tasks. PreGress performs multi-task pre-training using our carefully designed objectives, including degree centrality prediction and attribute reconstruction, to jointly capture structural and attribute information. To support heterogeneous ranking criteria, we design lightweight, task-specific prompt modules that adapt a frozen ranking backbone to downstream tasks without full retraining. Experiments on six public graphs and two real-world query-to-item benchmarks---Yelp2018 and MovieLens-100K---together with a controlled five-criterion graph-access study demonstrate strong ranking quality with low task-specific state overhead.

AI.tldr: PreGress is the first ranking-native graph pre-training and prompting framework that uses multi-task pre-training (degree centrality prediction + attribute reconstruction) with lightweight task-specific prompt modules to adapt a frozen backbone across diverse node ranking criteria without full retraining, achieving strong ranking quality with low task-specific overhead.
AI.motivation: Exact graph-based ranking is computationally prohibitive at scale. Existing GNN-based ranking approximations are task-specific and require retraining per criterion. Graph pre-training methods exist but their objectives are misaligned with node ranking, yielding suboptimal transferability. A unified, ranking-native pre-training framework adaptable to heterogeneous ranking criteria without full retraining is needed.
AI.method: PreGress employs (1) multi-task pre-training with two carefully designed objectives: degree centrality prediction (capturing structural information) and attribute reconstruction (capturing attribute information); (2) a frozen ranking backbone shared across tasks; and (3) lightweight, task-specific prompt modules that adapt the frozen backbone to downstream ranking criteria, eliminating full retraining per task.
AI.result: Experiments on six public graphs and two real-world query-to-item benchmarks (Yelp2018, MovieLens-100K), plus a controlled five-criterion graph-access study, demonstrate PreGress achieves strong ranking quality while maintaining low task-specific state overhead compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: PreGress demonstrates that ranking-native pre-training with prompting is both feasible and effective, enabling a single frozen backbone to serve multiple node ranking criteria with minimal per-task parameters, thus advancing scalable and transferable graph-based ranking.

title: Knowing You Is Everything: LLM Agents Achieve Near-Perfect Profile-Consistent Reaction Prediction in Social Media Simulation
summary: Autonomous AI agents in social media present concrete risks to democratic discourse and platform governance, while also offering tools for pre-deployment recommender system testing. A central open question is whether persona-prompted LLMs can simulate individual-level social media reactions with sufficient accuracy to support either application, and how accuracy depends on profile completeness, model selection, and the generalization challenge posed by novel post content. This study benchmarks twelve LLM configurations on binary like/dislike prediction across 296 survey-based agent profiles and 26 ground-truth-mapped posts under three profile conditions, with leave-post-out machine learning classifiers as baselines. Across full-profile conditions, accuracy ranges from 75.54% to 96.68%, with a 30-point spread attributable primarily to model selection and confirmed by paired McNemar tests with agent-level bootstrap intervals. GPT-5.5 Pro accuracy degrades monotonically from 96.68% under a full profile to 62.32% under a reduced profile and to 51.00% with demographics alone, the last indistinguishable from the majority-class baseline, which confirms that demographic inference provides negligible predictive signal. Supervised classifiers collapse to 15.4% under leave-post-out, while LLMs sustain genuine zero-shot generalization unavailable to trained methods. Adaptive reasoning improves accuracy substantially for some models. Inter-model agreement is nearly double for posts with direct profile anchors (mean \k{appa} = 0.44) than for posts without them (\k{appa} = 0.23), and the least heterogeneous configuration homogenizes 34% of simulated population reactions. Results validate LLM-based simulation for recommender system stress-testing while documenting the behavioral accuracy that makes large-scale synthetic agent swarms a credible threat to public opinion.

AI.tldr: LLMs can simulate individual-level social media reactions with high accuracy using full profiles (up to 96.68%), but accuracy collapses when profiles are reduced. LLMs uniquely achieve zero-shot generalization to novel posts where supervised classifiers fail (15.4%). Results validate LLM-based simulation for recommender testing but also confirm the credible threat of synthetic agent swarms to public opinion.
AI.motivation: Determine whether persona-prompted LLMs can accurately simulate individual-level social media reactions (like/dislike), and how this accuracy depends on profile completeness, model choice, and generalization to novel content — motivated by both beneficial applications (pre-deployment recommender system testing) and risks (autonomous agents manipulating democratic discourse).
AI.method: Benchmarked 12 LLM configurations on binary like/dislike prediction across 296 survey-based agent profiles and 26 ground-truth-mapped posts under three profile conditions (full, reduced, demographics-only). Used leave-post-out ML classifiers as baselines. Evaluated with McNemar tests, agent-level bootstrap intervals, and inter-model agreement (Cohen's kappa).
AI.result: Full-profile accuracy: 75.54%–96.68% (30-point spread driven by model selection). GPT-5.5 Pro degraded from 96.68% (full) → 62.32% (reduced) → 51.00% (demographics-only, at chance). Supervised classifiers collapsed to 15.4% under leave-post-out; LLMs sustained zero-shot generalization. Inter-model agreement: κ=0.44 for posts with profile anchors vs. κ=0.23 without. Least heterogeneous configuration homogenized 34% of simulated reactions.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based simulation is validated for recommender stress-testing, but the demonstrated behavioral accuracy confirms that large-scale synthetic agent swarms pose a credible threat to public opinion. Demographic inference alone provides negligible predictive signal; model selection and profile completeness are critical determinants of simulation fidelity.

title: Biomedical Knowledge Composition: A Software Engineering Perspective
summary: Biomedical research has accumulated vast molecular, clinical, and population data, yet translating this wealth into actionable knowledge remains constrained by technical and organizational difficulties. This article presents a unified treatment of two perspectives on biomedical knowledge infrastructure. The first introduces the biomedical domain to software engineers: it explains why knowledge graphs (KGs) are the central integrative data structure in modern biomedicine, characterizes five data harmonization challenges (identifier mapping, entity resolution, schema alignment, evidence integration, and provenance tracking), surveys application domains from drug discovery to digital twins, and profiles six representative KG systems with contrasting choices. The second perspective asks why engineering biomedical knowledge infrastructure remains so difficult. We argue that a contributing root cause is limited adoption of software tooling and practices that make development in other mature domains - particularly web engineering - reliably composable and reproducible: package management, typed namespaces, canonical interchange formats, service composition protocols, reproducible pipelines, and lifecycle governance. Against this backdrop, eight open engineering challenges for biomedical data integration are catalogued, each with partial solutions but no universally adopted stack. Crucially, the article shifts emphasis from describing deployed KG instances toward the reproducible process of assembling them: reusable build pipelines, versioned dependencies, and engineering practices that let others compile and customize a KG from source rather than consuming a static artifact. Together, the two perspectives provide domain grounding for newcomers and a research agenda for software engineers seeking to make transformative contributions to biomedical knowledge infrastructure.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a dual perspective on biomedical knowledge infrastructure: (1) an introduction for software engineers to knowledge graphs (KGs) as the central integrative data structure in biomedicine, covering harmonization challenges, application domains, and representative systems; and (2) an argument that limited adoption of mature software engineering practices (package management, typed namespaces, reproducible pipelines, lifecycle governance) is a root cause of persistent difficulty. The paper catalogs eight open engineering challenges and advocates shifting focus from static KG artifacts to reproducible, compilable, version-controlled build pipelines.
AI.motivation: Biomedical research has amassed vast molecular, clinical, and population data, but translating this into actionable knowledge is hindered by technical and organizational barriers. The paper identifies a critical gap: biomedical knowledge infrastructure lacks the composable, reproducible software engineering tooling and practices common in mature domains like web engineering, limiting scalability and reuse.
AI.method: The paper is a survey and position piece structured as two perspectives: (1) a domain primer characterizing five data harmonization challenges (identifier mapping, entity resolution, schema alignment, evidence integration, provenance tracking), surveying applications (drug discovery to digital twins), and profiling six representative KG systems; (2) a critique identifying six missing software engineering practices (package management, typed namespaces, canonical interchange formats, service composition protocols, reproducible pipelines, lifecycle governance) and cataloguing eight open engineering challenges with partial solutions.
AI.result: The paper identifies eight open challenges in biomedical data integration, each with partial but no universally adopted solution. It observes that current practice over-emphasizes describing deployed KG instances rather than the reproducible process of assembling them. The authors advocate for reusable build pipelines, versioned dependencies, and engineering practices enabling compilation and customization of KGs from source.
AI.conclusion: Biomedical knowledge infrastructure would benefit substantially from adopting mature software engineering practices from web engineering. The path forward should shift emphasis from static KG artifacts toward reproducible assembly processes, providing both domain grounding for newcomers and a concrete research agenda for software engineers aiming to make transformative contributions.

title: SurakshaEval: An Indic Safety Benchmark for Multilingual LLMs
summary: Existing safety evaluation datasets for large language models (LLMs) predominantly focus on English and Western contexts, often overlooking the linguistic diversity and culturally grounded safety risks present in other languages. To address this gap, we introduce SurakshaEval, a novel safety benchmark composed of human-written prompts spanning real-world scenarios, explicitly designed for ten major Indian languages - Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu, along with English. SurakshaEval includes both generic prompts common across India and region- and language-specific prompts that capture localized sociocultural sensitivities. We benchmark a broad range of state-of-the-art LLMs on SurakshaEval, establish baseline safety performance, and identify recurring failure modes, including over-refusal, missed detection of implicit bias, and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings. Our results show that even strong multilingual LLMs struggle to reliably meet nuanced safety requirements when operating in Indic languages, particularly in native scripts. These findings highlight the urgent need for safety evaluation frameworks that incorporate region-specific data and structured assessment protocols, enabling the development and deployment of AI systems that operate securely, ethically, and in alignment with diverse societal values. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/SurakshaEval. Warning: This paper contains text that may be offensive or unsafe.

AI.tldr: SurakshaEval is a multilingual safety benchmark covering ten Indic languages plus English, featuring human-written prompts that test LLMs on both generic and culturally-specific safety risks. Benchmarking reveals that even strong multilingual LLMs struggle with nuanced safety in Indic languages, particularly in native scripts, showing failure modes like over-refusal, missed implicit bias, and insufficient contextual awareness.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety evaluation datasets are overwhelmingly English- and Western-centric, neglecting the linguistic diversity and culturally grounded safety risks present in other languages, especially Indian languages spoken by over a billion people.
AI.method: The authors created SurakshaEval, a benchmark of human-written prompts covering real-world safety scenarios in ten major Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu) plus English. The dataset includes both pan-India generic prompts and region/language-specific prompts capturing localized sociocultural sensitivities. They benchmarked a broad range of state-of-the-art LLMs to establish baseline safety performance and analyze failure modes.
AI.result: Even strong multilingual LLMs fail to reliably meet nuanced safety requirements in Indic languages, especially in native scripts. Key failure modes include over-refusal, missed detection of implicit bias, and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings.
AI.conclusion: There is an urgent need for safety evaluation frameworks incorporating region-specific data and structured assessment protocols to enable secure, ethical, and culturally aligned AI deployment across diverse linguistic communities.

title: Shape Mutating Expert Compression:LorExperts and BTExperts
summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models deliver high capacity at low per-token compute, but deploying them cheaply requires compressing their many expert weight matrices. Expert pruning (e.g., REAP) and merging reduce cost but sacrifice accuracy and require retraining the router; low-rank delta decomposition of experts (e.g., D^2-MoE) preserves all experts and the router, but degrades sharply as the expert count grows because a single shared component cannot approximate many near-orthogonal experts.
  Because MoE expert weights are near-orthogonal, a single shared component (as in prior delta decomposition) scales poorly with the expert count; we show that experts nonetheless organize into functional co-activation communities that are decoupled from weight similarity. Building on this, we introduce LorExperts, a router-preserving compression method that clusters experts, keeps one full-precision dominant per cluster, and represents the remaining members as low-rank corrections to their local dominant. LorExperts retains all experts and the original router (no router retraining). At ~50% expert compression on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, LorExperts preserves downstream accuracy and perplexity better than the baselines on most of the tasks; the margin over D^2-MoE grows with expert count E. We further give a reconstruction fine-tuning procedure for LorExperts, and BTExperts, a tree organization of dominants and corrections that enables inference-time amortization of shared computation.

AI.tldr: LorExperts compresses MoE models by clustering experts into functional communities, keeping one full-precision dominant expert per cluster and representing others as low-rank corrections, preserving the original router and avoiding retraining. It outperforms prior compression methods, especially as expert count grows.
AI.motivation: Deploying Mixture-of-Experts language models cheaply requires compressing their many expert weight matrices. Existing methods either prune/merge experts (sacrificing accuracy and requiring router retraining) or use low-rank delta decomposition (D^2-MoE), which degrades sharply with increasing expert count because a single shared component cannot approximate many near-orthogonal experts. The authors observe that despite near-orthogonality, experts organize into functional co-activation communities decoupled from weight similarity, motivating a community-based compression approach.
AI.method: LorExperts clusters MoE experts into functional co-activation communities, retains one full-precision dominant expert per cluster, and represents the remaining experts as low-rank corrections (LoRA-style) relative to their local dominant. This is router-preserving (no router retraining). The authors also introduce: (1) a reconstruction fine-tuning procedure for LorExperts, and (2) BTExperts, a tree-based hierarchical organization of dominants and corrections that enables inference-time amortization of shared computation.
AI.result: At ~50% expert compression on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, LorExperts preserves downstream accuracy and perplexity better than baselines (REAP, D^2-MoE) on most tasks. The margin over D^2-MoE grows with expert count E, validating that local community-based decomposition scales better than a single shared component.
AI.conclusion: MoE experts form functional co-activation communities that enable effective compression via local low-rank corrections. LorExperts provides a router-preserving, retraining-free compression method that scales well with expert count, and the BTExperts tree extension further amortizes inference computation.

title: The Field Knows: Cross-Dimensional Geometry from Navigation to Black Holes
summary: We introduce a continuous metric field framework trained by a single causal contrastive loss. The framework encodes a scene into coefficients of a fixed symmetric matrix basis, assembles them into a Lie algebra element, and exponentiates the result to a Riemannian or Lorentzian metric. Across dimensions, this field discovers the full spectrum of geometric structures: from obstacle-avoiding geodesics in robot navigation across planar and manipulator configuration spaces, to event horizons of black holes in Lorentzian spacetime. Extensive zero-shot generalization studies demonstrate that the field captures transferable geometric structure rather than memorizing specific configurations. In the black hole setting, the causal loss spontaneously evolves genuine black-hole-like structures with the correct Lorentzian signature. The same loss, the same architecture, and the same training protocol produce the full range of geometric phenomena across dimensions. The field knows geometry, and geometry knows physics.

AI.tldr: A single causal contrastive loss trains a continuous metric field that encodes scenes into Lie algebra coefficients, which are exponentiated to produce Riemannian or Lorentzian metrics. The framework discovers diverse geometric structures — from robot navigation geodesics to black hole event horizons — and exhibits zero-shot generalization, demonstrating transferable geometric understanding rather than memorization.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified framework that can learn and represent the full spectrum of geometric structures (Riemannian and Lorentzian) across different dimensions and domains, using a single architecture and loss function, thereby demonstrating that geometry can be learned in a transferable, generalizable manner.
AI.method: The framework encodes a scene into coefficients of a fixed symmetric matrix basis, assembles them into a Lie algebra element, and applies the exponential map to obtain a Riemannian or Lorentzian metric. Training uses a single causal contrastive loss across all settings, with the same architecture and protocol applied uniformly across dimensions and domains.
AI.result: The method successfully discovers obstacle-avoiding geodesics in planar and manipulator configuration spaces for robot navigation, and spontaneously evolves black-hole-like structures with correct Lorentzian signature and event horizons in spacetime settings. Extensive zero-shot generalization experiments confirm the field captures transferable geometric structure rather than memorizing specific configurations.
AI.conclusion: A single loss function, architecture, and training protocol can produce the full range of geometric phenomena across dimensions. The learned metric field intrinsically captures geometry, and geometry in turn encodes physical structures, suggesting a deep connection: "The field knows geometry, and geometry knows physics."

title: Human-Simulation Interaction: From Prediction to Exploration in LLM Agent Simulations for Policy
comment: 4 pages. Position paper accepted to PoliSim@CHI 2026: LLM Agent Simulation for Policy, a workshop at CHI 2026 (CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
summary: Agent-based models have historically served as tools for generative explanation, constructing testbeds in which candidate micro-level behavioral rules can be tested for their capacity to produce observed macro-level phenomena. The integration of Large Language Models into agent-based simulation has expanded what these models can represent, but it has also introduced an unexamined shift in how users engage them. We argue that current generative agent-based models (GABMs) inherit the dominant interaction metaphor of conversational LLM interfaces - a question-answer pattern that positions users as consumers of system output rather than explorers of a possibility space. In the context of policy, where problems are wicked and ground truth is unknowable in advance, this metaphor produces a trust deficit that cannot be resolved through improved model accuracy alone. We open a design space we call human-simulation interaction, and argue that warranted trust requires interaction metaphors that restore the exploratory capacity simulation has historically supported.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that integrating LLMs into agent-based models has inadvertently shifted user interaction from exploration to a passive question-answer consumption pattern, creating a trust deficit in policy contexts. The authors propose "human-simulation interaction" as a design space for restoring exploratory capacity and warranted trust.
AI.motivation: Current generative agent-based models (GABMs) inherit the question-answer interaction metaphor of conversational LLM interfaces, positioning users as passive consumers rather than active explorers. In wicked policy problems where ground truth is unknowable, this metaphor produces a trust deficit that cannot be fixed by improving model accuracy alone. The authors seek to reclaim simulation's historical role as a tool for exploratory, generative explanation.
AI.method: This is a conceptual/position paper that articulates a critique and opens a design space. It draws on the history of agent-based modeling as a generative explanatory tool, contrasts this with the current LLM-integrated paradigm, and frames the problem of trust through the lens of wicked problems and warranted trust. The paper proposes "human-simulation interaction" as a new design space for rethinking how users engage with GABMs.
AI.result: The paper identifies a fundamental mismatch: GABMs currently adopt the conversational Q&A metaphor of LLMs, which reduces rich exploratory simulation to output consumption. This undermines warranted trust, particularly in policy domains where problems are wicked — characterized by uncertainty, value pluralism, and no definitive ground truth. The authors argue that restoring an exploratory interaction metaphor is essential for legitimate and trustworthy simulation-based policy insight.
AI.conclusion: Warranted trust in GABMs cannot be achieved through accuracy improvements alone. Instead, the field must develop "human-simulation interaction" — interaction metaphors that enable users to explore possibility spaces, interrogate assumptions, and engage iteratively with simulations, reclaiming the exploratory ethos of traditional agent-based modeling.

title: Targeted Counterfactual Fingerprinting for Black-Box LLM Ownership Verification
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are high-value assets that can be derived through redeployment, fine-tuning, quantization, or further alignment. Because deployed LLMs are commonly exposed only through query APIs, ownership verification must often rely on black-box text responses. This setting is difficult: generations are open-ended and can vary across repeated queries, while existing black-box fingerprints rely on signals that are fragile under a final-response interface, including full-text matching, soft behavioral features, or model-specific prompts designed not to transfer. We propose TCF (Targeted Counterfactual Fingerprinting), a black-box LLM fingerprinting framework that converts open-ended generation comparison into constrained-answer targeted counterfactual transfer. TCF restricts each verification query to a finite answer space, reducing the surface-form ambiguity that enters the verification score, and optimizes a prompt perturbation toward a counterfactual target different from the protected model's clean answer on the original prompt. Verification reduces to checking whether the suspect model's parsed final answer matches the recorded target. We introduce the source-model counterfactual margin (SCM), a protected-model-only quantity that certifies the target is unlikely before the perturbation and likely after it; SCM controls target selection, perturbation stopping, and fingerprint filtering. Under explicit derived-preservation and independent-transfer budgets motivated by local behavioral closeness, we derive a target-accuracy gap between derived and independent models. Across four LLM families, TCF achieves an average AUC of 0.9861, improving over TRAP, ProFLingo, and ZeroPrint by 0.07 to 0.19.

AI.tldr: TCF is a black-box LLM fingerprinting method that converts open-ended generation comparison into constrained-answer targeted counterfactual transfer, achieving AUC 0.9861 across four LLM families.
AI.motivation: LLMs are valuable IP assets but are exposed only via black-box query APIs, making ownership verification difficult. Existing black-box fingerprinting methods suffer from open-ended generation variability and fragile signals under final-response interfaces, necessitating a more robust approach.
AI.method: TCF restricts each verification query to a finite answer space to reduce surface-form ambiguity. It optimizes a prompt perturbation toward a counterfactual target — an answer different from the protected model's clean response. Verification checks whether the suspect model's parsed answer matches the recorded target. The framework introduces the Source-model Counterfactual Margin (SCM), a protected-model-only metric that certifies the target is unlikely before perturbation and likely after, controlling target selection, perturbation stopping, and fingerprint filtering. Under derived-preservation and independent-transfer budgets motivated by local behavioral closeness, a target-accuracy gap between derived and independent models is theoretically derived.
AI.result: TCF achieves an average AUC of 0.9861 across four LLM families, outperforming TRAP, ProFLingo, and ZeroPrint by margins of 0.07 to 0.19 AUC.
AI.conclusion: TCF provides a robust, black-box fingerprinting solution for LLM ownership verification by constraining answer spaces and leveraging counterfactual perturbation, substantially outperforming prior methods.

title: RVANNS: Mixed-Precision Indexing and Locality-Aware Graph Traversal on RISC-V
summary:
Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) on CPUs is increasingly constrained by candidate-vector movement and decoding rather than peak arithmetic throughput. Although the RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) provides vector-length-agnostic execution and LMUL-based register grouping, generic low-precision decoding still incurs conversion overhead, while irregular graph traversal generates scattered accesses that degrade cache locality and memory-level parallelism.
  We present RVANNS, an RVV-oriented ANNS engine that jointly optimizes vector representation and graph locality. Its Mixed-Precision Multi-Layer Index (MPMI) represents each vector with a dense 8-bit affine base and sparse FP16/FP32 residuals, fusing reconstruction with distance accumulation and aligning widening with LMUL-sized register groups. ROrder co-locates likely co-visited graph nodes and sorts remapped adjacency lists, transforming scattered payload probes into denser, predominantly forward-moving address streams.
  Integrated into Milvus, RVANNS achieves 3.39x and 4.94x speedups over scalar execution on real 128-bit and 256-bit RVV processors, respectively. Under controlled HNSW configurations, it improves throughput by 2.27--2.76x over RVV SIMD+FP32 and by 1.18--1.59x over the corresponding AVX-512 and SVE baselines. On Cohere10M, it further delivers 1.82--2.27x higher QPS/W than the evaluated GPU baselines.

AI.tldr: RVANNS is a RISC-V Vector Extension (RVV) based ANNS engine that uses mixed-precision multi-layer indexing and graph reordering to overcome memory bottlenecks, achieving significant speedups over scalar, SIMD, and GPU baselines on real RVV hardware.
AI.motivation: ANNS on CPUs is bottlenecked by candidate-vector movement and decoding overhead rather than arithmetic throughput. Existing RVV approaches suffer from (1) low-precision decoding conversion overhead, and (2) scattered memory accesses from irregular graph traversal that degrade cache locality and memory-level parallelism.
AI.method: Two-pronged approach: (1) Mixed-Precision Multi-Layer Index (MPMI) — stores vectors as 8-bit affine base plus sparse FP16/FP32 residuals, fusing reconstruction with distance accumulation and aligning widening operations with LMUL-sized register groups. (2) ROrder — co-locates likely co-visited graph nodes and sorts remapped adjacency lists, converting scattered payload probes into denser, predominantly forward-moving address streams.
AI.result: On real RVV hardware: 3.39× (128-bit) and 4.94× (256-bit) speedups over scalar execution. Under HNSW configurations: 2.27–2.76× throughput improvement over RVV SIMD+FP32, and 1.18–1.59× over AVX-512 and SVE baselines. On Cohere10M: 1.82–2.27× higher QPS/W than GPU baselines. Integrated into Milvus.
AI.conclusion: RVV-oriented joint optimization of vector representation and graph locality effectively mitigates the memory-bound nature of ANNS, enabling RISC-V vector processors to outperform comparable x86 and ARM SIMD implementations and even GPU baselines in energy efficiency.

title: Independent Patch Verification for Coding Agents with a Bidirectional Reconstruct-and-Verify Framework
summary: Autonomous coding agents powered by large language models can now generate code patches directly from bug reports, but a fundamental gap remains: once a patch is produced, no mechanism independently verifies whether it truly resolves the reported problem. Prior work has sought to address this through iterative self-refinement and inference-time scaling, but these approaches either review the patch under the same interpretation that produced it or broaden candidate generation without verifying individual patches, and neither provides an explicit verification signal for assessing patch correctness. We propose RETRACE, a training-free post-generation verification framework that derives such a signal through bidirectional reconstruction and reconciliation. When a coding agent generates a candidate patch for an issue, RETRACE performs forward reconstruction to build an explicit repair rationale from the issue and the agent's trajectory; backward reconstruction then independently infers, from the patch and its trajectory alone and without access to the original issue, a description of the problem the patch appears to address, and compares this reconstruction against the original issue to produce an alignment verdict; a reconciliation stage then checks the consistency between the forward rationale and the patch, diagnoses the source of any misalignment, and either submits the patch or produces targeted revision guidance. Evaluated on SWE-bench Verified with two backbones (GPT-5-mini and MiniMax-2.5), RETRACE lifts Pass@1 by 7.0% and 3.6% respectively on the mini-SWE-agent scaffold, and delivers comparable gains on OpenHands without modification. Ablation experiments show that both the forward and backward stages contribute to the overall improvement and that adding reconciliation yields further gains.

AI.tldr: RETRACE is a training-free post-generation verification framework for autonomous coding agents. It verifies whether a generated patch truly resolves a bug by performing bidirectional reconstruction: forward reconstruction builds a repair rationale from the issue and agent trajectory, while backward reconstruction infers the original problem from the patch alone and compares it against the actual issue. A reconciliation stage diagnoses misalignments and provides revision guidance. Evaluated on SWE-bench Verified, RETRACE improves Pass@1 by 7.0% (GPT-5-mini) and 3.6% (MiniMax-2.5) on mini-SWE-agent, with comparable gains on OpenHands.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous coding agents lack an independent verification mechanism to confirm whether a generated patch actually resolves the reported bug. Existing approaches either review patches under the same interpretation that generated them (iterative self-refinement) or broaden candidate generation without verifying individual patches (inference-time scaling). Neither provides an explicit verification signal for assessing patch correctness.
AI.method: RETRACE employs a three-stage, training-free framework: (1) Forward Reconstruction — constructs an explicit repair rationale from the original issue and the agent's trajectory; (2) Backward Reconstruction — independently infers a problem description solely from the patch and its trajectory (without access to the original issue), then compares this reconstructed description against the original issue to produce an alignment verdict; (3) Reconciliation — checks consistency between the forward rationale and the patch, diagnoses sources of misalignment, and either submits the patch or generates targeted revision guidance.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, RETRACE improved Pass@1 by 7.0% with GPT-5-mini and 3.6% with MiniMax-2.5 on the mini-SWE-agent scaffold. Comparable gains were achieved on OpenHands without any modification. Ablation studies confirmed that both forward and backward stages contribute to performance improvement, and adding the reconciliation stage yields further gains.
AI.conclusion: RETRACE demonstrates that bidirectional reconstruction with reconciliation provides an effective, training-free verification signal for patch correctness in autonomous coding agents. The framework is scaffold-agnostic and consistently improves Pass@1 across different backbone models.

title: Detection of Self-Introductions in Legislative Testimony
comment: Presented at AAIRC-AI4 conference, Las Vegas, NV, USA August 2026 https://ai4.io/aairc-ai4/
summary: Self-introductions are common in legislative committee testimonies. Successfully detecting them and extracting the speaker's name is enormously helpful in the task of speaker identification in the context of government meetings. In this paper, we present a pipeline for detection of self-introductions in legislative committee testimony using machine learning. We construct a training dataset from 1.54 million utterances spanning five state legislative sessions, apply a name-matching heuristic to generate automatic labels, and train three classifiers: a decision tree, random forest, and XGBoost to find self-introductions and extract the speaker's name. We construct a feature set combining bag-of-words, positional context, structural signals, introductory phrase indicators, and discourse context features. Among the three classifiers, XGBoost achieves the best performance with an F1 score of 0.9747 and the fewest total errors; adding fine-tuned BERT probability features improves this further. As an extension, we score the full candidate dataset with a fine-tuned BERT classifier and add BERT probability outputs as features. This BERT-augmented XGBoost model improves F1 from 0.9747 to 0.9782 and reduces total test errors from 241 to 207. The primary gain over the decision tree baseline (F1 0.9323) is driven by discourse context features and the boosting ensemble strategy; BERT provides a modest complementary signal. Analysis of false positives reveals that a minority are genuine self-introductions mislabeled due to name inconsistencies in the source data, indicating that measured metrics modestly understate true performance.

AI.tldr: A machine learning pipeline for detecting self-introductions in legislative testimony, using XGBoost augmented with fine-tuned BERT features, achieving an F1 score of 0.9782. Discourse context features and boosting provide the primary gains, and analysis reveals metrics understate true performance due to labeling inconsistencies.
AI.motivation: Self-introductions in legislative committee testimonies are common and detecting them to extract speaker names significantly aids speaker identification in government meetings. Automating this process addresses a practical need in processing large volumes of legislative speech data.
AI.method: A pipeline is built using 1.54 million utterances from five state legislative sessions. A name-matching heuristic generates automatic labels. Three classifiers (decision tree, random forest, XGBoost) are trained on a feature set combining bag-of-words, positional context, structural signals, introductory phrase indicators, and discourse context features. XGBoost is further augmented with probability outputs from a fine-tuned BERT classifier as additional features.
AI.result: XGBoost achieves the best base performance (F1 = 0.9747). The BERT-augmented XGBoost improves to F1 = 0.9782 and reduces total test errors from 241 to 207. The primary gains over the decision tree baseline (F1 = 0.9323) come from discourse context features and boosting; BERT provides a modest complementary signal. False positive analysis reveals some are genuine self-introductions mislabeled due to name inconsistencies, suggesting real performance is slightly higher than measured.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively detects self-introductions and extracts speaker names from legislative testimony. Boosting with engineered discourse features drives most of the improvement, while BERT offers supplementary gains. Labeling noise from name inconsistencies means reported metrics modestly underestimate true model performance.

title: From token probabilities to calibrated confidence: An empirical study of mathematical question answering
summary: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) aims to estimate the probability that a generated answer is correct, while calibration aligns these estimates with empirical accuracy. Prior work has shown that token probabilities are often overconfident, we investigate whether these readily available signals can nevertheless provide well-calibrated confidence estimation for mathematical question answering. We compare single-pass estimators, which reuse token probabilities from the original generation, with multi-pass estimators, which obtain additional confidence signals through verification or stochastic forward passes. While individual token probabilities can be highly saturated, we find that aggregating token probabilities over the full sequence captures small but consistent differences between correct and incorrect generations, yielding more informative confidence estimates. Multi-pass methods can yield calibrated confidence estimates. We study two such approaches: self-verification through re-prompting, including a lower-cost in-situ variant, and Monte Carlo Dropout, which derives confidence from variation across stochastic forward passes. We further evaluate two post-hoc calibration methods, Platt scaling and isotonic regression, both of which substantially reduce in-domain calibration error. However, their data efficiency varies with dataset difficulty, and the calibration mappings often transfer asymmetrically across datasets and models.

AI.tldr: Investigates confidence estimation for LLMs on mathematical QA, comparing single-pass token-probability aggregation with multi-pass methods (self-verification, MC Dropout). Finds that aggregating token probabilities captures informative differences between correct/incorrect answers, multi-pass methods yield calibrated estimates, and post-hoc calibration (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) reduces error but transfers asymmetrically.
AI.motivation: LLM token probabilities are often overconfident, but it is unclear whether these signals can still provide well-calibrated confidence estimation for mathematical question answering. The authors aim to systematically investigate whether readily available token probabilities, when properly aggregated or supplemented with multi-pass signals, can yield reliable confidence estimates.
AI.method: Compares single-pass estimators (aggregating token probabilities across the full generated sequence) with multi-pass estimators including self-verification via re-prompting (with a lower-cost in-situ variant) and Monte Carlo Dropout (confidence from variance across stochastic forward passes). Evaluates post-hoc calibration using Platt scaling and isotonic regression to correct miscalibration.
AI.result: Aggregating token probabilities over full sequences captures small but consistent differences between correct and incorrect generations. Multi-pass methods yield calibrated confidence estimates. Both Platt scaling and isotonic regression substantially reduce in-domain calibration error, but data efficiency varies with dataset difficulty, and calibration mappings transfer asymmetrically across datasets and models.
AI.conclusion: Token-probability aggregation provides informative confidence signals despite saturation. Multi-pass approaches offer calibrated estimates, and post-hoc calibration methods are effective in-domain but exhibit asymmetric transferability, highlighting practical limitations for deployment across varying datasets and models.

title: TeXFix-Bench: An Empirically Grounded Multi-Format Benchmark for LLM-Based Document Source Repair
summary: Scientific and technical writing depends on markup sources that must compile: LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown pipelines fail on missing delimiters, mismatched environments, broken imports, or package conflicts. Existing document-repair evaluations inject faults with ad-hoc edits that lack an empirical fault model. We present TeXFix-Bench, a multi-format benchmark for LLM-based full-source document repair grounded in a mined fault taxonomy. A Grounded-Theory study of localized hard-crash LaTeX faults from TeX Stack Exchange, GitHub commits, and package documentation (168 verified faults, dual open coding at $κ$=0.34) yields an 18-category taxonomy instantiated as DocMut: 48 AST-aware operators across three formats. A three-model cross-benchmark shows DocMut faults are 5.6-9.2 pp harder to repair than pattern-based mutations on the same seeds, and a real-error case study (88 mined human crashes, 67.0% repair success) brackets both synthetic sets from below. We construct 10,437 instances from 743 openly licensed seeds and evaluate seven LLMs under a fixed zero-shot protocol with provider-pinned routing, collecting 48,651 attempts at about USD 200 total inference cost. A complete 6,613-instance x 7-model balanced matrix confirms all rankings. A pinned engine gate yields a 27.5-point intention-to-treat compile spread (56.7-84.2%). Typst is markedly harder than LaTeX and Markdown. A restoration oracle over 28,129 compiling repairs shows that 13.6-18.5% of compiling repairs materially alter document text, and restoration rank diverges from compile rank: the model with the lowest compile rate restores content best among its successes. Compile success alone overstates repair quality. We release the taxonomy, DocMut, and all campaign artifacts.

AI.tldr: TeXFix-Bench introduces a benchmark for LLM-based document repair using a fault taxonomy mined from real-world LaTeX errors. It includes 10,437 repair instances across LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown, evaluates seven LLMs with 48,651 attempts at ~$200 total cost, and reveals that compile success overstates repair quality—models with lower compile rates can better preserve document content.
AI.motivation: Existing document-repair evaluations rely on ad-hoc fault injection without an empirical fault model. The authors aim to ground repair evaluation in real-world fault distributions and assess whether compile success is a sufficient metric for repair quality.
AI.method: A Grounded-Theory study of 168 verified hard-crash LaTeX faults from TeX Stack Exchange, GitHub commits, and package documentation yields an 18-category taxonomy (inter-coder agreement κ=0.34). This taxonomy is instantiated as DocMut: 48 AST-aware mutation operators across LaTeX, Typst, and Markdown. From 743 open-source seeds, 10,437 repair instances are constructed. Seven LLMs are evaluated under fixed zero-shot prompting with provider-pinned routing. A restoration oracle measures whether compiling repairs alter document text.
AI.result: DocMut faults are 5.6–9.2 percentage points harder to repair than pattern-based mutations. A real-error case study (88 mined crashes, 67.0% repair success) brackets both synthetic sets from below. A pinned-engine gate yields a 27.5-point compile spread (56.7–84.2%). Typst proves markedly harder than LaTeX and Markdown. Critically, 13.6–18.5% of compiling repairs materially alter document text, and restoration rank diverges from compile rank: the model with the lowest compile rate achieves the best content restoration among its successes.
AI.conclusion: Compile success alone overstates repair quality; content preservation must be measured alongside. The grounded fault taxonomy (DocMut) produces more challenging and ecologically valid repair tasks than ad-hoc mutation. All artifacts—taxonomy, DocMut, benchmark, and evaluation data—are publicly released.

title: EvalConvoLearn: An Open-Source Framework for Evaluating Grounded Learner Simulations in Tutoring Conversations
comment: Poster at the Impactful and Responsible AI Systems for Education workshop, as part of the Festival of Learning 2026
summary: Conversational learner simulations are valuable tools for testing learning theories, evaluating instructional materials and automated tutors, or powering teachable agents. Recently, large language models (LLM) have enabled richer, more naturalistic interactions with simulated learners; however, no open framework exists for evaluating whether such simulations faithfully reproduce real learner behavior. We introduce EvalConvoLearn, an open-source framework that assesses learner simulations along two axes: learning behavior (skill-conditioned mastery outcomes) and conversational quality (talk moves, error type distributions, question rate, turn length). EvalConvoLearn measures how closely a simulated learner approximates answer distributions observed in data by grounding metrics in authentic tutoring conversation datasets, and anchoring generated tutor responses in existing tutor utterances. The framework is demonstrated on a dataset of tutoring dialogues, including results for two LLM-based learner simulations, and the published GitHub code.

AI.tldr: EvalConvoLearn is an open-source framework for evaluating LLM-based conversational learner simulations by measuring fidelity along two axes: learning behavior (skill-conditioned mastery) and conversational quality (talk moves, error types, question rate, turn length), using authentic tutoring dialogue datasets as ground truth.
AI.motivation: LLMs have enabled richer simulated learner interactions, but no open framework exists to systematically evaluate whether these simulations faithfully reproduce real learner behavior.
AI.method: The framework grounds evaluation metrics in authentic tutoring conversation datasets, comparing simulated learner answer distributions against observed data, and anchors tutor responses in existing tutor utterances to ensure ecological validity. It assesses two axes: learning behavior (skill-conditioned mastery outcomes) and conversational quality (talk moves, error type distributions, question rate, turn length).
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on a tutoring dialogue dataset with results from two LLM-based learner simulations, and the code is published on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: EvalConvoLearn provides the first open, systematic evaluation framework for conversational learner simulations, enabling researchers to quantitatively assess simulation fidelity against real learner data.

title: Privacy-Preserving Data Drift Detection and Recovery for Large-Scale LLM Applications via Proxy Representations
summary: LLM applications deployed at scale face a fundamental challenge: privacy constraints prevent direct inspection of user interactions, making it difficult to obtain any representative evaluation dataset or to track the ongoing evolution of production traffic. We present ProxyDrift, a framework that (i) identifies and measures drift between production traffic and offline evaluation sets, and (ii) constructs and refreshes those evaluation sets accordingly; all without access to raw user data. Our approach operates entirely on non-PII proxy representations: structured, multi-dimensional descriptors derived from LLM-based classification of user interactions. We introduce (1) a chance-calibrated, redundancy-aware (RA) alignment score that aggregates per-dimension drift measurements via mutual information; (2) a conditional sampler that generates synthetic proxies respecting inter-dimensional dependencies; (3) a roundtrip consistency analysis that exposes generator/classifier disagreements and guides proxy taxonomy refinement; and (4) a feedback-linkage analysis that ties per-dimension and per-value proxy distributions to user satisfaction, surfacing actionable failure and success modes. Serving hundreds of millions of users, ProxyDrift enables continuous drift monitoring and targeted synthetic data generation without exposing sensitive user data. Experiments confirm strong roundtrip consistency, discriminator-level indistinguishability of synthetic queries from human queries, and tight end-to-end alignment (RA~0.9) with production.

AI.tldr: ProxyDrift is a privacy-preserving framework that detects and measures distribution drift between production LLM traffic and offline evaluation datasets using non-PII proxy representations, then constructs refreshed synthetic evaluation sets—all without accessing raw user data.
AI.motivation: LLM applications at scale cannot directly inspect user interactions due to privacy constraints, which prevents obtaining representative evaluation datasets and tracking production traffic evolution. A drift measurement and dataset refresh mechanism is needed that operates without raw user data access.
AI.method: ProxyDrift operates on non-PII proxy representations: structured, multi-dimensional descriptors from LLM-based classification of user interactions. Key components: (1) a chance-calibrated, redundancy-aware (RA) alignment score using mutual information to aggregate per-dimension drift; (2) a conditional sampler generating synthetic proxies respecting inter-dimensional dependencies; (3) roundtrip consistency analysis exposing generator/classifier disagreements to refine proxy taxonomy; (4) feedback-linkage analysis linking proxy distributions to user satisfaction for actionable failure/success mode discovery.
AI.result: Deployed at scale serving hundreds of millions of users, ProxyDrift achieved strong roundtrip consistency, discriminator-level indistinguishability of synthetic queries from human queries, and tight end-to-end alignment (RA ~0.9) with production.
AI.conclusion: ProxyDrift enables continuous drift monitoring and targeted synthetic data generation without exposing sensitive user data, successfully bridging the gap between production traffic and offline evaluation under strict privacy constraints.

title: DREAM Technical Report
summary: Industrial recommender systems commonly use cascaded retrieval, ranking, and re-ranking pipelines. Although efficient, these pipelines fragment information and objectives across modules, rely on rigid rules, and have limited awareness of real-time intent, leaving session-level shifts among browsing, comparison, and purchase insufficiently addressed. We present DREAM (Developing Recommender Engine with Agentic Methods), an autonomous optimization control architecture that adds a perception-aware, orchestrable, and auditable policy layer atop existing pipelines without replacing them. DREAM has two core components. First, a three-tier Intent Engine fuses on-device signals into structured L0/L1/L2 intent representations; its edge-cloud trigger chain reduces reporting volume to approximately 8.7%. Second, a Meta Engine uses a MetaModel for layered M1-to-M2-to-M3 reasoning: intent summarization, strategy planning informed by Strategy Memory, and parameter translation. It dispatches the resulting parameters through a unified outlet with safety guardrails. A Reward Dual Loop continuously optimizes both components by combining offline simulation for strategy-space exploration with online feedback for outcome calibration, forming a cycle of generation, execution, evaluation, and experience accumulation. Large-scale A/B tests on Taobao's homepage feed show that re-ranking control alone improves IPV by 2.06%, Core IPV by 2.39%, and GMV by 0.88%. Extending control to fine ranking raises these gains to 2.71%, 3.06%, and 1.31%, respectively, while consistently improving PV by more than 1%. These gains require neither replacement of pipeline models nor compromise of serving stability, supporting agentic meta-control as a viable paradigm for industrial recommendation.

AI.tldr: DREAM introduces an agentic meta-control layer atop existing industrial recommender pipelines, using a three-tier Intent Engine and a Meta Engine with layered reasoning to dynamically optimize retrieval, ranking, and re-ranking. A/B tests on Taobao show significant gains in IPV, Core IPV, and GMV without replacing underlying models.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommenders use cascaded pipelines (retrieval → ranking → re-ranking) that fragment information and objectives across modules, rely on rigid hand-crafted rules, and lack awareness of real-time session-level intent shifts (browsing, comparison, purchase). These limitations leave substantial optimization potential untapped, motivating an architecture that can orchestrate across modules without costly pipeline replacement.
AI.method: DREAM adds a perception-aware, orchestrateable, and auditable policy layer atop existing pipelines. It comprises: (1) a three-tier Intent Engine that fuses on-device signals into structured L0/L1/L2 intent representations, using an edge-cloud trigger chain that reduces reporting to ~8.7% volume; and (2) a Meta Engine employing a MetaModel for layered M1→M2→M3 reasoning — intent summarization, strategy planning informed by Strategy Memory, and parameter translation — dispatching parameters through a unified outlet with safety guardrails. A Reward Dual Loop continuously optimizes both components via offline simulation (strategy-space exploration) and online feedback (outcome calibration), forming a generate-execute-evaluate-accumulate cycle.
AI.result: In large-scale A/B tests on Taobao's homepage feed, re-ranking control alone improved IPV by 2.06%, Core IPV by 2.39%, and GMV by 0.88%. Extending control to fine ranking raised gains to 2.71%, 3.06%, and 1.31% respectively, with consistent PV improvements exceeding 1%. These gains required no replacement of pipeline models and did not compromise serving stability.
AI.conclusion: Agentic meta-control is a viable paradigm for industrial recommendation, delivering measurable business gains without disrupting existing infrastructure. DREAM demonstrates that a lightweight, auditable policy layer can effectively coordinate fragmented pipeline modules and respond to real-time user intent, supporting broader adoption of agentic methods in production recommender systems.

title: From Single Chatbots to Governed Agent Ecosystems: An Agentic AI Pattern Catalogue and Orchestration Framework for Mission-Critical Hospital Information Management Systems
summary: Hospitals are racing to embed AI, while coping with the surge in adaptation of the technology in other industries, into the triage management, documentation, scheduling, and revenue-cycle workflows, yet most deployments remain as fragmented pilots that stall at the edge of production, exposing patients and institutions to operational fragility, ungoverned risk, and mounting technical debt. At the same time, the global AI-in-healthcare market is projected to exceed nearly USD 1 trillion by 2034, according to the report of Fortune Business Insights, amplifying the financial consequences of architectural missteps and failed scaling strategies. This research proposes a compliance-first Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework, purposely built for HIMS, moving beyond the single LLM chatbots and towards a governed ecosystem of autonomous and semi-autonomous agents. The framework extends by adding (i) a taxonomy of Agentic roles, (ii) a formal risk-stratification model that maps each pattern to risk tiers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and governance hooks, and (iii) a unified orchestration runtime capable of coordinating multi-agent workflows across EHR/HIMS landscapes such as Epic, Cerner, and MEDITECH. Technically the framework combines vLLM-based inference, optimized paging memory, confidential computing, and MCP based on-premise deployment, enforcing end-to-end encryption and policy-as-code controls aligned with HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, India's DPDP and DISHA Acts, ISO 27001, ISO 27002, ISO 14971 and IEC 62304. We exhibit how the proposed architecture is capable and efficient to reduce the documentation time, integration effort, and AI pilot attrition while constricting the governance and auditability, offering hospital leaders and governing authorities an urgently needed blueprint to convert AI investment into sustainable clinical, operational, and financial ROI

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a compliance-first Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework for Hospital Information Management Systems (HIMS), moving beyond single-chatbot deployments toward a governed multi-agent ecosystem with formal risk stratification, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and unified orchestration across major EHR platforms, demonstrating reductions in documentation time, integration effort, and AI pilot attrition while ensuring regulatory compliance.
AI.motivation: Most hospital AI deployments remain fragmented pilots that fail to reach production, creating operational fragility, ungoverned risk, and technical debt. With the global AI-in-healthcare market projected to approach USD 1 trillion by 2034, architectural missteps carry enormous financial consequences. There is an urgent need for a structured, governable framework that moves beyond ad-hoc LLM chatbots toward compliant, scalable multi-agent systems.
AI.method: The framework comprises three core components: (i) a taxonomy of Agentic roles tailored for healthcare workflows; (ii) a formal risk-stratification model mapping each AI pattern to risk tiers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and governance hooks; and (iii) a unified orchestration runtime coordinating multi-agent workflows across EHR/HIMS platforms (Epic, Cerner, MEDITECH). The technical stack leverages vLLM-based inference, optimized paging memory, confidential computing, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-based on-premise deployment with end-to-end encryption and policy-as-code controls aligned with HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, India's DPDP/DISHA, ISO 27001/27002, ISO 14971, and IEC 62304.
AI.result: The proposed architecture demonstrates capability in reducing documentation time, integration effort, and AI pilot attrition while strengthening governance and auditability, thereby offering a blueprint for converting AI investment into sustainable clinical, operational, and financial ROI.
