AI.conclusion: A compliance-first, agentic AI orchestration framework provides hospital leaders and governing authorities with an urgently needed, production-ready blueprint to scale AI deployments responsibly, bridging the gap between fragmented pilots and governed, multi-agent ecosystems that deliver measurable returns across clinical, operational, and financial dimensions.

title: GALA: Graph-Augmented LLM Agents for Root Cause Analysis and Incident Response in Microservices
comment: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26), October 12--16, 2026, Munich, Germany
summary: Microservice root cause analysis (RCA) requires correlating failures across heterogeneous telemetry within complex service dependency graphs. Existing methods often rely on a single telemetry modality; recent LLM-based approaches can suffer from unconstrained exploration and hallucination; and most systems stop at fault ranking without producing actionable incident response. We present GALA+, a graph-augmented LLM agentic framework centered on graph-guided investigation, which uses service dependencies to bound exploration and refine diagnosis through localized multi-modal evidence. For initial hypothesis generation, GALA+ combines complementary telemetry signals with STRIX, a novel trace- and graph-structure-aware scoring module. GALA+ then produces ranked diagnoses, incident summaries, and stratified action recommendations. We further introduce SURE-Score, a human-guided evaluation framework co-developed with industry SRE experts for assessing RCA-specific output quality beyond conventional text similarity metrics. On two microservice benchmarks, GALA+ consistently achieves the strongest overall results, surpassing the best LLM-based baseline by more than 25 percentage points in AC@1, while also receiving the highest ratings from both SURE-Score and independent human SRE evaluation.

AI.tldr: GALA+ is a graph-augmented LLM agentic framework for microservice root cause analysis that constrains exploration via service dependencies, integrates multi-modal telemetry with a novel trace-structure-aware scoring module (STRIX), and produces ranked diagnoses with actionable incident response. It introduces SURE-Score, a human-guided SRE evaluation framework. GALA+ outperforms baselines by >25 pp in AC@1 and achieves top human ratings.
AI.motivation: Existing microservice RCA methods are limited by reliance on single telemetry modalities, LLM-based approaches suffer from unconstrained exploration and hallucination, and most systems only rank faults without providing actionable incident response guidance.
AI.method: GALA+ employs a graph-augmented LLM agentic framework with graph-guided investigation that uses service dependency graphs to bound exploration and refine diagnosis through localized multi-modal evidence. It combines telemetry signals with STRIX, a trace- and graph-structure-aware scoring module for hypothesis generation, and outputs ranked diagnoses, incident summaries, and stratified action recommendations. Evaluation uses SURE-Score, a human-guided framework co-developed with SRE experts.
AI.result: On two microservice benchmarks, GALA+ consistently achieves the strongest overall results, surpassing the best LLM-based baseline by more than 25 percentage points in AC@1, while also receiving the highest ratings from both SURE-Score and independent human SRE evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Graph-guided investigation with bounded LLM exploration, multi-modal telemetry fusion via STRIX, and actionable incident response generation significantly advances microservice RCA. The SURE-Score framework provides a more meaningful evaluation standard aligned with practitioner needs.

title: Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
summary: Reasoning language models increasingly use test-time compute to improve performance, but existing evaluations typically study this compute one question at a time. Yet when multiple problems share an end-to-end cost or latency constraint, models must decide how to divide limited inference compute among them. We introduce an exam-style evaluation framework for studying this setting, in which a model must distribute one shared token budget across questions with different difficulty and point values to maximize its total score. Across several open and frontier reasoning models, we find that models fail to allocate a shared budget strategically across questions of varying difficulties and values. Models behave largely as greedy sequential solvers: they prioritize questions by presentation order, front-load effort on early questions, and remain insensitive to value, with these tendencies becoming more pronounced as the number of questions grows. Explicit planning prompts spread compute more evenly but do not produce value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. The same behavioral pattern extends from mathematical to code reasoning. These findings establish global budget allocation as a distinct capability that is not captured by conventional per-question evaluation and remains a challenge for current reasoning models.

AI.tldr: Reasoning models fail to strategically allocate a shared token budget across questions of varying difficulty and point value, instead behaving as greedy sequential solvers that prioritize by presentation order. This reveals global budget allocation as a distinct, unevaluated capability gap.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of reasoning language models examine test-time compute on a per-question basis. In real-world scenarios, multiple problems share an end-to-end cost or latency constraint, requiring models to strategically distribute limited inference compute across questions with different difficulty and value. This capability has not been studied.
AI.method: The authors introduce an exam-style evaluation framework where models must distribute one shared token budget across questions with varying difficulty and point values to maximize total score. They test several open and frontier reasoning models, including explicit planning prompts, across both mathematical and code reasoning domains.
AI.result: Models consistently fail to allocate budget strategically. They behave as greedy sequential solvers: prioritizing by presentation order, front-loading compute on early questions, and remaining insensitive to question value. These tendencies intensify as question count grows. Explicit planning prompts spread compute more evenly but do not enable value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. The pattern holds across both math and code domains.
AI.conclusion: Global budget allocation is a distinct capability not captured by conventional per-question evaluation and remains a significant challenge for current reasoning models, indicating a key direction for future improvement.

title: TEMPER: Tensorized Efficient Manifold-constrained Parameterization for Expressive Residual Routing
summary: Residual connections rely on a static residual pathway, and are essential for training deep neural networks. Hyper-connections (HC) increase the expressivity of residual routing by incorporating multiple residual streams and learning dynamic information flow, while manifold-constrained (mHC) variants stabilize training through doubly stochastic residual mixing. However, a generator-level bottleneck remains in existing methods: they use dense, unstructured generators for pre-branch aggregation, residual mixing, and post-branch redistribution, which results in parameter count growing rapidly with the number of streams. To address this issue, we propose \underline{\textbf{T}}ensorized \underline{\textbf{E}}fficient \underline{\textbf{M}}anifold-constrained \underline{\textbf{P}}arameterization for \underline{\textbf{E}}xpressive Residual \underline{\textbf{R}}outing (\textbf{TEMPER}), which represents these generators as multi-way tensors over the input-stream, feature, and output-stream modes, and parameterizes them using tensor networks. Such a structured low-rank formulation is shown to preserve token-dependent manifold-constrained routing interface while substantially reducing parameter growth. It also promotes interpretability and intuition, as: i) tensor ranks control the dimensionality of the learned routing subspace, with full ranks recovering dense routing; while ii) the generator approximation errors bound differences in routing logits and, consequently, in the routed-block outputs. Comprehensive experiments show that TEMPER matches or outperforms existing methods across language modeling and commonsense reasoning tasks, while requiring substantially fewer additional parameters. At eight residual streams, TEMPER achieves the best CORE score while using about $84\%$ fewer additional parameters than mHC, thus showing a stronger performance-parameter efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: TEMPER proposes a tensorized low-rank parameterization for hyper-connections in residual networks, drastically reducing parameter growth with stream count while maintaining or improving performance.
AI.motivation: Existing hyper-connection and manifold-constrained hyper-connection methods use dense, unstructured generators for aggregation, mixing, and redistribution, causing parameter count to explode quadratically with the number of residual streams, creating a bottleneck at scale.
AI.method: TEMPER represents the three generator matrices (pre-branch aggregation, residual mixing, post-branch redistribution) as multi-way tensors over input-stream, feature, and output-stream modes, and parameterizes them using tensor networks. This structured low-rank formulation preserves token-dependent manifold-constrained routing while bounding routing-logit and output differences via generator approximation error. Tensor ranks control the routing subspace dimensionality, with full ranks recovering dense routing as a special case.
AI.result: TEMPER matches or exceeds existing methods on language modeling and commonsense reasoning benchmarks. At eight residual streams, it achieves the best CORE score while using approximately 84% fewer additional parameters than manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC), demonstrating superior performance-parameter efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Tensorized efficient parameterization provides a compelling solution to the parameter-scaling problem in multi-stream residual routing, enabling expressive, stable, and parameter-efficient deep networks.

title: CMU-Drive and V2V-VLA: Cooperative Multi-agent Unified Driving with Reasoning Benchmark and Vehicle-to-Vehicle Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently achieved impressive performance for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet existing approaches are primarily designed for an individual single autonomous driving agent with limited support for cooperative perception, reasoning, and planning. We present Cooperative Multi-agent Unified Driving with Reasoning (CMU-Drive), a closed-loop end-to-end benchmark for evaluating cooperative autonomous driving with multiple connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) operating in safety-critical driving scenarios with background traffic participants. We further propose Vehicle-to-Vehicle Vision-Language-Action (V2V-VLA), a cooperative VLA model that integrates cooperative driving into a single forward pass by jointly generating driving actions, future waypoints, language reasoning, and communication policies. Experiments on CMU-Drive establish the first benchmark and baseline for cooperative VLA driving and provide a foundation for future research on multi-agent, closed-loop, end-to-end cooperative autonomous driving. Our code, benchmark, and model checkpoint will be publicly released to facilitate open-source research.

AI.tldr: CMU-Drive introduces a multi-agent closed-loop benchmark and the V2V-VLA model for cooperative end-to-end autonomous driving, integrating language reasoning, action generation, and communication in a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models for autonomous driving are limited to single-agent settings and lack support for cooperative perception, reasoning, and planning among multiple connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) in safety-critical scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) CMU-Drive, a closed-loop end-to-end benchmark featuring multiple CAVs with background traffic in safety-critical scenarios, and (2) V2V-VLA, a cooperative VLA model that jointly produces driving actions, future waypoints, language-based reasoning, and vehicle-to-vehicle communication policies in a single forward pass.
AI.result: The paper establishes the first benchmark and baseline results for cooperative VLA driving on CMU-Drive, providing a foundation for future multi-agent cooperative autonomous driving research.
AI.conclusion: Cooperative VLA driving is a promising direction; CMU-Drive and V2V-VLA together offer an initial platform and baseline to catalyze further open-source research in multi-agent, closed-loop, end-to-end cooperative autonomous driving.

title: Differential Privacy for Markov Chain State Trajectories
summary: Data-driven systems may require state trajectories of Markov chains to function because these trajectories contain information that is useful to the system, e.g., a product's credit risk, a user's physical location, or a user's internet browsing behavior. However, sharing such state trajectories can reveal sensitive information about users, which presents a privacy threat. Therefore, we develop a new framework for privatizing the state trajectories in a Markov chain using differential privacy. Our framework privatizes state trajectories online, in the sense that a private state trajectory is generated at the same time as the sensitive one it approximates. We treat Markov chains as weighted directed graphs whose edge weights are the negative logarithms of the transition probabilities. Then, each state in a private state trajectory is chosen by minimizing its distance to the corresponding state in the sensitive state trajectory, where the notion of distance is equal to the total edge weight along a shortest path. We prove that with high probability the private state trajectory remains close to the sensitive one, which maintains high utility for downstream uses of private data. Additionally, we prove that private state trajectories are consistently in the typical set of state trajectories generated by the underlying Markov chain, which means that private state trajectories have similar statistical properties to actual state trajectories produced by the underlying Markov chain. Numerical simulations show that under $3$-differential privacy, the mechanism we introduce exhibits up to an $80\%$ decrease in entropy compared to the state of the art, which illustrates that private state trajectories generated by our framework more closely resemble their corresponding sensitive state trajectory while maintaining the same level of privacy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a differential privacy framework for online privatization of Markov chain state trajectories, using shortest-path distance on a weighted graph (edge weights = negative log transition probabilities) to select private states. It provides theoretical guarantees on proximity to sensitive trajectories and membership in the typical set, with simulations showing up to 80% entropy reduction over prior art under 3-differential privacy.
AI.motivation: Data-driven systems increasingly rely on Markov chain state trajectories (e.g., credit risk, location, browsing behavior), but sharing these trajectories leaks sensitive user information. Existing privatization methods degrade utility too much, so there is a need for a mechanism that preserves both privacy and the statistical fidelity of trajectories.
AI.method: The framework treats a Markov chain as a weighted directed graph where edge weights are the negative logarithms of transition probabilities. Given a sensitive state trajectory, the mechanism generates a private trajectory online by selecting, at each step, the state that minimizes the shortest-path distance (total edge weight) to the corresponding sensitive state. Differential privacy is achieved by adding calibrated noise to this distance-minimizing selection process.
AI.result: The authors prove that with high probability, private trajectories remain close to sensitive ones (utility guarantee) and belong to the typical set of the Markov chain (statistical fidelity). Numerical simulations under 3-differential privacy show up to 80% entropy reduction compared to the state of the art, meaning private trajectories more closely match the sensitive ones at equal privacy levels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed shortest-path-based privatization mechanism for Markov chain trajectories achieves a superior privacy–utility trade-off, substantially outperforming existing methods in preserving trajectory fidelity while maintaining formal differential privacy guarantees.

title: MetaStrategy: Generative Ranking with Executable LLM Strategies
summary: Industrial recommender systems rank heterogeneous content under coupled user, business, commercial, and experience objectives. Existing generative ranking methods typically construct item sequences directly, making them difficult to integrate with mature predictive models, operational rules, and field-level guardrails. We present MetaStrategy, a framework that instead generates a structured, executable ranking strategy. Conditioned on request context, a large language model (LLM) policy emits a typed JSON bundle controlling objective weights, content and category preferences, experience constraints, and position policies. A deterministic validator and compiler instantiate an isolated Generator that competes atomically with incumbents under the list-level Evaluator of the Generator-Evaluator (GE) architecture. We train the policy in a production-path replay environment that re-executes logged requests through the current re-ranking stack without user exposure. The method combines selection, relative-rank, and baseline-lift rewards, a self-competitive curriculum that feeds frequent strategies back as competitors, and Evaluator-routed reward-augmented on-policy distillation that transfers complementary 4B-parameter Teachers into a compact 0.8B-parameter Student. We deploy MetaStrategy in Taobao Homepage Guess You Like through diff-triggered nearline generation; LLM inference remains outside synchronous ranking, with no observable increase in response time (RT). In a seven-day user-randomized online A/B test, MetaStrategy wins 27.93% of treatment-side GE calls and significantly improves click page views (click PV) by 2.11%, item-detail page views (IPV) by 3.12%, and transaction amount by 2.83%.

AI.tldr: MetaStrategy is an LLM-based framework for industrial recommender systems that generates structured, executable ranking strategies (JSON bundles) rather than ranking items directly. Deployed on Taobao's homepage, it improved click PV (+2.11%), IPV (+3.12%), and transaction amount (+2.83%) in online A/B tests without increasing response time.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommenders must balance coupled objectives (user engagement, business goals, commercial constraints, experience quality), but existing generative ranking methods output item sequences directly, making them hard to integrate with mature predictive models, operational rules, and field-level guardrails. A strategy-level generation approach is needed instead.
AI.method: The MetaStrategy framework uses an LLM policy conditioned on request context to emit a typed JSON bundle specifying objective weights, content/category preferences, experience constraints, and position policies. A validator and compiler produce an isolated Generator that competes atomically against incumbent strategies under the Generator-Evaluator (GE) architecture's list-level Evaluator. Training occurs in a production-path replay environment using selection, relative-rank, and baseline-lift rewards, plus a self-competitive curriculum and Evaluator-routed reward-augmented on-policy distillation from 4B-parameter Teachers into a 0.8B-parameter Student model. Deployment uses diff-triggered nearline generation, keeping LLM inference outside the synchronous ranking path.
AI.result: In a seven-day online A/B test on Taobao's "Guess You Like" homepage, MetaStrategy won 27.93% of treatment-side GE calls and delivered statistically significant lifts: click PV +2.11%, IPV +3.12%, and transaction amount +2.83%, with no observable RT increase.
AI.conclusion: Generating structured ranking strategies via LLMs, rather than direct item sequences, is a practical and effective paradigm for industrial recommenders. It enables seamless integration with existing infrastructure, supports multi-objective optimization, and achieves strong online business gains without latency overhead.

title: Contextual Value Alignment via Multilayer Combinatorial Fusion
summary:
Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values remains a major challenge, especially for trustworthy AI. While existing approaches such as RLHF, CAI, and their variants have achieved promising results, they often rely on a single-agent framework and a unified reward system. This limits their ability to capture ethical pluralism, adapt to diverse moral contexts, and reflect the dynamics of multi-agent moral reasoning.
  In this work, we propose a framework that utilizes multilayer combinatorial fusion for contextual value alignment (MCF-CVA). At the first layer of the framework, it instantiates multiple moral agents, each fine-tuned to represent a distinctive value. Their outputs are then expanded combinatorially using both score- and rank-combinations as well as average and weighted aggregations. These combined models are then reduced to the same number of initial moral agents. This expansion and reduction (EAR) process continues for multi-layers until a stopping criterion is reached.
  The MCF-CVA framework leverages cognitive diversity between agents to mitigate conflicts and redundancies across multiple agents, producing responses that better reflect contextual human values. The framework using the EAR algorithm is performed on the dual architecture of Euclidean score space and Kemeny rank space. Empirical evaluations demonstrated that the proposed framework outperforms single-agent baselines, multi-agent single-layer results, and previous aggregation approaches on standard metrics, showing that the MCF-CVA framework provides a robust and effective mechanism for advancing contextual value alignment in LLMs.

AI.tldr: MCF-CVA proposes a multi-layer, multi-agent framework for aligning LLMs with human values by iteratively expanding and reducing outputs from diverse moral agents using both score-based and rank-based combinatorial fusion, outperforming single-agent and single-layer baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment methods (RLHF, CAI) rely on single-agent frameworks with unified reward systems, which fail to capture ethical pluralism, adapt to diverse moral contexts, or reflect the dynamics of multi-agent moral reasoning.
AI.method: The MCF-CVA framework instantiates multiple moral agents, each fine-tuned to a distinct value. It applies an Expansion and Reduction (EAR) process across multiple layers: outputs are combinatorially expanded using score-combinations, rank-combinations, and average/weighted aggregations, then reduced back to the original number of agents. This operates in dual Euclidean score space and Kemeny rank space, leveraging cognitive diversity to mitigate conflicts and redundancies.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show MCF-CVA outperforms single-agent baselines, multi-agent single-layer results, and prior aggregation approaches on standard metrics.
AI.conclusion: The MCF-CVA framework provides a robust and effective mechanism for advancing contextual value alignment in LLMs by effectively harnessing cognitive diversity across multiple moral agents through multilayer combinatorial fusion.

title: Pseudo2CodeQA: A Benchmark for LLM-Based Structured Algorithmic Reasoning in Code Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance in natural language-to-code generation; however, their ability to follow structured algorithmic reasoning remains insufficiently understood. We introduce Pseudo2Code, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the impact of structured pseudocode on code generation quality and algorithmic faithfulness. The benchmark consists of 300 manually validated real-world programming tasks spanning multiple domains and three difficulty levels (Easy, Medium, and Hard). Each task contains a problem description, structured pseudocode, reference implementation, and executable test suite. To ensure benchmark reliability, we adopt a dual-stage human validation protocol and release fully executable benchmark instances. Beyond the benchmark, we propose the Pseudo2Code Agentic Framework, a multi-stage pipeline that leverages pseudocode as an explicit intermediate reasoning representation for code generation. We evaluate both commercial and open-source language models using a rubric-based evaluation framework that measures correctness, completeness, relevance, clarity, reasoning quality, and pseudocode adherence, complemented by execution-based testing. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Pseudo2Code Agentic Pipeline consistently outperforms strong commercial and open-source baselines, achieving an overall score of 4.78 compared to 4.31 for the strongest baseline model. Furthermore, a human evaluation study involving 100 benchmark tasks shows strong agreement between human judgments and automated assessments. Our findings provide empirical evidence that structured pseudocode improves functional correctness, reasoning quality, and algorithmic faithfulness in code generation. We release Pseudo2Code to support future research on structured reasoning, interpretable code generation, and reliable AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: Pseudo2Code introduces a benchmark and agentic framework showing that structured pseudocode significantly improves code generation quality, with a multi-stage pipeline achieving a score of 4.78 vs. 4.31 for the best baseline.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at code generation but their ability to follow structured algorithmic reasoning is poorly understood. There is a need to systematically evaluate whether pseudocode as an intermediate representation enhances functional correctness, reasoning quality, and algorithmic faithfulness.
AI.method: The authors construct Pseudo2Code, a benchmark of 300 manually validated programming tasks (Easy/Medium/Hard) with problem descriptions, pseudocode, reference implementations, and test suites, validated via a dual-stage human protocol. They also propose a Pseudo2Code Agentic Framework — a multi-stage pipeline using pseudocode as explicit intermediate reasoning. Evaluation uses rubric-based scoring (correctness, completeness, relevance, clarity, reasoning quality, pseudocode adherence) plus execution-based testing, complemented by a 100-task human evaluation study.
AI.result: The Pseudo2Code Agentic Pipeline achieves an overall score of 4.78, outperforming the strongest baseline (4.31). Human evaluation on 100 tasks shows strong agreement with automated assessments, confirming that structured pseudocode improves functional correctness, reasoning quality, and algorithmic faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: Structured pseudocode is an effective intermediate representation for improving code generation. The Pseudo2Code benchmark and framework are released to support future research on structured reasoning, interpretable code generation, and reliable AI-assisted software development.

title: Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP): Hallucination Detection in LLMs from Hidden States
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent and useful responses but remain prone to hallucinations. We introduce Prompt Embedding Probes (PEP), a white-box method for answer-level hallucination detection from the hidden states of a frozen LLM. PEP extends standard linear probes by augmenting the input with a small number of learnable prompt embeddings. We evaluate PEP on TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MedQA using Qwen3 models at multiple scales. PEP improves hidden-state-based detection over standard linear probes in the main in-distribution setting. We further evaluate PEP for pre-generation prediction, cross-model transfer, and out-of-distribution generalization. PEP remains effective in the pre-generation and cross-model settings, whereas robust cross-dataset transfer remains difficult. These results show that prompt-based adaptation can strengthen hidden-state probing while keeping the backbone frozen and adding only a small number of trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: PEP introduces learnable prompt embeddings to augment linear probes for detecting hallucinations in LLMs from hidden states, improving detection performance across in-distribution, pre-generation, and cross-model settings while keeping the LLM frozen.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate fluent responses but are prone to hallucinations. Existing hidden-state probing methods for hallucination detection are limited in performance, motivating a more effective probing approach that remains lightweight and non-invasive to the base model.
AI.method: PEP extends standard linear probes by prepending a small number of learnable prompt embeddings to the LLM's hidden state representations before classification. The backbone LLM remains entirely frozen; only the probe (linear classifier plus prompt embeddings) is trained. Evaluated on TriviaQA, GSM8K, and MedQA using Qwen3 models at multiple scales. Tested across four scenarios: main in-distribution, pre-generation prediction, cross-model transfer, and out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.result: PEP consistently outperforms standard linear probes for answer-level hallucination detection in the in-distribution setting. It remains effective in pre-generation and cross-model transfer settings. However, robust cross-dataset transfer remains challenging.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based adaptation via learnable prompt embeddings is a practical and effective way to strengthen hidden-state probing for hallucination detection, requiring only a small number of additional trainable parameters while keeping the backbone LLM frozen.

title: CommitKV: Lifecycle-Aware KV Cache Compression via Commit Transitions for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Multi-turn Reasoning-and-Acting (ReAct) agents accumulate growing trajectories of reasoning, tool calls, and observations. Their key-value (KV) caches grow accordingly, increasing memory use and attention cost during model inference. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce these costs by evicting states with low attention scores. However, low attention in the current turn does not imply future irrelevance, as temporarily inactive information may become important later. Snapshot-based eviction methods therefore do not explicitly distinguish temporarily dormant information from information that appears to have completed its role. In this paper, we present CommitKV, which identifies KV lifecycles through commit transitions. Specifically, CommitKV first divides completed agent events into token pages and compares each eligible page's deletion effect before a tool-call commit and after the commit's returned observation has been incorporated. Based on these paired measurements, CommitKV distinguishes dormant pages from high-to-low completion candidates. It then applies a greedy joint test, accepting candidates for retirement only when their combined post-commit effect remains bounded. Finally, at a later compression checkpoint, accepted pages are excluded, a bounded set of pages awaiting post-commit measurement is protected, and the remaining KV states are retained within the cache budget using the same token indices for keys, values, and absolute positions. These mechanisms ensure that CommitKV can distinguish dormant information from information that has completed its observed role and can be safely removed. Experiments on various benchmarks show that CommitKV reduces agent memory use, accelerates end-to-end inference, and achieves higher accuracy than existing KV cache compression methods.

AI.tldr: CommitKV introduces a lifecycle-aware KV cache compression method for multi-turn ReAct agents that distinguishes temporarily dormant information from completed information via commit transitions, enabling safer eviction than attention-score-based methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn ReAct agents accumulate long KV caches, increasing memory and attention costs. Existing methods evict low-attention states, but low current attention does not guarantee future irrelevance — temporarily dormant information may later become important. Snapshot-based eviction fails to distinguish dormant from truly completed information.
AI.method: CommitKV identifies KV lifecycles through commit transitions. It partitions completed agent events into token pages, then measures each page's deletion effect both before a tool-call commit and after the commit's returned observation is incorporated. Pages are classified as dormant or high-to-low completion candidates via paired measurements. A greedy joint test accepts candidates for retirement only when their combined post-commit effect remains bounded. At compression checkpoints, accepted pages are evicted, pages awaiting post-commit measurement are protected, and remaining KV states are retained within budget using consistent token indices for keys, values, and absolute positions.
AI.result: Experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that CommitKV reduces agent memory usage, accelerates end-to-end inference, and achieves higher accuracy than existing KV cache compression methods.
AI.conclusion: CommitKV provides a principled, lifecycle-aware alternative to attention-score-based KV cache eviction for multi-turn ReAct agents, effectively distinguishing dormant from completed information to achieve safer compression with improved memory, speed, and accuracy.

title: Controlled Memory Interference in Continual LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables AI agents to maintain continuity across sessions, personalize behavior, and evolve through accumulated experience. Yet memory evolution is not simply a process of storing more information: new experiences may reinforce, revise, or interfere with existing memory states. Existing systems mainly emphasize memory construction and relevance-based retrieval, but several memories may remain simultaneously relevant while differing in state, temporal validity, or authority. We introduce Controlled Memory Interference (CMI), a controlled diagnostic and data-generation framework for studying how agent memory evolves under different memory relationships. Across controlled memory evolution, benign accumulation has limited effects, whereas relationship-specific interference sharply suppresses update plasticity with little stability gain, either by blocking target-memory exposure or by disrupting its downstream use. Lexical and Dense retrieval exhibit distinct interference pathways, while poisoning is more sensitive to update-authority cues than to recency alone. Beyond diagnosis, CMI provides targeted examples for interference-aware memory learning, improving the distinction between valid updates and interference-inducing memories while preserving performance on original memory tasks. These findings show that memory evolution is shaped not only by memory scale, but also by interactions among accumulated experiences. More broadly, memory interference emerges as an important factor for reliable continual agent memory systems.

AI.tldr: CMI introduces a diagnostic framework for studying how agent memory evolves under conflicting experiences, revealing that relationship-specific interference sharply suppresses update plasticity with minimal stability gain. The framework also generates targeted examples for interference-aware learning, improving the distinction between valid updates and interference-inducing memories.
AI.motivation: Existing agent memory systems focus on construction and relevance-based retrieval but neglect how multiple simultaneously relevant memories with conflicting states, temporal validity, or authority create interference. Memory evolution involves more than accumulation — new experiences can reinforce, revise, or interfere with prior states, yet this dynamic is poorly understood.
AI.method: CMI is a controlled diagnostic and data-generation framework that systematically studies memory evolution under different memory relationships. It evaluates benign accumulation versus relationship-specific interference, examines distinct interference pathways in Lexical and Dense retrieval, and tests sensitivity to update-authority cues versus recency. The framework also generates targeted examples for interference-aware memory learning.
AI.result: Benign accumulation shows limited effects, while relationship-specific interference sharply suppresses update plasticity with little stability gain. Lexical and Dense retrieval exhibit distinct interference pathways. Poisoning is more sensitive to update-authority cues than recency. Interference-aware learning improves distinction between valid updates and interference-inducing memories while preserving original task performance.
AI.conclusion: Memory evolution is shaped not only by scale but by interactions among accumulated experiences. Memory interference emerges as a critical factor for building reliable continual agent memory systems.

title: Evaluation of Motivational Interviewing Counsellors with Task-Aware Multi-Stage LLM-Based Simulated Clients
summary: The development and benchmarking of Large Language Model (LLM)-based Motivational Interviewing (MI) counsellors now often rely on LLM-based simulated clients. Prior work on simulated clients, however, has not aligned with the specific tasks fundamental to the MI therapy approach. A key task is evoking, in which the counsellor first elicits the client's ambivalence and then strengthens the client's motivation for change. We present Evoke-Sim, a task-aware, multi-stage LLM-based client simulation framework for evaluating MI counsellors in smoking cessation, designed specifically for the evoking MI task. Evoke-Sim employs structured client profiles, an evoking-specific three-stage conversation flow, and a reveal policy that regulates which client profile information might be disclosed at each stage. We show that compared to existing profile-grounded simulated clients, Evoke-Sim is better at differentiating levels of MI quality using task-aware evaluation metrics, while reducing non-grounded client statements and premature disclosure of client information, setting a higher standard for the evaluation of LLM-based MI counsellors.

AI.tldr: Evoke-Sim is a task-aware, multi-stage LLM-based simulated client framework for evaluating MI counsellors, specifically designed for the evoking task in smoking cessation. It uses structured profiles, a three-stage conversation flow, and a reveal policy to better differentiate MI quality while reducing ungrounded statements and premature disclosures.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based simulated clients for evaluating MI counsellors are not aligned with the specific tasks fundamental to MI therapy — particularly the evoking task, where the counsellor elicits ambivalence and strengthens motivation for change. Current profile-grounded simulators lack task-aware design, leading to poor differentiation of MI quality, ungrounded client statements, and premature information disclosure.
AI.method: The authors propose Evoke-Sim, a multi-stage LLM-based client simulation framework with three components: (1) structured client profiles capturing relevant background and ambivalence; (2) an evoking-specific three-stage conversation flow mirroring the MI evoking process; and (3) a reveal policy that controls which profile information is disclosed at each stage. The framework is instantiated for smoking cessation counselling.
AI.result: Compared to existing profile-grounded simulated clients, Evoke-Sim better differentiates levels of MI quality using task-aware evaluation metrics, reduces non-grounded (hallucinated) client statements, and reduces premature disclosure of client profile information.
AI.conclusion: Evoke-Sim sets a higher standard for evaluating LLM-based MI counsellors by introducing task-aware, multi-stage simulation grounded in MI theory, and demonstrates the importance of aligning simulated client design with the specific therapeutic tasks being evaluated.

title: SkillsMetric: Mapping the Detection Boundary of Static Analysis for Malicious Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills---structured packages of instructions and scripts that augment LLM-based agents---are rapidly proliferating, yet their security properties remain under-explored. We present \textsc{SkillsMetric}, a five-stage static analysis framework that scores skill packages along pattern density, statistical anomaly, dataflow taint, import anomaly, and capability mismatch dimensions. We construct an adversarial evaluation dataset of 2{,}266 skills spanning 16~attack types across code-level, system-level, and semantic-level threats, and evaluate on the full SkillMD-138K corpus. Our framework achieves an AUC of 0.93 and 5-fold cross-validated F1 of 73.4\%$\pm$0.5\%, with strong detection of data exfiltration (93\%) and steganographic payloads (93\%). Crucially, we identify fundamental blind spots: \emph{host destruction} attacks using common shell commands evade all five stages (0\% detection), and \emph{prompt injection} via natural-language manipulation achieves only 42\% detection. These findings establish that static analysis alone is insufficient for skill security, motivating defense-in-depth architectures that combine fast static pre-screening with semantic review.

AI.tldr: SkillsMetric is a five-stage static analysis framework for evaluating the security of LLM agent skill packages. Tested on 2,266 adversarial skills across 16 attack types and the full SkillMD-138K corpus, it achieves AUC 0.93 and F1 73.4%, but critically fails on host destruction (0% detection) and prompt injection (42%), demonstrating static analysis alone is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Agent skills—structured instruction/script packages for LLM-based agents—are proliferating rapidly, but their security properties have not been systematically studied. This gap creates risk as skills gain access to sensitive systems and data.
AI.method: SkillsMetric employs a five-stage static analysis framework scoring skills along: (1) pattern density, (2) statistical anomaly, (3) dataflow taint, (4) import anomaly, and (5) capability mismatch. The authors constructed an adversarial evaluation dataset of 2,266 skills covering 16 attack types (code-level, system-level, semantic-level) and evaluated on the full SkillMD-138K corpus.
AI.result: The framework achieves AUC 0.93, 5-fold cross-validated F1 of 73.4% ± 0.5%. Strong detection on data exfiltration (93%) and steganographic payloads (93%). However, host destruction attacks using common shell commands achieve 0% detection, and prompt injection via natural-language manipulation achieves only 42% detection.
AI.conclusion: Static analysis alone is insufficient for skill security due to fundamental blind spots. The authors recommend defense-in-depth architectures combining fast static pre-screening with semantic review to address threats that evade purely static approaches.

title: TSPORec: Token Selection via Preference Optimization for LLM-Based Sequential Recommendation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for improving recommendation systems. The effectiveness of LLMs arises from their ability to harness rich textual information and their capacity to model heterogeneous user preferences based on users' interaction history. However, due to the large-scale and deep architectures, LLM-based sequential recommendation approaches generally incur high inference costs, resulting in a low return on investment. To mitigate this cost, many existing approaches resort to using only the first few tokens of item descriptions, which inadvertently discards valuable information contained in the full text, thereby leading to suboptimal recommendation performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Token Selection approach for Preference Optimization in LLM-based sequential Recommendation, i.e., TSPORec, which accurately pinpoints informative tokens throughout the entire textual content to improve recommendation performance. Specifically, we design a three-stage pipeline to select informative tokens and introduce a novel proxy reward to facilitate the implementation. TSPORec not only enhances recommendation performance but also improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments across two models and datasets demonstrate the superb performance (up to 31.25%) and efficiency (up to 63.4%) of our approach compared with six baseline approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/WNQzhu/TSPORec.git.

AI.tldr: TSPORec is a token selection method that identifies informative tokens from full item descriptions to optimize LLM-based sequential recommendation, achieving up to 31.25% performance improvement and 63.4% efficiency gain over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based sequential recommenders incur high inference costs due to large-scale architectures. Many approaches truncate item descriptions to only the first few tokens to reduce cost, but this discards valuable information and degrades recommendation quality. A method is needed that retains full-text information while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: TSPORec uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) token-level importance scoring across full item descriptions, (2) selection of the most informative tokens based on these scores, and (3) preference optimization using a novel proxy reward signal. The approach selectively retains semantically rich tokens while pruning redundant ones, enabling efficient LLM inference without sacrificing information fidelity.
AI.result: Evaluated across two models and two datasets against six baselines, TSPORec achieved up to 31.25% improvement in recommendation performance and up to 63.4% improvement in computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: TSPORec demonstrates that selective token retention — rather than naive truncation — effectively balances the trade-off between recommendation quality and inference cost in LLM-based sequential recommenders. The code is publicly available.

title: IntelliAudit: Using Large Language Models to Evaluate Audit Controls
summary: IT audits require auditors to judge whether heterogeneous organizational evidence satisfies semantic security and compliance controls. This judgment is difficult to automate because relevant evidence is distributed across policies, records, spreadsheets, and operational artifacts, and because audit conclusions depend on evidentiary sufficiency rather than keyword matching. We present IntelliAudit, a retrieval-grounded multi-agent system for IT audit evidence evaluation. Given a control and an evidence corpus, IntelliAudit retrieves relevant artifacts, generates an evidence-grounded assessment, challenges adverse findings, adjudicates disagreements, and produces an auditor-facing recommendation with cited evidence, rationale, missing-evidence analysis, and remediation guidance. We instantiate IntelliAudit on ISO/IEC 27001 and evaluate it across multiple simulated organizations using expert auditor review and audit-readiness user feedback. The evaluation shows that IntelliAudit can support control interpretation, evidence-grounded reasoning, and audit-preparation workflows, while also revealing the importance of human oversight for calibrating sufficiency judgments and correcting overly permissive recommendations. These results suggest that retrieval-grounded multi-agent systems can assist audit evidence review, but should remain decision-support tools rather than autonomous certification systems.

AI.tldr: IntelliAudit is a retrieval-grounded multi-agent system that automates IT audit evidence evaluation by retrieving relevant artifacts, generating assessments, challenging findings, adjudicating disagreements, and producing auditor-facing recommendations with cited evidence and missing-evidence analysis. Evaluated on ISO/IEC 27001, it demonstrates utility as a decision-support tool but requires human oversight for sufficiency calibration.
AI.motivation: Automating IT audit judgments is difficult because evidence is distributed across heterogeneous artifacts (policies, records, spreadsheets, operational documents) and audit conclusions rely on evidentiary sufficiency assessments rather than simple keyword matching. Existing approaches lack the capacity for retrieval-grounded, multi-perspective reasoning about semantic compliance.
AI.method: IntelliAudit employs a multi-agent architecture that: (1) retrieves relevant evidence from a corpus given a control statement; (2) generates an evidence-grounded compliance assessment; (3) uses an adversarial agent to challenge adverse findings; (4) adjudicates inter-agent disagreements; and (5) synthesizes a final recommendation with cited evidence, rationale, missing-evidence analysis, and remediation guidance. The system is instantiated on ISO/IEC 27001 controls and evaluated across simulated organizations.
AI.result: Expert auditor review and audit-readiness user feedback demonstrate that IntelliAudit can support control interpretation, evidence-grounded reasoning, and audit-preparation workflows. However, the evaluation also reveals that the system can produce overly permissive recommendations and requires human oversight to calibrate sufficiency judgments appropriately.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-grounded multi-agent systems can meaningfully assist IT audit evidence review, but they should function as decision-support tools rather than autonomous certification systems, given the persistent need for human judgment in calibrating evidentiary sufficiency and correcting overly permissive outputs.

title: A Unified Issue Resolution Benchmark for Requirement Clarification, Planning, and Code Generation for Coding Agents
summary: Large language model-powered coding agents are increasingly used to modify existing code repositories, for example, by adding features or fixing bugs. Yet existing repository-level benchmarks typically evaluate only whether the final patch passes tests. Satisfying a user request requires a long chain of interdependent reasoning and decisions: an agent must recover explicit and implicit requirements, formulate a repository-grounded implementation plan, and translate it into correct code. A pass/fail outcome cannot characterize how an unsuccessful trajectory diverges from the requirements and implementation process needed for a correct patch. To address this gap, we introduce SWE-RPG, a repository-level benchmark that combines executable patch evaluation with validated ground-truth references (GTs) for (1) Requirement Clarification and (2) Implementation Planning. These intermediate GTs support retrospective, GT-aligned diagnosis of complete coding-agent trajectories across clarification, planning, code generation, and artifact submission. SWE-RPG comprises 163 tasks from 31 Python and Java repositories, including 113 bug fixes and 50 feature additions. We evaluate 3 coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, with 6 large language model backends, including Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Terra. Results show that the evaluated popular coding agents still struggle to implement user requests in existing repositories, achieving an average resolved rate of only 31.5% on SWE-RPG. Intermediate-GT diagnosis further identifies implicit requirement recovery as the main bottleneck, accounting for 24.5%--46.0% of agent runs. This result suggests implicit-requirement recovery as a key candidate direction for improving coding agents. The benchmark data and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/Xin-Zhou-smu/SWE-RPG-Bench.

AI.tldr: SWE-RPG is a repository-level benchmark with 163 tasks across 31 Python/Java repos that augments standard pass/fail evaluation with ground-truth references for Requirement Clarification and Implementation Planning, enabling trajectory-level diagnosis. Evaluation of 3 agents × 6 LLM backends reveals a 31.5% average resolve rate, with implicit requirement recovery identified as the primary bottleneck (24.5%–46.0% of runs).
AI.motivation: Existing repository-level benchmarks only evaluate final patch correctness (pass/fail), which fails to capture where and how an agent's reasoning trajectory diverges from the necessary requirements and implementation process. There is a need for fine-grained, intermediate diagnostic signals to understand agent failures.
AI.method: SWE-RPG introduces validated ground-truth references for two intermediate stages: (1) Requirement Clarification (explicit and implicit) and (2) Implementation Planning. These enable retrospective, GT-aligned diagnosis across the full trajectory (clarification → planning → code generation → submission). The benchmark contains 163 tasks (113 bug fixes, 50 feature additions) from 31 Python and Java repositories. Three coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) were evaluated with six LLM backends (including Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Terra).
AI.result: The evaluated agents achieved an average resolved rate of only 31.5% on SWE-RPG. Intermediate-GT diagnosis revealed that implicit requirement recovery is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 24.5%–46.0% of agent runs, making it a key area for improvement.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents still significantly struggle with repository-level modification tasks. Moving beyond pass/fail evaluation to trajectory-level diagnosis reveals that recovering implicit requirements is the critical weakness. SWE-RPG provides the infrastructure to benchmark and diagnose this gap, pointing toward implicit-requirement recovery as a high-priority research direction.

title: APEX-VW: A Document-Level English-Spanish Post-Editing Dataset in the Healthcare Domain
summary: Post-Editing (PE) of Machine Translation (MT) output often involves repeating the same lexical and terminological corrections across many segments, especially in specialised and highly repetitive documents. Despite substantial work on Automatic Post-Editing (APE), most available corpora operate at the sentence level, others are synthetic, and overall not designed to study how corrections propagate in realistic Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) workflows. This paper presents the APEX-VW (Automatic Post-Editing eXperiments on Virtual Wards) Corpus, a new open English-Spanish (EN-ES) dataset built from recent NHS virtual-ward documents and professional PE in Trados Studio, with controlled MT, terminology, and quality assurance settings. The corpus contains seven document-coherent source texts totalling 42k words, translated with four MT systems representing different paradigms and then post-edited by professional translators. Unlike prior resources such as WMT APE corpora, eSCAPE, MLQE-PE, or LangMark, the dataset preserves document order and CAT-tool context, making it suitable for research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop translation support. The paper describes the corpus design, data preparation, PE setup, and initial corpus statistics, and positions the resource as a benchmark for document-level APE and propagation-aware assistive tools.

AI.tldr: APEX-VW is a new open EN-ES document-level post-editing corpus (42k words, 7 documents) built from NHS virtual-ward texts with professional PE in Trados Studio across four MT systems. It preserves document coherence and CAT-tool context to enable research on correction propagation, terminology normalisation, and document-level APE.
AI.motivation: Existing APE corpora are predominantly sentence-level, synthetic, or fail to capture how lexical/terminological corrections propagate across segments in real CAT workflows — a critical gap for studying document-coherent post-editing in specialised, repetitive domains.
AI.method: Construction of the APEX-VW corpus: seven document-coherent EN source texts from NHS virtual-ward documentation were translated using four distinct MT paradigms, then professionally post-edited in Trados Studio under controlled MT, terminology, and QA settings, preserving document order and CAT-tool context.
AI.result: The resulting corpus comprises 42k words across seven documents × four MT systems, with document-level coherence and CAT-context metadata intact. Initial corpus statistics are provided, and the resource is positioned as a benchmark for propagation-aware, document-level APE research.
AI.conclusion: APEX-VW fills a key resource gap by offering a realistic, document-coherent, professionally produced PE corpus that supports research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop translation assistance beyond the sentence level.

title: Adaptive KappaSharp: Condition-Number Shaping for Preferential Bayesian Optimization
summary: Preferential Bayesian optimization (PBO) optimizes objectives accessible only through pairwise user comparisons. The standard approach fits a Gaussian process surrogate for observed pairwise comparisons (PairwiseGP) using the Laplace approximation and selects queries with the Expected Utility of Best Option (EUBO) acquisition function. EUBO queries new candidates at each step, producing pairs that share no candidates with previous queries. Each such pair forms an isolated component in the comparison graph, removing one degree of freedom from the likelihood Hessian and making it rank-deficient. This deficiency is structural and cannot be resolved by changing the surrogate modeling approach. Existing approaches to remedy this issue either waste query budget by forcing comparisons to stay connected, or apply uniform regularization that also perturbs directions already well-constrained by the observed comparisons. We propose KappaSharp that enables a diagonal correction to the Hessian to reduce its condition number, with larger corrections where the prior uncertainty is higher. The correction is only applied in the model fitting step, not query selection. An adaptive variant of KappaSharp is also presented that activates the correction only when the surrogate is confident about recent comparisons, avoiding unnecessary corrections when the problem is well-conditioned. On 11 benchmarks (5--20 dimensions), including a 16-dimensional controller tuning problem in plasma medicine, Adaptive KappaSharp outperforms the standard PBO baseline, with up to +10.9% ($p{=}0.003$).

AI.tldr: Preferential Bayesian optimization suffers from rank-deficient Hessians due to isolated pairwise comparisons. The authors propose KappaSharp, a diagonal Hessian correction that is stronger where prior uncertainty is high, applied only during model fitting. An adaptive variant activates the correction only when the surrogate is confident. Adaptive KappaSharp outperforms the standard PBO baseline across 11 benchmarks, with up to +10.9% improvement.
AI.motivation: In standard PBO using PairwiseGP with Laplace approximation and EUBO acquisition, each new query pair forms an isolated component in the comparison graph. This structurally removes one degree of freedom from the likelihood Hessian, making it rank-deficient. Existing remedies either waste query budget by forcing connectivity or apply uniform regularization that perturbs well-constrained directions. The authors aim to resolve this deficiency efficiently without these drawbacks.
AI.method: KappaSharp applies a diagonal correction to the Hessian to reduce its condition number, with larger corrections applied where the prior uncertainty is higher. The correction is exclusively applied during model fitting, not during query selection, preserving the EUBO acquisition logic. An adaptive variant, Adaptive KappaSharp, activates the correction only when the surrogate is confident about recent comparisons, thereby avoiding unnecessary regularization when the problem is already well-conditioned.
AI.result: Evaluated on 11 benchmarks ranging from 5 to 20 dimensions — including a 16-dimensional controller tuning problem in plasma medicine — Adaptive KappaSharp consistently outperforms the standard PBO baseline, achieving up to +10.9% improvement (p = 0.003).
AI.conclusion: Adaptive KappaSharp provides a principled, efficient solution to the structural rank-deficiency problem in PBO by applying targeted, uncertainty-aware Hessian corrections only when needed, leading to significant and statistically robust performance gains over the standard approach.

title: Harnessing Abundance: A Generativity Perspective on Human-GenAI Collaboration
summary: Research on human-GenAI collaboration yields conflicting findings: GenAI can enhance creativity yet reduce collective diversity, with uneven benefits across skill levels. Rather than treating these as contradictions, we argue they reflect a core feature of GenAI: abundance. GenAI makes ideas, drafts, and recombinations plentiful, potentially expanding the hypothesis space and surfacing unanticipated possibilities. However, abundance alone doesn't ensure better outcomes. We propose generative fit as a unifying mechanism explaining when abundance yields productive creativity and when it backfires. Drawing on Generativity Theory, generative fit captures how well a system's generative potential complements a community's generative capacities. We develop a conceptual framework for collaborative human-GenAI settings where participants share goals, depend on one another, and must integrate diverse contributions. By mapping abundance to cognitive, social, and organizational factors of collective creativity, we explain apparent tradeoffs and offer actionable implications for designing workflows that convert abundance into valued creative outcomes.

AI.tldr: GenAI introduces abundance into creative collaboration, which can enhance or undermine outcomes. The authors propose "generative fit" — the alignment between a system's generative potential and a community's generative capacities — as a unifying mechanism explaining when abundance yields productive creativity versus when it backfires.
AI.motivation: Resolve conflicting findings in human-GenAI collaboration research: GenAI can boost individual creativity but reduce collective diversity, with uneven benefits across skill levels. These contradictions are reframed not as paradoxes but as manifestations of a core property — abundance — requiring a unifying theoretical mechanism.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual framework grounded in Generativity Theory, mapping the effects of GenAI-induced abundance across cognitive, social, and organizational factors of collective creativity. It synthesizes existing empirical findings and introduces the construct of "generative fit" as an explanatory mechanism.
AI.result: The framework explains apparent tradeoffs in human-GenAI collaboration: when generative fit is high, abundance expands the hypothesis space and surfaces valuable unanticipated possibilities; when fit is low, abundance overwhelms, homogenizes output, or exacerbates skill-based inequities. Actionable design implications for collaborative workflows are derived.
AI.conclusion: Generative fit serves as a critical lens for designing human-GenAI systems, shifting focus from whether GenAI helps or harms creativity to under what conditions abundance is productively channeled. Future research should empirically validate the framework and develop interventions that align generative potential with community capacities.

title: Whose Refusal Is It? The Unmeasured Contribution of Black-Box Multimodal Guardrails
summary:
A black-box guardrail is evaluated as though the safety number it earns were its own. It is not. A defended pipeline holds two components that can refuse (the guardrail, and the target model out of its own alignment), and every reported metric is a sum over both. We show that the guardrail's actual share of the safety credited to it runs from none of it to essentially all of it, decided by two variables no evaluation records: which channel carries the payload, and what text the harness places in the defense's internal read.
  The split is recoverable at no extra cost, because a guard block replaces the model's response and the two counts are therefore disjoint. On a text guard across two open-weight targets: with the payload rendered as pixels the guard blocks nothing and the model produces every refusal the system makes; reading the encoded prompt the attacker actually sent, the guard produces a minority of the refusals attributed to it; reading the unencoded request behind the attack, it blocks almost everything and the model falls silent. The blindness is not inaccuracy: the same guards block no benign image inputs either, so their image-channel decision is a constant.
  Granting the unencoded request inflates measured benefit substantially for a guard gate, less for a caption-mediated re-check, and not at all for a majority-vote smoother; the ordering reproduces in an independent replicate. Isolating the grant within one defense shows it does not improve detection: the harm-verdict stage contributes nothing, while the stage that regenerates the answer carries the effect. Nor is the inflated setting careless; the reference implementation builds every stage from a single prompt field that cannot distinguish what the attacker sent from what the benchmark records, so faithful porting supplies it silently. Previously published figures of our own are among those revised.

AI.tldr: Black-box evaluations of guardrails conflate the safety contributions of the guardrail itself and the target model's intrinsic alignment; the split can be recovered by noting that a guard block and a model refusal are disjoint events. The guardrail's apparent efficacy depends heavily on unreported variables—payload channel and internal prompt construction—ranging from zero to near-total credit. Rendering payloads as pixels blinds text guards, while exposing the unencoded request inflates guard metrics; the effect localizes to response regeneration, not harm detection, and silently propagates through reference implementations.
AI.motivation: Black-box safety evaluations of defended LLM pipelines treat aggregate refusal metrics as attributable to the guardrail, ignoring that the target model also refuses prompts from its own alignment. This conflation prevents understanding how much safety a guardrail actually contributes and obscures critical confounding variables in evaluation design.
AI.method: The authors decompose the aggregate refusal count into two disjoint components: guard-blocked responses and model-generated refusals. They systematically vary two unreported variables—(1) the channel carrying the adversarial payload (text tokens vs. rendered pixels) and (2) the text exposed to the guardrail's internal processing (encoded attacker payload vs. unencoded benign request)—across two open-weight target models. They test three defense architectures: a guard gate, a caption-mediated re-check, and a majority-vote smoother, with an independent replication. They isolate the effect to the response-regeneration stage by comparing the harm-verdict and answer-regeneration stages within a single defense.
AI.result: When payloads are rendered as pixels, the text guard blocks nothing and the model produces all refusals. When reading the encoded attacker prompt, the guard accounts for only a minority of refusals. When reading the unencoded request, the guard blocks nearly everything and the model falls silent—inflating measured benefit substantially for guard gates, less for caption-mediated re-checks, and not at all for majority-vote smoothers. The harm-verdict stage contributes nothing to detection; the response-regeneration stage carries the entire effect. The unencoded-request inflation arises silently from reference implementations that build all stages from a single prompt field.
AI.conclusion: Guardrail evaluations must decompose safety metrics into guard-blocked vs. model-refusal components—recoverable at no extra cost—and must report what text the guardrail actually reads and through which channel the payload arrives. Failure to do so inflates or obscures true guardrail efficacy, and previously published figures (including the authors' own) require revision.

title: IntHQ: Task-Interactive Hierarchical Query on Dual-Stream Representations for Generative Recommendation
summary: Multi-task learning over heterogeneous data is fundamental to modern recommendation, while generative models are emerging as the backbone of next-generation recommenders. However, the integration of multi-task learning into the generative paradigm remains largely unexplored. Existing multi-task recommenders, in both discriminative and generative paradigms, extract task-relevant features from a single task-agnostic representation and wire tasks into a predefined conversion funnel. We show that this scheme is inherently prone to a threefold collapse. Source collapse, where task-specific signals are injected late and diluted in the shared latent space. Relational collapse, where task dependencies are either implicitly absorbed by the backbone or statically fixed by predefined funnels. Hierarchical collapse, where tasks depend on features at different scales and shift across training stages. We propose IntHQ, a multi-task generative recommender with three components, each alleviating one collapse. Dual-Stream Decoupling (DSD) injects task identity into computation stream early and separates the shared context stream from the task-specific stream, alleviating signal dilution. Task-Interactive Modeling (TIM) replaces the predefined funnel with explicit cross-task interaction, letting each task condition on the realized outcomes of its predecessors with learned, input-adaptive strength. Hierarchical Querying (HQ) lets each task gather multi-scale information across different layers at different training stages. In offline evaluations, IntHQ consistently outperforms competitive encoder backbones under four representative task-head configurations. Deployed in production on Amap, serving hundreds of millions of users for travel recommendation, IntHQ yields a 1.60\% relative UVCTR lift.

AI.tldr: IntHQ is a multi-task generative recommender that addresses three forms of collapse (source, relational, hierarchical) via Dual-Stream Decoupling, Task-Interactive Modeling, and Hierarchical Querying, achieving offline gains and a 1.60% relative UVCTR lift in production on Amap.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-task recommenders—both discriminative and generative—extract task-specific features from a single task-agnostic representation and wire tasks into a predefined funnel, which leads to three collapses: (1) source collapse (task signals diluted in shared latent space), (2) relational collapse (task dependencies implicitly absorbed or statically fixed), and (3) hierarchical collapse (tasks needing features at different scales across training stages are underserved). The integration of multi-task learning into generative recommenders remains underexplored.
AI.method: IntHQ introduces three components: (1) Dual-Stream Decoupling (DSD) — injects task identity early, separating a shared context stream from a task-specific stream to prevent signal dilution. (2) Task-Interactive Modeling (TIM) — replaces predefined funnels with explicit, learned, input-adaptive cross-task interactions where each task conditions on predecessors' realized outcomes. (3) Hierarchical Querying (HQ) — enables each task to gather multi-scale information across different layers at different training stages.
AI.result: In offline evaluation, IntHQ consistently outperforms competitive encoder backbones across four representative task-head configurations. Deployed in production on Amap serving hundreds of millions of users, it yields a 1.60% relative UVCTR lift.
AI.conclusion: IntHQ effectively addresses the threefold collapse problem in multi-task generative recommendation, demonstrating both strong offline performance and real-world production impact at scale.

title: QuantumMind: Constraint-Grounded Agentic Reasoning for Speedup Analysis in Quantum Computing
summary: Identifying a meaningful quantum speedup requires more than matching a classical problem to a familiar quantum primitive: the claim must preserve the task, respect access and output models, expose required promises, and remain within a defensible complexity scope. We present QuantumMind, an auditable agentic workflow for generating and conservatively screening quantum-acceleration hypotheses. A fixed sequence of typed, role-specialized actions formalizes the public task, analyzes structure and classical bottlenecks, matches a source-linked registry of quantum primitives and barriers, and constructs a scoped candidate scheme. A deterministic ten-check validator assigns the authoritative verdict; completed states are compiled into a Quantum Acceleration Evidence Graph and passed through a downward-only research screen that cannot strengthen the decision. We evaluate QuantumMind against seven task-adapted prompting and agentic controls on 582 identical open-discovery tasks. Under the frozen Open-Discovery Score (ODS), QuantumMind obtains 53.1 mean ODS, exceeding the strongest baseline by 17.3 points (48.2% relative), and wins 355 of 582 paired tasks against that baseline. It passes the graph audit on 99.8% of tasks, compared with 43.6% for the strongest baseline, and ranks first in all seven task families. The results indicate that typed state transitions and deterministic evidence control contribute beyond fluent generation alone.

AI.tldr: QuantumMind is an auditable agentic workflow that systematically generates and screens quantum-acceleration hypotheses using typed state transitions and a deterministic ten-check validator. It outperforms seven baselines on 582 open-discovery tasks, achieving a 53.1 mean Open-Discovery Score (48.2% relative improvement) and passing graph audits on 99.8% of tasks.
AI.motivation: Identifying meaningful quantum speedup claims requires rigorous preservation of task, access/output models, promises, and complexity scope. Existing approaches relying solely on fluent generation lack the structured, auditable reasoning needed to produce defensible quantum-acceleration hypotheses.
AI.method: The authors propose QuantumMind, an agentic workflow featuring: (1) a fixed sequence of typed, role-specialized actions that formalize the task, analyze structure and classical bottlenecks, match against a source-linked registry of quantum primitives and barriers, and construct scoped candidate schemes; (2) a deterministic ten-check validator that assigns an authoritative verdict; (3) compilation into a Quantum Acceleration Evidence Graph; and (4) a downward-only research screen that cannot strengthen the decision. Evaluation compares against seven task-adapted prompting and agentic baselines on 582 identical open-discovery tasks using the frozen Open-Discovery Score (ODS).
AI.result: QuantumMind achieves a mean ODS of 53.1, exceeding the strongest baseline by 17.3 points (48.2% relative improvement). It wins 355 of 582 paired tasks against that baseline, passes the graph audit on 99.8% of tasks (vs. 43.6% for the strongest baseline), and ranks first across all seven task families.
AI.conclusion: Typed state transitions and deterministic evidence control contribute significantly beyond fluent generation alone, demonstrating that structured, auditable agentic workflows can more reliably produce and screen quantum-acceleration hypotheses.

title: Memoir: Learning, Verifying, and Evolving False-Positive Memories for Static Application Security Testing Tools
summary: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools have become indispensable in modern secure software devel- opment. However, these tools often generate false-positive (FP) alerts, imposing substantial manual inspection costs and reducing the trust from developers. Existing FP reduction methods still face two primary challenges. First, the large differences among SAST tools and vulnerability categories make it difficult for these methods to learn recurring patterns in historical false positives. Moreover, the knowledge used by these methods are largely static and cannot be updated as newly validated cases accumulate. To address these challenges, we propose Memoir, a memory- driven framework for identifying false positives by transform- ing historical FP alerts into reusable semantic memories. It consists of two key modules. First, historical semantic memory construction converts historical FP alerts into structured semantic memories through LLM-guided annotation, pattern clustering, and memory synthesis to capture reusable behavioral patterns. Moreover, memory-driven identification and evolution retrieves relevant memories and performs semantic verification against taxonomy consistency and security invariants before making the final prediction. It then incorporates verified predictions back into the memory repository, allowing the knowledge base to evolve as new cases accumulate. We evaluate Memoir on CWE- Bench-Java to demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world security analysis. Specifically, Memoir achieves an F1-score of 99.43% with a Recall of 98.88% and perfect Precision, consistently outperforming other baselines. Furthermore, an industrial case study on production software systems from a top IT company shows that the learned memory base generalizes effectively across different SAST tools without retraining.

AI.tldr: Memoir is a memory-driven framework that reduces SAST false positives by converting historical FP alerts into reusable semantic memories via LLM-guided annotation, pattern clustering, and memory synthesis. It achieves 99.43% F1-score on CWE-Bench-Java and generalizes across SAST tools without retraining.
AI.motivation: SAST tools are essential for secure software development but generate many false-positive alerts, leading to high manual inspection costs and reduced developer trust. Existing FP reduction methods struggle due to (1) large variability across SAST tools and vulnerability categories, hindering pattern learning, and (2) static knowledge bases that cannot evolve as new validated cases accumulate.
AI.method: Memoir consists of two modules: (1) Historical semantic memory construction — transforms historical FP alerts into structured semantic memories using LLM-guided annotation, pattern clustering, and memory synthesis to capture reusable behavioral patterns. (2) Memory-driven identification and evolution — retrieves relevant memories, performs semantic verification against taxonomy consistency and security invariants, makes final predictions, and incorporates verified predictions back into the memory repository for continuous knowledge evolution.
AI.result: On CWE-Bench-Java, Memoir achieves an F1-score of 99.43% (Recall: 98.88%, Precision: 100%), consistently outperforming all baselines.
