An industrial case study on production software from a top IT company demonstrates that the learned memory base generalizes effectively across different SAST tools without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Memoir effectively addresses SAST false-positive reduction by converting historical FP knowledge into evolving semantic memories. Its strong performance on benchmarks and industrial systems, along with cross-tool generalizability, demonstrates its practical value for reducing manual inspection costs and improving developer trust in SAST tools.

title: DialectS2S: End-to-End Speech Dialogue Modeling for Low-Resource Chinese Dialects
summary: Current end-to-end speech dialogue models are primarily optimized for mainstream languages and remain limited in low-resource dialect scenarios due to the scarcity of dialect speech data. Moreover, during dialect adaptation, the semantic representation space of speech dialogue models continuously evolves, while conventional speech supervision remains unchanged, leading to semantic inconsistency between hidden representations and speech targets and degrading speech stability and naturalness. To address these issues, we propose DialectS2S, an end-to-end speech dialogue model for Chinese dialects. We first develop a scalable dialect speech dialogue synthesis pipeline for efficient data construction. We further introduce a two-stage post-training strategy with self-aligned speech supervision, which aligns the semantic content of speech supervision with the evolved semantic representations of the model to improve dialect speech generation quality. Experimental results show that DialectS2S consistently outperforms existing baselines across multiple Chinese dialects in speech dialogue, achieving substantial improvements in dialect consistency, response quality, and speech intelligibility. Our work provides an efficient and scalable solution for end-to-end speech dialogue modeling in low-resource dialect scenarios. To facilitate future research and practical applications, we fully open-source the DialectS2S framework, including model checkpoints, training datasets, and fine-tuning code.

AI.tldr: DialectS2S is an end-to-end speech dialogue model for low-resource Chinese dialects that uses a scalable data synthesis pipeline and a two-stage post-training strategy with self-aligned speech supervision to address semantic inconsistency during dialect adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current end-to-end speech dialogue models focus on mainstream languages and perform poorly on low-resource dialects due to data scarcity. Additionally, during dialect adaptation, the model's semantic representation space evolves while conventional speech supervision remains static, causing semantic inconsistency that degrades speech stability and naturalness.
AI.method: (1) A scalable dialect speech dialogue synthesis pipeline for efficient training data construction. (2) A two-stage post-training strategy with self-aligned speech supervision that dynamically aligns speech supervision targets with the model's evolving semantic representations, thereby resolving representation–target mismatch.
AI.result: DialectS2S consistently outperforms existing baselines across multiple Chinese dialects, achieving significant improvements in dialect consistency, response quality, and speech intelligibility.
AI.conclusion: DialectS2S offers an efficient, scalable solution for end-to-end speech dialogue in low-resource dialect settings. The full framework is open-sourced to promote further research and practical deployment.

title: CONFER: Conflict-Aware Evidence Negotiation for Regime-Calibrated Weak Supervision in Multimodal Emotion Recognition
summary: Multimodal emotion recognition often treats self-reported labels as reliable supervision while overlooking self-report unreliability and cross-modal conflict. We propose \textbf{CONFER}, a graph-based conflict-aware evidence negotiation framework for weakly supervised multimodal emotion recognition. CONFER represents each modality expert as a node with a predictive belief, boundary-based uncertainty, and runtime reliability estimated from historical out-of-fold performance and current-sample uncertainty. Uncertainty-aware compatibility and reliability-directed asymmetric edge weights govern iterative message-passing negotiation, followed by peer-supported prediction readout. Conflict reduction, residual disagreement, and mean modality uncertainty further characterize three regimes---Consensus, Dissent, and Ambiguity---for sample-specific weak-label calibration. We evaluate CONFER on AMIGOS, MAHNOB-HCI, and DEAP under subject-dependent 10-fold and strict leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols. CONFER achieves competitive performance, reaching \textbf{0.873} accuracy on AMIGOS-V and \textbf{0.854} accuracy on MAHNOB-V under strict LOSO evaluation. Further analyses show larger negotiation gains on high-conflict samples and improved robustness to weak-label corruption, indicating that cross-modal conflict provides useful information for both directional modality coordination and supervision-reliability estimation.

AI.tldr: CONFER is a graph-based framework for weakly supervised multimodal emotion recognition that treats modalities as nodes negotiating via uncertainty-aware belief propagation. It explicitly models self-report unreliability and cross-modal conflict to improve both prediction accuracy and robustness to label corruption.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal emotion recognition methods treat self-reported labels as ground truth, ignoring two critical issues: (1) self-reports are inherently unreliable as supervision, and (2) cross-modal conflict (disagreement among modalities) is typically discarded rather than leveraged as informative signal for both coordination and supervision-quality estimation.
AI.method: CONFER models each modality expert as a graph node carrying: (a) a predictive belief, (b) boundary-based uncertainty, and (c) runtime reliability derived from historical out-of-fold performance and current-sample uncertainty. Nodes exchange messages via asymmetric directed edges governed by uncertainty-aware compatibility and reliability. After iterative negotiation, a peer-supported readout produces predictions. Additionally, three sample-level regimes — Consensus, Dissent, and Ambiguity — are identified using conflict reduction, residual disagreement, and mean modality uncertainty for weak-label calibration.
AI.result: Under strict LOSO evaluation, CONFER achieves 0.873 accuracy on AMIGOS-V and 0.854 on MAHNOB-V. It shows larger negotiation gains on high-conflict samples and stronger robustness to weak-label corruption compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal conflict, rather than being a nuisance, provides valuable information for directional modality coordination and supervision-reliability estimation. Explicitly modeling self-report unreliability and enabling conflict-aware negotiation yields both competitive accuracy and improved robustness in multimodal emotion recognition.

title: Agent-MD: Selective LLM Intervention with Event-Driven Escalation for Stateful GCMC--MD Campaigns
summary: Long-running molecular simulation campaigns require repeated continuation from saved states, provenance-aware progression, adaptive assessment, and occasional interpretation of workflow conditions that cannot be resolved safely by fixed rules. Here, we present Agent-MD, a framework that places large language model (LLM) reasoning selectively at campaign construction and event-triggered review, while routine simulation, analysis, continuation, archiving, and state progression are handled by a persistent rule-based campaign agent using approved policies and explicit state records. Agent-MD was demonstrated in a grand canonical Monte Carlo-molecular dynamics (GCMC-MD) water-vapor desorption campaign comprising five montmorillonite systems and three sequential relative-humidity states (RH = 0.9-0.3-0.1). Across 15 system-RH states, the workflow completed 120 segmented simulation cycles with state-specific sampling lengths and provenance-aware restart inheritance. Routine production required no live reasoning-agent invocation, while one state reached a review boundary; two preserved incidents were subsequently evaluated through blinded reasoning-agent replay, which identified the underlying workflow problems and recommended appropriate follow-up actions. The simulations also revealed distinct composition-dependent low-RH responses, with Ca-bearing montmorillonite retaining more interlayer water and maintaining a larger basal spacing than the Na- and K-bearing systems, while the highest-charge Na system retained more residual water under dry conditions. These results demonstrate that long-running scientific workflows need not place every operation inside an LLM reasoning loop: selective reasoning can instead be combined with deterministic execution, structured evidence, and validated control handoffs to provide reproducible and auditable agent-assisted molecular simulation.

AI.tldr: Agent-MD integrates LLM reasoning selectively at campaign construction and event-triggered review points within a rule-based molecular simulation workflow, demonstrated on a GCMC-MD water-vapor desorption campaign across 15 system-RH states, showing that combining deterministic execution with targeted LLM oversight yields reproducible, auditable agent-assisted simulations.
AI.motivation: Long-running molecular simulation campaigns require repeated continuation from saved states, provenance tracking, adaptive assessment, and occasional interpretation of workflow conditions that cannot be resolved by fixed rules alone. The authors aim to demonstrate that LLM reasoning can be deployed selectively rather than pervasively, avoiding unnecessary overhead while still handling edge cases.
AI.method: Agent-MD framework with a dual architecture: (1) a persistent rule-based campaign agent that handles routine simulation, analysis, continuation, archiving, and state progression using approved policies and explicit state records; (2) LLM reasoning invoked only at campaign construction and event-triggered review boundaries. Demonstrated via a GCMC-MD water-vapor desorption campaign on five montmorillonite systems across three sequential RH states (0.9→0.3→0.1), totaling 120 segmented simulation cycles. Blinded reasoning-agent replay was used to evaluate preserved incidents.
AI.result: Routine production across 15 system-RH states required no live reasoning-agent invocation. One state reached a review boundary; two preserved incidents were evaluated via blinded reasoning-agent replay, which correctly identified workflow problems and recommended follow-up actions. Scientifically, Ca-bearing montmorillonite retained more interlayer water and larger basal spacing under low RH than Na- and K-bearing systems; the highest-charge Na system retained more residual water under dry conditions.
AI.conclusion: Long-running scientific workflows benefit from combining selective LLM reasoning with deterministic execution, structured evidence, and validated control handoffs, rather than placing every operation inside an LLM reasoning loop. This approach yields reproducible and auditable agent-assisted molecular simulation.

title: Customized Tourist Navigation in Urban Contexts Following General Trends and Individual Preferences
summary: Navigating an unfamiliar city poses significant challenges, and tourists are among the groups more likely to experience them, particularly when attempting to locate a point of interest (POI). Various factors, such as language barriers or a lack of precise information, further complicate this issue by making it difficult for visitors to explore efficiently. To address these issues, we introduce the tool "Personalized Assistant for Tourist Hints" (PATH), which is based on a methodology for estimating personalized tourist routes. PATH computes optimal paths to specified locations guided by two tailored heuristics: tourist frequency and POI preference. This integration enables efficient and personalized navigation, guiding users toward attractions that best match their preferences. We evaluated our methodology through a case study in Viterbo, Italy, using a dataset comprising over 1000 routes from 265 tourists who visited the city during different periods. To validate our approach, we tested it with 238 new tourists and collected expert assessments from 86 local specialists. User satisfaction was measured through a structured questionnaire, which revealed highly positive feedback regarding the relevance and quality of the recommended routes, also when compared with existing routing applications and approaches proposed in the literature. These results demonstrate PATH's potential to enhance urban exploration by providing an adaptable and user-centric solution for tourist navigation.

AI.tldr: PATH is a personalized tourist navigation tool that computes optimal routes to points of interest using two heuristics—tourist frequency and POI preference—validated through a case study in Viterbo, Italy with 265 historical tourists, 238 new users, and 86 local experts, yielding highly positive satisfaction feedback.
AI.motivation: Tourists navigating unfamiliar cities face significant challenges—language barriers, imprecise information, and difficulty locating points of interest—that hinder efficient urban exploration. Existing routing applications lack adequate personalization to address these issues.
AI.method: The PATH tool estimates personalized tourist routes by computing optimal paths using two tailored heuristics: (1) tourist frequency, and (2) POI preference. This dual-heuristic approach guides users toward attractions matching their individual preferences. Validation employed a dataset of 1000+ routes from 265 tourists, tested with 238 new tourists, and evaluated via expert assessments from 86 local specialists using structured questionnaires.
AI.result: User satisfaction questionnaires revealed highly positive feedback on route relevance and quality. PATH outperformed existing routing applications and literature-proposed approaches in comparative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: PATH demonstrates strong potential to enhance urban exploration by delivering an adaptable, user-centric solution for personalized tourist navigation.

title: HaloMark: A Spectral Threshold for Embedding-Vector Watermarking under C2PA
summary:
Foundation-model embeddings are now a primary data asset, but the content-provenance machinery built for images and audio does not transfer to them. C2PA binds to an asset with a stable bit-level or perceptual identity; embeddings have neither, since quantisation, projection, fine-tuning, and windowed averaging reshape them in normal use and break any fixed hash.
  We present HaloMark, a watermark for embedding vectors cryptographically bound to a C2PA manifest. It composes four standard primitives -- a block-diagonal orthogonal rotation, public whitening, an input-dependent LSH commitment, and a per-vector nonce -- around one protocol change: the producer signs the LSH commitment c into the C2PA sidecar, and the verifier reads c from the manifest instead of recomputing it. Recomputing is fragile under whitening, which flips the commitment bucket on 62% of inputs at cos = 0.96; reading the signed c reduces the verifier's score to T = T_null + beta(A)*epsilon, so security turns on a single scalar beta, which we bound rigorously for linear and non-adaptive attackers and characterise empirically for the adaptive case.
  We evaluate against an adversary holding polynomially many clean/watermarked pairs under one key with full sidecar visibility, across eight baselines and ten adaptive attackers including denoising-autoencoder removal. The eleven encoders separate at an empirical threshold eff_rank(Sigma)/d ~= 0.19: above it, detection AUROC stays at 0.98 or higher across every in-budget attack on the three encoders we sweep in full, and at 0.965 or higher under single-seed DAE removal on the rest; below it every variant we tested fails. Why the threshold is dimension-uniform is left open. Deployed as a Qdrant admission filter, the verifier runs at 284 us and 24 bytes of sidecar per vector, validated end-to-end against three C2PA reference-SDK bindings.

AI.tldr: HaloMark is a watermarking scheme for embedding vectors that cryptographically binds to a C2PA manifest by signing an LSH commitment into the manifest sidecar, enabling robust verification despite whitening and other common embedding transformations. It achieves high detection AUROC (>0.98) when the effective rank-to-dimension ratio exceeds ~0.19, with a fast verifier (284 μs, 24 bytes/vector) deployable as a Qdrant admission filter.
AI.motivation: Existing C2PA content-provenance machinery relies on stable bit-level or perceptual identity (fixed hashes), which breaks for foundation-model embeddings due to routine transformations like quantization, projection, fine-tuning, and windowed averaging. A provenance solution tailored to the unique properties of embedding vectors is needed.
AI.method: HaloMark composes four primitives: a block-diagonal orthogonal rotation, public whitening, an input-dependent LSH commitment, and a per-vector nonce. The key innovation is a protocol change: the producer signs the LSH commitment c into the C2PA sidecar manifest, and the verifier reads c directly rather than recomputing it (which is fragile under whitening). This reduces the verifier's score to T = T_null + beta(A)*epsilon, with security governed by a single scalar beta, rigorously bounded for linear/non-adaptive attackers and empirically characterized for adaptive ones.
AI.result: Across eight baselines and ten adaptive attackers (including DAE removal), encoders with eff_rank(Σ)/d > ~0.19 maintain detection AUROC ≥ 0.98 under all in-budget attacks (≥0.965 under single-seed DAE removal). Below this threshold, all variants fail. The verifier operates at 284 μs and 24 bytes of sidecar per vector, validated end-to-end against three C2PA reference-SDK bindings.
AI.conclusion: HaloMark provides the first cryptographically bound provenance watermark for embedding vectors compatible with C2PA. The empirical eff_rank(Σ)/d ≈ 0.19 threshold cleanly separates robust from fragile encoders, though why this threshold is dimension-uniform remains an open question.

title: Listwise Cross-Encoder Fine-Tuning vs. Agentic Instruction Tuning for LLM Rerankers: A Systematic Study in Medical Procedure Reranking
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Code available at https://github.com/matanf-healthee/listwise-crossencoder-reranking
summary: Reranking medical procedures against patient queries is a critical component of health insurance information retrieval, complicated by a substantial lexical gap between patient language and clinical nomenclature. We present a systematic comparison of two reranking paradigms for this production task: (1) small cross-encoders (MedCPT, MiniLM-L12) fine-tuned with listwise learning-to-rank objectives across layer freezing configurations, and (2) Qwen3-Reranker-4B, a 4B-parameter instruction reranker whose prompt is iteratively refined via an agentic optimization loop driven by GPT-4.1. On a purpose-built dataset of 2,647 queries across 708 insurance services, we find that a 109M-parameter cross-encoder fine-tuned with ListNet outperforms the 4B-parameter model by 2.6 percentage points on NDCG@3 and 13.3 points on Spearman correlation - at 37x fewer parameters. We report practical findings, a scalable LLM based dataset construction pipeline, and deployment trade-offs relevant to production reranking systems. We release our code and a sample dataset to support reproducibility and adaptation to other domains.

AI.tldr: A 109M-parameter cross-encoder fine-tuned with ListNet outperforms a 4B-parameter instruction reranker (Qwen3-Reranker-4B) by 2.6 NDCG@3 points and 13.3 Spearman correlation points on medical procedure reranking, at 37x fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Health insurance information retrieval suffers from a substantial lexical gap between patient queries (lay language) and clinical procedure nomenclature. Reranking is critical to bridge this gap, but it is unclear whether small, fine-tuned cross-encoders or large instruction-tuned rerankers are more effective and practical for production deployment.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare two paradigms: (1) small cross-encoders (MedCPT, MiniLM-L12, ~109M params) fine-tuned with listwise learning-to-rank objectives (e.g., ListNet) under various layer freezing configurations; (2) Qwen3-Reranker-4B, a 4B-parameter instruction reranker with prompts iteratively refined via an agentic optimization loop driven by GPT-4.1. Evaluation uses a purpose-built dataset of 2,647 queries across 708 insurance services. A scalable LLM-based dataset construction pipeline is also introduced.
AI.result: The 109M-parameter cross-encoder fine-tuned with ListNet outperforms the 4B Qwen3-Reranker by 2.6 percentage points on NDCG@3 and 13.3 points on Spearman correlation, despite having 37x fewer parameters. Practical deployment trade-offs and findings are reported.
AI.conclusion: Small, domain-specific cross-encoders with listwise fine-tuning can surpass much larger general-purpose instruction rerankers on specialized medical procedure retrieval tasks, offering a more parameter-efficient and deployment-friendly solution. The released code, dataset, and pipeline support reproducibility and domain adaptation.

title: Guixu: Valuation-Driven Data Discovery for Autonomous AI Agents with On-Chain Attestation
comment: This paper has been accepted for presentation at VLDB 2026
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on external data to complete downstream tasks such as model training and decision support. However, existing data discovery systems remain largely retrieval-oriented: they surface candidate datasets from heterogeneous sources, but provide limited support for estimating task-specific utility, selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, or incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. This paper presents Guixu, a valuation-driven data discovery system for autonomous agents. Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline with proxy-label propagation and multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. Guixu integrates agentic payment protocol to enable budget-constrained data procurement workflows. Guixu leverages on-chain data market and attestation signals for verifiable data discovery. Our demonstration highlights how Guixu enables an agent to move beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval toward task- and budget-aware, trustworthy data discovery and procurement. Attendees can interactively explore the full workflow, from NL task specification and multi-source search to data valuation and verifiable transaction feedback.

AI.tldr: Guixu is a valuation-driven data discovery system that enables autonomous agents to go beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval by incorporating task-aware data valuation, budget-constrained procurement, and verifiable trust signals via on-chain attestations.
AI.motivation: Existing data discovery systems are largely retrieval-oriented — they surface candidate datasets but lack support for (1) estimating task-specific utility, (2) selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, and (3) incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. Autonomous agents need these capabilities to make informed data procurement decisions.
AI.method: Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline combining proxy-label propagation with multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. It integrates an agentic payment protocol for budget-constrained procurement and leverages on-chain data markets with attestation signals for verifiable discovery.
AI.result: The demonstration showcases an end-to-end workflow where an agent moves from natural language task specification and multi-source search through data valuation to verifiable transaction feedback, enabling interactive exploration by attendees.
AI.conclusion: Guixu advances data discovery beyond retrieval toward a valuation-driven paradigm that jointly addresses task awareness, budget constraints, and trustworthiness — key requirements for autonomous agent data procurement.

title: Software Engineering for and with GUI Agent
summary: GUI agents have advanced rapidly, producing a growing body of frameworks, benchmarks, and applications. However, this growth has outpaced the maturity of the field. GUI agents remain technically brittle, incompletely engineered, and insufficiently validated for sustained real-world use. They are evolving into closed-loop software systems. Within these systems, model reasoning is coupled with interface perception, execution feedback, recovery, and human oversight. This evolution calls for a software engineering perspective that remains largely absent from existing research. We address this gap by reviewing 336 GUI-agent papers from January 2018 to April 2026. Five research questions examine the research landscape, architectures, evaluation, software lifecycle concerns, and future opportunities. Our findings show that the field has expanded sharply since 2024, while mobile and web settings remain dominant. Architectures increasingly adopt modular perceive-reason-act loops, but recovery, human escalation, safety enforcement, and auditability remain underdeveloped. This architectural imbalance extends to evaluation. Evaluations are becoming more interactive, but they remain centered on task success and are difficult to compare across protocols. More broadly, existing studies provide limited support for testing beyond benchmarks and for maintaining agents after release. Observability, privacy engineering, and systematic human oversight are also underdeveloped. Together, these findings show that capability improvements alone cannot ensure deployment readiness. Future research should connect dependable execution with lifecycle-centered testing and reproducible evaluation. It should also integrate permission and privacy controls with cost-aware, human-centered governance. This integration is necessary to build dependable, maintainable, secure, and deployable GUI-agent systems.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 336 GUI-agent papers (2018–2026) reveals that while the field has grown rapidly, architectures and evaluations remain immature from a software engineering standpoint. Key gaps exist in recovery, human oversight, safety, auditability, observability, and lifecycle testing, highlighting the need to shift focus from raw capability toward dependable, maintainable, and deployable systems.
AI.motivation: GUI-agent research has expanded quickly but lacks a software engineering perspective. Agents are becoming closed-loop systems coupling reasoning with perception, execution feedback, and human oversight, yet the field has not matured to address the engineering challenges of reliability, maintainability, security, and real-world deployability.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 336 GUI-agent papers published between January 2018 and April 2026. They structured the review around five research questions covering: the research landscape, agent architectures, evaluation practices, software lifecycle concerns, and future research opportunities.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The field expanded sharply after 2024, with mobile and web domains dominating. (2) Architectures increasingly adopt modular perceive-reason-act loops, but recovery mechanisms, human escalation, safety enforcement, and auditability remain underdeveloped. (3) Evaluations are growing more interactive yet remain centered on task success, with poor cross-protocol comparability. (4) Testing beyond benchmarks, post-release maintenance, observability, privacy engineering, and systematic human oversight are all under-addressed.
AI.conclusion: Capability improvements alone are insufficient for deployment readiness. Future work must bridge dependable execution with lifecycle-centered testing and reproducible evaluation, and integrate permission/privacy controls with cost-aware, human-centered governance to build GUI-agent systems that are dependable, maintainable, secure, and deployable.

title: Commitment Before Realization: When Classifier-Free Guidance Becomes Unnecessary in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is usually kept on throughout masked diffusion language model decoding, although its benefit varies across prompts and over time. We study when CFG is actually needed by comparing, from any partial output, the probability of eventual constraint satisfaction under continued CFG and under base-only continuation. Their difference defines the remaining value of guidance. Guidance dependence is highly prompt-specific. Many prompts already succeed without CFG, while for others it provides no measurable benefit or can be harmful. For prompts that do benefit, the gain is often concentrated early. We define the commitment horizon $\astar$ as the earliest point from which switching all remaining decoding to the base model reduces final success by no more than a chosen tolerance. Under the base model, the corresponding success probability, or committor, is a martingale. To first order, CFG's per-step effect is governed by the covariance between the guidance logit direction and the successor committor. This gives a local account of when guidance can help, but it does not by itself locate the horizon. Among prompts with an observed preterminal horizon, $\astar$ is usually early and varies more within constraint families than between them. Freezing each prompt at its own cross-fitted horizon is noninferior to full CFG on all 13 subtasks at the prespecified margin, even while many tokens remain masked. This separates commitment from realization. The boundary also identifies a later region in which higher parallelism adds only a small cost in constraint success, although fluency still degrades with parallel width. For failed trajectories, reopening committed positions improves recovery in both failure modes.

AI.tldr: CFG benefit is prompt-specific and often concentrated early; the commitment horizon—where one can switch to base-model decoding with minimal success loss—is usually preterminal, enabling guidance-free completion without sacrificing constraint satisfaction.
AI.motivation: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is applied uniformly throughout masked diffusion language model decoding, yet its benefit is neither universal across prompts nor constant over decoding steps. The authors seek to identify *when* CFG is actually needed, and whether it can be safely turned off after a certain point.
AI.method: The authors define the *remaining value of guidance* as the difference in probability of eventual constraint satisfaction between continued CFG and base-only continuation from any partial output. They introduce the *commitment horizon* (a*) as the earliest step where switching entirely to the base model reduces final success by no more than a chosen tolerance. The committor (success probability under the base model) is shown to be a martingale. CFG's per-step effect is related, to first order, to the covariance between the guidance logit direction and the successor committor. Cross-fitted horizons are used to freeze prompts at their own horizon and compare against full CFG across 13 subtasks.
AI.result: Many prompts succeed without CFG; for others, CFG provides no measurable benefit or is harmful. For prompts that do benefit, the gain concentrates early. The commitment horizon is usually preterminal and varies more within constraint families than between them. Freezing at the cross-fitted horizon is noninferior to full CFG on all 13 subtasks at the prespecified margin. Higher parallelism after the horizon adds only small cost to constraint success, though fluency degrades. For failed trajectories, reopening committed positions improves recovery.
AI.conclusion: CFG can be safely curtailed after a prompt-specific commitment horizon without sacrificing constraint satisfaction, separating commitment from realization. This enables more efficient decoding, though fluency and failure recovery require additional consideration.

title: V-Simba: Unleashing the Architectural Potential of RL in Visual Continuous Control
summary: Improving sample efficiency remains a core challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), especially in real-world settings like robotics, where data collection is costly. This challenge is pronounced in visual RL, where high-dimensional inputs often obscure learning signals. While prior work in visual RL has focused on algorithmic solutions, such as better dynamics models or exploration strategies, recent advances in state-based RL show that architectural design alone can lead to significant gains in sample efficiency. This raises an important question: Can these architectural principles transfer to visual RL? In response, we introduce V-Simba, a simple yet effective visual RL architecture inspired by the Simba architecture from state-based RL. Built on top of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with data augmentation, V-Simba modifies the architecture by adding normalization layers to stabilize training and using pointwise convolutions to reduce computation. Despite its simplicity, V-Simba matches or outperforms the state-of-the-art methods across the DMC, Adroit, and Meta-World benchmarks, while being more computationally efficient than DrQ-v2. We make our code publicly available at https://github.com/DAVIAN-Robotics/V-Simba.

AI.tldr: V-Simba adapts the Simba architecture from state-based RL to visual RL, adding normalization and pointwise convolutions on top of SAC with data augmentation. It achieves state-of-the-art or better performance on DMC, Adroit, and Meta-World benchmarks while being more computationally efficient than DrQ-v2.
AI.motivation: Sample efficiency is a critical bottleneck in visual RL, particularly in robotics. While architectural innovations have recently driven gains in state-based RL, their potential in visual RL remains underexplored. The authors investigate whether architectural design principles (specifically those of Simba) can transfer from state-based to visual RL.
AI.method: V-Simba builds on Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with data augmentation. It incorporates two key architectural modifications inspired by the state-based Simba architecture: (1) normalization layers to stabilize training, and (2) pointwise convolutions to reduce computational overhead. The architecture is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods without requiring new algorithmic components.
AI.result: V-Simba matches or surpasses state-of-the-art methods across three visual RL benchmarks: DMC (DeepMind Control), Adroit (dexterous manipulation), and Meta-World (multi-task manipulation). It also demonstrates superior computational efficiency compared to DrQ-v2.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design principles from state-based RL can be effectively transferred to visual RL. V-Simba demonstrates that simple, well-motivated architectural changes — rather than complex algorithmic innovations — can yield substantial gains in both sample efficiency and computational efficiency for visual continuous control tasks.

title: An IMU Dataset for Human Activity Recognition to Support Independent Living in Smart Homes (IMU-HAR-IL)
summary: This document introduces HAR-IMU-IL, a dataset developed for human activity recognition (HAR) using inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors within a smart home environment with a focus to support objective functional assessment of older adults' independent living (IL). In particular, HAR-IMU-IL includes recordings of 50 participants performing 17 clinically relevant activities of daily living, spanning 4 functional domains essential for independent living: mobility, hygiene, nutrition and hydration, and medication intake. The dataset was collected using 30 IMU sensors, comprising both wearable and object-mounted devices integrated within a real-world residential setting. The dataset includes multi-sensor inertial data captured under realistic, unconstrained conditions, together with detailed annotations ensuring high temporal accuracy and consistency across sensors. A comprehensive data collection protocol was implemented to preserve ecological validity and enable reliable multi-sensor synchronisation. HAR-IMU-IL provides a large-scale, functionally grounded resource for advancing and benchmarking machine learning and artificial intelligence approaches for HAR in home settings. We further demonstrate its utility by developing models capable of accurately recognising both activities and broader functional domains using wearable and object-mounted sensors. These capabilities highlight the dataset's potential to enable applications in continuous activity monitoring, functional health assessment, smart home automation, and assistive technologies that support independent living.

AI.tldr: HAR-IMU-IL is a multi-sensor IMU dataset featuring 50 participants performing 17 ADLs across 4 functional domains in a real smart home, designed to support objective functional assessment and machine learning for independent living monitoring.
AI.motivation: Existing HAR datasets lack ecologically valid, multi-sensor IMU data collected in real residential settings with clinically relevant activity annotations tied to functional domains essential for assessing older adults' capacity for independent living.
AI.method: The authors collected data from 50 participants using 30 IMU sensors (wearable and object-mounted) in a real-world smart home. A rigorous protocol ensured temporal synchronization, detailed annotations, and ecological validity across 17 ADLs spanning mobility, hygiene, nutrition/hydration, and medication intake domains. Benchmark models were developed to validate the dataset's utility for both activity-level and functional-domain-level recognition.
AI.result: The resulting HAR-IMU-IL dataset provides large-scale, functionally grounded, multi-sensor inertial data with high temporal accuracy. Demonstrator models successfully recognized both individual activities and broader functional domains using wearable and object-mounted sensor modalities.
AI.conclusion: HAR-IMU-IL fills a critical gap by offering ecologically valid, clinically annotated IMU data for smart home HAR. It enables advances in continuous activity monitoring, functional health assessment, smart home automation, and assistive technologies supporting older adults' independent living.

title: Toward Metacognitive One-Shot Indirect Prompt Injection: Strategy Abstraction Via Outcome-Conditioned Reflection
summary: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which malicious instructions embedded in external observations manipulate subsequent agent decisions and actions. Most existing adaptive attacks rely on repeatedly querying and refining against the target agent, whereas realistic attackers may have only a single opportunity to interact with an unknown target agent. We propose SAVOR (Strategy Abstraction Via Outcome-Conditioned Reflection), which shifts attack adaptation from test-time iteration to offline strategy distillation. SAVOR performs outcome-conditioned reflection over successful and failed trajectories collected from disjoint training environments, validates context-conditioned candidate strategies, and iteratively consolidates them into a reusable strategy memory. At test time, the frozen memory guides the generation of a single payload for each unseen target, requiring only one target-agent query and no target-agent feedback. Across two benchmarks and three victim models, SAVOR attains the highest average attack success rate in all six settings, leading the strongest prior attack by 2.5 to 11.8 points and the same injection channel without strategy learning by 23.1 points on Agent Security Bench, which holds out attacker tools, and 28.6 points on OpenClaw-IPI, an executable benchmark we introduce that holds out attack goals and verifies attacks through tool interactions and execution receipts. A memory learned under one defense also transfers to another.

AI.tldr: SAVOR proposes offline strategy distillation for indirect prompt injection attacks against LLM agents, learning reusable attack strategies from training trajectories to generate effective single-shot payloads without target-agent feedback, achieving state-of-the-art attack success rates across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive attacks on LLM agents require repeated querying and refinement against the target, which is unrealistic in real-world scenarios where attackers have only a single interaction opportunity with an unknown target. There is a need for attack methods that can succeed in one shot without target-agent feedback.
AI.method: SAVOR shifts attack adaptation from test-time iteration to offline strategy distillation via three stages: (1) outcome-conditioned reflection over successful and failed trajectories from disjoint training environments, (2) validation of context-conditioned candidate strategies, and (3) iterative consolidation into a reusable strategy memory. At test time, the frozen memory guides single-payload generation for unseen targets requiring only one query and no feedback.
AI.result: Across two benchmarks (Agent Security Bench and the newly introduced OpenClaw-IPI) and three victim models, SAVOR achieved the highest average attack success rate in all six settings, outperforming the strongest prior attack by 2.5–11.8 points and the same injection channel without strategy learning by 23.1–28.6 points. Learned strategies also transferred across different defenses.
AI.conclusion: Offline strategy distillation via outcome-conditioned reflection is a highly effective paradigm for IPI attacks, enabling strong single-shot performance without target feedback. The approach also yields transferable attack strategies across defenses, and the newly introduced OpenClaw-IPI benchmark provides a more realistic evaluation framework with executable verification.

title: Weather- and Location-Aware Agentic Dining Recommendation: Leveraging LLM World Knowledge for Region-Sensitive Contextual Reasoning
comment: 5 pages. An agentic LLM system that reasons over combined location and weather context for region-sensitive dining recommendation. Working prototype implemented and briefly deployed end-to-end
summary: Context-aware recommender systems have long recognized that factors such as location, time, and weather shape where and what people choose to eat. Existing weather-aware food and point-of-interest recommenders, however, typically treat weather generically -- mapping conditions to preferences through hand-crafted rules or specially trained context models -- and do not capture that the culturally appropriate response to weather is itself region-specific: a rainy evening calls for hot tea and fried snacks in one culinary culture and for very different comfort food in another. Encoding such weather-by-region-by-cuisine interactions as explicit rules or training data is brittle and does not scale. We present a weather- and location-aware agentic dining-recommendation system that takes a different approach: a large language model (LLM) orchestrates tools for location and weather retrieval and then reasons in natural language over the combined context, drawing on the cultural and culinary world knowledge already latent in the model to produce region-sensitive, weather-appropriate recommendations without per-region rule tables or specialized training. We describe the agent architecture, the tool-orchestration flow (Google location services and a weather service feeding an OpenAI LLM), and the reasoning mechanism, and we report on a working prototype that was implemented and briefly deployed end-to-end. We discuss design trade-offs -- cost, latency, ambiguity handling, and fallbacks -- and we are explicit about limitations, including the absence of a formal user study and the risk of cultural stereotyping in locality-based inference. The contribution is architectural: a simple, extensible pattern for incorporating environmental and cultural context into agentic recommendation through LLM reasoning rather than engineered rules.

AI.tldr: Proposes an agentic dining-recommendation system where an LLM orchestrates weather and location tools, then reasons over combined context using its latent cultural knowledge to produce region-sensitive, weather-appropriate recommendations without hand-crafted rules or specialized training.
AI.motivation: Existing weather-aware food recommenders treat weather generically via hand-crafted rules or trained context models, failing to capture that culturally appropriate responses to weather are region-specific (e.g., rainy-evening comfort foods differ across culinary cultures). Encoding weather-by-region-by-cuisine interactions as explicit rules or training data is brittle and does not scale.
AI.method: An LLM-based agent architecture that orchestrates external tools (Google location services, a weather service) to retrieve context, then performs natural-language reasoning over the combined location-weather context. The system draws on culinary and cultural world knowledge already latent in the LLM to generate recommendations, avoiding per-region rule tables or specialized training. A working prototype was implemented and briefly deployed end-to-end.
AI.result: A working end-to-end prototype was implemented and briefly deployed, demonstrating the architectural pattern. Design trade-offs (cost, latency, ambiguity handling, fallbacks) are discussed. No formal user study was conducted.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is architectural: a simple, extensible pattern for incorporating environmental and cultural context into agentic recommendation through LLM reasoning rather than engineered rules. Limitations include the absence of a formal user study and the risk of cultural stereotyping in locality-based inference.

title: Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: Are Embodied VLMs Ready for Safety-Critical Scenarios?
summary: Theory of Space framework (ToS) assesses the spatial understanding of curiosity-driven Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under partial observability. As AI techniques are increasingly applied to safety-critical scenarios, it is crucial to understand whether VLMs possess robust spatial memory and make reliable decisions. In this paper, we assess whether VLMs' decisions are based on physical evidence or are corrupted by visual-language biases, if their memory processes align with human cognitive patterns, and how they respond to environmental hazards. We extend the ToS framework into a safety-critical, goal-driven pipeline, named Explore, Map, Remember, and Decide (EMRD). We then quantify Exploration Competence (Explore) through metrics of environmental coverage and temporal efficiency, assess Spatial Fidelity (Map), evaluate, with a suite of psychological metrics, Memory Persistence (Remember), and measure, using focal-point metrics, Cognitive Decision-Making (Decide). Our results show that in terms of decision-making capabilities, VLMs frequently select evacuation points based on pre-trained textual priors while lacking the spatial grounding to justify their choices. We also show that spatial reasoning degrades in low-light conditions, but it is not affected by texture and colour tampering. Our findings suggest that VLM memory fundamentally diverges from human cognition, creating unpredictable risks of misalignment.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Theory of Space (ToS) framework into a safety-critical, goal-driven pipeline (EMRD) to evaluate VLMs' spatial understanding under partial observability, finding that VLMs rely on textual priors over spatial grounding, degrade in low-light conditions, and diverge fundamentally from human cognitive memory patterns.
AI.motivation: As VLMs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical scenarios, it is essential to determine whether their decisions are grounded in physical evidence or corrupted by visual-language biases, whether their memory processes align with human cognition, and how they respond to environmental hazards under partial observability.
AI.method: The authors extend the Theory of Space (ToS) framework into the EMRD pipeline: (1) Explore — quantifying exploration competence via environmental coverage and temporal efficiency metrics; (2) Map — assessing spatial fidelity; (3) Remember — evaluating memory persistence using a suite of psychological metrics; (4) Decide — measuring cognitive decision-making via focal-point metrics.
AI.result: VLMs frequently choose evacuation points based on pre-trained textual priors rather than spatial grounding. Spatial reasoning degrades in low-light conditions but is unaffected by texture and color tampering. VLM memory fundamentally diverges from human cognition, creating unpredictable misalignment risks.
AI.conclusion: VLM spatial reasoning and memory are unreliable for safety-critical applications due to over-reliance on language priors, vulnerability to lighting conditions, and fundamental misalignment with human cognitive patterns, posing risks for real-world deployment.

title: OpenCodeReview: Determinism over Non-Determinism for Cost-Effective Agent-Based Code Review
summary: LLM-based code review agents promise scalable, always-on review, yet current systems suffer from two intertwined weaknesses: (1) non-determinism--unbounded tool use makes review outcomes unstable, and (2) context locality--the reviewer's access remains bounded to the diff, capping discoverable issue depth. Both give rise to three challenges: misaligned context retrieval, a coherence-efficiency trade-off in multi-file pull requests, and hallucinated comments that erode trust. To address these, we introduce OpenCodeReview, built on deterministic engineering for uncertain agents: rather than granting maximal freedom, we inject determinism at three deliberate pipeline points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses a multi-layer rule system to deterministically select files and review criteria, eliminating variability of agent-driven triage. Grounded File Review replaces free-form exploration with a curated tool set exposed through a ReAct loop, while file-level parallel SubAgents balance context coherence against efficiency and recover cross-file dependencies on demand. Independent Reflection introduces a falsification-first filter under an asymmetric information boundary--the reflector sees only the diff, not the agent's tool-augmented exploration--removing hallucinated comments without self-reinforcing bias, improving precision while preserving recall. On AACR-Bench (200 real-world PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-verified comments), OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream coding agents (e.g., Claude Code and Codex) across six LLM backends, achieving up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) while consuming 5-15x fewer tokens. We open-source OpenCodeReview at https://github.com/alibaba/open-code-review.

AI.tldr: OpenCodeReview is a deterministic pipeline for LLM-based code review that addresses non-determinism and context locality via Rule-Guided Dispatch, Grounded File Review with parallel SubAgents, and Independent Reflection. It achieves up to 2.17× higher SEM-F1 over mainstream agents while using 5–15× fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based code review agents suffer from (1) non-determinism due to unbounded tool use, making review outcomes unstable, and (2) context locality, where the reviewer is bounded to the diff, limiting discoverable issue depth. These weaknesses cause misaligned context retrieval, a coherence-efficiency trade-off in multi-file PRs, and hallucinated comments that erode trust.
AI.method: OpenCodeReview injects determinism at three pipeline points: (1) Rule-Guided Dispatch — a multi-layer rule system deterministically selects files and review criteria, eliminating agent-driven triage variability. (2) Grounded File Review — replaces free-form exploration with a curated tool set in a ReAct loop; file-level parallel SubAgents balance context coherence with efficiency and recover cross-file dependencies on demand. (3) Independent Reflection — a falsification-first filter under asymmetric information boundaries (reflector sees only the diff, not the agent's tool-augmented exploration) removes hallucinated comments without self-reinforcing bias, improving precision while preserving recall.
AI.result: On AACR-Bench (200 real-world PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-verified comments), OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream coding agents (including Claude Code and Codex) across six LLM backends, achieving up to 2.17× higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) while consuming 5–15× fewer tokens.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic engineering for uncertain agents — injecting constrained, predictable decision points into an otherwise unbounded agent loop — significantly improves both review quality and efficiency. OpenCodeReview demonstrates that limiting agent freedom at strategic pipeline stages yields more reliable, trustworthy, and cost-effective automated code review.

title: Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) iteratively refine a sequence, allowing earlier predictions to be revised as context evolves. This rollback capability distinguishes them from irreversible autoregressive generation, but makes inference costly. Every denoising update alters the global context, forcing both prompt and response states to be recomputed even though only response tokens are revisable. Key-value (KV) caching could reduce this cost, yet conventional caching assumes immutable historical states and is therefore difficult to reconcile with rollback.In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback (Archer), a training-free KV caching method for rollback-capable DLMs. Archer asymmetrically keeps the mutable response synchronized with the current hypothesis while reusing prompt K/V within a bounded state neighborhood. Although prompt representations also change under bidirectional attention, their token identities remain fixed; bounded reuse therefore amortizes repeated prompt computation without caching mutable response states. It also delays feedback from tentative tokens, reducing premature reinforcement of transient high-confidence errors and giving rollback more opportunity to correct them. Our analysis characterizes prompt reuse as a reversibility-aligned cache boundary, bounds its state-dependent approximation error, and gives a decoder-margin condition for preserving full-refresh decisions.Existing DLM acceleration often trades quality for speed. Archer shifts this frontier, attaining the best mean performance of 33.63% together with a 2.57x mean speedup on the main suite. Across evaluated settings, it improves Pass@1 by up to 3.05 points and reaches up to 2.95x speedup. Controlled analyses connect the quality gain to delayed prompt feedback and validate state-aware refresh. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hxnng/Archer.

AI.tldr: Archer is a training-free KV caching method for diffusion language models that asymmetrically reuses prompt hidden states while keeping response states mutable, achieving both quality improvements (up to +3.05 Pass@1) and speedups (up to 2.95x) by amortizing prompt computation and delaying feedback from tentative tokens.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable iterative refinement with rollback capability, but inference is costly because every denoising update requires recomputing both prompt and response states — even though only response tokens change. Conventional KV caching assumes immutable states and cannot handle rollback. The authors aim to reduce this cost without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: Archer introduces asymmetric KV caching: prompt K/V states are reused within a bounded neighborhood despite bidirectional context changes, while response states remain synchronized with the current hypothesis. The method bounds state-dependent approximation error, characterizes prompt reuse as a reversibility-aligned cache boundary, and provides a decoder-margin condition for triggering full refreshes. It also delays feedback from tentative tokens to reduce premature reinforcement of transient errors.
AI.result: Archer achieves a mean performance of 33.63% with 2.57x mean speedup. Pass@1 improves by up to 3.05 points, and speedup reaches up to 2.95x. Controlled analyses confirm quality gains stem from delayed prompt feedback and state-aware refresh mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Archer shifts the quality-speed frontier for DLM inference, demonstrating that training-free asymmetric KV caching with bounded prompt reuse can simultaneously accelerate generation and improve output quality by mitigating premature error reinforcement.

title: Router Sensitivity Under Lightweight Fine-Tuning Identifies Prunable Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models decouple total parameters from per-token compute, but deployment still requires storing every expert. Recent theory shows that pruning experts with the smallest router-norm changes during fine-tuning can preserve accuracy, but assumes full fine-tuning. We test whether lightweight adaptation can recover this signal. We briefly fine-tune with a parameter-efficient adapter, rank experts by the induced $\ell_2$ router change, and prune the least-changed experts in one shot. On Mixtral-8$\times$7B-Instruct (44.83% MMLU-Pro), router-only LoRA trains 0.002% of parameters and outperforms all-module LoRA at matched rank with half the experts removed (27.54% vs. 24.42%); signal quality declines as adaptation spreads to attention and expert weights. Accuracy improves monotonically with LoRA rank, reaching 28.76%. IA3, which leaves router weights frozen, matches direct router adaptation, whereas unconstrained additive adapters degrade the signal. Router-guided MMLU-Pro accuracy decays quasi-linearly rather than collapsing, remains nearly 1.8 times that of magnitude-based or random pruning at maximal compression, and reduces memory by 49% and per-token latency by 37%. At 25% compression, retention is competitive with methods using full activation statistics. The criterion also transfers to Qwen1.5-MoE fine-tuned for mathematics, retaining 49.7% mean accuracy over eleven benchmarks with half the experts removed while random pruning falls to single digits. Router sensitivity under lightweight fine-tuning therefore makes provably motivated expert pruning practical at scale.

AI.tldr: Lightweight fine-tuning with parameter-efficient adapters (e.g., LoRA on router only) reveals router-weight sensitivity signals that enable effective one-shot expert pruning in MoE models, preserving accuracy far better than magnitude or random pruning while reducing memory by 49% and latency by 37%.
AI.motivation: Prior theory shows that pruning experts with the smallest router-norm changes during full fine-tuning preserves accuracy. However, full fine-tuning is computationally expensive. The authors investigate whether lightweight, parameter-efficient adaptation (e.g., LoRA, IA3) can recover the same pruning signal at a fraction of the cost, enabling practical expert pruning at scale.
AI.method: The method applies a parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapter (primarily LoRA on router weights only) to briefly fine-tune an MoE model. Experts are then ranked by the induced ℓ₂ norm change in their associated router parameters. The experts with the smallest router change are pruned in one shot. Variants tested include applying adapters to attention modules, expert weights, and using IA3 or additive adapters. The approach is evaluated on Mixtral-8×7B-Instruct (MMLU-Pro) and Qwen1.5-MoE (mathematics benchmarks).
AI.result: Router-only LoRA (0.002% of parameters) outperforms all-module LoRA at matched rank with 50% experts removed (27.54% vs. 24.42% MMLU-Pro). Accuracy improves monotonically with LoRA rank (up to 28.76%). IA3 matches direct router adaptation; unconstrained additive adapters degrade the signal. Router-guided pruning yields quasi-linear accuracy decay, ~1.8× better than magnitude/random pruning at maximal compression, with 49% memory and 37% latency reduction. At 25% compression, retention is competitive with full-activation-statistics methods. On Qwen1.5-MoE, 49.7% mean accuracy is retained across 11 benchmarks with half the experts removed, while random pruning collapses to single digits.
AI.conclusion: Router sensitivity under lightweight fine-tuning provides a provably motivated, practical signal for expert pruning in large MoE models, enabling substantial compression with minimal accuracy loss and negligible adaptation cost, making it viable at scale.

title: Mendel Gödel Machine: Recursive Self-Improving Coding Agents via Comparative Evolution
comment: Project Page at https://reallcz.github.io/MGM; Code at https://github.com/RealLcz/MGM
summary: Self-improving coding agents that iteratively rewrite their own source code have demonstrated impressive performance on coding tasks. However, existing solutions generally derive self-modification from a single failure trajectory at a time, overlooking rich comparative signals available in the agent's expanding archive of past attempts. According to Mendelian principles of controlled inheritance, we introduce Mendel Gödel Machine (MGM). In addition to the general single-trajectory clonal mutation, MGM includes two new types of self-modification that better utilizes evidences accumulated: the reaction-norm mutation edits an agent based on its trajectories on multiple tasks simultaneously, and the cross-lineage hybridization edits an agent using the trajectory of a reference agent from another lineage on the same task. Under an additive fitness landscape model, we prove theoretically and demonstrate via controlled surrogate simulation that the new strategies facilitate a faster and better convergence over single-trajectory baselines. Experiments on SWE-bench and Polyglot confirm MGM's consistent improvement in performance, efficiency, and generalizability.

AI.tldr: Mendel Gödel Machine (MGM) introduces two novel self-modification strategies for coding agents—reaction-norm mutation (multi-task trajectories) and cross-lineage hybridization (cross-agent trajectories)—inspired by Mendelian genetics. Theoretically and empirically, MGM outperforms single-trajectory baselines on convergence, performance, and generalizability.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improving coding agents rely on single failure trajectory for self-modification, ignoring the rich comparative signals from the growing archive of past attempts across tasks and lineages. The authors aim to leverage these signals for more efficient and effective agent evolution.
AI.method: MGM extends the standard clonal mutation with two Mendelian-inspired strategies: (1) reaction-norm mutation, which edits an agent using its trajectories on multiple tasks simultaneously; (2) cross-lineage hybridization, which edits an agent using a reference agent's trajectory from a different lineage on the same task. The approach is analyzed under an additive fitness landscape model and evaluated via surrogate simulation and real benchmarks (SWE-bench, Polyglot).
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and surrogate simulations demonstrate faster and better convergence over single-trajectory baselines. Experiments on SWE-bench and Polyglot confirm consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging comparative signals from an agent's expanding archive via Mendelian-inspired mutation and hybridization strategies yields superior self-improvement compared to single-trajectory clonal approaches.

title: Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication
summary: Interdisciplinary project-based learning requires students to negotiate differences in language, assumptions, priorities, and working practices. These differences are difficult to surface in text-based team communication, where discussions can become fragmented and AI tools are often used as private side channels rather than shared supports for collective sensemaking. We present Spritz, a Discord-based LLM technology probe that explores how AI might mediate disciplinary boundaries in student project teams. Spritz monitors group chat for signals of semantic or pragmatic boundaries, prompts members to articulate their perspectives through private channels, and returns anonymized syntheses to the shared discussion. We conducted a technology probe study and co-design workshop with 12 university students from technical, business, and design backgrounds. Participants experienced Spritz during a simulated interdisciplinary resource-allocation task and reflected on AI's role in collaboration. Findings show that participants valued AI mediation not only as cognitive support for boundary crossing, but also as a relational buffer. Spritz helped organize fragmented discussion, surface implicit expectations, and clarify divergent interpretations, while softening interpersonal pressure around disagreement and concession. Participants further imagined future AI mediators as switchable roles, including strategic advisors, cross-domain translators, and perspective challengers. However, these expanded roles introduced a central design tension: the neutrality that made AI acceptable as a mediator became unstable when AI began to advise, challenge, or influence team decisions. We contribute empirical insights and design considerations for AI systems that mediate interdisciplinary collaboration in text-based communication while preserving human agency, trust, privacy, and accountability.

AI.tldr: Spritz is a Discord-based LLM probe that mediates interdisciplinary student team communication by detecting disciplinary boundaries, privately eliciting perspectives, and returning anonymized syntheses — revealing that AI mediation serves as both cognitive support and relational buffer, while raising tensions around neutrality when AI takes on advisory or challenging roles.
AI.motivation: Interdisciplinary project-based learning requires negotiating differences in language, assumptions, and working practices, but these differences are difficult to surface in text-based team communication. Discussions fragment, and AI tools are typically used privately rather than as shared sensemaking supports — motivating the need for AI systems that mediate disciplinary boundaries collaboratively.
AI.method: The authors designed Spritz, a Discord-based LLM technology probe that monitors group chat for semantic/pragmatic boundary signals, privately prompts members to articulate perspectives, and returns anonymized syntheses to the shared channel. A technology probe study and co-design workshop were conducted with 12 university students from technical, business, and design backgrounds, using a simulated interdisciplinary resource-allocation task followed by reflective co-design sessions.
AI.result: Participants valued AI mediation for both cognitive boundary-crossing support and as a relational buffer — it organized fragmented discussions, surfaced implicit expectations, clarified divergent interpretations, and reduced interpersonal pressure around disagreement. Co-design revealed participants wanted switchable AI roles (strategic advisor, cross-domain translator, perspective challenger), but these expanded roles created a tension: AI's perceived neutrality as mediator became unstable when it advised, challenged, or influenced decisions.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes empirical insights and design considerations for AI systems that mediate interdisciplinary collaboration in text-based communication, emphasizing the need to balance expanded AI roles with preserving human agency, trust, privacy, and accountability — particularly the paradox that mediation requires neutrality, but more proactive AI roles inherently undermine it.

title: Treating Statewide CORS Networks as Spatially Distributed Sensors for GNSS Integrity Monitoring under Unintentional and Deliberate Threats
summary: State departments of transportation (DOTs) in the United States increasingly rely on statewide continuously operating reference station (CORS) networks to support high-precision Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-based positioning and timing for intelligent transportation systems. These networks also provide continuous observations that can support regional GNSS integrity monitoring. This study develops and demonstrates a framework that treats a statewide CORS network as a spatially distributed sensor system for identifying unintentional (environmental) and intentional (cyber) interference when GNSS measurements deviate from expected spatial patterns. We develop a graph-based Network Consistency Framework (NCF) that evaluates each station against its spatial neighborhood using four metrics: neighborhood residual, spatial gradient, residual, and graph smoothness. These metrics are combined into a Network Consistency Index (NCI). The framework is demonstrated using two consecutive days of four-constellation observations from 50 stations in the Alabama DOT-maintained CORS network, using changes in vertical total electron content (ΔVTEC) and the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI) as spatially coherent observables. The framework quantified network-wide spatial consistency and identified localized anomalies. Detected anomalies indicate stations whose observations deviated from the surrounding regional network, signaling potential integrity issues. Determining whether anomalies result from receiver faults, localized interference, spoofing, or other causes requires further investigation. This study introduces statewide CORS networks as regional GNSS integrity observatories and presents the NCF and NCI for graph-based spatial integrity monitoring. Transportation agencies can implement the framework using existing CORS observations to monitor network integrity and identify localized anomalies.

AI.tldr: A graph-based Network Consistency Framework (NCF) using four spatial metrics combined into a Network Consistency Index (NCI) is developed to monitor GNSS integrity across statewide CORS networks, detecting both environmental and cyber interference through spatially coherent ionospheric observables (ΔVTEC and ROTI).
AI.motivation: State DOTs increasingly depend on CORS networks for high-precision GNSS positioning/timing in intelligent transportation systems, yet lack a systematic method to leverage these networks as spatially distributed sensors for detecting unintentional (environmental) and intentional (cyber) GNSS interference and integrity anomalies.
AI.method: A graph-based Network Consistency Framework (NCF) treats the CORS network as a graph, evaluating each station against its spatial neighborhood using four metrics: neighborhood residual, spatial gradient residual, graph smoothness, and a composite Network Consistency Index (NCI). Demonstrated on 50 stations from the Alabama DOT CORS network over two days using four-constellation GNSS observations, with ΔVTEC and ROTI as spatially coherent ionospheric observables.
AI.result: The framework successfully quantified network-wide spatial consistency and identified localized anomalies where station observations deviated from surrounding regional patterns, flagging potential integrity issues — though root cause determination (receiver faults, interference, spoofing, etc.) requires further investigation.
AI.conclusion: Statewide CORS networks can serve as regional GNSS integrity observatories using the proposed NCF/NCI graph-based approach. Transportation agencies can implement this framework with existing CORS observations for continuous spatial integrity monitoring and anomaly detection.

title: Search-Based Generation of Undetected Quantum Circuit Mutants
summary: Quantum mutation analysis is emerging as an essential technique for evaluating test suites due to the limited availability of real faulty quantum programs. However, existing quantum mutation analysis tools use fixed gate-based mutations, resulting in easy-to-detect mutants, which reduces their effectiveness in assessing the quality of test suites. We propose QUMUG, a search-based approach for generating challenging mutants by utilising parameterisable quantum gates. QUMUG employs search algorithms to optimise mutation parameters and find non-equivalent mutants passing a given test suite. In our evaluation over 30 quantum programs, QUMUG produced mutants that are three times more challenging than the mutants generated by existing tools. Among the four evaluated search algorithms, the genetic algorithm was the most effective, generating an average of 494 undetected mutants per program with a 99.67% success rate and 94.3% non-equivalent ratio. The generated mutants demonstrated their effectiveness by requiring the addition of five times more test cases to the test suite than the mutants generated by existing tools. We also analysed the behaviour of higher order mutants in quantum circuits, and showed that while first order mutations are more effective for enhancing the test suite, higher order mutants highlight the need for new unique test cases.

AI.tldr: QUMUG uses search algorithms (notably genetic algorithms) to generate parameterized gate-based mutants for quantum programs that are three times harder to detect than those from existing tools, achieving a 99.67% success rate and 94.3% non-equivalent ratio.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum mutation analysis tools rely on fixed gate-based mutations that produce easy-to-detect mutants, undermining their utility for robust test suite assessment. The scarcity of real faulty quantum programs further motivates the need for more challenging synthetic mutants.
AI.method: QUMUG employs search-based optimization over parameterizable quantum gates to generate non-equivalent mutants that evade a given test suite. Four search algorithms were evaluated, with genetic algorithms proving most effective. The approach also analyzes first-order versus higher-order mutant behavior in quantum circuits.
AI.result: QUMUG produced mutants three times more challenging than existing tools. The genetic algorithm generated an average of 494 undetected mutants per program (99.67% success rate, 94.3% non-equivalent ratio). Mutants required five times more additional test cases to detect compared to baseline mutants. Higher-order mutants highlighted the need for unique test cases.
AI.conclusion: Search-based parameterized mutation is a viable and effective strategy for quantum mutation analysis. First-order mutations are more practical for test suite enhancement, while higher-order mutants expose gaps requiring novel test cases.

title: Wisdom in Unity: The Role of Multilingual Training in Figurative Language Identification in Proverbs
summary:
Although multilingual approaches to figurative language identification are not new, the shift beyond language homogeneous training data requires a clearer understanding of the contribution of translated multilingual supervision. We examine this question using 742 proverb concepts across 6,787 translated instances in seven languages. We evaluate five models, including multilingual encoders and instruction tuned LLMs, under progressively increasing levels of multilingual supervision. Moreover, we introduce a multidimensional annotation framework for proverbs that characterizes them through four complementary figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific.
  Our findings show that approximately 50% of the translated multilingual training data is sufficient to achieve near-optimal figurative language identification performance. We further show that combining diverse figurative forms yields the strongest overall performance. A notable finding is that the least frequent figurative form, Culture Specific, exhibits the largest performance gains under multilingual supervision. Furthermore, the Moral/Advisory and Culture Specific forms contribute most to the performance of instruction-tuned LLMs on figurative language identification. These findings motivate multilingual figurative language identification to move beyond metaphor-centric taxonomies toward concept level multidimensional frameworks that explicitly model complementary forms of figurative meaning.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how translated multilingual supervision affects figurative language identification, using 742 proverb concepts across seven languages. It finds that ~50% of translated training data achieves near-optimal performance, and introduces a multidimensional annotation framework capturing four figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific. Culture Specific forms benefit most from multilingual supervision, and combining diverse figurative forms yields the strongest results, especially for instruction-tuned LLMs.
AI.motivation: The shift beyond language-homogeneous training data in figurative language identification necessitates understanding how translated multilingual supervision contributes to model performance, particularly beyond metaphor-centric taxonomies toward richer, multidimensional frameworks of figurative meaning.
AI.method: The authors use 742 proverb concepts with 6,787 translated instances across seven languages. They evaluate five models (multilingual encoders and instruction-tuned LLMs) under progressively increasing levels of multilingual supervision. They also introduce a multidimensional annotation framework classifying proverbs along four figurative forms: Metaphorical, Moral/Advisory, Cause-Effect, and Culture Specific.
AI.result: Approximately 50% of translated multilingual training data suffices for near-optimal figurative language identification. Combining diverse figurative forms yields the strongest overall performance. The least frequent form, Culture Specific, shows the largest gains under multilingual supervision. Moral/Advisory and Culture Specific forms contribute most to instruction-tuned LLM performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings advocate moving beyond metaphor-centric taxonomies toward concept-level, multidimensional frameworks that explicitly model complementary figurative forms. The disproportionate benefit of multilingual supervision for culture-specific figurative meaning highlights the value of cross-lingual data.

title: LLM-Based Embeddings for Program Analysis and Optimization
summary: Recent advances have highlighted the potential of machine learning, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), for analyzing and optimizing programs. We present the first application of program embeddings from LLMCompiler---an LLM massively pretrained on intermediate representation (IR) code---to representative program analysis and optimization tasks. We generate program embeddings directly from source and IR code using a simple approach: split programs into chunks, independently embed each chunk with pretrained LLMs, and then aggregate the chunk embeddings into a single program embedding.
