Our experiments show that combining source and IR code embeddings achieves an error rate of 1.54\% in algorithm classification, a 12\% improvement over the current state-of-the-art, and a competitive accuracy on heterogeneous device mapping. These findings suggest that training a performance-aware LLM for embedding IR code might yield state-of-the-art results in code optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first use of LLMCompiler (an LLM pretrained on IR code) for generating program embeddings from source and IR code. By chunking programs, embedding chunks, and aggregating them, the combined source+IR embeddings achieve state-of-the-art algorithm classification (1.54% error rate, 12% improvement) and competitive device mapping performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown promise for program analysis and optimization, but their application to embedding intermediate representation (IR) code for downstream tasks remains underexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging LLMCompiler, a model massively pretrained on IR, to generate high-quality program embeddings that can improve tasks like algorithm classification and heterogeneous device mapping.
AI.method: The approach is straightforward: (1) split programs into chunks, (2) independently embed each chunk using the pretrained LLMCompiler model, and (3) aggregate chunk embeddings into a single program-level embedding. Both source code and IR code are used as input modalities, with their embeddings combined for downstream tasks.
AI.result: Combining source and IR code embeddings yields a 1.54% error rate on algorithm classification, improving over the prior state-of-the-art by 12%. Competitive accuracy is also achieved on heterogeneous device mapping. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of IR-pretrained embeddings for code optimization.
AI.conclusion: Training a performance-aware LLM specifically for embedding IR code shows strong potential to achieve state-of-the-art results across code optimization tasks, suggesting a promising direction for future research in ML-driven compiler optimization.

title: An Agentic AI Framework Overcomes Fundamental Limitations of Large Language Models for Glaucoma Detection from Fundus Photography
summary: Large language models (LLMs) show promise in medical image interpretation but suffer from hallucination, limited accuracy, and run-to-run inconsistency. We developed and validated an agentic AI framework integrating LLMs with specialized deep learning tools for glaucoma detection from fundus photography. The workflow had three steps: (1) LLM initial assessment; (2) function calling to invoke specialized tools for image quality (QAModel, FundaQ-8), glaucoma classification (SwinV2-Tiny), and optic disc/cup segmentation (SegFormer-B0); and (3) LLM reflection integrating the initial impression with tool outputs. Two LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5.4 mini) were evaluated on two public datasets (ORIGA, n=100; RIM-ONE-v3, n=100) under uncropped and cropped fields of view; all images were independently graded by a masked fellowship-trained glaucoma specialist. The agentic workflow improved classification accuracy by 16 to 47 percentage points across all conditions, reaching within 6 points of the specialist; on RIM-ONE-v3 the best configurations matched the specialist accuracy of 88%. LLM-alone approaches failed in two ways: GPT-5.4 mini showed positive bias (sensitivity 95-100%, specificity 0-5%), while Gemini 2.5 Flash varied stochastically between runs; the agentic workflow corrected both. Cup-to-disc ratio error fell 15-50% (MAE 0.156-0.228 to 0.104-0.132), and correlation with specialist grading rose from weak (r=0.12-0.39) to moderate-strong (r=0.59-0.84). Run-to-run consistency rose from near-random (kappa as low as -0.01) to near-perfect (kappa up to 0.96). Integrating LLMs with specialized tools addressed key limitations of LLM-alone approaches, including over-diagnosis and run-to-run variability. Gains held for both LLMs, suggesting generalizability across backbones, and may signal a shift from monolithic models toward orchestrated multi-agent systems in medical AI.

AI.tldr: An agentic AI framework combining LLMs with specialized deep learning tools significantly improves glaucoma detection accuracy, consistency, and cup-to-disc ratio estimation compared to LLM-alone approaches, matching specialist-level performance in some configurations.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise in medical image interpretation but are undermined by hallucinations, limited accuracy, and stochastic run-to-run variability. The authors aim to determine whether integrating LLMs with specialized vision tools via an agentic workflow can overcome these limitations for glaucoma detection.
AI.method: A three-step agentic workflow: (1) LLM initial assessment of fundus images, (2) function calling to invoke specialized tools for image quality (QAModel, FundaQ-8), glaucoma classification (SwinV2-Tiny), and optic disc/cup segmentation (SegFormer-B0), and (3) LLM reflection integrating the initial impression with tool outputs. Two LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5.4 mini) were evaluated on ORIGA (n=100) and RIM-ONE-v3 (n=100) under both uncropped and cropped fields of view, with a masked glaucoma specialist as ground truth.
AI.result: The agentic framework improved classification accuracy by 16–47 percentage points, reaching within 6 points of specialist accuracy; on RIM-ONE-v3, the best configuration matched the specialist's 88% accuracy. LLM-alone GPT-5.4 mini showed extreme positive bias (sensitivity 95–100%, specificity 0–5%), while Gemini 2.5 Flash varied stochastically; both were corrected. Cup-to-disc ratio MAE fell 15–50% (from 0.156–0.228 to 0.104–0.132), and correlation with the specialist rose from weak (r=0.12–0.39) to moderate-strong (r=0.59–0.84). Run-to-run consistency improved from near-random (kappa ≥ -0.01) to near-perfect (kappa ≤ 0.96).
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLMs with specialized tools via an agentic framework effectively addresses over-diagnosis, inconsistency, and inaccuracy in LLM-alone medical image interpretation. Gains generalized across both LLM backbones and held across datasets and fields of view, suggesting a potential paradigm shift from monolithic models toward orchestrated multi-agent systems in medical AI.
